**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN brand guidance names Obviously for display typography, but the available Adobe Type OTF in corporate SharePoint links to a Typekit EULA and reports OS/2 fsType 4. Possession of that desktop asset does not establish permission to convert and self-host it as a webfont.

## 2026-07-20 — Queue the resolved TTS model; trial Dolly v3 as a separate profile

**Status:** accepted (dev trial complete; Adelaide promoted as the controlled real-station pilot)

**Context:** A forensic comparison of manual Melbourne job `6f2dcabe…` and scheduled Adelaide job `38f43727…` found that both job records reported Dolly Traffic on `eleven_multilingual_v2`, but they did not use the same synthesis model. The manual mapping copied voice id and settings into `BroadcastQueueMessage` but omitted `Model`; the ElevenLabs adapter therefore substituted the deployed global default `eleven_v3`. The scheduled poller passed Multilingual v2 explicitly. Speaker embeddings and synthesis-history rows confirmed the resulting voice-character split. The persisted job metadata described intent, not the model actually sent.

**Decision:** (1) Treat the resolved TTS model as required queue data: `ToBroadcastQueueMessage` copies the persisted `Job.VoiceConfig` voice id, model, settings, and pace boost; `ToBroadcastRequest` rejects a message without a resolved model before orchestration. (2) Have `ElevenLabsAudioSynthesizer` return the effective model actually sent, and use that value in `SynthesisRecord`, so duration calibration is keyed to execution rather than intent. (3) Keep the current Dolly Multilingual-v2 profile intact for comparison/rollback and create a separate dev **Dolly Traffic - v3** profile (`vp-6ae5197f3b4545e9b723ae30c25db9ba`, voice `081vkDcbgbIsSiFEYxT0`, stability 0.5 Natural, similarity 0.7, style 0, speaker boost off). Assign only `TEST STATION` in single-voice mode while the operator compares three independent same-script v2/v3 pairs. Do not change real-station assignments until the human listening verdict.

**Rationale:** Configuration propagation must be deterministic before a model-quality decision is meaningful. A separate profile makes the trial explicit, reversible, and voice-specific; it avoids changing the global default or silently moving Jeffrey/other voices. Three independent realizations guard against selecting one unusually good stochastic take.

**Consequences:** Backend deployed healthy to dev. Regression coverage proves the job's resolved model reaches the queue, missing-model messages fail clearly, the adapter reports default and override models, and synthesis history persists the provider-effective model. Full non-integration suite: Domain 1217, Application 502, Functions 396, Infrastructure 1198 passed (22 skipped live/integration tests). Poller proof `caca45a4b15a40f88d72602ba1524cd3` rendered `Dolly Traffic - v3` on `eleven_v3`, included weather and two fuel summaries, and finalized at 30.0s; the matching synthesis-history row independently records `ModelId=eleven_v3`. The blind comparison page and six exact-30s WAVs are at `/tmp/dolly-v3-comparison-20260720/`.

**Post-deploy manual-path proof:** ad-hoc job `adfbfedde57247d990fc2d6e7f12e0a4` was created with Dolly Multilingual v2, traversed `JobService` → queue → worker, reached `WAITING_APPROVAL`, and finalized at 30.0s. The newest matching synthesis-history row records `ModelId=eleven_multilingual_v2`, proving the repaired manual path no longer falls through to the platform `eleven_v3` default.

**Human listening verdict:** The blind page mapped Candidate A to Multilingual v2 and Candidate B to Eleven v3. B won all three rounds. In Round 1, A had slightly better spacing/cadence, but B had materially better voice character and pronounced Keilor correctly where A did not. B won Round 2 and Round 3 by far; Round 3 B was the overall favourite. This establishes a repeatable model-level preference rather than a single lucky take, while retaining a concrete cadence issue to monitor.

**Controlled promotion:** Adelaide/KIIS 102.3 moved from the original Dolly Multilingual-v2 profile to **Dolly Traffic - v3**; Brisbane, Darwin, and Sydney remain on v2 as controls and immediate rollback. Adelaide's active pronunciation version contains 15 alias rules and zero phoneme rules, so it is v3-compatible. Poller-fired proof job `287d14a0b2484f10938b5f62b755d2cb` persisted Dolly Traffic - v3 / `eleven_v3` / stability 0.5 / similarity 0.7, resolved the ElevenLabs pronunciation dictionary version, included real Adelaide traffic plus weather and two fuel summaries, and finalized at 30.0s. Audio pre-review matched 100% of significant words with zero suspect words or number mismatches; synthesis history independently recorded `ModelId=eleven_v3`. The schedule was restored disabled on its original production cron with `NextRunAt=null`.

## 2026-07-21 — Park the PoC unilaterally; propose RG deletion to the ARN Technology Lead

**Status:** accepted (park executed; deletion proposed, awaiting the ARN Technology Lead)

**Context:** The PoC (`ARN-AUE-RSG-TNP`, ARN Sub) was still running an always-on P0v3 plan with its poller firing every minute. A 30-day App Insights audit (2026-07-21) showed the environment is a pure idle burner: 43,200 `SchedulePoller` executions and ~734K table transactions with **zero** bulletins generated, zero HERE/ElevenLabs/OpenAI calls, zero API/console traffic, and zero Logic App runs. Dependency checks confirmed nothing current touches it: the repo has no references to PoC resource names, ADO holds only the three IBP service connections (the former PoC connection was deleted 9 Jul) with all variable groups pointing at IBP resources, and the CI failure webhook posts to an IBP Logic App.

## 2026-07-21 — Dispatcher model: the poller enqueues, the queue executes; concurrency is queue-governed

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Scheduled bulletins ran the full generation pipeline (p50 25–36 s, p99 ~90 s per market) in-process inside the singleton `SchedulePoller` timer tick, while manual and recovered jobs ran via `broadcast-queue`. Three costs: (1) control-plane starvation — a busy clock slot (many markets at 5–7 am, capped at 4 parallel) ran the tick for minutes, delaying the NEXT tick's fallback-deadline/escalation sweeps against a 3-minute dead-air budget; (2) fidelity asymmetry — `BroadcastQueueMessage` carried no delivery style or pronunciation locator, so a recovered scheduled job silently regenerated WITHOUT its station's delivery/pronunciation config (same divergence class as the 2026-07-20 Dolly model drift); (3) scale asymmetry — the in-process burst was pinned to the timer-singleton instance while queue work scales out. Separately, Azure OpenAI TPM quota is now effectively unlimited (confirmed 2026-07-21), retiring the 2026-07-06 429-storm rationale for the 4-market cap.

**Decision:** (1) The poller is a pure dispatcher + watchdog: resolve station config, persist the job, enqueue a **full-fidelity** `BroadcastQueueMessage` (now carries `StationId`, `DeliveryStyle` policy + id/version, `PronunciationLocator`, alongside voice/model/settings/pace/content/fill-order — snapshot-at-dispatch, same philosophy as queueing the resolved TTS model), advance `NextRunUtc`. All generation executes on `BroadcastQueueProcessor`. Continuity is intentionally NOT on the message: it is persisted on the job and restored by orchestrator enrichment. (2) Stale-job recovery re-resolves delivery/pronunciation from the schedule (fail-soft) so the recovery lane matches. (3) Dispatch publish failure marks the job Failed + FailedNotCovered card. (4) Generation concurrency is queue-governed: host.json `batchSize` 16→32, `newBatchThreshold` 8→16, per instance × autoscale; `SchedulePollerMaxParallelMarkets` (4→8) now bounds only resolution+enqueue, jitter default 8→2 s. Pollerless alternatives were evaluated and rejected: Storage-queue timer-chains lose self-healing and need a reconciliation poller anyway; Service Bus scheduled messages require Premium (~AU$1k+/mo) for the PE posture; Durable timers poll internally while adding replay semantics. The watchdog is irreducibly temporal ("no audio by deadline" is the absence of an event), so a 1-minute clock exists in every design; ours costs ~$0.20–0.40/mo on an always-on plan.

**Rationale:** One execution lane gives uniform lease dedupe, retry classification, poison handling, and autoscale to scheduled runs; the tick becomes O(seconds) regardless of market count, so the dead-air watchdog can never be starved by generation. Snapshot-at-dispatch kills the two-lane divergence bug class at the contract level. Not-unbounded concurrency: with TPM unconstrained, the remaining ceilings are per-instance memory/CPU during audio assembly and ElevenLabs concurrency — 32/instance × autoscale covers every realistic burst (12 markets today) with headroom, without inviting resource thrash.

**Consequences:** The codemaps' long-standing description ("poll schedules, enqueue due broadcasts") is now literally true. Full backend suite green at baseline (Domain 1217 / Application 502 / Functions 396 / Infrastructure 1198, 22 skip); poller tests rewritten to dispatch semantics (publish expectations, dispatch-failure → Failed + notification). `*-ai-throttling` runbook row and the task-board quota ask updated to the unlimited-TPM reality. Deployed to dev + live-verified via a poller-fired bulletin (see CONTEXT.md same day).

**Addendum (2026-07-21, same day) — live verification exposed and fixed a masked race: the in-flight worker grace.** First live poller-fired job (`f0a182d6…`, sydney) went `FALLBACK_USED` in 23 s: with generation no longer blocking the singleton tick, the next tick's fallback sweep covered the deadline-passed job WHILE its queue worker was mid-generation (the old model masked this — a tick physically could not sweep during its own in-process generation; the trigger recipe's ~5-min arming makes the deadline land seconds after dispatch). Fix: `ProcessFallbacksAsync` now defers a deadline-passed job whose worker is demonstrably alive — active pipeline status (`Requested…AudioReady`) touched within a 2-minute grace (`InFlightGraceMinutes`; workers advance status every few seconds, so a silent job is crashed and gets covered next tick — the dead-air guarantee keeps a bounded delay). Re-verified live on job `562ccb4e…` (sydney): dispatched 02:53:35Z, the 02:54:00Z sweep logged "worker is active … deferring", audio landed 02:55:00Z → `WAITING_APPROVAL` with the FULL station config through the queue — Dolly Traffic / `eleven_multilingual_v2` (not the ARN Hudson default), weather present, 2 fuel summaries, exact 30.0 s. Two regression tests added (defer-when-active, cover-when-stale); three existing fallback-test fixtures aged past the grace to keep modelling crashed workers. Application suite 504/504.

## 2026-07-21 — Remove no-bulletins heartbeat alert (fundamentally incompatible with drive-time-only schedules)

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** IBP-AUE-{ENV}-FNA-APP01-no-bulletins (Sev1, deployment/modules/alerts.bicep) fired repeatedly in dev (4x/7d) and test (2x/7d), emailing the dev action group receiver. Investigation found it fires because all dev market schedules are Enabled=false (no auto-broadcast). But computing real gaps from live per-market cron expressions (e.g. adelaide, brisbane) showed drive-time-only schedules have normal broadcast-free windows of 11-17h (weeknight, and Sat-afternoon-to-Sun-morning), far exceeding the alert's fixed 6h lookback. The rule would false-positive nightly even in a fully healthy, fully-enabled production deployment -- its description ('during expected service hours') was aspirational; the KQL had no time-of-day or schedule-awareness at all.

**Decision:** Deleted the live scheduledQueryRules resource IBP-AUE-{ENV}-FNA-APP01-no-bulletins in dev, test, and prod (prod's copy was already disabled). Removed the bulletinHeartbeatAlert resource from alerts.bicep and renumbered the remaining alert comments (now 6 rules, was 7). Updated docs/operations/as-built.md, runbook.md, and slo.md to drop references.

**Rationale:** A fixed wall-clock silence window cannot distinguish 'pipeline broken' from 'no broadcast was scheduled right now' for a drive-time-only broadcast pattern, in any environment -- not just dev. Making it correct would require a schedule-aware rewrite (per-market: was a cron-due run missed) with no clear ROI, since the failure modes it targets (stuck poller, broken pipeline) are already covered by no-executions, poison-queue, ai-throttling, errors-alert, and synthesis-failures.

**Consequences:** Silent pipeline stalls during an actual scheduled broadcast window are no longer caught by a heartbeat -- covered instead by the other 6 alerts plus manual job-status review. If a schedule-aware version is wanted later, it needs a per-market cron-due check, not a fixed lookback window. alertRuleIds output in alerts.bicep now returns 4 IDs instead of 5.

## 2026-07-21 — Job-lifecycle security remediation: state-before-side-effect guards, optimistic revision binding, real audit identity, atomic playout writes

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** A security review of the job-approval/publish/delivery path found five related gaps: (1) `PublishJobAsync` delivered audio to Zetta playout BEFORE checking the job was `Approved`/`FallbackUsed`, so a delivery could fire against a job in the wrong state, discovered only when the subsequent status transition failed; (2) `ApproveJobAsync` accepted any job regardless of status, so a mid-pipeline job could be force-approved; (3) `SaveJobAsync` failures were silently ignored in several lifecycle methods, letting a job proceed in-memory while the persisted row stayed stale; (4) reject/reject-to-fallback/regenerate stamped the literal string `"operator"` instead of the authenticated caller, so the audit trail could not say who actually acted; (5) the web UI already gated `publish` to Admin, but the server accepted it from any Operator — an API caller could bypass the UI's own rule. Separately, the operator console had no way to guard against acting on a bulletin that had moved on since it was loaded (stale-tab double-approve), and `SmbFileWriter` wrote the watched filename directly, so the playout poller could observe a partially-written file mid-transfer.

**Decision:** `JobService.PublishJobAsync`/`ApproveJobAsync` now validate the job's current status — and an optional caller-supplied `expectedEtag` revision precondition — before any side effect; publish only delivers audio after confirming `Approved`/`FallbackUsed`. Every lifecycle method (`ApproveJobAsync`, `RejectJobAsync`, `RejectToFallbackAsync`, `PublishJobAsync`, `RegenerateJobAsync`, `MarkFailedAsync`) now returns the `SaveJobAsync` failure instead of swallowing it. `RejectJobCommand`/`RejectToFallbackCommand` gained a `By` field carrying the authenticated caller (threaded from `ClientPrincipal`); domain `Job.Approve`/`Publish` gained `byObjectId` and persist `ApprovedByObjectId`/`PublishedByObjectId` (immutable Entra object id) alongside the existing mutable display-name field. `POST /api/jobs/{id}/publish` moved out of the Operator role group in `RouteRoleMatrix` so it falls through to the Admin-only default, matching the web UI exactly. Every job DTO now exposes `Etag`; approve/publish accept an optional `expectedEtag` body field and return a conflict with no side effects on mismatch (web always sends the etag it loaded; the mock API mirrors the semantics). `TableStorageJobRepository.SaveJobAsync` reconciles a 412 by comparing a new material-column fingerprint (`Job.ConcurrencyFingerprint`, captured on load) against the freshly-read row: an unchanged fingerprint means only a concurrent log append happened underneath (merge logs, retry with the fresh ETag), a changed fingerprint is a real concurrent state change (surfaced as a conflict, never silently overwritten). `SmbFileWriter` now writes to a sibling `.part` temp filename and atomically renames it onto the watched filename on success. `BroadcastOrchestrator`'s duplicate-queue-worker finalize guard was widened to also refuse `WaitingApproval` and `Rejected` jobs. The web `JobActions.tsx` fallback-publish button now opens a confirm dialog before combining auto-approve + delivery in one click.

**Rationale:** Every fix follows the same principle — validate state and identity BEFORE causing an external effect, never after. Delivering audio then discovering the state transition should have been rejected leaves no clean rollback (the vendor already has the file); checking first is free and correct. Optimistic concurrency via ETag is the standard low-cost way to stop a stale-tab operator action from clobbering a newer state without adding a lock service. A material-column fingerprint (rather than the raw storage ETag) is what makes the reconcile-on-412 retry safe: it lets a routine concurrent log append merge and retry automatically while still surfacing a genuine state race as a conflict. Persisting the Entra object id (not just a display name) is what makes `ApprovedByObjectId`/`PublishedByObjectId` durable audit evidence — display names can be renamed or reissued. Atomic rename-on-write is the standard fix for a poller that watches a filename for existence rather than completion.

**Consequences:** Callers of `IJobService.ApproveJobAsync`/`PublishJobAsync` gained optional trailing parameters (`expectedEtag`, `byObjectId`) — additive, existing callers unaffected. `RegenerateJobAsync` gained a `by` parameter (default `"unknown"`) for the same reason. Any script or integration that called `POST /api/jobs/{id}/publish` as an Operator now gets 403 and must use an Admin principal. `RejectionEntry`/`StatusHistoryEntry` (now their own `Domain/Models` files, extracted off `Job.cs` in the same pass) always carry the real caller instead of `"operator"` going forward; historical entries are unaffected. No behavior change for callers that never pass `expectedEtag` — the precondition is opt-in.

## 2026-07-21 — Backend domain-folder structure and collaborator-split convention

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The Functions and Application projects had grown as flat file dumps (~48 and ~58 root-level files) with several god files (ScriptGenerationEngine 124KB, LlmScriptGenerator 112KB, SchedulePollerService 44KB, TrafficEvidenceBuilder 32KB, JobsHttpTrigger 29KB, VoiceProfilesHttpTrigger 22KB), making navigation and safe change hard.

**Decision:** (1) Application is organized into domain folders with matching namespaces: `Broadcasting/` (orchestrator + generation pipeline collaborators), `Scheduling/` (poller, schedule/coverage services), `Jobs/`, `Libraries/` (the per-station versioned-library services, ex-`Services/`), `ConfigTransfer/`, `Access/`, `Metrics/`; `Commands/`, `Mapping/`, `ConfigImport/`, `Validation/` unchanged. (2) Functions is organized into `Triggers/{Http,Queues,Timers}/`, `Middleware/`, `Auth/`, `Http/`, `Metrics/`, `ConfigTransfer/`; Program.cs + host/app settings + `Contracts/` stay at root. (3) God files are split into `internal sealed` collaborator classes with primary constructors, hand-`new`ed by their owner when the owner's public constructor must stay stable (BroadcastOrchestrator.BuildCollaborators, SchedulePollerService, LlmScriptGenerator precedents) — no new interfaces, no DI-registration growth for internals. Namespace always follows folder.

**Rationale:** Folder/namespace grouping reflects the domain (a bulletin flows Scheduling → Broadcasting → Jobs) instead of file kind; the collaborator convention splits responsibility without widening public surface or churning DI/tests. Splits were verified behavior-preserving: `[Function]` names (88) and routes (81) byte-identical, DI registrations unchanged, full non-integration suite green at identical counts (3374 passing).

**Consequences:** New Application/Functions code goes into the matching domain folder with the matching namespace — do not add files at project root. New oversized-class splits should follow the collaborator pattern. Remaining large-but-cohesive single-responsibility files (TableStorageJobRepository 42KB, HereTrafficProvider 41KB, TrafficNarrativeSummarizer 42KB incl. partial, CorridorAggregator 42KB, AudioPipelineService 34KB, MarketSchedule 31KB, JobService 30KB, ElevenLabsClient 29KB) were assessed and deliberately left whole — they are single-seam vendor adapters, repositories, or aggregates where a split adds indirection without cohesion gain.

## 2026-07-21 — Job persistence contract is machine-verified (round-trip suite + schema drift gates)

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The Job ↔ Table Storage boundary produced six production incidents (silent 30K-cap column drops that blanked a whole market, publish 409-forever ETag desync, fingerprint merge races, swallowed save failures, hot-partition scans, market-key mismatch starving per-market lookups). The contract — ~60 columns, six conditionally gzip-compressed, Option↔nullable conversion, enum-string parsing, ETag + material-column fingerprint — lived only as hand-written mapping code with nothing guaranteeing Save→Load identity, and the Python harvest/eval tooling re-implements the same parsing blind.

**Decision:** (1) `JobPersistenceRoundTripTests` asserts whole-aggregate Save→Load ≡ identity through the real (mocked-TableClient) repository path, with a reflection ratchet: any new public `Job` property fails the suite until it is populated in the builder, mapped both directions, and listed. (2) The mapping/compression contract lives in `JobEntityMapper` (row shapes in `JobEntity.cs`); the repository keeps queries and the ETag/fingerprint retry policy. (3) `docs/reference/job-table-schema.md` documents the radioJobs contract for non-C# consumers and is drift-gated by a reflection test over `JobEntity`. (4) Market ids and market-scoped storage keys normalize exclusively via `Domain.ValueObjects.MarketKey.Normalize` (was 8 scattered `Trim().ToLowerInvariant()` sites).

**Rationale:** Every incident in this seam was a contract violation nobody could see. Generator-enforced completeness + round-trip identity makes adding a `Job` field safe (the previously scariest routine change); the schema doc + gate keeps the Python consumers honest; one named normalization prevents the next mildura-style silent lookup miss.

**Consequences:** Adding a `Job` field now REQUIRES: populate `CreateFullyPopulatedJob`, map in `JobEntityMapper.MapToEntity` AND `MapToDomain`, add to the ratchet list, update `job-table-schema.md` (tests name each step on failure). Never normalize a market string inline — use `MarketKey.Normalize`. Known accepted behaviors, characterized in tests: incompressibly-oversized columns drop with a warning (rest of the row persists); whitespace-only `Option<string>` values normalize to None on reload (latent gotcha, documented in the suite).

## 2026-07-22 — Backend NuGet dependency refresh — pins for two majors

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Task: ensure the backend project (.NET solution) has no known package vulnerabilities and is up to date. dotnet list package --vulnerable already reported zero known vulnerabilities pre-change; dotnet list package --outdated showed ~20 top-level packages behind latest (mostly Microsoft.Extensions.* 10.0.3/10.0.8 -> 10.0.10 patch releases, Azure.Identity/Storage.Blobs/Storage.Queues minor bumps, Cronos, SMBLibrary, Azure.Extensions.AspNetCore.Configuration.Secrets, Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker(.ApplicationInsights/.Extensions.Storage.Queues), WireMock.Net, xunit.runner.visualstudio, coverlet.collector, Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk) plus two majors: Azure.Search.Documents 11.7.0->12.0.0 and Microsoft.ApplicationInsights.WorkerService 2.23.0->3.1.2, and NSubstitute 5.3.0->6.0.0.

**Decision:** Bumped every package in Directory.Packages.props to its latest stable version, including Azure.Search.Documents to 12.0.0 (its 12.0.0 breaking changes only obsolete two legacy Skill enum members we do not use; StyleExamplesService's SearchClient usage is unaffected) and all Microsoft.Extensions.*/Azure.Storage.*/Azure.Identity/Functions.Worker.* packages. Kept two deliberate pins, each documented inline in Directory.Packages.props: (1) Microsoft.ApplicationInsights.WorkerService stays at 2.23.0 (latest stable 2.x) because 3.x's OpenTelemetry-based core drops ITelemetryInitializer/ITelemetryProcessor, which Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker.ApplicationInsights depends on -- the Functions team confirmed (github.com/Azure/azure-functions-dotnet-worker#3322) they will not ship a 3.x-compatible release, and 3.x throws TypeLoadException at Functions startup. (2) NSubstitute stays at 5.3.0 because 6.0.0 enables nullable annotations on Arg.Is<T>/Arg.Any<T>, turning their predicate parameter into a nullable reference type; with the repo's TreatWarningsAsErrors + Nullable=enable, that alone produced 127 CS8600/CS8602/CS8604 errors across every test project's substitute call sites (isolated by reverting only NSubstitute and confirming a clean build) for zero functional or security benefit.

**Rationale:** Both blocked upgrades are pure library-surface friction (a confirmed upstream incompatibility bug report, and an opt-in nullable-strictness change the library's own BreakingChanges.md flags as disable-able) with no security advisory attached to the versions we kept. Chasing them would mean either an unsupported/broken telemetry pipeline in production, or mechanically touching 100+ scattered test call sites purely to satisfy new nullable annotations -- churn with no functional payoff. Every other package, including one full major version (Azure.Search.Documents), moved to latest because its breaking changes don't touch our usage.

**Consequences:** dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive: zero vulnerable packages across all 11 projects (unchanged, was already zero). dotnet list package --outdated: only the two pinned packages remain behind latest, both with an inline justification comment in Directory.Packages.props pointing at this decision. Full solution build: 0 warnings / 0 errors (TreatWarningsAsErrors). Full non-integration test run (Category!=Integration&Category!=E2E): 3,387 passed, 0 failed, 22 skipped (live-verification tests gated behind real API keys) across all 7 test projects. The redundant Scriban.Signed 7.2.5 override was left in place with an updated comment (WireMock.Net.Minimal 2.13.0 now declares the same 7.2.5 floor itself, so the pin is no longer strictly load-bearing but remains a deliberate explicit security floor).

## 2026-07-22 — Web perf: lazy-load on-demand Studio dialogs off route chunks

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** User asked for immediately-applicable web performance wins with zero UI degradation/regression, following the same-day npm dependency-refresh pass. Baseline npm run perf (Lighthouse desktop, mock build, 7 routes): stations was the clear outlier — score 78 (vs 88-93 elsewhere), TBT 316ms (vs 89-157ms), LCP 1823ms (vs 1247-1475ms), page weight 642KB (heaviest). Root cause: StationsPage.tsx statically imported TriggerStudio, ScheduleStudio, and ScheduleDetailStudio (~1,470 combined lines) even though all three only ever render behind a truthy state flag set by a user action (Create/Edit/Trigger/View) -- never on the initial station-list paint. All three transitively import MapPicker+ShapeEditors (~1,700 lines of Leaflet coverage-area drawing code), which vite.config.ts's manualChunks already isolates into a 'vendor-map' chunk (Leaflet itself) but which was still being pulled into the eagerly-loaded route chunk's static import graph. The identical pattern (one eagerly-imported, conditionally-rendered Studio dialog) also existed on DeliveryPage, PronunciationPage, and VoicesPage, each smaller in absolute terms (26-32KB studios) but the same shape of waste.

**Decision:** Converted all 6 Studio components (StationsPage: TriggerStudio, ScheduleStudio, ScheduleDetailStudio; DeliveryPage: DeliveryStyleStudio; PronunciationPage: PronunciationDictionaryStudio; VoicesPage: VoiceStudio) to React.lazy() + a local Suspense fallback={null} wrapper around each conditional render block -- the exact pattern already used for every top-level route in App.tsx, just applied one level down to conditionally-rendered dialogs/sheets instead of whole pages. No visual or behavioral change: each was already gated behind '{flag && <Component/>}', so the only difference is the module's JS is now fetched on first open (typically already prefetched/cached) instead of bundled into the page's initial chunk. Left OnAirPage's CoverageHome/QueueBeam/ReviewPane alone -- those are the page's primary, always-visible content on every visit, so lazy-splitting them would trade a real perf win for a guaranteed loading-flash regression on the busiest page; the win here is specifically for content that is genuinely conditional.

**Rationale:** This is the single highest-value, lowest-risk fix available: it needed zero new dependencies, zero design changes, and matches an established in-repo convention exactly (App.tsx's route-level lazy()), so there was no new pattern to review or learn. Verified via the existing npm run perf harness (not a new one-off benchmark) so the win is durably tracked by the same regression gate that would catch a future reversion.

**Consequences:** Route chunk sizes: StationsPage 139.25KB->18.73KB (-87%), DeliveryPage 31.20KB->8.02KB, PronunciationPage 26.07KB->8.20KB, VoicesPage 31.85KB->10.16KB. New on-demand chunks appear only after the relevant user action: TriggerStudio 9.81KB, DeliveryStyleStudio 23.29KB, PronunciationDictionaryStudio 19.82KB, VoiceStudio 23.92KB, a shared map-picker chunk 29.42KB (deduped across the three schedule/trigger studios that need it). npm run perf re-run: stations score 78->93, TBT 316ms->52ms (-83%), LCP 1823ms->1509ms (-17%); every other route's TBT also dropped substantially (e.g. home 133ms->34ms, voices 123ms->8ms) from the smaller shared bootstrap. Live mock-mode browser verification (CDP): all 6 studios open with correct content, including MapPicker's Leaflet coverage editor inside the Coverage tab of the New Station dialog -- zero regression. Full verification green: tsc -b clean, eslint clean, vitest 597 passed/3 skipped/0 failed, vite build clean. Follow-up recommendation (not implemented this session, needs its own ESLint-gated rollout): adopt React Compiler 1.0 (GA Oct 2025) -- this stack (Vite 8 + @vitejs/plugin-react v6, which dropped Babel for oxc) needs @rolldown/plugin-babel + reactCompilerPreset() rather than the older react({babel:{...}}) form; install eslint-plugin-react-compiler first and fix Rules-of-React violations project-wide before flipping compilationMode from 'annotation' to 'all'.

## 2026-07-22 — Canonical script stays written; pronunciation is pinned, visible on air, and preserved through re-voice

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Pronunciation dictionaries deliberately alter speech without altering editorial copy. The review UI previously showed only canonical text, so an operator could not tell that `Greensborough` would be spoken using an alias. More seriously, the direct edit/re-voice queue message omitted the original job's `PronunciationLocator`, so an unrelated edit could synthesize new audio without the station dictionary. Resolving the current station dictionary during re-voice would be equally wrong because the library may have changed since the bulletin was generated.

**Decision:** The script remains canonical written copy. Jobs expose and persist the exact provider dictionary id and provider version id used for synthesis. Review mode gives matching canonical terms a visible glow and a rich pronunciation-dictionary popover that names the substitution and pinned library version. Edit mode remains a native text area, arranged sentence-per-line, with a pointer-transparent live mirror that recomputes the same highlights and popovers as the draft changes. It does not replace the canonical terms, expose raw timing in hover copy, or duplicate matches in a separate panel or count; timed words in the read-only script remain click-to-seek targets. Re-voice carries the complete persisted locator through `RegenerationQueueMessage` and `BroadcastWithTraffic`; an incomplete or historical locator resolves to none, never to the current dictionary. Frontend matching loads the historical version by provider version id, applies case/word-boundary/model compatibility rules, and never mutates the script text.

**Rationale:** The operator needs both truths at once: trustworthy editorial copy and an explicit account of what listeners will hear. Pinning the original version makes re-voice reproducible and auditable; silently adopting current rules would change on-air behavior after review, while rendering respellings directly into the script would corrupt the canonical record and make editing awkward.

**Consequences:** `JobDetailDto` now carries `PronunciationVersionId`; regeneration contracts carry a nullable `PronunciationLocator`; the review and Config & audit surfaces show exact or explicitly unavailable pronunciation provenance. Live dev verification on job `018661b3e01a4c1396a7ee5df5b105ff` preserved dictionary `uYDhCfPEaG4qA33L23Mb` version `tCAi7AQzdwj7ge7E2B4K` across an unrelated `Cloudy` → `Overcast` edit. The regeneration trace recorded that exact locator attached to ElevenLabs, and Azure Speech heard the canonical `Greensborough` as “Greenieborough,” confirming that the on-air pronunciation path—not the written script—changed.

## 2026-07-22 — React Compiler evaluated for web — not adopted (measured, not assumed)

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Follow-up to the 2026-07-22 Studio lazy-load perf fix: tested whether adopting React Compiler 1.0 (GA Oct 2025) would give a further, real win, per the user's explicit ask to test it rather than just recommend it. Pre-flight: eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1 (already installed) has fully absorbed the compiler's own Rules-of-React lint rules (immutability, purity, set-state-in-render, error-boundaries, refs, globals, etc. -- all already enforced as 'error' via reactHooks.configs.recommended.rules); only two compiler-specific advisory rules (preserve-manual-memoization, incompatible-library) were pre-emptively set to 'off' with a comment deferring them until adoption. Temporarily flipped both to 'warn' and ran eslint across all ~450 files: only 3 warnings total, all benign 'Compilation Skipped' (existing useMemo in use-script-verification.ts/VoiceStudio.tsx kept as-is unoptimized; TriggerStudio.tsx's react-hook-form watch() correctly flagged incompatible) -- zero errors, confirming the codebase was already exceptionally compiler-ready. Wired the compiler for real: installed babel-plugin-react-compiler@1.0.0 + @rolldown/plugin-babel (the actual current API is , not the  form some 2026-04 blog posts describe -- that package's pre-1.0 API had already changed between when those posts were written and npm's current 0.2.3), gated behind  so vitest transforms stayed untouched.

**Decision:** Not adopted. Measured on all three of this repo's own perf harnesses, with-vs-without on the SAME lazy-load-fixed baseline: (1) npm run perf (cold-load Lighthouse, 7 routes) -- scores flat (+/-1 point, noise), LCP flat-to-slightly-worse on every route, page weight up 10-25KB per route everywhere with zero exception. (2) Build output -- every route/component chunk grew 18-49% (OnAirPage 159KB->230KB, StationsPage 19KB->28KB, VoiceStudio 24KB->32KB, shared 'components' chunk 59KB->80KB) from the compiler's inserted memoization slots (_c() cache arrays), and cold build time went from ~570ms to ~8.6s (15x) with an explicit rolldown PLUGIN_TIMINGS warning flagging the Babel pass as the dominant build cost. (3) npm run perf:runtime (timespan/interaction probe, the metric the compiler is actually designed to help) was genuinely promising on the FIRST paired run -- idle-onair and audio-review both ~15-19% faster with the compiler on, at both 1x and 4x throttle -- but did NOT replicate on a second paired run on the same machine (one 4x sample swung to 1730ms vs the first run's 408ms, a >4x outlier the harness's own median-of-3 couldn't fully absorb), consistent with this doc's already-documented CPU-throttle noise caveat (devtools throttling multiplies live host load, and this session had multiple background jobs competing for the same machine). Two paired runs is not enough to distinguish a real interaction-latency win from host noise in either direction.

**Rationale:** The decision rests on what's NOT noisy: bundle size and build time are deterministic build outputs, not timing samples, and both moved unambiguously in the wrong direction. The one metric that would need to show a clear, reliable win to justify that cost (steady-state re-render latency) did not survive a second measurement on the same hardware. This matches the React team's own honest framing (Instagram ~12%, Quest Store 2.5x fewer re-renders) -- those are gains on apps with duplicate-render fat still on the table; this app's hottest re-render loops (on-air board ticks, audio-waveform requestAnimationFrame) were ALREADY hand-optimized in three prior sessions (use-second-tick isolation, the AuroraHero/AuroraWash CSS-animation-to-compositor fix, and this same day's Studio lazy-load), so there is little duplicate-render fat left for the compiler to remove, while its bundle-size cost is unconditional and paid on every route regardless of how re-render-heavy that route is.

**Consequences:** vite.config.ts and eslint.config.js left exactly as they were before this experiment (git diff confirms zero residue). babel-plugin-react-compiler and @rolldown/plugin-babel installed then npm-uninstalled; package.json/package-lock.json verified clean of both. Re-ran npm run perf after reverting: scores 89-96 and weights match the post-lazy-load baseline exactly (e.g. stations 602KB, home 462KB) -- confirms nothing was left in an inconsistent state. Re-evaluate only if (a) a future profiling session finds a genuinely re-render-heavy, NOT-yet-hand-optimized hot path where the compiler's target scenario actually applies, or (b) the ecosystem (@rolldown/plugin-babel, which is pre-1.0 and changed its public API between two blog posts written months apart) stabilizes enough that the build-time and bundle-size tax drops. The eslint-plugin-react-hooks 'preserve-manual-memoization'/'incompatible-library' rules stay 'off' with their existing comment -- that comment's reasoning still holds.

## 2026-07-23 — CC-010 resolved: retention figures self-decided instead of waiting on ARN Legal

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** main.bicep's publishedAudioDeleteAfterDays / unpublishedAudioDeleteAfterDays / auditExportsDeleteAfterDays had sat at the CC-010 placeholder (0 = keep forever) since the storage lifecycle module shipped, pending an exact figure from ARN Legal. CC-002 (9 Jun compliance call) already established the floor and rationale — audio >=90 days (60-day Code retention window after a complaint, plus 30 days for the complaint itself), audit/approval text logs 2-3+ years (cheap to keep, useful for a later dispute) — but nobody had picked concrete day-counts from that range.

**Decision:** Pick concrete figures from the CC-002 range ourselves rather than keep waiting indefinitely: publishedAudioDeleteAfterDays=90 (the CC-002 floor), unpublishedAudioDeleteAfterDays=30 (never-aired candidates are a short debugging window, not evidence, so no reason to hold them as long as aired audio), auditExportsDeleteAfterDays=1095 (3 years, the upper end of CC-002's 2-3+ year range). Set live in main.test.bicepparam and main.prod.bicepparam 2026-07-23; main.bicep's descriptions and defaults (still 0, for any environment that doesn't set them explicitly) updated to stop calling these ARN-pending placeholders.

**Rationale:** The CC-002 call already gave us everything needed to compute a defensible figure; the outstanding ask was purely 'give us the exact number', which we can derive ourselves without changing the legal position. Leaving the params at 0 (keep forever) indefinitely was the more conservative-looking choice but not actually the agreed one, and it left a lifecycle-policy gap open for no reason once the range was known. ARN Legal can still ask for a change later — this isn't presented as unchangeable, just no longer something we're blocked waiting on.

**Consequences:** retention ask to ARN Legal is marked RESOLVED, not withdrawn (unlike CRA guidelines / data-training review, which are genuinely non-blocking and dropped). docs/canonical/production-readiness.md rows 94/96 updated to reflect concrete figures instead of 'awaiting ARN Legal'. Bicep template + all four param files validated to compile (az bicep build / build-params).

## 2026-07-23 — ElevenLabs v2/v3 model-family handling: four bugs found by live reproduction and fixed

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** User asked whether the system correctly branches ElevenLabs behavior by resolved model family (v3 vs v2-family), suspecting theoretical audit findings might not hold up in the real dev environment. Rather than trust static code review, every candidate bug was reproduced live against dev before fixing: (1) ModelSelector.SelectModel (the no-profile ad-hoc/default-voice fallback path) ignored a voice's verified base models entirely, always defaulting to the configured preferred model regardless of capability -- reproduced live by triggering an ad-hoc /broadcast with Dolly Traffic (a v2-only PVC, ModelIds=[multilingual_v2, turbo_v2_5, ...], no v3) and no profile/model override: the created job resolved Model=eleven_v3, exactly the IVC-fallback/accent-drift failure mode. (2) ElevenLabsClient.BuildTtsPayload's supportsStyle/supportsSpeed/supportsSpeakerBoost checks matched only "multilingual_v2"/"turbo_v2", missing eleven_flash_v2_5 -- confirmed both by ElevenLabs' own docs (speed available for all models except v3) and by a live A/B: pre-fix, Speed 1.0 vs 1.4 on eleven_flash_v2_5 produced statistically identical raw synthesis duration/WPM; a target-duration-matched clean re-test post-fix showed WPM scaling correctly (112/173/218 at Speed 0.7/1.0/1.2). (3) similarity_boost was sent unconditionally to every model including v3, which ElevenLabs silently ignores -- config-only, not independently observable live, verified by source + updated unit test. (4) A newly-discovered, deeper bug beyond the original audit: the Director (IScriptDirector/DeliveryDirector) genuinely applies and synthesizes v3 audio tags on real (non-ScriptOnly) bulletins, but AudioFinalizer.SaveFinalBroadcastResultAsync (the terminal WaitingApproval save, the one that matters) never wrote TaggedScriptText/DeliveryStyleId/DeliveryStyleVersion -- reproduced live on the isolated demo-coast test market by temporarily assigning a real delivery style and firing it through the actual scheduled-poller path (ad-hoc /broadcast never carries DeliveryStyleId, so this required the real poller, not the shortcut endpoint).

**Decision:** Fixed all four in the same batch, each verified live against a fresh dev deploy before/after: (1) ModelSelector now depends on IVoiceProvider + IMemoryCache, fetches the voice catalog once (5 min cache), and applies the existing VoiceModelResolver.Resolve(voice.ModelIds, languageSelectedModel) to the no-profile fallback path -- unknown voice id or a provider failure degrades to the prior language-only behaviour, never blocking selection. IModelSelector.SelectModel became SelectModelAsync; both call sites (StationConfigResolver.DefaultVoice, JobService.CreateJobAsync) now await it. (2) BuildTtsPayload's three model-family flags collapsed into one shared isV2Family check (multilingual_v2 OR turbo_v2 OR flash_v2), closing the flash_v2_5 gap and preventing the three checks from drifting apart again. (3) similarity_boost now gated by the same isV2Family flag (0.0 for v3, matching how style/speed/speaker-boost were already treated) instead of always forwarding the caller's value. (4) GenerationAttemptOutcome's success tuple widened to carry the tagged script alongside the plain one end-to-end (ScriptGenerationEngine -> BroadcastOrchestrator -> AudioFinalizer.FinalizeAudioAsync/RevoiceExistingScriptAsync -> SaveFinalBroadcastResultAsync), which now independently sets TaggedScriptText/DeliveryStyleId/DeliveryStyleVersion from DeliveryTags.HasTags(taggedScript), mirroring PersistScriptOnJob's exact logic rather than depending on an earlier intermediate save having landed correctly.

**Rationale:** Live reproduction over static trust: the session repeatedly found that plausible code-level fixes did not match observed dev behaviour until traced with real jobs, App Insights traces, and (for bug 4) two rounds of temporary diagnostic logging deployed to dev -- this caught that the Director's LLM call is itself non-deterministic (fails open to a plain script on some attempts), which had been mis-read as a persistence bug in an earlier session. Fixing ModelSelector at the root (capability-aware, matching the established VoiceModelResolver/2026-06-26 pattern) closes a KNOWN GAP that decision explicitly left open, rather than leaving a second capability-blind path alongside the fixed VoicesHttpTrigger display path. Widening AudioFinalizer to independently persist provenance (rather than trusting PersistScriptOnJob's earlier ScriptReady-stage save) makes the FINAL, terminal, operator-facing job state self-sufficient regardless of whatever intermediate save behaviour exists upstream.

**Consequences:** Verified: full backend suite green (Domain 1217, Application 543, Functions 402, Infrastructure 1034/22 skipped, ArchitectureTests 14 -- zero failures) after every change; each of the four fixes independently confirmed live against a fresh dev deploy (job resolved model, WPM-vs-speed A/B, and a real demo-coast poller-fired job showing populated TaggedText/DeliveryStyleId/DeliveryStyleVersion). New: ModelSelector's voices-list cache (5 min, keyed once) adds one ElevenLabs GetVoicesAsync call per cache window on the ad-hoc/default-voice fallback path only -- profile-driven jobs (all real stations) are unaffected. IModelSelector.SelectModel is now SelectModelAsync (breaking signature change, 2 production call sites + 6 test files updated). Residual, not fixed here: the Director's own tag-application success rate is LLM-dependent and non-deterministic -- a bulletin with a real delivery style assigned will sometimes still air neutral when the LLM fails open on every retry attempt; this is pre-existing, documented, fail-safe-by-design behaviour, not a persistence defect. Zero delivery styles remain assigned to any real (non-demo) station -- a product decision, not addressed in this batch. AudioFinalizer.cs and WordTargetEnforcer.cs briefly carried temporary [DIAG]/[DIAG-EXTEND]/[DIAG-POSTIF] LogWarning instrumentation during live bisection -- removed before the final clean redeploy; no residue shipped.

## 2026-07-24 — Zetta delivery gains a third transport: AD DS-authenticated Azure Files drop (AzureFilesDrop)

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** the ARN Technology Lead added an Azure Files SMB share (name 'informationbulletins', distinct from the existing blob container of the same name) to the same drop account (ibpauetststaftp01) used for the proven BlobDrop/SFTP transport (2026-07-17 decision), with Azure Files identity-based auth configured against ARN's on-prem AD (ausradio.net.au domain join, defaultSharePermission StorageFileDataSmbShareReader). He granted the AD group sg_GB Zetta 'Storage File Data SMB Share Reader' and asked (1) whether Read is sufficient for Zetta's SMB pull or whether Zetta 'moves' the file locally (needing write/delete), and (2) whether the app can write bulletins into the new share. Confirmed live via az: the share exists (Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/fileServices/shares, SMB-enabled), a private endpoint for the file subresource (ibp-aue-tst-pep-ftp02) is already wired to privatelink.file.core.windows.net in the test VNet, and Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor/Reader are already assigned to ARN's own AD groups — all provisioned by the ARN Technology Lead outside our template, same pattern as the drop account itself.

**Decision:** Added DeliveryTransport.AzureFilesDrop (third option alongside Smb/BlobDrop) and AzureFilesDropFileWriter : IDeliveryFileWriter, using Azure.Storage.Files.Shares with the app's existing managed identity (TokenCredential). Critically, Azure Files OAuth-over-REST needs ShareClientOptions.ShareTokenIntent=Backup on every call AND the 'Storage File Data Privileged Contributor' role (GUID 69566ab7-960f-475b-8e7c-b3118f30c6bd) — NOT the 'Storage File Data SMB Share *' roles, which only cover on-prem AD DS/Kerberos SMB mounts (what sg_GB Zetta uses) and lack the readFileBackupSemantics/writeFileBackupSemantics data actions OAuth-over-REST requires. roles-delivery-drop.bicep now grants both Storage Blob Data Contributor and Storage File Data Privileged Contributor to the Function App's managed identities unconditionally whenever a drop account is configured, so flipping zettaTransport never needs a fresh role deploy. New params zettaDropFileShareName (default 'informationbulletins') threaded through main.bicep/function-app.bicep exactly like zettaDropContainerName. Test bicepparam switched zettaTransport to 'AzureFilesDrop' for live verification; BlobDrop remains fully implemented and is a one-line revert away. On the ARN Technology Lead's permission question: recommended sg_GB Zetta stay at Reader — our delivery always overwrites the same stable filename per market ({MarketId}_TRAIN_TRAFF.wav), so nothing on our side ever needs Zetta to delete/move the source; only bump to Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor if Zetta's own import empirically needs to clear the file after pulling it.

**Rationale:** The SMB Share RBAC roles (Reader/Contributor/Elevated Contributor) are scoped for Kerberos-authenticated on-prem SMB clients and are the correct roles for Zetta's own AD identity, but they deliberately exclude the two backup-semantics data actions that gate OAuth/REST access — granting them to our own managed identity would silently 403 on every write. The Privileged Contributor role exists specifically for exactly this scenario (a service identity that owns and writes into a share it doesn't NTFS-ACL itself into), bypassing per-file/directory ACLs account-wide, which matches a delivery-drop writer that just needs to land files. Keeping BlobDrop and AzureFilesDrop as sibling transports (not a replacement) means the already-proven SFTP path is never at risk while the new SMB-native path — closer to Zetta's own ingest mechanism and free of the SFTP vendor-egress-IP-allowlisting friction — gets a real trial.

**Consequences:** Backend build 0/0 across the full solution; 19/19 AzureFilesDropFileWriter + BlobDropFileWriter + ZettaFileDeliveryService tests green. az bicep build/build-params clean for main.bicep and main.test.bicepparam. roles-delivery-drop.bicep redeployed standalone against ibpauetststaftp01 (both Function App slots) ahead of the next full main.bicep deploy. Pending: full main.bicep + code deploy to test to actually exercise AzureFilesDropFileWriter end-to-end and confirm a real bulletin WAV lands in the share for Zetta to mount; production Zetta network/host details remain blocked on ARN playout regardless of transport choice.

## 2026-07-26 — Every no-retry generation failure covers its slot from the standby chain, not just content-limited

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The first authenticated load burst on TEST (11 markets, one clock tick — see `docs/operations/load-testing.md` §Results 26 Jul) produced two jobs that failed the *same* final grounding hard gate for the same class of reason (a duplicated claim), yet reached different terminal states: `mildura` → `FallbackUsed`, `goldcoast` → `Failed`. Root cause: `BroadcastOrchestrator.GenerateBroadcastAsync` routed to the fallback chain **only** for `FailureDisposition.ContentLimited`; every other failure fell through to `MarkJobFailedAsync`. Mildura had also tripped the content-limited underrun so it carried that disposition and was covered; goldcoast had only the grounding failure and was not. Compounding it, the grounding gate returned an untyped `Result.Failure(string)` so it defaulted to `Retryable`, and `ScriptReviewLoop` (~L376) rebuilt the failure from `.Error` alone, discarding any metadata a caller did set. `JobWatchdog` still covered the slot at the fallback deadline, so this was never dead air, but recovery was deferred through the whole operator review window and raised an intervention card for something the standby chain could have filled silently. It also reads as an "unplanned error" against SC-01's *"10 consecutive scheduled bulletin cycles with zero unplanned errors"*.

**Decision:** Cover the slot immediately for every generation failure the queue will not redeliver, using `QueueFailurePolicy`'s existing classification as the authority rather than inventing a second one. (1) `ScriptReviewLoop` types final-grounding exhaustion as `OperationalFailure.Permanent("broadcast.final_grounding_failed", …)` — the refine budget is spent and the gate rejected the script on every attempt, so re-running the pipeline over the same fetched content is not expected to clear it (the reasoning the content-limited path already applies); the transient sibling paths (reviewer unavailable, refine failed) stay untyped/retryable on purpose. (2) That method now returns the `Result` itself instead of rebuilding `Failure(finalGrounding.Error)`, so the disposition survives. (3) `BroadcastOrchestrator` routes `ContentLimited | SafetyRejected | Permanent` into a generalised `HandleUnairableAsync` (was `HandleContentLimitedAsync`), tagging the fallback with a new `FallbackReasons.QualityGateFailed` and `quality_gate_*` metrics so the console can explain *why* the slot was covered. `Conflict` is excluded (job already terminal, nothing to cover); `Retryable`/`InvalidInput` still fall through to queue redelivery with the watchdog as the net.

**Rationale:** `QueueFailurePolicy` already encodes which dispositions get no second chance (`ContentLimited`, `SafetyRejected`, `Conflict`, `Permanent`). Deriving the fallback decision from that existing contract makes the invariant checkable in one sentence — *if the queue will not retry it, cover the slot now* — instead of adding a parallel list to keep in sync. Typing the gate rather than special-casing the orchestrator keeps the knowledge where the judgement is made.

**Consequences:** `scripts/verify.sh` green — backend 3220 tests (Application 543→545), web 595, 0 failures. Two new `BroadcastOrchestratorTests`: a never-approving reviewer now proves the standby is applied with `FallbackReasons.QualityGateFailed` and the job is never persisted `Failed`, and that the surfaced failure carries `Permanent`/`broadcast.final_grounding_failed`. The metadata-discard bug at `ScriptReviewLoop` ~L376 was found by the second test failing for the *wrong* reason — rebuilding a `Result` from `.Error` silently downgrades disposition anywhere else it is done. Safety rejections now also reach the standby chain, which they did not before. Unchanged: `JobWatchdog` remains the deadline net for `Retryable` exhaustion and for the no-standby-available case.

## 2026-07-27 — Local gate scoped by changed paths and run in parallel lanes

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The local CI mirror `scripts/verify.sh` (2026-07-17 decision) enforced its invariant the blunt way: every gate, always, serially. Measured on the current tree the full gate is 369s of phases. That made the honest gate expensive enough to avoid, and avoidance is what actually happened — the pre-push hook ran only `--quick`, which skips backend E2E and web perf. Two of the three gates the 2026-07-17 incident broke were therefore un-run locally by default. The cost was concrete: `BroadcastPipelineE2ETests` had been failing since 21 Jul (d9e61be made the approve/publish `ExpectedEtag` precondition mandatory; the E2E test still posted an empty body and got 428) and nobody saw it for six days, because nothing was pushed to CI after 22 Jul and every local run used the quick gate.

**Decision:** Keep the invariant — no gate whose inputs changed may be skipped — but satisfy it by SCOPE and CONCURRENCY rather than by brute force. (1) Gates are selected from the changed paths (`classify_path`), with the default branch escalating to every area so an unrecognised path fails safe/slow, never unsafe/skipped. (2) Selected gates run as parallel lanes (backend, eslint, web build chain, bicep, gitleaks); lanes never share a build directory, so the backend chain stays serial within itself (bin/obj) as does the web chain (.tsbuildinfo). (3) The pre-push hook now runs the full scoped set, bounded by the actual push range passed as VERIFY_RANGE, instead of the gate-skipping `--quick`; an unbounded push (new branch, several refs) escalates to every area. (4) `--full` remains the unscoped exact CI mirror, `--quick` the fast-subset escape hatch, `--explain` a dry run. (5) Report shows a per-phase timing table and dumps full output only for lanes that failed.

**Rationale:** CI already runs these as parallel jobs (Build & Test: Backend / Bicep / Secret scan / dependency scan; Package: Frontend) — only the local mirror serialised them, so parallelising is convergence with CI, not a new risk. Scoping is sound because the gate builds and tests the WORKING TREE, and the scope set is the union of the push range, tracked modifications and untracked files, so anything that will be compiled is classified. Measured on this tree: serial sum 369s vs 209s wall unscoped (the backend lane — build 10s + unit 83s + E2E 116s — is the critical path and exactly equals wall time); a docs-only push is 3.3s end-to-end; a web-only push is ~92s (computed from the measured web-lane phases). Scope detection itself needed care: classifying via `$(classify_path ...)` forked a subshell per path and the tree carries ~28k untracked files (26k of presentation footage), costing 38.1s to decide there was nothing to do; assigning to a variable and collapsing paths to their first two components (lossless — no rule discriminates deeper) took that to 0.197s.

**Consequences:** verify.sh --full is green across all 10 phases (backend build/unit/E2E, web lint/typecheck/unit/build/perf, bicep, gitleaks). Running the honest gate immediately surfaced two real defects, both now fixed: (1) BroadcastPipelineE2ETests now sends the reviewed revision's ETag on approve and a fresh one on publish, and asserts 428 for a missing precondition so a silent relaxation back to 'optional' fails the suite — the ApproveJobRequest / PublishJobRequest doc comments still claimed 'absent means no precondition', the stale text that let the drift go unnoticed, and are corrected to mandatory. (2) scripts/e2e-backend.sh's fresh-slate wipe was unreachable whenever Azurite was already running — precisely the scenario its own comment describes — so consecutive local E2E runs 409'd on seeded 'E2E Hudson' voice profiles; it now restarts an Azurite serving our data directory, refuses to reuse a foreign one squatting on ports 10000-10002, and offers ARN_E2E_REUSE_AZURITE=1 for the fast dev loop. Adding a new top-level directory escalates every push to the full gate until classify_path learns it — deliberate, and the failure mode is slowness, not a skipped gate.

## 2026-07-27 — Frontend quality gates: Tailwind conformance, scored Lighthouse categories, and a dark-mode capture axis

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The frontend quality harness measured three things well and three things not at all. (1) Nothing checked Tailwind class usage: 102 findings existed in web/src with no gate — 18 deprecated v4 classes, 5 arbitrary values with named equivalents, and a real defect where `block line-clamp-1` on the Adjust rundown detail rows resolved to display:block, so the single-line clamp never applied. (2) `lighthouse@13.4.1` was already a devDependency and already ships the `agentic-browsing` category (13.3+), but `perf-audit.mjs` requested `onlyCategories: ['performance']` — accessibility and agentic-browsing had never been scored. First measurement: a11y 0.93–1.00, agentic 0.33–0.67, with `button-name` failing on 28 unnamed `<SelectTrigger>` combobox buttons (WCAG 4.1.2 A), `label-content-name-mismatch` on the queue rows and the Cards/Table toggle (2.5.3), `aria-sort` on a `<button>` where it is not an allowed attribute, H1→H3 heading skips on four gallery pages, and CLS 0.146 on /jobs. (3) `ux-audit.mjs` never controlled the theme: the app runs next-themes with `enableSystem`, so the captured theme depended on the headless browser's prefers-color-scheme — an uncontrolled variable in a harness whose value is byte-stable determinism, and the `.dark` half of the token set was never screenshotted or axe'd.

**Decision:** Add the three missing layers, each enforced rather than documented. (1) `web/.oxlintrc.json` — oxlint + oxlint-tailwindcss compile `src/index.css` to build the real design system and gate on it, in two tiers: unambiguous rules (deprecated/duplicate/unnecessary-arbitrary/hardcoded-colour/prefer-theme-token/dark-without-light/unknown-class) are errors wired into `npm run lint`, which CI already runs; rules that need adjudication against the compiled stylesheet (`no-conflicting-classes`, `prefer-scale-token` at step 1) are warnings. `no-contradicting-variants` is OFF — 11 of its 12 findings were the twMerge composition pattern, where a caller's `focus:text-destructive` neutralises the primitive's own `focus:text-accent-foreground` and is therefore required. (2) `perf-audit.mjs` requests all three categories and gates both quality scores at 100, recomputing each from its auditRefs so a waived audit (`llms-txt`, no anonymous agent on an Entra-gated console) leaves the bar for everything else untouched. (3) `ux-audit.mjs` gains a theme axis: capture variants are viewports x themes, the variant id IS the existing `vp` key (`desktop` / `desktop-dark`), so every artifact path, stored finding and resolved box stays valid. Theme is driven through next-themes' own storage-event channel, not by forcing a class. Accessible names on `SelectTrigger` are required in the TYPE, not by convention. `web/docs/UI-INVENTORY.md` is generated from the TypeScript checker and its freshness is gated by verify.sh.

**Rationale:** Each layer catches a class the layer above it structurally cannot. A VLM reviewing a screenshot cannot know `bg-gradient-to-r` is deprecated or that `block` beat `line-clamp-1` in the cascade; only a linter reading the compiled design system can. axe run once per page cannot score a category or weigh audits; only Lighthouse can. And neither can see a theme that is never rendered. Enforcing in the type system where possible is the same reasoning one level down: 28 unnamed comboboxes accumulated under a convention, and zero can accumulate under a required prop. The two-tier lint split exists because `no-conflicting-classes` was verified WRONG on this codebase — it claims `animate-in` beats `duration-300` on animation-duration, and the compiled CSS shows the opposite (.animate-in @93476 at 150ms, .duration-300 @95005 at 300ms) because tailwindcss-animate v1 is bridged through `@config` and emits later than the plugin models; that pair is allow-listed with the offsets recorded. A gate that is right by construction earns errors; a gate that needs a human to check the stylesheet earns warnings.

**Consequences:** Tailwind gate: 0 errors, 0 warnings. 25 distinct rewrites across 33 sites were verified byte-equivalent against the compiled CSS before landing (e.g. max-w-[80rem] -> max-w-7xl both resolve to 1280px); the dead v3 `filter` class was removed after confirming v4's `invert`/`blur-*` each emit the full filter composition themselves. Lighthouse: all 7 routes now score a11y 100 and agentic-browsing 100, up from 0.93–1.00 and 0.33–0.67. Fixes: `SelectTrigger` requires `aria-label`|`aria-labelledby` in its props type and all 28 call sites are named; queue rows and the Cards/Table toggle are named from content so the accessible name contains the visible text; `aria-sort` moved from the sort button to its `<th>`; four gallery card titles and the scope-group header promoted h3->h2; and the On-air board is top-anchored with schedules' loading state threaded through, which removed both the 0.146 CLS and a false 'No stations configured' flash on every cold load. UX audit: 20 targets x 8 variants, dark captures confirmed (mean luminance 28 vs 227 light). Equalising the two axe passes with a warm-up theme cycle turned '5 dark-only violations' into 0 — they were lazily-mounted subtrees the earlier light pass had missed, so the harness is now more accurate in light too and reports 46 axe findings (up from 45) that a follow-up triage pass should work through. Runtime 217s. Costs: two devDependencies (oxlint, oxlint-tailwindcss); the audit is ~2x longer; UI-INVENTORY.md must be regenerated when a shared component's props change or verify.sh fails.

## 2026-07-27 — Duration trimming budgets for the weather/fuel close, and reports itself to the job log

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Four bulletins in the 25-26 Jul dev sample lost their trailing weather and/or fuel line between the AI safety review and the audio, with nothing in `LogsJson` to explain it. Verified from the `llm-call-captures` blobs: the close survives the writer, the reviewer and the Safety call (whose response is only `{"safe":true,"violations":[]}` — it returns a verdict, not a script), then is absent from both the persisted `ScriptText` and the word timings. Root cause is `BulletinDurationFitter.FitByTrimming`, called from `AudioPipelineService` CASE 3: when a read overruns beyond the pitch-preserving speed-up budget the pipeline measures where each sentence lands in the TTS alignment, drops sentences, and re-synthesises. The mechanism is deliberate and correct; three things around it were not. It drops by POSITION, not priority — and the prompt's fill order is traffic, then weather, then fuel, so the close is always last and therefore always the first thing sacrificed. It logs only to `ILogger`, never `LogJobAsync`, so the operator-facing timeline never mentioned it. And the pre-synthesis `Synthesizing audio (N words)` job-log line is the PRE-trim count and was never corrected, so the timeline actively overstated what aired. Published job `19be05d7` aired ending flat on a four-road roll-call with no close at all.

**Decision:** `FitByTrimming` now budgets for the close FIRST. The trailing contiguous run of locked sentences (`PolishLockPolicy.IsWeatherOrFuel` — the same lexicon the polish gate already treats as unchangeable) is identified as the close, its cost is subtracted from the slot budget, and the overrun is taken out of the TRAFFIC items instead. Only the TRAILING run counts, so a weather mention earlier in the read is ordinary content. When the close alone cannot fit the budget, or every sentence is locked, it degrades to the previous leading-prefix trim rather than dropping all the traffic. Separately, `ScriptGenerationEngine` now compares the spoken word count against the pre-synthesis count and writes a `Read overran the Ns slot — trimmed to fit (X -> Y words)` line to the job log, and the comment asserting "The pipeline does not mutate text" is corrected — it does, and that is exactly why `FinalScript` is the thing persisted.

**Rationale:** A bulletin that ends mid-list is a worse on-air artifact than one that covers one fewer road: the close is short, cheap and structural, while the marginal traffic item is the least important thing in the read by construction (worst-first ordering). Reusing `PolishLockPolicy` rather than inventing a second lexicon keeps one definition of "this sentence carries exact factual numbers". Making the trim visible was non-negotiable independent of the editorial change — a decision that alters what airs and appears nowhere in the operator's timeline is unauditable, and the misleading pre-trim count is what kept it hidden through four jobs.

**Consequences:** `BulletinDurationFitter` gains a private `LockedTailStart`; class and method docs corrected (they described the old drop-by-position behaviour). `ScriptGenerationEngine` gains the trim log line. Four new tests in `BulletinDurationFitterTests` cover close preservation, a multi-sentence weather+fuel close, degradation when the close cannot fit, and the all-locked case; the five existing tests are unchanged and still green, so the no-close path is unaltered. Behaviour change: a trimmed overrun now airs one fewer traffic item and keeps its close.

## 2026-07-27 — Fuel prices are normalised to spoken words deterministically

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Job `5dfe174e` aired `Unleaded's cheapest at $1.79 in Chermside West` while nine sibling bulletins said the same kind of figure in words. Measured live on 2026-07-27, the same market on the same config produced `$1.78` on one run and `a dollar seventy-eight` on the next — the prompt asks for spoken numbers, but the instruction is unreliable under sampling variance. An LLM review pass does not close it: replaying the real captured review prompt against the affected script flagged it 0 times in 6, because a numeral is a rendering defect, not a fidelity one, and the reviewer is looking for fidelity.

**Decision:** New `SpokenPriceNormalizer` (Domain/Services), wired into the same always-on chain as `ClosureVerbNormalizer`/`ClearRoadLabelNormalizer`/`TimeOfDayNormalizer` at all three `LlmScriptGenerator` exits (generate, refine, polish). `$1.79` becomes `a dollar seventy-nine`, `$2.19` becomes `two dollars nineteen`; a single cents digit reads as tens (`$1.8` is a dollar eighty); whole dollars omit cents. Only the currency form is touched — temperatures, distances and drive-times are untouched. A 3-decimal wholesale figure (`$1.779`) is deliberately left alone, since it is not a price we voice and rounding it here would invent a number the data did not supply.

**Rationale:** This is precisely the failure class the deterministic normalizer suite exists to close, and the suite already had the shape to copy. Fixing it in code rather than the prompt makes it structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged, and costs no tokens and no latency.

**Consequences:** New `SpokenPriceNormalizer.cs` + `SpokenPriceNormalizerTests.cs` (16 tests, including the observed `$1.79`/`$1.78`/`$2.19` cases and the non-currency negatives). Runs after the polish gate's own comparison, so locked weather/fuel lines are normalised consistently on both sides and the byte-identical lock check is unaffected.

## 2026-07-27 — The durable market-feedback corpus rejects workflow artifacts and duplicates

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** One operator reject click forks into two channels, both fed the same `notes` string: the per-job `RejectionHistory` (which builds the authoritative `<producer-feedback>` block for the next regeneration) and the durable per-market corpus (`RetainMarketFeedbackAsync`, replayed into EVERY future bulletin for that market as `<operator-notes>` — "Recurring mistakes to avoid"). The corpus is a rolling window of 8 per market that never expires, so slots are scarce. The console sends a hardcoded `notes: 'Script edited and re-voiced'` whenever an operator hand-edits a script (`use-bulletin-review.ts`), which is a workflow event, not an editorial lesson. On 2026-07-26 it occupied 7 of Melbourne's 8 slots, leaving the single real lesson ("Lead with the motorway closure") one click from eviction; Brisbane's window was 5/5 stale `[test]` fixtures. Nothing deduplicated either.

**Decision:** New pure `MarketFeedbackPolicy.IsDurableLesson(notes, existing)` (Domain/Services) gates the corpus write: known workflow-artifact stems are rejected, and a note already present in the market's current 8-entry window is rejected as a duplicate (case-insensitive, trimmed). `JobService.RetainMarketFeedbackAsync` consults the same window the generator actually replays, so "already known" means exactly "the writer is already seeing this". The duplicate lookup fails OPEN — a read failure stores the note anyway.

**Rationale:** Fixing this at the corpus boundary rather than in the console cleans every writer at once and cannot be bypassed by a client. Filtering here loses nothing: a rejected note still lands in the job's own `RejectionHistory` and still drives the very next regeneration through `<producer-feedback>`; only the claim on a permanent market-wide slot is refused. Failing open on the dedupe read is deliberate — dropping real operator feedback because a lookup failed is worse than storing a possible duplicate. Note the near-miss: the duplicate copy of a note across the TWO channels is load-bearing and was NOT removed — measured on the real captured Draft prompt, stripping the `<operator-notes>` copy dropped producer-feedback compliance from 6/8 to 0/8.

**Consequences:** New `MarketFeedbackPolicy.cs` + `MarketFeedbackPolicyTests.cs` (6 tests). `JobService` gains `RecentFeedbackTextsAsync` and the `MarketFeedbackWindow` constant (8, matching `MarketContentFetcher`), plus three new `JobServiceContentTests` covering the console note, the duplicate, and the fail-open path. `JobWatchdog`'s "Expired unapproved" note never reached the corpus (it rejects via `job.Reject` directly, not `JobService`), and still does not.

## 2026-07-27 — Prompt-cache work: token usage is now measured; retention and static-first reordering both rejected on measurement

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** A stack review asked what recent technology could give a big, cheap win. The frontend is already on Vite 8/Rolldown (vite build 0.88s), TypeScript 7 native (tsc -b 0.99s vs TS6 6.95s), React 19, Tailwind 4, oxlint and .NET 10, so the only unexploited lever found was prompt caching. Four gpt-5.6-luna production captures (job-diagnostics/*/llm_calls) all reported cached_tokens: 0 on ~6.2k-token Drafts, against 34.8% on the older gpt-5.4-mini corpus (63 calls, 164k input tokens) -- and from gpt-5.6 onward Azure bills cache WRITES on top of discounted reads, so a never-read cache is a pure cost. That headline turned out to be a four-sample artifact; the truth needed live measurement, which nothing in the app could provide because the raw usage object was captured but never parsed.

**Decision:** Ship the measurement, reject both changes. (1) ADOPTED: LlmTokenUsage (Domain) + TokenUsageParser (Infrastructure) lift input/cached/output/reasoning tokens out of every Responses API body; ResponsesTransport parses them on BOTH transport paths and emits one structured log line per call (InputTokens/CachedTokens/CacheHitRatio/OutputTokens/ReasoningTokens/JobId), and LlmCallRecord carries them as a first-class field. (2) REJECTED: prompt_cache_retention='24h'. (3) REJECTED and reverted: reordering prompts/draft.md static-first.

**Rationale:** Measured live against the dev arn-draft/arn-review Foundry agents on 2026-07-27, not assumed. Retention: accepted by both endpoints and latency-neutral (+12ms p50, +0.6%, n=10 interleaved), but it does not do the one thing it was wanted for -- across a 14-minute inter-slot gap the agent path cached 3,840 tokens WITH '24h' and 2,816 WITHOUT it (the cache simply survived either way), and on the raw-model path the '24h' arm cached 0 after the gap while the in_memory arm cached 3,840. No benefit, so no config. Static-first reordering: a synthetic arm with a 5.7k-token static block looked spectacular (0/5 hits and 0.0% cached variable-first, vs 5/5 and 96.6% static-first, 5.6% FASTER at p50). It did not survive contact with Arn's real prompt sizes. Interleaved A/B on the actual old and new templates, both arms pre-warmed, 32 calls over two runs: OLD 33.0% cached (7/16 hits), NEW 38.2% (9/16) -- directionally consistent but marginal, while the SAME old arm swung 60.9% to 5.2% between runs with no code change. Cache warmth dominates prompt ordering by an order of magnitude, because Arn's draft user message is only ~1.5k tokens against the agent's 2,764-token server-side instruction block, so the ~40-token variable head displaces almost nothing. A prompt reorder changes what the model reads first and would need full regression-corpus validation; that risk budget is not worth a gain inside the noise. Also confirmed disqualified: Chat Completions caches gpt-5.6-luna reliably (89.1%) where the Responses API is erratic, but at 16.4s per call vs 1.3s -- it would wreck the pipeline. prompt_cache_key made no measurable difference (71.3% hit rate with and without, n=10 each) and one probe carrying it took 61s, so it is not used.

**Consequences:** New LlmTokenUsage.cs, TokenUsageParser.cs, TokenUsageParserTests.cs (12 tests); LlmCallRecord gains an optional trailing Usage parameter (source-compatible, both call sites updated). Cache behaviour is now queryable in Log Analytics per call and per stage without cracking capture blobs, which is the prerequisite for revisiting this with production data instead of four samples. The metric is logged rather than pushed through IBroadcastMetrics because that interface lives in Application, which Infrastructure must not reference (LayerDependencyTests). prompts/draft.md is unchanged (git-reverted; verified line 1 still opens with the targetSeconds/city interpolation). Re-open this only if the new per-call CacheHitRatio shows a sustained low rate across real bulletins -- and note that Safety prompts (~688 tokens) sit under the 1,024-token floor and can never cache at all.

## 2026-07-27 — web/.prettierignore covers generated dirs, so npm run format is usable again

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** npm run lint was failing on a clean tree with prettier/prettier errors in src/. The cause was upstream: .prettierignore listed only dist, coverage and the generated live-traffic snapshot, so 'prettier --write .' (the npm run format script) rewrote 440 files -- audit/ 280, dist-mock/ 135, perf/ 12 -- against roughly 10 real sources. A format command that produces a 440-file diff is one nobody runs, which is exactly how formatting drift accumulated in src/ unnoticed. .oxlintrc.json already carried the correct ignore list; .prettierignore had drifted from it.

**Decision:** Add dist-mock, audit and perf to web/.prettierignore alongside the existing dist/coverage entries, plus the generated docs/UI-INVENTORY.md and docs/ui-inventory.json (emitted by scripts/ui-inventory.mjs, same rationale as the live-traffic snapshot). Fix the outstanding src/ violations with a scoped 'eslint src --fix' rather than a repo-wide reformat.

**Rationale:** Keeping the two ignore lists in step is the actual fix -- the lint failure was a symptom. Scoping the autofix to src/ mattered because the working tree carried ~130 unrelated in-flight web changes at the time; a repo-wide reformat would have mixed formatting churn into someone else's uncommitted work.

**Consequences:** npm run lint exits 0. 'prettier --list-different .' drops from 440 files/24.2s to 10 files/6.3s. The 10 remaining are docs and config (README, CONTEXT.md, CODEMAPS/MODULES.md, .oxlintrc.json and similar), deliberately left alone. Keep .prettierignore and .oxlintrc.json's ignorePatterns in step when either changes.

## 2026-07-27 — Frontend defect remediation: solve colour to the AA floor, and fix the instruments that mis-reported

**Status:** accepted
