Multi-voice round-trip proven lossless by parsing a three-id window and replaying the save payload. Two reported items were downgraded rather than fixed as described: the duplicate window-id counters do NOT corrupt data because window mutations are index-based (tested - the right row is removed), and the four version-history Restore labels were already honest except voices, which now also reads "Restore as new version"; the draft-versus-immediate behaviour split across the four libraries is left as a product decision. Also corrected: the pronunciation audition renders the SAVED dictionary, so editing rules now clears a stale clip rather than leaving it beside unsaved edits.

## 2026-07-29 — Per-role model plumbing deleted; unused Foundry deployments removed; dev deployed at HEAD

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The remaining config-drift open items needed a decision rather than more investigation. Per-role Azure OpenAI deployments were fully provisioned in IaC but never consumed: function-app.bicep declared param roleDeployments and never read it, so no agent role was ever pinned to its own capacity bucket. Separately, the dev Foundry account carried deployments nothing referenced.

**Decision:** Delete rather than wire. Removed roleModelDeployments from main.bicep and all three bicepparams, the per-role deployment resource and the roleDeployments output from ai-services.bicep, and the dead roleDeployments parameter from function-app.bicep. AzureAIOptions's per-role override (DraftModel and siblings) is deliberately kept: pinning a role now takes a deployment plus an app setting rather than standing IaC. Deleted three deployments from the dev Foundry account: gpt-5.4-mini, gpt-5.4-mini-draft and gpt-5.6-luna-draft. Retained gpt-5.6-terra, which the first audit pass wrongly called an orphan - it is the pinned independent judge in every and is run by the CI EvalGate stage, so deleting it would have broken CI. Also completed the three LOW findings: all three HERE base URLs are now explicit in appsettings.json, four eval-history docs retagged from arn-draft-natural-v53 to arn-draft, and canberra/hobart dropped from CityMappings. Deployed the full stack to dev at the current working tree.

**Rationale:** The 429s that motivated per-role capacity isolation were retired by the dispatcher model (decisions.md 2026-07-21), and the shared deployment sits at 1900 of 10000 TPM, so the isolation solves a problem that no longer exists. The audit's cost justification also evaporated on inspection: every deployment is GlobalStandard, i.e. consumption-billed, so idle capacity is a rate limit rather than a reservation and costs nothing. Deleting inert wiring is better than completing it, because dormant plumbing that looks wired is exactly the trap the whole drift audit exists to remove.

**Consequences:** Verified live on dev after deploy: POST /api/broadcast rejects a missing, blank, unknown-profile and unknown-voice request with the exact four messages; GET /api/voices/profiles serves provider-resolved base voice names for all 5 profiles; auth unchanged (authenticated 200, unauthenticated 401, health 200) with no AadClientSecret app setting; and a real Gold Coast bulletin (job e9e3e656) rendered a prompt reading 'a 30-second traffic bulletin for Gold Coast radio' with zero occurrences of the old mangled 'Goldcoast'. Backend suite green (Domain 1310, Application 580, Functions 487, Infrastructure 1288, Architecture 14, ExternalSmoke 3). NEW deferred item: the deploy script's post-deploy validation now reports Zetta__Username and Zetta__Password as unresolved Key Vault references - the same shape as AadClientSecret, but genuinely needed when Zetta:Transport is Smb, so the fix is to emit them conditionally on zettaEnabled rather than remove them. That the validation flagged two rather than three confirms removing AadClientSecret closed a real wart.

## 2026-07-29 — verify.sh --full was not the CI mirror it claimed: frontend Playwright E2E was missing

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** CI run 2668 (the first test/prod promotion attempt) failed its Package stage on 8 frontend Playwright specs, blocking Deploy_Test and Deploy_Prod. The failing commit range contains four commits landed by a concurrent session, two of them explicitly frontend; the failing specs target UI affordances (an Adjust tab, a re-voice button, an assign-operator button) that Playwright can no longer resolve. Both that session and this one ran ./scripts/verify.sh --full and saw it green before pushing. AGENTS.md documents --full as 'every gate, every area, no scoping - the exact CI mirror'. It was not: CI's Package stage runs npm run e2e (Playwright, mock mode) and gates every deployment on it, and verify.sh had no web E2E phase at all. Its only e2e reference was scripts/e2e-backend.sh.

**Decision:** Added a 'web e2e' phase running 'cd web && npm run e2e' to verify.sh's web lane, inside the SLOW_TAIL branch alongside the backend E2E and the web perf budget. So --full and the default scoped run include it, --quick drops it, matching how every other slow gate is already treated. Updated the --quick help text and the slow-tail banner to name it.

**Rationale:** A gate documented as the CI mirror must actually mirror CI, or it manufactures false confidence in exactly the situation it exists to prevent: a green local run immediately followed by a red pipeline that blocks deployment. Putting it in the slow tail rather than the default fast path keeps --quick usable for tight loops while making the honest pre-push gate honest. Placing it in the web lane means it runs in parallel with the backend lane, so wall time grows by roughly the Playwright run minus existing web slack rather than by its full duration.

**Consequences:** verify.sh --full now runs the same frontend suite CI does, and will FAIL until the 8 specs are green again - which is correct, because master is currently un-deployable for that reason. The blocking regression itself was NOT fixed here: it sits in a concurrent session's active frontend area, the affordances the specs target are absent from the current source, and adjudicating whether the removals were intentional or accidental needs that session's intent rather than a guess. Test and prod promotion (CI 2668) remains blocked until it is resolved.

## 2026-07-29 — Promotion gate grades its bulletin panel on dev, not the environment being promoted

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** CI 2686 deployed dev and test at HEAD, then EvalGate_Test failed: 'could not list schedules on test: HTTP Error 401 Unauthorized'. The promotion gate drives the target Function App's own API (GET /api/schedules, PUT /api/schedules/{m} to arm the poller, GET /api/jobs) with the ADO service connection's management token. Test and prod deliberately exclude the ARM audience from Easy Auth (least-privilege finding 2026-07-16), so every call is rejected at the platform before the worker runs — verified live with one token: test returns 401 + Content-Length 0 + WWW-Authenticate: Bearer, dev returns 200 + Server: Kestrel. Enabling allowArmAudience on test was considered and rejected on TECHNICAL grounds, not policy: an ARM-audience token carries no app role for api://{clientId}, so it would clear Easy Auth and then 403 in AuthorizationMiddleware, which requires Operator or Admin. Dev only works because Auth__DevFallbackRole adds a role to every parsed principal ('a dev-only authorization bypass', ClientPrincipal.TryFromJson), and Program.cs aborts host startup if that setting is present on a TST/PRD site. So the audience flag would move 401 to 403 and change nothing else, while widening the authenticated surface to every ARM token in the tenant.

**Decision:** Retarget the promotion gate to dev and rename the stage EvalGate_Test -> EvalGate_Promote, since a stage named for an environment it does not touch is the same stale-mirror class fixed across the codebase on 2026-07-29. Deploy_Prod still depends on it, so prod is still gated on a real-bulletin panel; the panel now runs on dev, where Deploy_Dev has already shipped the exact build being promoted. Pass the panel explicitly (markets: sydney,melbourne,brisbane,adelaide,perth,goldcoast,darwin,mildura) because every dev schedule is deliberately disabled and the gate would otherwise exit 2 on 'no enabled schedules' — it arms and reverts each schedule itself, so Enabled never gated triggering, only default resolution. Raise the ARN ask for one Operator app-role assignment per environment on the TEST/PROD API app registrations, which would let the gate grade the real target without re-enabling the ARM audience.

**Rationale:** Prod has no listeners pre-go-live, so three weeks of staleness costs nothing, but an ungated prod deploy would. Grading on dev keeps a real generation-through-TTS panel in front of prod using live HERE traffic, real Azure OpenAI and real ElevenLabs; what it loses is the target environment's own data and config, which is a smaller loss than dropping the gate. The alternative that grades the real target needs an Entra write the Arinco guest cannot perform. Panel size is not cosmetic: these are RATE thresholds, so at n=5 a min of 0.85 is unsatisfiable below a perfect 5/5 — the first run FAILED (structural 4/5 = 0.80, target_shape 3/5 = 0.60) and the same code PASSED at n=8 (structural 8/8, target_shape 6/8), which is the script's own default cap.

**Consequences:** Prod promotion is unblocked and gated. Verified by running the gate twice live on dev, 8 markets, 8 of 8 bulletins triggered and harvested: gazetteer 8/8 (no fabricated roads), safety 0.99, continuity 0.88, structural 8/8, atn_style 4/8, target_shape 6/8 = GATE PASS. Two findings recorded rather than papered over: (1) target_shape passed at EXACTLY its 0.75 floor, zero margin, so one more short bulletin fails the gate; (2) scripts have drifted shorter since the calibration baseline — median 83 words to 77, 2.77 wps to 2.57 — while the grader assumes 3.1 wps against a pipeline calibrated at 2.85, so its band already sits above natural output. The two thin bulletins read WELL on inspection (Brisbane covered five roads plus weather and fuel in 70 words), so the defect is under-filling the slot and padding to length, not incoherence. Both are noted in gates.promotion.yaml with an explicit instruction not to lower the floor. The drift-watch stage still targets dev and is unaffected.

## 2026-07-29 — The real-bulletin quality panel stops blocking prod and moves to the scheduled path

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Build 2694 was the FIRST time the promotion gate ever executed end to end. Every earlier run either skipped it or 401'd before grading (2686 failed on auth, 2668 skipped, 2657/2646/2638/2630 predate the stage). It was wired in as a Deploy_Prod dependency without a single green run to calibrate against. When it finally ran it failed two ways: a HARD gazetteer failure that turned out to be a grader bug, and arn_atn_style 0.12 against a 0.20 floor.

**Decision:** Deploy_Prod now depends on Deploy_Test. The panel moves to a new scheduled stage, EvalQualityPanel, running the same 8-market dev panel on the existing eval cron alongside EvalDrift. Two real defects found while investigating are fixed and kept: (1) arn_gazetteer_factuality graded a genuine HERE-supplied road as fabricated because HERE names carry a direction qualifier - 'M80 METROPOLITAN RING ROAD(NORTHBOUND)' - and the suffix rule could not see past the parenthetical; _norm now drops a trailing parenthetical group. (2) promotion_gate.py ran run_suite with --repeats 1 while the golden gate uses --repeats 3 on the same LLM judges; it now uses 3.

**Rationale:** Four evidenced reasons, none of them 'the gate is inconvenient'. First, it had never passed, so blocking prod on it was aspirational rather than validated. Second, it cannot be catching a generation regression against prod: git log --since 2026-07-16 -- prompts/ is empty, so prod already runs these exact prompts. Third, its one hard check - zero fabricated road names - already blocks every push deterministically and for free through final-bulletin-det/gates.yaml in the golden gate, so the panel duplicated the valuable part and added three LLM judges on top. Fourth, those judges grade 8 bulletins generated at whatever minute CI runs against thresholds calibrated on a 46-row FULL-DAY corpus; two panels 90 minutes apart on 2026-07-29 scored atn_style 0.50 and 0.12 on identical code. A deploy gate must be deterministic. This is a monitoring instrument and the repo already had the right home for it. Keeping it on the schedule preserves the signal it uniquely provides - it GENERATES fresh bulletins through the live poller/LLM/TTS path, where EvalDrift only harvests bulletins that already happened - and finally builds the pass/fail history the gate never had.

**Consequences:** Prod can promote on the deterministic gates that actually pass: Build, Package, backend unit + E2E, frontend Playwright, golden Foundry evals (including the hard zero-fabricated-roads floor), bicep lint, gitleaks, and a successful Deploy_Test. The gazetteer fix is verified against two real corpora: the failing CI panel now grades 8/8, and the 46-row 2026-07-16 baseline still scores 0.978 - identical to its documented calibration - and still catches its one genuinely ungrounded road ('Military Road'), so the check was corrected, not weakened. --repeats 3 measured: at the documented 0.39 style rate and n=8, a single pass fails spuriously 11.7% of the time versus 3.8% for the median of three, and medians round toward failure. Two standing quality gaps are now recorded in gates.promotion.yaml rather than silenced: bulletins drop the ATN opener/advice framing and read as bare road lists (atn_style), and scripts drift short (median 83 words to 77, 2.77 to 2.57 wps) against a grader assuming 3.1 wps while the pipeline calibrates at 2.85. Promote the panel back in front of Deploy_Prod once its scheduled history shows it passing consistently.

## 2026-07-29 — Operators are recorded at sign-in by the SWA roles bridge, not by /operators/me

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** TEST showed an empty Operators page after the token-first work was deployed. Two independent causes, both proven live: Graph is 403 (no ARN consent), and self-registration on GET /operators/me can never fire behind Static Web Apps, because SWA forwards only userRoles to a linked backend on normal /api/* calls. With no oid claim the caller has no directory object id, and registering a SWA userId would create a row no Entra state can explain. So nobody would ever appear on TEST or PROD, no matter how often they signed in; dev only had a row because an Easy Auth path supplied an oid.

**Decision:** Register the person on the one call that does receive the AAD claims: the SWA rolesSource function (POST /api/GetRoles), which SWA invokes at sign-in and which already walks claims[] to map app roles. New Functions/Auth/OperatorRegistrar plus an OperatorIdentity record hold the logic, shared with /operators/me (Easy Auth direct, where the header carries oid). OperatorAssignment gains UserPrincipalName, RolesAtSignIn and LastSignInUtc; ClientPrincipal now parses a UPN from preferred_username/upn/email or userDetails. The repository treats a null on any of the three as unchanged, so an admin editing markets or a config import cannot erase sign-in identity, and an empty incoming role list never erases stored roles. Only the sign-in path sets LastSignInUtc, so the per-page-load /operators/me call does not write. When a sign-in arrives with no oid the app logs a warning naming the claim TYPES present (never values), so the gap is self-diagnosing.

**Rationale:** The rolesSource payload is the only place the AAD claims reach the backend behind SWA, so it is the only place registration can work there. Storing what the token presented also removes the reason to chase ARN for Graph consent: the console can show a person's email and role from their own sign-in, leaving consent to buy only pre-population of people who have never signed in. Registration is fire-and-forget because failing it would fail sign-in itself.

**Consequences:** Live-proven on TEST 2026-07-29 by posting both payload shapes to the deployed /api/GetRoles: with an oid, 'Registered or refreshed operator a50de7bf-... as the Arinco deploy operator with role(s) [Admin]'; without one, roles still mapped and 'no oid claim ... Claim types present: [name, roles]'. Rows appear on first sign-in, so an already-signed-in session must sign out and back in once. The console shows sign-in roles for Assignment-source rows with explicit provenance instead of 'Role unknown'. Graph consent is demoted to optional pre-population. **Confirmed with a REAL sign-in the same day, not just synthetic payloads:** the caller's own row was deleted (14:51:46), the SWA session cookie was cleared, and a fresh silent-SSO login recreated it (14:55:03) as 'Registered or refreshed operator a50de7bf-... as the Arinco deploy operator with role(s) [Admin]' alongside 'Mapped 1 AAD app role(s)'. So the real rolesSource payload does carry oid, name, preferred_username and roles; `/.auth/me` independently shows the objectidentifier claim URI, which the parser accepts alongside the short 'oid' form.

**Follow-on (same day):** the standing "Entra directory not connected" banner was deleted from OperatorsPage, along with the raw Graph 403 body it disclosed. `DirectoryStatus: Unavailable` is the STEADY state until an ARN tenant admin consents, so the alert would have rendered on every visit for the life of the product and taught operators to ignore warnings — and a provider error body does not belong in front of them. The page header already states the model ("people appear here after signing in"), each row states its own provenance, and the 403 stays in App Insights for whoever is debugging it. The empty state now reads "No one has signed in yet" instead of "No previously assigned operators are available". Verified on deployed TEST: the Operators table shows the Arinco deploy operator with his UPN, an Admin badge, "From Assignment" and "Entra could not be read. The role shown is the one their token carried at their last sign-in", with no banner anywhere on the page.

**Defect found by the same dry run (fixed same day):** scoping a person to a station renamed them. `UpsertOperatorAssignment` builds the row with `DisplayName ?? string.Empty` and the station dialog sends `markets` only, so the update wrote a blank name through and the console fell back to showing the raw UPN — an operator display name became `operator@arn.com.au` the moment an admin scoped the operator. The repository now treats a blank display name as "not supplied", the same convention already used for the three sign-in fields, so a markets-only edit preserves name, UPN, sign-in roles and last sign-in. Pre-existing bug, not introduced by the sign-in work, but only visible once rows existed for people other than the caller. Proven on deployed TEST: markets `cairns-4ca` → `cairns-4ca,sydney` while the operator display name and `Operator` survived.

## 2026-07-30 — ARN-configurable editorial layer: kernel vs editorial split of the writer prompt

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Script quality was bottlenecked on Arinco's deploy cycle. prompts/system.md (660 lines, 24 sections) mixed correctness invariants with pure editorial taste, so an ARN request as small as 'stop saying busy' needed a code change. the ARN Head of Content raised exactly that: 'busy' is an approved word in the road-feel list (system.md:329) and 'looking good'/'moving nicely' are the mandated clear-road phrases (system.md:491). RISK-33 (MaxCorridors=5 dropping real congested roads) was likewise a product decision blocked on a const. system.md:121 went further and told the model to IGNORE ARN guidance asking for a sign-off or advice framing, while gates.promotion.yaml records 'bulletins drop the ATN opener/advice framing' as a standing gap - our prompt overriding ARN's own house style.

**Decision:** Split the writer prompt on the correctness-vs-taste line. prompts/system/_manifest.txt declares 22 ordered slots: 8 Arinco-owned kernel slots (role preamble, product goal, priority order, data-only, output contract, input handling, missing fields, final self-check) and 14 ARN-editable editorial blocks (wrappers-and-advice, voiceability, select-and-order, length, atn-style-target, road-feel-language, anchors-and-locations, closures-and-blockages, shared-condition-grouping, clear-roads, weather-and-fuel, time-of-day, numbers, repetition-and-freshness). EditorialBlock is a versioned append-only aggregate scoped Global/Market/Station, resolved MOST-SPECIFIC-WINS with a single winner per key - deliberately unlike GuidanceComposer, which composes additively, because a prompt section cannot be half-replaced. Managed via /api/editorial (reads Operator, writes Admin) with a preview endpoint returning the exact assembled prompt. Priority order stays kernel because it is the meta-rule ranking factual safety above house style.

**Rationale:** Seeds are byte-identical slices of the original file and a golden-fixture test asserts that assembling with zero overrides reproduces prompts/system.md byte-for-byte, so the migration is provably behaviour-neutral rather than argued to be. Composition fails safe in one direction only: a failed lookup, an empty composition, or text that sanitises away all fall back to the shipped seeds, because a read in the network default style is recoverable and a writer missing its data-only rule is not. Overrides must also ride in the draft user prompt as a delta: Draft runs as Foundry agent arn-draft, which holds instructions server-side and rejects a request-side instructions field, so a system-only override composed and previewed correctly yet produced a byte-identical bulletin on dev. Overrides use StripDelimiters rather than Sanitize because an editorial block is a multi-line markdown section and Sanitize collapses newlines, which delivered ARN's text shaped unlike the seed it replaced.

**Consequences:** ARN can change how bulletins are written per market or station without a redeploy, and every change is versioned with rollback. That also moves script-quality ownership: the golden eval baseline validates Arinco's seeds, not ARN's overrides, so a pre-publish eval showing the quality delta before a block goes live is required follow-on work and is the reason to gate publishing rather than trust it. The Foundry agents still carry the seed prompt server-side, so re-provisioning them with the kernel alone is the natural next step. Editorial numeric constants (drive-time threshold, tier caps, MaxCorridors, continuity caps, monitored routes) remain hardcoded and are the remaining bottleneck.

## 2026-07-30 — Eval datasets exclude ARN filler statements from the judged script

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The 2026-07-29 promotion panel scored `arn_atn_style` 0.12 against a 0.20 floor, and the two SPARSEST markets scored worst of all eight (mildura 0.32, darwin 0.40). Investigating the judge rubric explained why: its contract says "NEVER penalise the absence of a sign-off, station tag, greeting, or safety close. Penalise their PRESENCE (wrapper text does not belong in the copy)." Wrapper text is exactly what ARN's filler statements are — six of mildura's eight library entries are safety platitudes ("Please stay alert out there and stick to the speed limit.", "Drive safe, Mildura."). `ScriptGenerationEngine` appends filler verbatim AFTER generation, review/refine, word-target compliance, safety and delivery direction, and its own comment states filler "never passes through any LLM call, so it is never critiqued, reworded, or cut. It is ARN's own editorial content." `harvest_dataset.py` nevertheless fed the full post-filler `ScriptText` to every grader as `response`, so the generator was being scored on words it neither wrote nor can change — and penalised hardest in exactly the markets where the pipeline had to lean on filler most.

**Decision:** `harvest_dataset.py` removes ARN filler statements from the judged text. A single query against the `fillerStatements` table (PartitionKey `FillerStatements`, RowKey = market) yields each market's library; matching text is removed from both `response` and `prior_bulletin`, longest-first so a short statement cannot partially match a longer one. Removal is exact rather than heuristic because insertion is verbatim by contract. `target_sec` deliberately keeps the FULL slot: filler covers a gap the generator was asked to fill (`fillerGapSeconds = TargetDurationSeconds - trafficOnlyDuration`), so an intact target keeps `arn_target_shape` honest about under-fill instead of letting filler words mask it. No new dataset columns — the 13-column schema is preserved, so no eval object rebuild and no lost run history.

**Rationale:** Judging generation quality on ARN's own approved copy measures the wrong thing, and it was not a small distortion: it inverted the result. It made the sparsest markets look like the worst writers when they were simply the ones carrying the most station boilerplate. Excluding filler also removes a latent false positive from the HARD gazetteer gate, since filler names roads ('The Sturt Highway and Calder Highway are Mildura's two main links') that need not appear in that bulletin's HERE evidence.

**Consequences:** Measured on the same 8 scripts with --repeats 3, changing only the judged text: arn_atn_style 0.12 -> 0.38, a 3.2x lift that clears the 0.20 floor with no change to a single generated word. arn_target_shape fell 1.00 -> 0.75 exactly as predicted, because filler had been masking real generator under-fill; that is now visible rather than hidden. gazetteer, safety and structural stayed at 1.00. Only the two sparse markets carried filler at all (darwin -29 words, mildura -23); the six dense markets were untouched, confirming filler is a sparse-market slot-filler. arn_continuity_semantic is now the gate blocker at 0.50, but it was ALREADY failing at 0.75 before this change and is the noisiest criterion in the suite - it swings 0.50 to 0.88 across runs on identical scripts, and brisbane dropped 0.20 with its text completely unchanged. Continuity stability is the next thing to look at, separately. Both the promotion gate and the scheduled drift watch call harvest_dataset.harvest, so both inherit this automatically.

## 2026-07-30 — Cairns pilot station switched from 4CA to Star 102.7 FM

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The project manager asked on 24 Jul (email 'Cairns Pilot Station - Switch to Star' to the pilot station stakeholders) whether the Cairns pilot could run on STAR 102.7 FM instead of 4CA. The reason given: Star has more announcers on shift, so pilot faults get noticed and resolved faster. The request sat unread for six days while the 13 Jul record (KIIS 90s SYD and 4CA) remained the standing decision, and a station name was quoted to ARN playout ahead of confirmation. Confirmed verbally with the project manager on 30 Jul.

**Decision:** The pilot stations are KIIS 90s SYD (Sydney, NSW) and Star 102.7 FM (Cairns, QLD). This supersedes the 13 Jul record, which named 4CA for Cairns. The market id stays cairns-4ca: job partitions (Job_{market}), the Zetta market-code app setting, coverage, priority roads, pronunciation dictionaries, guidance, filler lines and operator market scoping all key off it, and renaming would mean re-seeding every one of them three weeks from SG3 for no operator-visible gain. Operators see the station name, not the id. Station renamed to 'Star 102.7 FM' and the schedule to 'Cairns Star 102.7 Traffic' on dev and test.

**Rationale:** The switch is a configuration change, and the reason is sound: more announcers in the loop during a pilot means faults are caught by people rather than by us reading logs. Keeping the market id is the smaller of two evils, but it is drift of exactly the kind the 29 Jul config-drift audit was about, so it is recorded here rather than left implicit.

**Consequences:** Cairns coverage geometry, priority roads and the pronunciation dictionary are city-level and carry over unchanged. Two things need ARN input: whether the ARNTN workbook holds a Star 102.7 clock row (Cairns has been running an invented dev clock since 13 Jul, because the workbook had no 4CA row), and whether the assigned voice profile still suits Star's format rather than 4CA's. PROD still carries '4CA 846 AM' because it is parked and its API is unreachable while stopped; correct it on the next prod resume. Every current-state doc is updated; historical status reports, week-in-review decks and the archive keep their original wording as records.

## 2026-07-30 — Prompts have one source of truth: git, with Foundry as a deployment target

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Reasoning about writer behaviour from the repo gave the wrong answer, and it cost an afternoon. prompts/system.md is 18.6KB, is loaded at startup by PromptLibrary, and reads like the authoritative writer prompt — but every environment with DraftAgentName set (dev, test, prod) routes Draft through the arn-draft Foundry agent, whose instructions were hand-tuned in the Azure portal and existed NOWHERE else. An audit of all seven role agents found arn-draft (11,628 chars, 'v37, renamed from arn-draft-natural-v53') and arn-polish (6,497 chars, 'trial v5') portal-only: no diff, no review, no history, and no copy if the project were recreated. provision-foundry-agents.sh said so in its own header — 'NOT MANAGED HERE: the Draft and Polish agents are hand-tuned portal agents'. arn-review was already git-managed and verified byte-identical to prompts/review-system.md; the other four carry a deliberate 167-char neutral shim because a writer-style instruction breaks a JSON-returning role.

**Decision:** Git is the source of truth; Foundry is a deployment target. The two portal-only prompts were exported verbatim to prompts/agents/arn-draft.md and prompts/agents/arn-polish.md, and provision-foundry-agents.sh now manages all seven role agents from git rather than five. A new deployment/scripts/check-foundry-agent-drift.sh fetches every live agent and fails on any difference from git, including the neutral shim, so an unmapped agent cannot be silently unchecked. prompts/README.md is the authoritative map of which prompt each code path actually sends, and the WARNING now sits on PromptLibrary.SystemInstructions itself, at the exact line that created the false impression.

**Rationale:** Exporting fixes the past; the drift check fixes the future, because a portal edit is one click and leaves no trace in the repo. Comparison normalises only trailing newlines — jq always emits one and a text file may not end with one, so raw-byte comparison reported all seven as drifted on the first run. Verified against dev: all 7 agents match git. Deliberately behaviour-neutral: nothing was pushed, no prompt text changed, and the provisioner was not re-run, because 'whatever is in use now' had to stay in use. system.md is kept rather than deleted — the raw-model path still needs it and prompts/system/ must assemble back to it byte-for-byte.

**Consequences:** Any future prompt question can be answered from the repo, and the drift check gives a one-command answer to 'is what I am reading what is running'. It needs Azure auth and a live endpoint, so it belongs on the deploy path rather than in verify.sh, which runs offline. Two writer prompts still coexist by design (agent path vs raw-model path) and they are NOT the same text — unifying them so prompts/system/ builds the agent instructions would make ARN's editorial blocks bind natively instead of via a user-message delta, but it changes writer behaviour and must be eval-gated. Separately, _shared-rules.md and review-system.md still carry Arinco's editorial vocabulary and the reviewer enforces it, which is why an ARN block can be vetoed into a fallback.

## 2026-07-30 — Zetta file names are ARN's exact strings, and a hyphenated market needs a JSON code map

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN playout issued the playout naming convention on 30 Jul: [SYD]KIIS90s_TRAFF and [CAI]STAR1027_TRAFF, one file per station, same name every time, written to the share root. He also confirmed Zetta re-ingests on overwrite, stamps its own date/time plus an expiry so a replayed file cannot air, and DELETES the file once ingested, which makes the file disappearing a usable delivery confirmation. He declined a separate test folder because his autoloader wildcard-matches per market. Two things in our implementation collided with that: the delivery service uppercased the market code, which would have written [SYD]KIIS90S_TRAFF.wav, one letter off the spec; and Azure rejects app-setting names containing a hyphen on Linux apps, so Zetta__MarketCodes__cairns-4ca cannot exist at all.

**Decision:** The code is written exactly as ARN supplied it: ZettaFileDeliveryService no longer uppercases it. Added ZettaOptions.MarketCodesJson, a single JSON object of market id to code that is merged over the per-key MarketCodes and wins on conflict, so any market id can carry a code regardless of app-setting name rules. Malformed JSON is ignored rather than throwing, leaving the per-key codes intact, because a broken setting must not take working markets off air. TEST now runs FileNamePattern={MarketId}_TRAFF, Zetta__MarketCodes__sydney=[SYD]KIIS90s and Zetta__MarketCodesJson={"cairns-4ca":"[CAI]STAR1027"}.

**Rationale:** The market code is ARN's identifier, not ours to normalise: uppercasing it was silent mangling of the same class as the market-code fallback removed on 29 Jul. The JSON map was chosen over renaming the market id, which would have meant re-seeding coverage, priority roads, dictionaries, guidance, filler lines, schedules and operator scoping across three environments, and over normalising keys on lookup, which would have made the setting name stop matching the market id.

**Consequences:** Proven on TEST 2026-07-30 with three bulletins driven trigger to publish: Cairns delivered as [CAI]STAR1027_TRAFF.wav (trace: 'Wrote 2646044 bytes to Azure Files drop ibpauetststaftp01/informationbulletins/[CAI]STAR1027_TRAFF.wav'), and two Sydney bulletins each logged 'Audio delivered to playout system' at job level, though adaptive sampling dropped their filename traces. The exact-case substitution is covered by unit tests for both a legacy uppercase code and [SYD]KIIS90s. ARN playout's delete-on-ingest means we can upgrade Delivered from 'file written' to 'playout has it' by watching for the file to disappear; not built yet. DEV and PROD still carry the old TRAIN_TRAFF pattern and codes, and PROD additionally cannot express a cairns code without MarketCodesJson, so both need the new settings before they deliver.

## 2026-07-30 — The reviewer and reviser read ARN's editorial blocks, so an ARN edit cannot cause dead air

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Handing ARN the writer's 14 editorial sections left the reviewer enforcing Arinco's vocabulary from `prompts/system/user/shared-rules.md` and `prompts/review-system.md`, both of which hard-code CLOSED synonym lists (clear-road wording, the ATN road-feel palette). An ARN clear-roads block saying 'running to schedule' produced a phrase absent from that list; the reviewer read it as an unsupported clear claim, the refine budget drained, and the bulletin fell back to a filler cart. Measured at 1 in 8 bulletins on dev (2026-07-30). Editorial control that can silently cause dead air is not shippable.

**Decision:** The eight vocabulary-bearing blocks (road-feel-language, clear-roads, closures-and-blockages, shared-condition-grouping, anchors-and-locations, repetition-and-freshness, numbers, wrappers-and-advice) now ride into the Review and Refine user messages as a STATION WORDING POLICY notice, via EditorialBlockKeys.CrossAgent and ContentFormatters.FormatCrossAgentEditorial. The other six (length, select-and-order, atn-style-target, voiceability, weather-and-fuel, time-of-day) are deliberately withheld: the reviewer is told never to judge those, so sending ARN's rules for them would invite the style policing it must not do. Only overridden blocks travel; seeds are already baked into the agent.

**Rationale:** The notice may only WIDEN accepted wording, never narrow it, and it says so in its own text. That single property is what keeps grounding intact under self-service editing: ARN can teach the reviewer a new phrase for a condition the data supports, but cannot teach it to accept a condition the data does not supply, nor to start policing style it is told to ignore. `review-system.md` now sanctions the notice as trusted configuration rather than content to judge, so it does not trip the reviewer's own prompt-injection defence. Shared rules and the road-feel vocabulary are now operator-editable surfaces resolved through the editorial block cascade, seeded from `prompts/system/user/` and deliberately kept outside the manifest slots.

**Consequences:** Fallback from an ARN wording override goes to zero: 27 bulletins on dev with the exact vetoing override live, 0 fallbacks, versus 1 in 8 before. Grounding demonstrably still bites - 5 of those 27 had the reviewer flag a real defect and the reviser fix it, including the writer over-applying ARN's clear phrase to roads the data said were delayed, which was correctly rejected. That is the widen-only property proven live rather than argued. ARN's policy is now the contract for writer, reviewer and reviser instead of the writer alone. Cost: the review and refine user messages grow by the overridden blocks only, and arn-review must be re-provisioned (done, drift check green).

## 2026-07-30 — The proven drop share IS production playout; test gets its own share and prod its own network path

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN playout answered the two remaining delivery questions on 30 Jul: "The folder we are using now will be the production folder. The two sites are both active sites and the reports are being dropped into the libraries for these stations. They will not play to air however until we give the content teams there the go ahead to start scheduling these." That closed the last ARN-gated integration item and simultaneously created three problems. First, the drop account `ibpauetststaftp01` lives in IBP-AUE-TST-RSG-STA01 with firewall default Deny and private endpoints only in the TEST VNet, while prod is an island VNet with zero peerings — prod had neither a network path nor any role assignment on it, so an approved prod bulletin could not be delivered at all. Second, our TEST environment was writing into the folder that feeds two live station libraries. Third, `main.bicep` hard-coded `Zetta__FileNamePattern={MarketId}_TRAIN_TRAFF` plus six never-confirmed three-letter codes, so the working convention existed only as hand-set app settings and the next deploy to test would have silently reverted ARN playout's file names.

**Decision:** The naming convention moved into IaC as `zettaFileNamePattern` + `zettaMarketCodesJson`, and the six legacy codes were deleted rather than kept — an unmapped market must fail delivery loudly, never guess a name. `Zetta__MarketCodes__*` per-key settings are no longer emitted at all; the JSON map is the only source of codes, since Azure forbids hyphens in app-setting names on Linux. A new `zettaDropAccountResourceGroup` lets an environment point across resource groups at the one ARN-built account, and `private-endpoints.bicep` gained a file-subresource endpoint (`{prefix}07`) plus a `privatelink.file.core.windows.net` zone in `network.bicep`, so prod reaches the share from its own VNet. TEST is pointed at a sibling share, `informationbulletins-test`, which the autoloader does not watch. The account carries a `CanNotDelete` lock named `ibp-playout-drop-protect`.

**Rationale:** Test and prod sharing one playout folder is only safe while nothing is scheduled to air; the moment ARN's content teams start scheduling, a UAT operator publishing a deliberately broken scenario would be putting audio into a live station's library. Relying on remembering to flip a setting at that point is the kind of guard that fails under time pressure, so the separation was made permanent now, while the flip was cheap and verifiable. Keeping the six unverified codes would have meant a market silently shipping a wrong file name the first time someone enabled it — the same silent-mangling class as the uppercase bug fixed earlier the same day. Adopting the hand-built account into Bicep was rejected: it carries ARN's AD DS join and share ACLs, and a template that re-declared those properties could reset Zetta's own access; a delete lock plus documentation gives the protection without the risk.

**Consequences:** Production delivery is proven, not just wired. Two poller-fired prod bulletins with full station config (real voice profile, pronunciation dictionary, weather, fuel, 30s) were approved, published and delivered on 30 Jul: `zetta.delivery.success` = 1 for both `sydney` and `cairns-4ca`, with the write logged as `ibpauetststaftp01/informationbulletins/[SYD]KIIS90s_TRAFF.wav`. Test delivery to the isolated share is proven by control plane, independent of telemetry sampling: `informationbulletins-test` reports `shareUsageBytes` 2,646,044, exactly one 30-second WAV. Nothing reaches either share without a human: `DeliverAsync` has exactly one caller, `PublishJobAsync`, which requires an Approved job and a matching ETag, and that has exactly one caller, the publish HTTP trigger — there is no timer or queue path that can auto-publish. Prod is deployed at HEAD and re-parked. Still open with ARN: nothing blocking, but ARN must tell us before the content teams start scheduling, and the remaining 11 markets' station IDs are post-pilot.

## 2026-07-30 — park.sh silences alerts before it touches anything

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Parking prod on 30 Jul, the B1 plan downgrade returned "No available instances ... App Service is attempting to increase capacity" six times over roughly ten minutes. `park.sh` disabled the alert rules and availability test as its LAST step, after a verification step that exits non-zero, so the run aborted with the Function App already stopped and its availability test still armed. A stopped prod then failed its synthetic health check and fired alerts into the interim Arinco on-call inbox, and the alerts had to be silenced by hand.

**Decision:** `toggle_alerts false` now runs FIRST, before the app is stopped and before the plan is touched. The SKU downgrade retries six times with 90-second backoff and, if it still fails, exits with the app stopped and alerts already quiet plus an explicit "retry the downgrade later" message.

**Rationale:** Every action park.sh takes deliberately makes a live-looking environment unhealthy, so monitoring must be quiet before the first of them, not after the last. Leaving alerts armed through a multi-minute capacity retry loop guarantees false pages on exactly the slow runs where a human is least likely to be watching. Alerts staying off after a failed park is the correct end state for an environment we intended to park; `resume.sh` re-enables them.

**Consequences:** Verified live the same day: prod re-parked in 49 seconds with "alerts + availability test disabled" as the first line of output and zero alert noise. A capacity-blocked park now self-heals instead of aborting halfway.

## 2026-07-30 — Named-individual voice and RISK-33 corridor cap retired as Arinco-chased reporting items

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** CONTEXT.md's Open Questions carried 'whether bulletins use a named individual voice' even though the 9 Jun compliance decision already named ARN Content as the decision-owner, with nothing new since. Separately, docs/canonical/risks.md's RISK-33 asked for an ARN 'product decision' on the MaxCorridors=5 busy-market corridor cap. Both kept surfacing in weekly status-meeting prep as if they were open questions Arinco needed to keep chasing ARN on, despite the 2026-07-30 ARN-configurable editorial layer having already made MaxCorridors an ARN-editable per-market/station setting (/editorial/settings) rather than a hardcoded constant -- the product decision this risk needed no longer requires a meeting, a redeploy, or Arinco at all.

**Decision:** Stop carrying either item as an active Arinco-chased open question or status-meeting agenda item. Named-individual voice remains recorded only in its original 9 Jun decision entry, as ARN's outstanding decision to make on its own timeline, not something Arinco re-raises. RISK-33 stays open as a genuine residual risk (a wrong default could still under-serve a busy market) but its mitigation is reworded from 'needs a product decision' to 'ARN can change this itself via the editorial settings UI, no Arinco action required'.

**Rationale:** Matches the discipline already applied in the 2026-07-23 asks-tracker trim: an item sitting on the active tracker or agenda implies work is pending on someone, and repeatedly re-surfacing a question already answered (voice: it was always ARN's) or already resolved by shipped capability (RISK-33: it is now self-service) burns meeting time and creates a false impression that either side is still waiting on the other.

**Consequences:** CONTEXT.md's Open Questions drops the named-individual-voice line (the underlying decision is untouched in decisions.md, 9 Jun entry). docs/canonical/risks.md's RISK-33 row and CONTEXT.md's Known Risks line are reworded to state the cap is ARN self-service, not an open ask. quality-tail item drops the 'RISK-33 corridor-cap product-decision proposal' framing. If ARN raises either topic itself, it is answered then; neither is proactively re-raised by Arinco in status reporting.

## 2026-07-30 — Second SoW trim: hub VNet moot, custom domain and Teams-channel rename are non-SoW polish

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The 2026-07-23 asks-tracker trim classified five items against the SoW and dropped what wasn't required. Six items on the the ARN Technology Lead section of arn-asks-2026-07-16.md were never put through that same check: action-group receivers, prod hub VNet migration, prod ops Teams channel nomination, custom domain CNAMEs, Graph directory permission for the Function App managed identities, and an app role for the CI pipeline service principal. Checked today against line by line: none of the six appears as a named SoW commitment. Two are already self-labelled in the tracker as non-blocking (Graph MI permission is 'OPTIONAL ENRICHMENT', the CI pipeline SP role is a 'QUALITY UPGRADE, not a blocker'), so those two were already correctly triaged, just not formally closed out. The other four had not been checked at all, and one of them, prod hub VNet migration, is now actively obsolete: the 2026-07-30 AzureFilesDrop private-endpoint decision gave prod its own file-subresource private endpoint in its own island VNet specifically so it would not need hub connectivity for Zetta, which was the VNet migration's whole reason for existing on this tracker.

**Decision:** Formally downgrade all four unchecked items, none silently deleted. (1) Prod hub VNet migration: recommend dropping as an active ask; the Zetta delivery need that motivated it is resolved by prod's own private endpoint, and no other SoW commitment depends on hub connectivity. Re-raise only if ARN has a separate reason to want it. (2) Custom domain CNAMEs: not a SoW commitment (the matrix has no CDN/custom-domain line); it is a self-imposed performance improvement (SWA has no CDN edge without it). Keep on file as a cheap, zero-downtime win if ARN ever supplies the CNAMEs, but stop treating it as an active ask needing chasing. (3) Prod ops Teams channel nomination: the underlying SoW commitment, 'Approval notifications and reminders - Teams', is already delivered and live on the interim channel; this ask is a branding/routing refinement on top of a met commitment, not a gap. Keep low priority. (4) Action-group receivers (on-call email/SMS): not literally named in the SoW text, but the 'Deliverable: Handover session to operational support teams' commitment implies a real ops team can receive alerts; keep pursuing, framed as handover readiness rather than an SoW blocker. Graph MI permission and the CI pipeline SP role keep their existing self-labelled non-blocking status, now cross-checked and confirmed correct.

**Rationale:** The same discipline that trimmed the first five items applies here: an item that isn't gating SG3, a named success criterion, or a real SoW line dilutes the ones that are, and repeatedly carrying it as an active ask implies work is pending on ARN that the contract never actually promised. Distinguishing 'not in the SoW' from 'in the SoW but already met' matters, because the Teams channel item is the latter, not the former - conflating the two would wrongly suggest ARN owes a fix rather than an optional polish.

**Consequences:** the ARN Technology Lead section items 5-7 annotated with their SoW status and rationale, not deleted, matching the audit-trail convention already used for items 3/8/9. CONTEXT.md's Current Goal already reflects hub VNet as likely moot. The active ARN ask surface for genuine SoW gaps is now: UAT window and participants, handover session scheduling, SMS/phone written election, and (as handover readiness rather than a contractual line) real action-group receivers.

## 2026-07-30 — The job audio proxy path carries a per-render token, so the console rebinds after a re-voice

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** An operator corrected the Perth dictionary's `Fremantle` respelling four times on job `3f8e788fa2ad47718e4e5784b385a480` (versions 3-6, minted 05:35, 05:36, 05:37 and 06:45) because each re-voice sounded identical. The pipeline was working correctly throughout: `RefreshPronunciation` re-resolved the dictionary before every re-voice, the job pinned the newly minted version each time, and all five renders are byte-distinct WAVs. The staleness was in the console. `pinMediaSrc` (web/src/features/jobs/lib/media-url.ts) deliberately keeps `<audio src>` stable when only a SAS token rotated, comparing URLs by path — an invariant that held while job audio was a timestamped SAS blob URL. The 2026-07-16 audio-proxy change replaced that with the constant path `jobs/{jobId}/audio`, so every re-voice compared equal, the element never reloaded, and the operator kept hearing the first take until a hard refresh. The duplicate-alias guard added 2026-07-28 (three stacked Toorak rules) was the same symptom treated one layer too high.

**Decision:** `JobsHttpTrigger.ResolveAudioUrlAsync` appends the blob filename as a render token: `jobs/{jobId}/audio/{renderToken}`. The route became `jobs/{jobId}/audio/{render?}`, and the token is a cache key only — the handler always streams the job's current audio and never resolves the token to a blob. No frontend logic changed.

**Rationale:** Restoring the "one render, one path" invariant fixes the bug where it broke rather than teaching the player about SAS parameter names, which would be brittle and would leave the same trap for any future stable-path media route. Ignoring the token server-side keeps the route from becoming an arbitrary-blob reader.

**Consequences:** Operators see a re-voiced take without refreshing. Rebinding resets `currentTime` to 0 on a genuinely new render, which is correct. The bare `jobs/{jobId}/audio` path still resolves, so older clients and `tools/arn/arn.py`'s relative-path handling are unaffected. Pronunciation-dictionary version history now over-counts real fixes: Perth Roads v3-v6 are four attempts at one problem, and v3 (`Free-mantle`) already read acceptably.

## 2026-07-30 — Publish returns to Operator; filler statements join the operator-owned per-market set

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** A re-evaluation of the Operator/Admin matrix against the Workshop 2 operating model found the Operator role could not complete the loop it exists for. `POST /jobs/{id}/publish` required Admin, so an operator-only account approved a bulletin and it stopped at `Approved` until an Admin clicked Publish — with an on-call review window of roughly 5:30am to 7pm and ~15 operators at full rollout, that puts an Admin on call for every slot. The Admin requirement was never an access-model decision: it arrived as a consequence line of the 2026-07-21 job-lifecycle security pass ("must use an Admin principal"), and contradicted four approved documents that all state Operator publishes — the 2026-05-24 RBAC decision, SDD sections 6.3 and 8.2, SC-05's verification steps, and `docs/operations/access-and-accounts.md`. The middleware's own class doc comment also still listed publish under Operator. Separately, `PUT /markets/{market}/filler-statements` fell to the Admin default despite being the same per-market whole-list PUT shape as priority roads and verified pronunciations (its trigger doc comment already claimed "both routes require Operator only"), and the Bulletin rules page showed operators the Style rules and Writer sections tabs whose writes are Admin — an edit-then-403.

**Decision:** (1) `/publish` joins the operator clause in `RouteRoleMatrix` alongside approve/reject/reject-to-fallback/regenerate. (2) `PUT /markets/{market}/filler-statements` becomes Operator. (3) `JobActions` no longer hides the Publish button from non-admins. (4) The Style rules and Writer sections tabs (trigger AND content) are gated on `isAdmin`, as Banned words already was. The role-matrix theory gains rows for publish, the three operator-owned per-market PUTs, and the three Admin-only editorial/compliance writes so a future relaxation of any of them fails the suite.

**Rationale:** Publish is the last step of the same review decision, not a separate privilege, and none of the controls that make it safe are the role: the market guard (`JobLifecycleHttpTrigger.PublishJob`), the ETag revision precondition, and the `Approved`/`FallbackUsed` status check inside `JobService.PublishJobAsync` are all untouched, so the 2026-07-21 hardening survives intact. Human-in-the-loop is unaffected — there is still no auto-publish path, and publish is still a named person's positive action. Filler statements sit with the operator for the same reason verified pronunciations do: the operator is the one who hears the line read badly on air. Hiding the two Admin-only tabs is the honest version of a boundary the backend already enforced; showing a save button that always 403s teaches operators to distrust the console.

**Consequences:** An operator can now take a bulletin from Waiting approval to delivered without an Admin. Admin keeps everything that changes how bulletins are written or where they go: station config, voices, delivery styles, pronunciation dictionaries, style rules, writer sections, banned words, operator assignments, config transfer, the activity audit, job deletion and ad-hoc broadcast. The ARN-facing docs that told operators to ask an administrator to publish are corrected (`operator-guide.md`, `faq.md`, `first-day.md`, `glossary.md`, `platform-overview.md`); the SDD and success criteria needed no change because they always described this. The remaining cockpit gap — saving a pronunciation rule still hit the Admin-only library PUT — was closed the same day by the job-scoped route in the next entry. Neither blocker was observable in dev, because `Auth__DevFallbackRole=Admin` adds Admin to every parsed principal there; TEST and prod carry no fallback, so UAT is where they would have surfaced.

## 2026-07-30 — A pronunciation fix is addressed by JOB, so it can be an operator's to make

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The last Admin gate inside the operator loop: saving a rule from the review cockpit called `PUT /pronunciation-dictionaries/{id}`, which is Admin. The frontend already granted the capability to operators (`use-pronunciation-verdicts.ts` sets `canManage = isAdmin || isOperator`), so an operator listening to a word read wrong could open the chip, type the respelling, press Save and get a 403. Opening the library PUT to Operator was the wrong fix: a dictionary is shared across stations and carries no market of its own, so that route has nothing to scope a market guard against — an operator in Cairns could have rewritten Sydney's dictionary. The browser also owned the read-modify-write, because the resource is a whole-list PUT: a one-word fix sent the entire rule set with an ETag, caught a 409 when someone else had edited, re-fetched and replayed — a round trip the operator waited through, and logic that had already produced one dev bug (appending a second rule for the same word, which the provider ignores, so the fix was silently dead).

**Decision:** New route `POST /api/jobs/{jobId}/pronunciation-rules` (Operator in `RouteRoleMatrix`), body `{ Word, Replacement }`. It resolves the dictionary the bulletin AIRED with — matching the library item that owns the provider dictionary id the job recorded, not whatever the station is assigned today — applies the edit, and mints a version. Market scoping comes free: the trigger runs `EnsureJobAccessAsync`, the same guard as approve/publish. The rule-set edit is a pure domain helper (`PronunciationRuleSetEditor.WithAlias`): alias only, and it REPLACES the word's rule rather than appending a second. The read-modify-write moves to `JobPronunciationService`, which replays once against a fresh read on a revision conflict. `PUT /pronunciation-dictionaries/{id}` stays Admin for library-wide editing. Activity audit files the change under the DICTIONARY (an explicit `ActivityPathResolver` row ahead of the generic `/jobs` rule; the response's top-level `Id` is the dictionary's, so the middleware's body fallback resolves it).

**Rationale:** Addressing the write by job is what makes the market guard possible, and the market guard is what makes the grant safe — the route shape follows the authorisation requirement rather than the resource. Keeping the replay server-side costs one internal retry instead of a browser round trip, and puts the "one rule per word" invariant in the domain, where the next caller inherits it rather than reimplementing it. Alias-only is not a preference: a phoneme rule is ignored by `eleven_v3` and DROPS every matched word on `eleven_multilingual_v2`, so one well-meant fix could take a whole dictionary off the read.

**Consequences:** The operator loop is now complete for an Operator-only account: review, approve, fix a pronunciation, re-voice, publish. The frontend lost its ETag/409 replay path and the test that covered it; three tests replace it (job-addressed payload with no rule list or ETag, no pending chip queued when the save failed, no server call when the dictionary already says exactly this). 15 new backend tests: the service (replace-not-append, case-insensitive match, already-correct writes nothing, no dictionary on the job, dictionary gone from the library, concurrent edit replayed WITHOUT losing the other operator's rule, sustained conflict stops after one replay), the domain helper (never emits phoneme, preserves the existing rule's flags and spelling, leaves a v2 phoneme rule for the same word alone), and the trigger (403 outside the job's market, and that a forbidden call reaches no service). Writing the sustained-conflict test found a real defect: the service dropped the typed failure metadata, so a 409 would have surfaced as a 500 — it now propagates. **Proven in the running app** (mock mode, one SPA session): the Adelaide Roads dictionary went v2/15 aliases → v3/16 with `Mooringe → Moor-inj` as the new rule, and the mark read "Queued: will say 'Moor-inj' — re-voice to apply".

## 2026-07-31 — The direct-SMB Zetta transport is deleted; the drop share made the playout side the SMB client

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The PoC shipped a delivery writer that opened SMB2 to Zetta's on-premises ingest share (!ZETTA_IMPORTS\Traffic) with a vaulted username/password, via the third-party SMBLibrary package. It was never enabled in any environment (Zetta__Enabled=false everywhere) because it needed a VPN/ExpressRoute path into ARN's playout VLAN plus service-account credentials. Two later transports superseded it on the same ARN-built drop account: BlobDrop (2026-07-17, proven by SFTP pull-back) and AzureFilesDrop (2026-07-24, proven end to end, and in PROD 2026-07-30). Both invert the direction: we write over Files/Blob REST on 443 with managed identity, and the playout side is the SMB client. The dead transport was still costing us: two unresolvable Key Vault references (Zetta--Username/Password, flagged by the deploy script's own validation on 2026-07-29 and deferred), six app settings emitted into every environment, a third-party SMB dependency, 'Smb' as the bicep and options DEFAULT, and client-facing architecture diagrams asserting that we write SMB into ARN's network.

**Decision:** DeliveryTransport.Smb, SmbFileWriter, its test class, the SMBLibrary package reference, and ZettaOptions.ServerAddress/ShareName/SubFolder/Domain/Username/Password are deleted. ZettaOptions.Transport now defaults to AzureFilesDrop and the bicep @allowed set is ['BlobDrop','AzureFilesDrop'] with the same default, so an environment that sets nothing gets the live transport rather than a dead one. function-app.bicep no longer emits Zetta__ServerAddress/ShareName/SubFolder/Domain/Username/Password at all. The LikeC4 model's 'direct SMB write (unused)' relationship is gone; the platform-architecture, bulletin-lifecycle and network-topology views now route delivery through arn.playoutDrop, and the delivers relationship kind's technology is 'Files REST' (its colour key renamed smblink -> dropfile, edge class smb -> drop). BlobDrop stays: it is proven, it shares the drop account and RBAC with AzureFilesDrop, and flipping to it is one app setting.

**Rationale:** A transport that was never enabled in three environments and is superseded by two proven ones is not a fallback, it is a liability: it kept a credential-shaped hole in the config (two dangling KV references), an SMB library in the dependency graph, and the wrong story in diagrams ARN reads. Keeping 'Smb' as the DEFAULT was the sharpest edge — a new environment that forgot to set zettaTransport would have selected the dead writer. Deleting it is also the honest version of the architecture: the SMB in this system belongs to Zetta's own Kerberos mount, not to us, and every artefact should say so. BlobDrop is kept rather than collapsing to one transport because it is genuinely proven, costs nothing to retain (same account, same role grants, no extra dependency), and is the tested escape hatch if Azure Files OAuth ever regresses.

**Consequences:** Backend build 0 errors / 0 warnings; 3,768 non-integration backend tests green (Domain 1355, Application 589, Functions 533, Infrastructure 1277 + 22 skipped, Architecture 14). ZettaFileDeliveryServiceTests' fixture now configures the drop account instead of SMB credentials. E2E is unaffected: it runs Zetta__Enabled=false and swaps in FakeDeliveryFileWriter. No environment changes behaviour — dev never delivered (Zetta__Enabled=false) and test/prod already pinned zettaTransport='AzureFilesDrop'; the six removed app settings disappear from all three on next deploy. The Zetta--Username/Password secrets, if they still exist in any vault, are now unreferenced and safe to delete (not deleted here). docs/reference/config-drift-audit-2026-07-29.md's deferred KV finding is closed by deletion; production-readiness.md's 'Zetta SMB retry' and 'post-write verification' rows are replaced by the delivery integrity + failure-handling rows that describe what actually runs; RISK-08 moves to Closed with the prod evidence. Diagram consequence: render.py's manual specs validate every edge against the model, so network-topology.yaml and platform-architecture.yaml had to be re-laid-out around the drop share.

## 2026-07-31 — ARN console domains landed on the AI.N naming; the custom domain alone does not fix latency

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The 2026-07-17 Option A decision was blocked on ARN DNS and had sat DEFERRED since, recorded as NXDOMAIN on live re-verification 29 Jul. the ARN Technology Lead created the CNAMEs under arn.com.au on 31 Jul, using the AI.N branding the project manager confirmed 21 Jul rather than the placeholder bulletins* names the 17 Jul decision had proposed: ain-dev, ain-test and ain point at the dev, test and prod SWA default hostnames respectively. All three were bound and validated the same morning (customDomains status Ready, SWA-managed GeoTrust TLS certs issued 31 Jul, auto-renewing, so ARN supplies no certificate). HTTPS answers 200 on dev and a 302 auth-redirect on test and prod, which is correct for Easy Auth. Measurement immediately after binding showed the latency problem was untouched: ain-dev.arn.com.au and the default hostname resolve to the SAME address (9.163.40.246) via azurestaticapps7.trafficmanager.net -> msha-slice-7-am2-0 -> the am2 stamp, geolocated Amsterdam NL (AS8075), with a 115KB JS asset still taking 1.0-1.4s TTFB and about 2s total from Melbourne. That is the identical stamp and the identical figures as the original 2026-07-01 finding.

**Decision:** Adopt the AI.N names as the platform's real addresses (ain.arn.com.au prod, ain-test, ain-dev), superseding the bulletins* names proposed on 17 Jul, and carry each in swaCustomDomain in the matching bicepparam so the binding is reproducible from IaC and not portal state. Separate the two halves of Option A explicitly in the records: the custom domain is DONE and is an ARN-visible naming and trust win, while enterprise-grade edge is the half that actually fixes latency and remains an Arinco action needing no ARN involvement. Enable the edge on dev first (swaEnterpriseEdge = true) to measure the real gain against the recorded Amsterdam baseline before spending on test and prod.

**Rationale:** The 17 Jul decision reasoned that functional names outlive a codename, but AI.N is confirmed product branding rather than a codename, so it is the durable choice and it matches the Teams channel naming already going to the project manager. Keeping the domain in IaC matters because the binding was performed by a direct ARM call, and an undeployed param would let the next deploy drift. Splitting the two halves in the records prevents the failure this measurement nearly hid: DNS arriving looks like the fix landing, when the custom domain is only the prerequisite and every page load still crossed to Amsterdam. Enabling on dev first buys a measured number for the same monthly cost as guessing, and the status report can then quote a measured improvement instead of a vendor claim.

**Consequences:** ARN ask 7 in arn-asks-2026-07-16.md is CLOSED with nothing outstanding on ARN; week10-focus A2 row 6 likewise. CONTEXT.md no longer lists console custom-domain DNS as remaining from ARN. RISK-free on rollback: the default hostnames keep working, so the names are additive. Dev edge enablement was initiated 31 Jul 01:5x UTC and reported enterpriseGradeCdnStatus Enabling; the ARM API returns HTTP 409 Conflict for any other write on the Static Web App while enablement is in progress, which is expected and not a fault. Budget a long provisioning window: dev was still Enabling 20 minutes after initiation, with ain-dev still resolving to the am2 stamp and per-asset timing unchanged (1.2-1.45s TTFB), so neither a stuck status nor an unimproved measurement during that window indicates failure, and the gain must be re-measured only once status reads Enabled. main.dev.bicepparam now sets swaEnterpriseEdge = true; test and prod remain false pending the dev measurement, at about USD 17.52 per app per month each. Stakeholder-visible links (Teams deep-links, decks, the walkthrough) should move to the ain names once the dev measurement confirms the edge behaves.

## 2026-07-31 — Dead-code sweep after the SMB removal: six items deleted, three prior 'fixed' claims disproven, eight decisions registered

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The SMB transport had been dead but shipped for two months. Rather than assume it was unique, four read-only audits ran in parallel over Domain+Application, Infrastructure+Functions, web/src, and deployment/tooling, each required to prove every negative with a recorded search. They found the same class in six more places, and — more usefully — found that three items an earlier audit recorded as FIXED were only partially fixed: CorridorSelectionOptions is still never bound (2026-07-30 F-1, recorded in CONTEXT.md as applied), the SYNTHESIZING_AUDIO/AUDIO_READY dead wire statuses were only removed from PipelineStepper.tsx and still ship through the backend enum, DTOs, mappings, watchdog, Teams labels, IsEditable and the whole frontend status ladder (2026-07-21), and Result<T>.Bind/BindAsync are test-only despite F-11 asserting the instance methods remained live.

**Decision:** Applied now, all unambiguous: (1) AzureAIOptions.UseManagedIdentity and its AiSettings__AzureAI__UseManagedIdentity app setting are deleted — auth is always the DI TokenCredential, so the flag was a knob that changed nothing; (2) regeneration-queue-poison is added to storage.bicep — RegenerationPoisonQueueTrigger listened on a queue IaC never created, so it 404-polled until the first poison move and QueueDepthMetricsTrigger had nothing to measure, and the comment claiming the -poison suffixes matched provisioned queues was false; (3) the Webhook__ConfigTouch instruction is removed from notifications.md and manual-steps.md — the setting was deleted on 2026-07-20 and the runbook still told operators to touch it; (4) FAILURE_STAGE_VALUES loses REQUESTED and SELECTING_INCIDENTS plus the matching label, because ToFailureStage maps Requested->REQUESTING and IncidentsSelected->GENERATING_SCRIPT so neither is ever on the wire; (5) three doc-comments still naming the removed 'Zetta SMB share' are reworded; (6) the two empty web/src/features/rules-pipeline directories are deleted. Registered but NOT actioned, in JobStatus.Delivered (never assigned, yet the SDD calls it shipped and the state-machine diagram draws it — implement the ACK now that Zetta's delete-on-ingest gives us the signal, or delete the claim), WebhookOptions.MaxRetries (a documented retry that does not exist, so one Power Automate blip drops an operator's card permanently), the two sources of truth for queue names, archive/unarchive being implemented on both sides but unreachable from the UI, CorridorSelectionOptions, SynthesisHistoryOptions' phantom blob repository, the never-read AiSettings--AzureAI--ApiKey vault secret, and a tail of never-read option properties, unconsumed bicep outputs and stale deploy.sh variables.

**Rationale:** The applied six share one property: no behaviour depends on them and each one lies to a reader — which is what makes them expensive. A knob that does nothing invites someone to flip it and conclude something else is broken; a runbook step naming a deleted setting wastes an operator's incident; a failure stage the pipeline cannot reach invites a branch on an impossible value. The eight registered items were held back because each carries a real choice (implement versus delete) that changes behaviour or product surface, and deciding those unilaterally inside a cleanup wave is how scope creep gets shipped. Recording the three disproven 'fixed' claims matters more than the individual items: the recurring failure mode is fixing a lie in one layer, writing it up as complete, and leaving it in every other layer.

**Consequences:**./scripts/verify.sh green on every gate after the changes (backend build 0/0, backend unit + E2E, web lint/ui-inventory/typecheck/unit/build/e2e/perf, bicep lint, gitleaks); web/docs/UI-INVENTORY.md regenerated. The next deploy of any environment stops emitting AiSettings__AzureAI__UseManagedIdentity and starts provisioning regeneration-queue-poison. New doc carries every finding with its proof, the three disproven claims, the eight open decisions ranked by harm, and the checked-and-clean coverage list; production-readiness.md's poison-queue row records the missing queue. Live app settings still carry the six deleted Zetta SMB keys plus UseManagedIdentity until each environment's next deploy — inert, because options binding ignores unknown keys. Separately confirmed while checking vault hygiene: the dev vault holds only 5 secrets and never held Zetta--Username/Password, so those app settings referenced secrets that never existed, exactly like AadClientSecret; the test and prod vault data planes are unreadable from outside the VNet by design, so their copies (if any) are now orphaned and need an in-VNet session or the documented temporary public-access round-trip to purge.

## 2026-07-31 — The top three dead-code decisions resolved: webhook retry implemented, queue names collapsed, JobStatus.Delivered deleted

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The 2026-07-31 dead-code audit registered eight open decisions. The three highest-harm ones each needed a real call rather than a mechanical edit. (1) JobStatus.Delivered was never assigned by any code path, yet solution-design.md called Delivered status tracking 'Shipped', the bulletin-state-machine diagram drew it as a state, functionality-catalog.md listed it in the status chain, and counted it as a good status. (2) WebhookOptions.MaxRetries had shipped since the PoC with [Range(0,5)], a default of 2, and a doc comment promising retries on transient failures, while WebhookNotificationService.PostAsync made exactly one POST and the client had no retry policy — so a single Power Automate blip dropped an operator's review card permanently, with only a log line. (3) Queue names had two sources: the QueueTrigger attributes hardcoded literals while QueuePublisher and QueueDepthMetricsTrigger read a bound QueueOptions, and Queues__* keys were being set by e2e-backend.sh, the E2E example settings, ExternalSmokeFixture and DependencyInjectionTests — divergence would have been silent, the publisher writing to a queue no trigger listens on.

**Decision:** (1) JobStatus.Delivered is DELETED, not implemented. Gone with it: the IsTerminal and IsSettled arms, the Approve_FromTerminal_Fails case, the E2E accepted-status list, harvest_dataset.py's GOOD_STATUSES entry, the state-machine diagram node (Published gains the sublabel 'written to the playout drop' and the spec header now records why there is no Delivered state), and the claims in solution-design.md, functionality-catalog.md and productionisation-backlog.md. A new open item replaces it: an unconsumed-delivery ALERT, which is what delete-on-ingest can actually support. (2) New Infrastructure/Notifications/WebhookRetryHandler, a DelegatingHandler following the existing RateLimitRetryHandler precedent: retries 5xx / 408 / 429 / transport errors / per-attempt timeouts, honours Retry-After, caps accumulated delay at 30s, and reads MaxRetries. The webhook HttpClient's global timeout is set to InfiniteTimeSpan because the handler now owns the per-attempt timeout — a global timeout would cut the retry budget. 17 unit tests. (3) QueueOptions is deleted. QueueNames gains BroadcastPoison and RegenerationPoison, and all four QueueTrigger attributes, QueuePublisher and QueueDepthMetricsTrigger read those constants; the Queues__* config keys are removed from every script, example and fixture.

**Rationale:** Delivered was deleted rather than built for two reasons, either sufficient. The drop file is OVERWRITTEN per station, so its disappearance identifies that station's most recent publish and not a specific bulletin — a per-job Delivered would be a guess presented to ARN as a fact, the exact failure class this audit exists to remove. And it is unverifiable in any environment we can exercise: prod is parked, and TEST writes to informationbulletins-test, a share the autoloader deliberately does not watch, so a file there is never ingested and never deleted. The real signal in delete-on-ingest is monitoring, not status, so it belongs in Azure Monitor beside the other alerts. The webhook retry went the other way because the gap was a live reliability hole with a documented contract already promising the behaviour, and a DelegatingHandler makes it unit-testable — a Polly policy on the client pipeline would have left the contract unverifiable. Queue names collapsed to the constants rather than teaching the attributes to read config, because attribute arguments must be compile-time constants and the %setting% binding-expression route would trade a silent divergence for a startup-time binding failure; nothing ever set those keys to a different value, and all four queues are provisioned by name in storage.bicep.

**Consequences:**./scripts/verify.sh green on every gate (backend build 0 errors / 0 warnings, backend unit + E2E, web lint/ui-inventory/typecheck/unit/build/e2e/perf, bicep lint, gitleaks). WebhookRetryHandlerTests: 17 passed — transient statuses retried, client errors not retried, exhaustion returns the last failure so PostAsync still logs it, MaxRetries=0 means one attempt, transport failures retried then rethrown, Retry-After honoured and counted against the 30s cap, caller cancellation not mistaken for a timeout. The backend E2E suite is the proof for the queue change: it drives the real Functions host through both queues. Behavioural change to watch: a retried webhook POST can duplicate a Teams card if the endpoint processed a request whose response was lost — deliberately accepted, since a duplicate card is noise an operator ignores while a dropped review card is a missed bulletin. bulletin-state-machine.png re-rendered and visually verified. The audit register now carries a 'Second pass' section, the renumbered five remaining open decisions, and the new unconsumed-delivery alert item.

## 2026-07-31 — A global pronunciation layer stacks UNDER the station dictionary, station locator first

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Asked why there is no global pronunciation dictionary. There was one: the PoC's redeploy-only ElevenLabsOptions.PronunciationDictionaryId pair, rejected by the Phase 0 review (docs/reference/phase-0-code-reviews.md:154 — Brisbane read Sydney's dictionary) and replaced on 2026-06-23 by the per-station versioned library. That code still exists as a disabled fallback in ElevenLabsClient.BuildTtsPayload:509-513 with no bicepparam setting any of its keys. What is genuinely missing is not global INSTEAD of per-station but global AND per-station together: rules true everywhere (NorthConnex, Bruce Hwy, M1, brand names) are copy-pasted into every station's rule set, so fixing one means editing eleven and any new station starts wrong. Three things block the stack: BuildTtsPayload emits a one-element locator array (ElevenLabsClient.cs:516), StationConfigResolver.ResolvePronunciationLocatorAsync returns one Option<PronunciationLocator> (StationConfigResolver.cs:183-213), and Job.PronunciationDictionaryId records a single aired locator that JobPronunciationService resolves an operator's word fix against (JobPronunciationService.cs:62-78).

**Decision:** Add PronunciationScope { Global = 0, Station = 1 } to the EXISTING PronunciationDictionary aggregate (not a second aggregate), with at most one active Global dictionary, and carry an ordered PronunciationStack value object through the synth path in place of the single Option<PronunciationLocator>. Emit the station locator FIRST and the global second.
