This ordering is not a preference: a live probe on 2026-07-31 (Dolly Traffic / eleven_v3, faster-whisper adjudicated) established that multiple locators UNION their rule sets and that on a word both layers define the FIRST locator in the array wins — [station, global] rendered the station's answer, [global, station] the global's. Keep Job.PronunciationDictionaryId meaning the STATION layer and add a parallel GlobalPronunciationDictionaryId/VersionId scalar pair, so the operator's one-word fix keeps targeting the station dictionary with no ambiguity rule and no change to JobPronunciationService. Global dictionaries are Admin-only to edit, are not station-assignable, cannot be deleted or archived while active (today's LibraryReferenceGuard cannot see them because no schedule references them), and promotion/demotion mints no version. Reuse the Guidance Global-first scope grouping (ScopeGroupedList + scope-grouping.ts) in the gallery and add an effective-stack toggle to the studio preview. Retire the dead ElevenLabsOptions global-config path in the same change. Full spec:

**Rationale:** Scope on the existing aggregate reuses versioning, the ElevenLabs round-trip, the rule editor, preview and restore — a parallel global aggregate would duplicate all of it, the exact mistake the 2026-06-23 decision avoided by reusing the library pattern. Global = 0, Station = 1 matches GuidanceScope (GuidanceEntry.cs:4-12) so narrower-wins is one vocabulary platform-wide. ElevenLabs accepts up to 3 locators applied in order, so two layers compose with NO server-side rule merging; the spare slot leaves room for a future Market layer. Encoding order in PronunciationStack.Of rather than at each call site means the counter-intuitive station-first rule is unit-testable in one place — getting it backwards would silently kill every station-local correction, the same failure class as the append-instead-of-replace bug fixed on 2026-07-28. Keeping the station id in the field it already occupies is what makes the operator fix path require zero ambiguity resolution. Refusing to let an operator edit the global keeps a correction made on one market's bulletin from changing ten other stations, which is why that route is market-guarded in the first place.

**Consequences:** IMPLEMENTED 2026-07-31 (backend + web); full spec and evidence in A station with NO dictionary assigned now starts reading with the platform-wide one — the main new risk, because the 2026-07-19 audit found aliases that made correct renderings worse, and a bad platform-wide rule degrades every station at once. Mitigation: the first platform-wide dictionary ships small and hand-picked, swept per pilot voice with scripts/pronunciation_sweep.py, not assembled from the eleven existing rule sets (§15 open decision, needs the the ARN voice consult VO consult). PronunciationStack replaced Option<PronunciationLocator> at ~20 sites; no new [Function] name or route, because scope rides the existing create/update bodies. NO queue-shape break, contrary to the original plan: both messages keep PronunciationLocator with its original name and meaning (the station layer) and gained GlobalPronunciationLocator alongside it, so an in-flight message enqueued before the deploy still carries exactly the dictionary it was dispatched with and no drain window is needed. radioJobs gained two plain scalar columns outside the gzip set (docs/reference/job-table-schema.md updated; the JobTableSchemaDoc and JobPersistenceRoundTrip completeness guards both fired and were satisfied). The dead ElevenLabsOptions global-config path was deleted, which also emptied ElevenLabsOptionsValidator — that class and its DI registration went too. One UI deviation: ScopeGroupedList was NOT reused (it renders dense bordered rows and fits neither a card grid nor a sortable table); the gallery groups with section headings via a new features/pronunciation/lib/scope-grouping.ts mirroring the guidance helper's Global-first shape. Gates: solution build 0 errors / 0 warnings, 3696 backend tests pass, web tsc + eslint clean, 701 vitest pass, production bundle builds. Verified on real audio through the shipped chain: the collision sentence rendered "Bravo" (station won the shared word), "Charlie" (platform-only rule still applied) and "Delta" (station-only rule applied), matching the design probe exactly. Four throwaway probe dictionaries remain in the ElevenLabs account, unassigned, because the provider has no delete for pronunciation dictionaries (405) — same disposition as the 2026-07-19 trial dictionary.

## 2026-07-31 — Azure Monitor alerts reuse the notification Logic App to reach Teams

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The only receiver on every environment's action group was the Arinco deploy operator, so no Azure Monitor alert reached anyone at ARN. The proper fix is ARN's on-call DL or the central mgt-aue-ibp-agp-* group, both outstanding on the ARN Technology Lead. Meanwhile each environment already had a working Teams path for the app's own approval and failure cards: a Consumption Logic App (IBP-AUE-{ENV}-LOA-APP01) with an authorised Teams API connection posting Adaptive Cards to a nominated channel. action-group.bicep already accepted webhookReceivers with useCommonAlertSchema; main.bicep simply never passed any.

**Decision:** Added main.bicep param routeAlertsToTeams (default false). When true and a webhook URL resolves, the action group gains a TeamsAlerts webhook receiver pointing at the notification Logic App's own trigger callback, with useCommonAlertSchema true. The Logic App gained an outer If, Is_azure_monitor_alert, that discriminates on the top-level schemaId and renders an alert Adaptive Card; the pre-existing Has_card job-card logic moved unchanged into its else. logic-app-notification.bicep gained an environmentLabel param so one channel can carry several environments. Enabled on dev only (routeAlertsToTeams = true in main.dev.bicepparam); test and prod stay default false. alertEmailReceivers is deliberately left populated.

**Rationale:** Reusing the existing Logic App avoids a second Teams API connection, and that interactive OAuth consent is the only step in this path a redeploy cannot perform. The URL is never a source value - it is resolved in-template from the Logic App's trigger callback, which carries a sig= and must stay out of the repo. Discriminating on schemaId rather than data.essentials.alertRule matters: Azure's own createNotifications test sends the full common alert schema with alertRule NULL, so an alertRule test routes every test payload into the job-card branch, where Compose_card calls formatDateTime on a null createdAt and fails the run. An email receiver is retained because a Logic App inside the subscription cannot be trusted to report that the subscription is down.

**Consequences:** Verified live on dev 2026-07-31, both directions. Alert path: action-group createNotifications produced Logic App run 08584161285042066718147841470CU01 with Compose_alert_card Succeeded and Post_alert_card Succeeded code=Created. Regression path: a schema-3.0 job payload posted to the same trigger produced run 08584161284348576895453150490CU22 with Post_card_passthrough Succeeded code=Created and the alert branch correctly skipped. Two bugs were found and fixed only because the test was run rather than reasoned about: the alertRule-vs-schemaId discriminator, and createArray() with no arguments which Logic Apps rejects outright (now json('[]')). Modules were deployed individually at RG scope because the full main.bicep dev deploy is blocked on an unrelated stuck SWA state - IBP-AUE-DEV-SWA-APP01 has sat at enterpriseGradeCdnStatus Enabling since 2026-07-31, which fails every staticSites write with 'A create or update operation is currently in progress'. Dev's own bicepparam sets swaEnterpriseEdge false and the module omits the property entirely when false, so the template did not set it; test and prod both read Disabled. The site itself serves 200 throughout. main.dev.bicepparam therefore carries routeAlertsToTeams = true which has not yet round-tripped through a full deploy.

## 2026-07-31 — Delivery style survived neither the slot trim nor the word guard; both are fixed

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** No dev or prod station had a delivery style assigned, so nobody had watched one air end to end. Building a same-station same-voice delivery comparison on demo-coast (DCOAST 101.7, Dolly Male Young, eleven_v3) exposed two independent faults that between them made the whole DeliveryStyle library a no-op on any real bulletin. First: BulletinDurationFitter.MapSentenceSpans segments with ScriptSentenceSplitter, which by contract EXCLUDES bracketed cues, and FitByTrimming rejoined those tag-free sentence texts. Every read that overran its slot - which is the normal case at 30s - was therefore re-synthesised with zero audio tags, and because ScriptGenerationEngine and AudioFinalizer both gate provenance on DeliveryTags.HasTags, the job also recorded no DeliveryStyleId or TaggedScriptText, so the loss was invisible on the console (dev jobs ee6ee37a, db319bcf). Second: DeliveryDirector.WordsEqual compared whitespace tokens including punctuation, while prompts/director.md rule 3 explicitly INVITES the director to capitalise for emphasis and add ellipses or an exclamation mark for weight. One added exclamation mark reverted an entire correctly-tagged bulletin to a flat read (dev job 32a5e344, logged as 'Delivery tags reverted: the tagged read changed the words'). FallbackReplayTests already carried the comment 'dev logs show tags rarely applied anyway' - that was this bug, mistaken for LLM flakiness.

**Decision:** SentenceSpan gained a Source field carrying the verbatim script slice for that sentence, tags included, exposed as SourceText with a fallback to Text. MapSentenceSpans attributes everything between the previous sentence and this one - inline tags above all - to the following sentence, and FitByTrimming rejoins SourceText instead of Text. Text still holds the spoken words, so word counting, calibration, the weather/fuel close detection and provenance are untouched. WordsEqual now compares only letter and digit tokens, case-insensitively, so capitalisation and added punctuation pass while any word or number change still fails - '$1.83' to '$183' remains a mismatch because digits are tokenised.

**Rationale:** The fitter fix belongs in the span, not the caller: the trim is the only consumer that reconstructs a script, and giving it the original slice is strictly more information than the stripped text, so no other reader changes behaviour. Tightening director.md to forbid punctuation instead of fixing the guard was rejected - ellipses and emphasis are a large part of how audibly different two styles can be, and the prompt's permission is the design intent while the punctuation-sensitive guard was simply too strict for it. The invariant the guard exists to protect is the spoken WORDS, which letter-and-digit tokenisation still enforces exactly.

**Consequences:** Both fixed and deployed to dev. Verified live on the three demo-coast comparison jobs (0235ecad hard urgency, 3c82fc0f calm advisory, c33e60cc warm breakfast): identical 75-word read, same station, same voice profile, same eleven_v3 model, 30.0s each, and 4 / 1 / 4 audio tags respectively surviving a trim on every one, each with its DeliveryStyleId and version pinned on the job. Word onsets diverge up to 0.92s across the three, mean 0.45s, so the reads genuinely differ in phrasing. New tests: BulletinDurationFitterTests covers tag attachment, the SourceText fallback and a tag-preserving trim; BroadcastOrchestratorTests covers the punctuation-and-caps accept and the changed-word revert. Domain 1360 and Application 593 green. Separately, deploying this tree exposed pre-existing config drift: dev still carried Zetta__Transport=Smb, removed from the enum earlier the same day, which crashed host startup with FormatException until the setting was set to the IaC default AzureFilesDrop. Any environment still on Smb will fail to start on the next deploy.

## 2026-08-02 — Operator-placed delivery tones travel as a verified toned script and suppress the director

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Delivery style is per-station and always-on, so there was no way to direct a single line of a single bulletin — the case that matters is a grave incident inside an otherwise ordinary read. Two things had to be settled before building it. First, measurement against live ElevenLabs on the pilot voice (Dolly original, eleven_v3, seed pinned, n=3 per variant, generation noise ±0.7%) showed the mechanics are far more fragile than the docs suggest: a tag steers only the next 4-5 words before the read reverts, so one tag on a 19-word line moved median pitch -2.8%, i.e. nothing. What works is two directives stacked at the opening plus varied directives at natural clause breaks joined by ellipses: -8.4%. Removing only the stacked opening took it to 0.0%. Swapping [solemn] for [sombre] — the same word to a person — took it to -2.8%. Second, tone bleeds: an untagged line following a directed one dropped 10.3%, harder than the line being directed, and tagging the way back out restored it. Single-shot A/B was actively misleading; several earlier conclusions were noise and were reversed once replicated.

**Decision:** The operator sets a tag per line in the review editor's line gutter, beside the words they are already editing, and one Re-voice applies words and tone together. The UI posts `tonedScript` — the approved words with the tags already placed — next to `editedScript`. `AudioFinalizer.ResolveTonedOrDirectedAsync` accepts it only when `DeliveryTags.WordsPreserved` confirms stripping the tags reproduces the approved words, and then synthesises it verbatim and SKIPS the delivery director entirely: one author per read. A rejected payload loses the tone, never the words. Tones are keyed by normalised sentence text, never by index, so editing a line drops its own tone instead of migrating it onto a neighbour. The dropdown carries only ElevenLabs' documented tags; anything typed, including several tags at once, is passed through unchanged.

**Rationale:** Sending the assembled text rather than structured marks avoids reimplementing tag placement in C# and reuses an invariant the codebase already enforces, so the backend needs one field and one guard. Suppressing the director is not an optimisation: the station style and hand-placed tones would otherwise both tag the same script. Presets are deliberately ElevenLabs' own list rather than the wording that measured best, because the effect is so sensitive to exact phrasing that a curated list would imply a reliability the model does not have — the free-text box is where real tuning happens, and the UI says the effect varies by voice and to audition before publishing. No expansion, companion directives or strength tiers ship: they were built, measured, and could not be made to reproduce the hand-tuned result reliably.

**Consequences:** Wired end to end and gated green (`./scripts/verify.sh`, all 12 phases). New tests: `BroadcastOrchestratorTests` covers verbatim synthesis of a toned read and refusal of one that altered the spoken words; `JobLifecycleHttpTriggerTests` covers the wire name surviving into the queue message; `ReviewScript.test.tsx` covers a tone-only change enabling Re-voice and sending the tagged read beside unchanged words. Deployed to dev 2026-08-02 and quality-tested against the live app, which found and fixed two defects. (1) A toned script carrying NO tags suppressed the station's delivery style and gave nothing back; it now falls through to the director. (2) `WordTimingBuilder` counted each tag as a word, so karaoke highlight and click-to-seek drifted by one per preceding tag — measured live at 74 words + 2 tags = 77 timings with `[solemn]` as the first entry. Tags are now excluded from alignment; re-verified live at 75 timings with or without tags and zero tag tokens. Refusal was confirmed live for four malformed payloads (altered word, nested brackets, over-length tag, reordered clauses): each logged the refusal and aired the approved words. The full operator loop was then driven in the deployed browser — type a tone, Re-voice — and produced `Operator delivery tones applied: 1 tag(s); station delivery style skipped`. One gap remains: tone changes measured duration in a way the estimator cannot see, because tags are stripped before estimation, so the post-synthesis fitter partly compresses the effect back out. Voice choice dominates everything: the docs are explicit, and Dolly is a PVC, which ElevenLabs states is not optimised for v3.

## 2026-08-03 - Tone costs time, never content; tone picker is a plain Select

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Two defects in the per-line delivery-tone feature shipped 2026-08-02.

The picker was a bespoke Popover+cmdk combobox. Every item was unclickable by mouse: shadcn's
`command.tsx` was generated against cmdk 0.x and matched `data-[disabled]` by attribute PRESENCE,
but cmdk 1.1.1 always emits `data-disabled="false"`, so every item resolved to
`pointer-events: none`. This was NOT limited to the picker - the global Ctrl+K palette had been
mouse-dead for as long as cmdk has been on 1.x. Item padding was also hand-tuned per element
(`h-8` items, `h-9` input, `px-3 py-3` empty state) rather than inherited.

Separately, a tag slows the read. Measured on the demo-coast pilot voice (Dolly Male Young,
eleven_v3, n=5 seeds, 74-word script): `[solemn]` on all five sentences costs +2.5% (within the
±2% generation noise), `[solemn] [slowly]` costs +4.2% (real, >2 sigma). The audio fitter absorbs
overrun by pitch-preserving stretch up to `MaxSpeedUpFactor` (1.15), and beyond that
`AudioPipelineService` CASE 3 DROPS trailing sentences and re-synthesises. So a delivery choice
could silently cut a road closure out of a bulletin.

**Decision:**
1. `command.tsx` matches `data-[disabled=true]`, restoring mouse interaction to every cmdk list.
2. The tone picker is a plain Radix `Select` - the control the other 20 pickers in the app use -
   so rows inherit uniform 32px/`6px 8px 6px 32px` geometry. Free text is a `Custom…` entry that
   swaps the trigger for an `Input` of identical width. Radix fires `onOpenChange(false)` BEFORE
   `onValueChange`, so the handover to the input is deferred a frame; doing it inline gets the
   input blurred straight back out by Radix's own focus restoration.
3. A tone may cost time, never content. `AudioFinalizer` compares the approved words against
   `AudioSynthesisResult.FinalScript`; if fitting the tagged read required trimming, the tagged
   take is discarded and the approved words are re-voiced plain. Same fail-open shape as the
   existing word-immutability guard.

**Rationale:** The mouse defect was a primitive bug, not a picker bug, so it is fixed in the
primitive where the palette benefits too. Reaching for `Select` rather than repairing the bespoke
combobox removes the padding drift at the source: the shared item geometry cannot drift if it is
never overridden. And gravity may only subtract energy, never add it - a solemn read of a cut
bulletin is worse than a flat read of a complete one, so when the two conflict the words win.

**Consequences:** Final duration was already pinned to the slot and still is - plain and
5-tag reads of the same script both finalise at exactly 30.0s with all 74 words. What tone
consumes is compression headroom (~4% of 15% worst case), not slot length. Verified live on dev:
a 148-word script for a 30s slot logged "Delivery tones dropped: the tagged read could not fit the
slot without cutting content" and aired 0 tags. Deliberately NOT done: reserving tone headroom in
the generator's word target, which would shorten every bulletin to benefit the tagged minority.

## 2026-08-03 - One v3 tag per sentence does not change the read; repeat it every ~5 words

**Status:** superseded by "v3 audio tags cannot deliver newsreader gravity" (2026-08-03) - the
density finding is real but it buys PACE, not tone, and pace alone was judged not worth the feature

**Context:** An operator set every sentence of the Gold Coast bulletin
(`fa754637c1b442748551adb42fa7e41c`) to `[solemn]` and reported it sounded unchanged. It was
unchanged - measured, not inferred. All numbers below are median F0 over whole clips on the pilot
voice (Dolly Male Young, eleven_v3, stability 0.5), n=5 fixed seeds per cell, on that exact script.

| Treatment | F0 | vs plain | Pace |
|---|---|---|---|
| plain | 208.4 Hz | - | 30.14 s |
| one `[solemn]` per sentence | 215.1 Hz | **+3.2% (d 2.14)** | +0.9% |
| `[solemn]` every 5 words | 200.2 Hz | **-3.7% (d 1.46)** | **+5.9% (d 2.14)** |

One tag per sentence does not merely under-deliver, it reads BACKWARDS - brighter and no slower,
which is why it sounded like the original but never better. ElevenLabs documents the cause: a tag
steers roughly the next 4-5 words and then delivery reverts, so one tag in front of a 25-word
sentence colours its opening clause and nothing else.

Three other levers were measured and rejected. Creative stability (0.0) instead of Natural: no
effect (+1.5%). Ellipses at clause boundaries: no effect (+0.6%). `speed` in voice_settings:
**eleven_v3 ignores it entirely** - 17.87 s / 18.03 s / 17.92 s across speed 1.0 / 0.85 / 0.7, so
pace cannot be dialled directly on v3 and tag density is the only way to slow a read.

Content also fights the tag: the same `[solemn]` treatment on an all-clear script ("moving nicely",
"clear run", "no dramas") has less to grip than on a fatal-crash script. Tone amplifies what the
words already say; it does not overrule them.

**Decision:** A tone repeats its tag across the line at the documented ~5-word span rather than
sitting once at the front, and the expanded read is shown to the operator verbatim so the
repetition is visible rather than hidden. A single-tag-per-line tone control is not shippable.

**Rationale:** The span is the provider's, not ours - honouring it is the difference between a
control that works and one that lies to the operator. Repetition is not hidden machinery so long
as the expanded read is shown verbatim, which is why this pairs with surfacing tags in the script
rather than behind a disclosure.

**Consequences:** A tone control that emits ONE tag per line should be treated as non-functional
regardless of how it is presented. Tag density also costs time (+5.9% here), which spends the
audio fitter's 15% compression headroom - the "tone costs time, never content" guard recorded
above is what keeps that from cutting a bulletin short. Measurement harness and clips:
`/tmp/gc-ab` (A/B page), regenerate with the ElevenLabs `with-timestamps` endpoint.

## 2026-08-03 - v3 audio tags cannot deliver newsreader gravity; only sounds work, never moods

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The per-line tone control shipped with presets like `[solemn]`, `[professional]`,
`[sympathetic]`. An operator applied `[solemn]` to every line of a bulletin and reported no
change. Listening tests on the pilot voice (Dolly Male TVO - `category=generated`, a DESIGNED
voice, not a clone, so the PVC caveat does not apply) settled it. Judged by ear by the product
owner, not by acoustic proxy:

| Tag | Class per ElevenLabs | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `[whispers]` | phonation | works, unmistakably |
| `[sighs]` | non-verbal | works |
| `[exhales sharply]` | non-verbal | works |
| `[clears throat]` | non-verbal | works |
| `[crying]` | non-verbal | works |
| `[short pause]` x3 at clauses | non-verbal | works |
| `[inhales deeply]` | non-verbal | nothing |
| single `[short pause]` / `[long pause]` | non-verbal | nothing |
| `[shouts]` | phonation | nothing (voice has no shouting exemplars) |
| `[excited]` `[sarcastic]` `[curious]` `[mischievously]` `[solemn]` `[sombre]` | direction | nothing |

ElevenLabs' own prompt template splits tags into **Directions** (`[happy]` `[sad]` `[excited]`
`[angry]` `[thoughtful]` `[surprised]`) and **Non-verbal** (`[laughing]` `[chuckles]` `[sighs]`
`[clears throat]` `[short pause]` `[long pause]` `[exhales sharply]` `[inhales deeply]`). The
results split on exactly that line, with one refinement: within Non-verbal, only tags that insert
an AUDIBLE EVENT land. `[inhales deeply]` is too quiet to register; a lone pause is swallowed.

**Decision:** Do not ship a delivery-tone control built on v3 audio tags. Every tag that works
inserts a non-speech artefact - a sigh, an exhale, a throat clear, a whisper, a sob - and none of
those can air in a professional traffic bulletin. Every tag that would express tone editorially
(the Directions class) is inert. The one usable-but-weak lever, repeated `[short pause]`, only
makes the read slower, which is what the operator originally rejected.

**Rationale:** A control that appears to work but does not is worse than no control. The failure
mode is an operator setting "solemn" on a fatality, hearing something close to the original, and
airing it believing gravity was applied. Also note `[professional]` / `[sympathetic]` /
`[reassuring]` ARE documented by ElevenLabs (a customer-service dialogue example) and still do
nothing - being in the docs is not evidence a tag functions.

**Consequences:** Gravity has to come from levers we already own and that demonstrably work: the
WORDS (the script generator can write shorter, harder sentences for a fatality) and PACE (our own
audio pipeline time-stretches; v3 ignores `speed` in voice_settings entirely - verified at 1.0 /
0.85 / 0.7 producing 17.87 / 18.03 / 17.92 s). If per-bulletin gravity is genuinely required, the
mechanism ElevenLabs points at is voice selection - "the most important parameter for Eleven v3" -
i.e. a second DESIGNED voice variant switched in on high-severity bulletins, not tags. That
trades against station voice identity and is a product decision, not an implementation one.

## 2026-08-03 - v3 tags INSERT and SWITCH; they cannot MODULATE

**Status:** SUPERSEDED and partly WRONG - see "Tag effect scales with the emotional latitude
of the words" below. Emotion tags DO modulate delivery; this entry generalised from
single-word tags tested at high similarity_boost, which suppressed the effect.

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Root-cause investigation into why `[solemn]`/`[sad]`-style tags change nothing.
Every candidate cause was eliminated by listening test, judged by the product owner:

| Suspect | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Our station voice lacks range | `[sad]` on Callum, a premade performative voice | no change |
| Stability too low | Creative 0.0 / Natural 0.5 / Robust 1.0 | all identical |
| Voice needs designing for range | new Voice Design voice, range-first prompt | no change |
| Tag class | `[whispers]` vs `[sad]`, same voice and settings | whispers works, sad does not |
| **Text has no emotion to select** | **`[sad]` on a grief line vs a traffic line** | **grief line reads sad** |

The decisive result: the grief line reads sad **with or without the tag**. Adding `[sad]`
explicitly adds little. So eleven_v3 infers delivery from the SEMANTICS OF THE TEXT; a direction
tag does not impose a delivery, it at most disambiguates one the words already support. A factual
road closure is affectively flat, so there is nothing for the tag to select and it is consumed
with no effect - at any voice, any stability, any setting.

Non-verbal tags are a different mechanism entirely: `[sighs]`, `[exhales sharply]`,
`[clears throat]`, `[whispers]`, `[crying]` INSERT an acoustic event rather than modulate prosody,
which is why they fire on flat text where direction tags cannot.

**Decision:** Tonality for bulletins is controlled through the SCRIPT, not through audio tags. Do
not ship, and do not further tune, a mood-tag control. Any future "make this read graver" affordance
must rewrite the words - short sentences, hard full stops, no softeners - because that is the only
input the model's delivery actually responds to.

**Rationale:** Every other lever is measured and closed. v3 ignores `speed` entirely (17.87 /
18.03 / 17.92 s at speed 1.0 / 0.85 / 0.7). Stability does nothing across its full range. Voice
choice does nothing for mood tags. Tag density buys pace, not tone, and was rejected on listening.
The words are the last lever standing, and they are also the one we already own end to end: the
generator writes them and the operator can already edit them.

**Consequences:** ARN operators get MORE tonal control this way, not less - the script editor is a
higher-bandwidth control than a six-item dropdown ever was. The useful build is an LLM-backed
"rewrite for register" action on the existing edit path (operator picks the register, sees the
reworded diff, approves, re-voices), which reuses the re-voice pipeline unchanged. Pause tags may
still be layered on top, as the one non-verbal tag class that is inaudible-as-artefact.

## 2026-08-03 - The under-slot expand refine only fires when there is unvoiced fill, and uses the shared feedback

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** An operator flagged deployed job `fa754637c1b442748551adb42fa7e41c` (goldcoast / "Gold Coast",
30 s, 02:07:10 AEST) for reading the same lines twice. HERE returned **0 corridors and 0 incidents**;
the only data was six good-run roads, of which `ContentFormatters.FormatGoodRuns` shows 4 on a quiet
read. The Draft correctly wrote 30 honest words naming all four. `LlmScriptGenerator` then fired its
under-slot expand refine with its OWN feedback string - "too short ... would leave dead air. Expand
it to about 109 words ... by naming more of the flowing roads already in the data" - which had no
escape hatch. Every road it had been shown was already voiced, so the only way to obey was to
restate: 100 words that named the same four roads twice more and closed on a road-less wrap-up. That
string also contradicted the shared style rules rendered into the same prompt ("never flag a script
for being short", "NEVER expand by restating an item the script already covers"). Nothing caught it:
`RollCallDetector` Rule A allows 6 clear names on a quiet read (Darwin ATN precedent) and dedupes, so
four-named-twice counts as four; Rule B's universe is incident-corridor names, empty here;
`RepeatedStatePhraseDetector` peaked at 2 against a threshold of 3; and `RedundantTailDetector` missed
the tail by two regex tokens. The conditional audit therefore fast-pathed past LLM review, and the
operator deleted the tail sentence by hand.

**Decision:** Four fixes at their own source.
1. The expand call now uses `SlotFitPlanner.ExpansionFeedback(targetWordCount)` - the same source
   `WordTargetEnforcer` already used, whose "If every data source is already voiced, return the
   script unchanged - a shorter honest read is the correct result" clause is the whole point. The
   local copy is deleted. `SlotFitPlanner`'s own doc comment already cited this failure mode on this
   market ("frozen-eval iter4, Gold Coast"); the duplicate string simply predated it.
2. **The emptiness test is now deterministic, not a model judgement.** A new `HasUnvoicedFill` gate in
   `LlmScriptGenerator` skips the expand call entirely unless a road `FormatGoodRuns` actually SHOWED
   the writer is still unnamed, or a present weather / fuel line has not aired. Escape hatch or not,
   asking a model to notice its own well is dry is unreliable: with fix 1 deployed, Queenstown job
   `958c2121` still volunteered a 5-word echo ("Murchison Highway's a clear run." for a road already
   voiced as "moving nicely"), which the grounding check then rejected into a filler-cart fallback.
   The capped-name cap itself moved into `ContentFormatters.NamedGoodRuns` so the gate and the prompt
   can never disagree about which roads the writer saw.
3. `RedundantTailDetector` widened for two independent near-misses on the shipped tail
   ("So, for the latest traffic picture, those four roads are all moving nicely..."): the
   back-reference now tolerates a count/qualifier between determiner and noun ("those FOUR roads")
   from a CLOSED token set, and the filler-close matches "for the latest traffic picture", not only
   the "traffic"-last form. Both feed the existing mechanical `Repair`, so the tail is now dropped
   with no LLM call - the same edit the operator made by hand.
4. `AudioFinalizer`'s `GeneratorInputSnapshot` capture moved INSIDE the `!context.RevoiceOnly` guard.
   It sat outside, so every operator re-voice overwrote `GeneratorInputJson` with the contextless
   re-voice context - this job's record kept its six `GoodRunRoadsJson` entries while the snapshot
   read zero, and a fixture built from it replayed as an empty script.
   `JobFixtureReplayTests.BuildSnapshot` now falls through to the sibling-column reconstruction when
   the captured snapshot is present but carries no evidence, so already-corrupted jobs stay replayable.

**Rationale:** One prompt cannot hold two contradictory length rules and be reliable - the model
follows the more specific, more urgent one, which was the hardcoded feedback. Deleting the duplicate
is strictly better than hardening it: the canonical helper is already battle-tested on this exact
defect. But the prompt is the wrong place to decide a question the code can answer exactly, hence
fix 2: "is there anything left to say" is a fact about the data, so no call is issued when the answer
is no - which also removes a wasted LLM round trip and a retry. The detector widening is defence in
depth, not the fix, and stays a closed token set so it cannot false-fire on a normal close that names
a real road. Fix 4 is why this class of job could not be reproduced at all, so it is a prerequisite
for regression-testing any future one.

**Consequences:** Deployed to dev (`arn deploy api --env dev`, health 200) and verified live:
- **the operator's exact frozen input**, replayed through the real generator
  (`export-prompts.py --build-fixture goldcoast-echo-padding --replay-fixture`), returns *"Gooding
  Drive, Markeri Street and Burleigh Road are all looking good, with Benowa Road also looking good."*
  - each road named once, no restatement, no wrap-up; Fabrication/Style/Safety all PASS (Style was
  FAIL before). Zero expand calls: the gate answers from the data.
- **Queenstown, poller-fired, before and after fix 2.** Same market, same 2-corridor shape: job
  `958c2121` FellBack on "the same road's clear condition is restated twice as separate content";
  job `d00c4d2e` lands WaitingApproval at 30.0 s / 76 words, every road named once, weather and fuel
  each aired once.
- **Gold Coast, poller-fired** (`df90e147`, Hot Tomato 102.9, 20 corridors / 24 incidents): a clean
  84-word read, no expand path taken - the busy case is unaffected.

The all-clear read is now honestly short, which is the designed content-limited outcome: a configured
station fills the remainder from weather / fuel / filler statements, and the operator's job had none because
"Gold Coast" matched no configured station (`goldcoast`'s station is **Hot Tomato 102.9**) - the
separate, operator-visible reason that bulletin had so little to work with. Committed as regression
fixture `test/corpus/regressions/goldcoast-echo-padding.json` plus unit regressions in
`LlmScriptGeneratorTests` (4 cases incl. the zero-call gate), `RedundantTailDetectorTests` and
`BroadcastOrchestratorTests` (the last verified to fail on the pre-fix code). NOT changed:
`RollCallDetector` (widening Rule B to good-run roads would false-fire on the Darwin all-clear
precedent it was tuned against) and the 109-word target for a 30 s slot, which is the intended
`WordTargetOvershoot` headroom. Ad-hoc `POST /api/broadcast` probes used to hunt a live zero-corridor
coverage resolve to the REAL market (`Location: "Gold Coast"` -> market `goldcoast`) and chain
same-day fallbacks onto it - seven such probes built a streak of 4 and were deleted via
`arn job delete`; use the poller path or clean up after.

## 2026-08-03 - Complete map of what can and cannot change v3 delivery

**Status:** accepted - investigation closed, all classes exhausted

**Context:** Final sweep. Roughly 60 clips judged by ear by the product owner on the pilot voice
(Dolly Male TVO, eleven_v3). Acoustic proxies were abandoned early - they reported "effects" that
were inaudible, and every real finding here came from listening.

**The rule:** v3 audio tags can **insert** a discrete acoustic event and can **switch** phonation
mode. They cannot **modulate** the ongoing delivery. Nothing that asks for a continuous change to
loudness, rate, pitch contour or emotional colour has any effect.

| Class | Examples | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Phonation-mode switch | `[whispers]` | WORKS |
| Inserted vocal sound | `[sighs]` `[exhales sharply]` `[clears throat]` `[crying]` | WORKS |
| Inserted silence | `[short pause]` repeated at clauses | WORKS (single one is swallowed) |
| Emotion / mood | `[sad]` `[excited]` `[solemn]` `[professional]` `[sympathetic]` | inert |
| Manner / delivery adverb | `[softly]` `[booming]` `[rushed]` `[drawn out]` `[slowly]` `[gently]` `[firmly]` `[monotone]` `[deadpan]` `[solemnly]` | inert |
| Voice choice | premade performative; Voice-Design voice built for range | no effect on tags |
| Stability | Creative 0.0 / Natural 0.5 / Robust 1.0 | no effect |
| `speed` in voice_settings | 1.0 / 0.85 / 0.7 | ignored by v3 outright |
| Our own request params | bare `{text, model_id}` vs seed + normalization + full settings | identical - not our bug |
| **Text semantics** | grief wording vs traffic wording | **the only real driver of prosody** |

`[softly]` failing while `[whispers]` succeeds is the decisive pair: whisper is a BINARY mode the
model can enter, "softly" is a continuous intensity it will not track. Same for `[slowly]` failing
while repeated `[short pause]` works - silence is insertable, rate is not modulable.

**Decision:** Tone is not controllable on eleven_v3 for traffic bulletins. The tags that function
all put a sigh, a throat clear, a sob or a whisper to air; the tags that would express tone do
nothing; and the one genuine driver - emotional vocabulary in the script - is unavailable to us
because traffic copy must stay factual (`prompts/safety.md` forbids editorialising).

**Rationale:** Every hypothesis was eliminated by listening, in this order: our voice lacks
range (no - a performative premade voice behaves identically), stability is wrong (no - all three
settings identical), the voice needs designing for range (no - a purpose-built one behaves the
same), our request parameters suppress it (no - a bare request behaves the same), the tag needs
semantic support (yes, but that is the TEXT working, not the tag - the grief line reads sad with
the tag removed), and finally that manner words might work where mood words do not (no - the
whole adverb class is inert). What survives is a single mechanical rule, stated above.

**Consequences:** What remains is pacing: repeated `[short pause]` and our own pipeline
time-stretch. Ship that as "read weight" if anything, named for what it does. Untested and
predicted inert by the rule above: CAPITALISATION (continuous emphasis). Predicted to behave like
pauses: ellipses (inserted silence). Neither is worth a feature on its own.

## 2026-08-03 - Tag effect scales with the emotional latitude of the words (FINAL)

**Status:** accepted - closes the tone investigation

**Context:** With the right configuration, v3 emotion tags work dramatically. Judged by ear:

| Text | Tag + config | Result |
|---|---|---|
| "I... really thought things would be different this time." | `[sad, subdued, voice trembling]`, stability 0.0, similarity 0.65, speaker_boost on | **"insanely aligned", dramatic and correct** |
| A fatal-crash traffic bulletin | same tag class, same config | real but "immensely subtle" |
| Same bulletin | similarity pushed to 0.45 / 0.30, richer directions, tag density, ellipses | **no meaningful gain** |

So the earlier "tags cannot modulate" conclusion was wrong, and so was the preset vocabulary and the
settings we sent. Three things had to be right at once and never were: COMPOUND natural-language
directions (`[grave, measured, subdued]`, not `[solemn]`), stability at Creative 0.0, and
similarity_boost lowered to ~0.65 with speaker_boost on. Our production path sent single-word tags
at stability 0.5 / similarity 0.75, which suppresses the effect.

**The governing rule:** a tag's effect is PROPORTIONAL TO THE EMOTIONAL LATITUDE OF THE SURROUNDING
TEXT. v3 conditions delivery on semantics; the tag biases a reading the words already permit. Emotive
copy gives it enormous room. Factual copy gives it almost none, and no setting recovers that.

**Decision:** No tone control for traffic bulletins. The capability is real but the content type
cannot use it - a road closure is affectively flat by construction, and adding emotional wording is
editorialising, which `prompts/safety.md` forbids.

**Rationale:** Everything that could amplify it on factual copy was tried and measured by ear:
lower similarity (0.45, 0.30 - also drifts off the station voice), richer directions, tags repeated
at every clause, ellipsis and line-break support, Creative stability, speaker boost. None moved it
past "subtle". Remixing the voice for range (prompt_strength 0.8, range-first description) produced
poor audio and was abandoned; the test voice was deleted.

**Consequences:** Ship no mood picker. Pacing (repeated `[short pause]`, plus our own time-stretch)
remains the only usable delivery lever for bulletins, and should be named "read weight" if shipped
at all. NOTE FOR FUTURE NON-TRAFFIC CONTENT: for anything with emotional latitude - station promos,
news reads, sponsor copy - the capability IS available and strong, using compound directions at
stability 0.0 / similarity ~0.65 / speaker_boost on. That is worth remembering rather than
concluding "v3 tags do not work".

## 2026-08-03 - Fatality register: the words carry it, and even then only just

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Final comparison on one fatal-crash bulletin, same facts throughout, at the config
proven to work (stability 0.0, similarity_boost 0.65, speaker_boost on). Judged by ear:

| Variant | Result |
|---|---|
| today's wording + `[grave, measured, subdued]` (TAG ONLY) | barely anything |
| reworded purely factual, no tag (WORDS ONLY) | "a bit better than the tag, but very subtly" |
| human framing + tag | "did change it a bit" - the best of the set, still modest |

The reworded factual version makes the death its own sentence and its own subject - "There's been a
fatal crash on the Monash Freeway. A person has died." - instead of burying it as a subordinate
clause explaining a road condition. That is the semantic latitude v3 responds to, and it is standard
broadcast practice: no speculation, no victim detail, no graphic content.

The human-framing version adds "Sad news on the roads this morning" and "please take care through
there". That is real traffic-radio register but IS editorial framing and needs ARN sign-off.

**Decision:** No operator tone control. If ARN wants gravity on fatalities, do it in the GENERATOR's
phrasing, not as a control: a fatality should be written with the death as its own sentence. The
compound tag and corrected voice settings may ride along automatically on high-severity bulletins,
but they are an amplifier, not the mechanism.

**Rationale:** The best achievable result on traffic copy is "changed it a bit", and it needs
editorial framing to get there. That does not justify an operator-facing feature, and it especially
does not justify one that looks more capable than it is. The phrasing change, however, stands on its
own merits - "A person has died" is clearer and more respectful copy than "after a fatal crash"
regardless of how it is synthesised. Do it as journalism, and take any tonal benefit as a bonus.

**Consequences:** Generator prompt work, not UI work. Needs an ARN editorial ruling on whether the
"Sad news…" / "please take care" register is permitted before it can be used. Tone as an operator
affordance is closed.

## 2026-08-03 - The tone effect does not reproduce; it was generation variance (CLOSES investigation)

**Status:** accepted - supersedes every "settings fix" recommendation above

**Context:** A single generation at `stability 0.0` / `similarity_boost 0.65` / `use_speaker_boost
true` with a compound direction sounded genuinely grave, and a backend settings change was
recommended on the strength of it. A blind A/B then killed it: 6 generations of that exact config
against 2 plain controls at today's settings, shuffled, same voice and words - all judged
indistinguishable.

v3 is not deterministic. The effect was a lucky draw, not a control. The same mistake was made
earlier in the session ("over-tagging drops words", from one 9.68s clip; three re-runs gave 18.2 /
18.3 / 19.1s), and repeated here despite that lesson.

**Decision:** No tone control, and NO backend voice-settings change. `stability`/`similarity_boost`
stay as they are - the proposed values bought nothing reproducible, and Creative is documented as
more hallucination-prone even though 20 runs found no drift.

**Rationale:** A control whose output depends on the draw is worse than no control: the operator
sets a tone, hears it work once, and thereafter trusts a read that is not being steered. Single-
generation evidence is not evidence for a non-deterministic model. Any future perceptual claim here
MUST be a blind, shuffled, multi-generation test - that is now the bar, and it is cheap.

**What IS established:** `similarity_boost 0.65` does not audibly change the station voice, so voice
identity was never the constraint. Non-verbal tags (`[sigh]`, `[whispers]`, `[clears throat]`)
remain reliable because they insert an acoustic event rather than modulate prosody - which is
exactly why the deployed job `d00c4d2e` produced the sigh and nothing else. A strong emotional
effect WAS heard once on genuinely emotive first-person copy, but it was never reproducibility-
tested and must not be relied on without one.

**Consequences:** Remove the operator tone affordance. Unrelated and more urgent: job `d00c4d2e`
reached air-ready containing "keep this person in your prayers during the day" - religious
editorialising about a road fatality that `prompts/safety.md` should have blocked. That is a real
safety-reviewer defect on the highest-risk content type and outranks anything tonal.

## 2026-08-03 - The documentation gates run in verify.sh, because the language contract was never actually enforced

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The 2026-07-28 decision that created the published ARN documentation set says the
language contract is "enforced by the build rather than by discipline". It was not. `build-docs-site.py`
carries the eleven-class leak guard and works, but its only caller was the `DocsSite` deployment job in
`deployment/pipelines/deploy-stage.yml`, gated behind `enableDeploy=true` AND a variable-group
`deployDocsSite=true`. `docs.py check` had no caller at all beyond the contributor instructions. In
`verify.sh`, every documentation path (`docs/*`, `*.md`, `.agents/*`, `architecture/*`) classified as
`inert`, so a docs-only push selected a secret scan and nothing else, and `docs-site/*` fell to the
default branch and escalated to every gate. By 2026-08-03 six body leaks had accumulated on published
pages - `poller` x3 in `integration-test-plan.md`, `RISK-13`/`RISK-28` in `open-items.md`, and the
organisation name in `known-limitations.md` - none of which any routine command would have reported. A
13-lane documentation audit found them; a strict build confirmed them in one second.

**Decision:** `verify.sh` gains a sixth lane. A new `docs` path class selects it, covering `docs/*`,
`docs-site/*`, `.agents/*`, `architecture/*`, `*.md`, `llms.txt` and the three documentation scripts;
`docs-site/*` and `llms.txt` move off the escalate-everything default so a docs push no longer drags in
the backend. The lane runs `./scripts/docs.py check` then `./scripts/build-docs-site.py` STRICT, serially,
because a frontmatter failure makes the leak report noise. `--allow-leaks` stays a mid-refactor reporting
flag and is never used by a gate.

**Rationale:** A guard nothing runs is documentation, not enforcement. The cost is about one second on a
docs-touching push, against a class of defect that reaches a client deliverable and that reading does not
catch at 31 pages. Putting it in `verify.sh` rather than only in CI means the pre-push hook covers it too,
which is where the invariant "no gate whose inputs changed may be skipped" actually bites.

**Consequences:** A docs-only push now costs the secret scan plus the two documentation gates. Adding an
ARN-facing page without frontmatter, or introducing a contract term, now fails locally before it fails a
reviewer. Six leaks were cleared in the same change. The signed cover
(`docs/deliverables/Handover-Pack/*.typ`) remains OUTSIDE the guard - it is Typst, not a published page -
and four of the audit's client-boundary defects were in it, so extending the guard to the cover source is
the obvious next step and is not done here.

## 2026-08-03 - Rewrite-for-register: an agent that reshapes the WORDS, staged for review

**Status:** accepted - implemented end to end

**Context:** Tone could not be reached by tagging alone. Verified by listening across ~90 clips: mood
tags (`[sad]`, `[solemn]`, `[professional]`) are inert on our voices; the tags that do work insert a
literal sigh, breath or throat-clear and cannot air; punctuation alone is real but weak. What DID
work, judged good by the product owner, combined three things: a reworded script with a short framing
line, one or two capitalised words plus ellipses, and one or two MANNER tags (`[quietly]`,
`[gently]`, `[brightly]`, `[warmly]`). The dominant ingredient is the words.

`IScriptDirector` cannot do that: it is word-immutable by contract, which caps it at "decent". And it
was never running anyway - all 6 delivery styles on dev are assigned to 0 of 13 schedules, with
`AllowedTags: ["[serious]"]`, a tag proven inert.

**Decision:** A second, operator-facing agent that MAY reshape the wording:
`prompts/delivery-writer.md` + `IDeliveryWriter` + `POST /jobs/{id}/retone`. The operator types one
plain sentence ("talk about this more calmly, it's about a death"); the agent returns rewritten text
into the editor. It never voices and never saves. The operator reads it, edits anything they
disagree with, auditions it (`POST /jobs/{id}/audition`, ~5s, no job mutation), then re-voices - at
which point the changed words go through the safety reviewer on the normal path.

**Rationale:** Changing words is the only lever that reaches the quality bar, and changing words is
exactly what must not happen unattended. Staging it - rewrite, read, audition, submit - keeps the
power and puts a human and the safety agent between it and air. The director stays as-is for the
unattended station-level path, where word-immutability is the right trade.

Three guards are enforced in code (`DeliveryRewriteValidator`, 26 unit tests) with up to 3 corrective
retries, because all three failures were observed in practice:
- a BANNED tag (sound-inserting or inert-mood) - it aired a real sigh, or silently did nothing;
- WORD GROWTH over 115% - the first version inflated a 31-word bulletin to 47 (+52%), which makes
  the duration fitter compress the read or trim a road off the end;
- a LOST FACT (named road or number) - a register change may reword freely, never drop a fact.

The agent also refuses to lift a bulletin carrying a death even when asked for energy, and splits
the register mid-bulletin instead (grave for the crash, bright after "Elsewhere").

**Caught by attempting the UI drive:** both hooks read `res.data.script` / `res.data.url`
directly. The API serialises PascalCase, so both calls returned 200 and the UI silently ignored
them - and the mock adapter answered camelCase, which hid it through every unit and mock-mode run.
Fixed by routing both through Zod schemas like every other response in the app, aligning the mock
to PascalCase, and adding a regression test that parses the real wire shape. The lesson is the
mock: a fixture that disagrees with the API about casing will hide a whole class of bug.

**Consequences:** Verified on deployed dev end to end: retone 4.6s (28->30 words, 1 tag), audition
6.5s with the job status unchanged, then re-voice -> "AI safety review passed", 1 tag aired, audio
finalised at 30.0s. Its brief encodes the session's LISTENING results rather than ElevenLabs'
documentation, which is wrong about this model in several places - so that brief must be updated from
evidence, not from vendor docs. Untouched and still true: the 6 delivery styles remain unassigned,
and voice choice matters more than any of this (Dolly Female Young is markedly flatter than Dolly
Male Young on identical text).

## 2026-08-03 - Delivery styles: three ARN pilot styles, and a non-v3 voice no longer disables direction

**Status:** implemented and assigned on dev (13/13 schedules)

**Decision:** ship three delivery styles built from verified manner tags, assign every station by
format, and scope the v3 gate to tags so a non-v3 voice still receives punctuation direction.

**Rationale:** the feature was inert - not because it was unbuilt, but because nothing was assigned
and half the network could not run it. Both had to change for a style to reach air.

**Context:** delivery styles had existed for weeks but were assigned to 0 of 13 schedules, so the
director never ran in the pipeline. Three styles were authored from the manner tags verified by
listening on 2026-08-03 (`[quietly] [gently] [brightly] [warmly] [firmly] [urgently]`), never from
ElevenLabs' documented mood tags, which are inert on our voices:

| Style | Palette | Stations |
|---|---|---|
| ARN Drive Authority | `[firmly] [urgently]` | Gold 96FM, DCOAST |
| ARN Bright Contemporary | `[brightly] [warmly]` | KIIS x4, Hot Tomato, Hot 100, Star 102.7 |
| ARN Measured Advisory | `[quietly] [gently]` | River 1467, 5AU, Magic FM, 7XS |

**The blocker found while testing:** 7 of 13 stations run professional voices, which resolve to
`eleven_multilingual_v2`. `DirectAsync` skipped the director outright on any non-v3 model, so a
delivery style on those stations was a silent no-op - assignment alone would not have fixed
anything. The v3 gate exists because non-v3 models SPEAK tags aloud, but capitalisation and
punctuation are model-agnostic. The gate is now scoped to the tags, not the direction: a non-v3
voice still gets directed with an EMPTY palette, which `prompts/director.md` treats as a deliberate
"punctuation and CAPS only" instruction. Prompt compliance is not a guarantee, so tags emitted
anyway are stripped in code before the word-immutability check. `DeliveryTags.SupportsTags` holds
the predicate so it is testable and fails safe (unknown model => no tags).

**Gravity is subtractive.** The first version guarded the fatality SENTENCE, so an energetic style
still aired "allow an extra TWENTY minutes!" in a bulletin about a death. Gravity is now judged over
the whole script, and may only ever remove devices - never grant one. An earlier draft said the
director "may still capitalise a status word", which contradicted the calm rule and made Measured
Advisory capitalise CLOSED on a death; where tone and gravity disagree the quieter instruction wins.

**Verified** (12-cell matrix, both TTS models x grave/clear x 3 styles): zero tags on non-v3 6/6;
no exclamation on any grave read 6/6; Measured Advisory never capitalises 6/6; clear roads still
lift. Poller-fired River 1467 job aired Measured Advisory - `[quietly]` in the synthesised text,
stripped from the displayed script, audio 30.0s against a 30s target.

**Consequences:** every station now has a style that actually reaches the read, including the seven
on professional voices. Tags remain impossible on non-v3 by two independent mechanisms (empty
palette, plus a code strip). A future model string containing "v3" is assumed tag-capable.

**Not fixed here:** the chronic quality-gate fallback (2 of 3 poller jobs) is pre-existing and
upstream of the director - Melbourne fell back on 07-31 before any of this work.

## 2026-08-03 - Two fallback causes, and a gate that could never pass on a capable machine

**Status:** implemented, deployed to dev, verified live

**Decision:** fix the two defects behind the poller fallbacks at their real causes, and bound the
browser gate by MEMORY rather than by core count or an environment flag.

**Rationale:** the previous session reported both poller failures as one "chronic quality-gate
fallback". Diagnosis showed they were three separate bugs, only one of which was a quality problem.

**Context:** three separate defects, diagnosed from App Insights exception stacks and job
`LogsJson` rather than inferred from the fallback status.

**Context - fallback cause 1, a crash reported as a timing problem.** `RollCallDetector.Repair`
sliced the gap between consecutive road mentions. Two corridor names can match OVERLAPPING spans
when one contains another - "Ring Road" inside "Northern Ring Road" - so the slice ran backwards and
threw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException("length ('-20')")`. The exception escaped the review loop; the
job never advanced past INCIDENTS_SELECTED; the watchdog swept it 2m43s later as `missed-window`. So
a deterministic crash discarded a finished 83-word APPROVED script and surfaced to the operator as a
deadline miss. Mentions are now collapsed to non-overlapping spans (longest match wins) and counted
after collapsing, since one road named once must not count twice toward the roll-call cap.

Worse than the bug was its invisibility, so the ten mechanical post-LLM repairs now run through one
fail-open helper: a repair that throws keeps the unrepaired script - already airable, having passed
review and safety - logs the fault against the job, and names the detector. A cosmetic polish pass
must never cost a station its bulletin.

**Context - fallback cause 2, an abbreviation the writer had to expand.** HERE emits abbreviated
road types and contracted place names. `Trl`, `W'mooloo` and `HT` had no entry in
`RoadNameFormatter.SpokenExpansions`, so source text kept them while the writer correctly read
"Trail", "Woolloomooloo", "Harbour Tunnel" - and the grounding reviewer flagged the expansion as a
NAME_SPELLING violation whose hard gate binned the script. Measured across 69k chars of live
incident/corridor text (34 jobs): those three were the only unmapped forms, so the map stays
measured rather than becoming a gazetteer. Expanding at SOURCE keeps the fidelity gate strict -
writer and reviewer now see the same spoken name. `ToSpeakable` also descends into hyphen segments,
because the spaced-hyphen tightening glues "Toll Plaza - W'mooloo" into one token. Rule 9 of
`prompts/review-system.md` was additionally restated as a PRINCIPLE (judge the base name, never the
road-type suffix) since its enumerated allowlist will always be incomplete.

**Context - the browser gate.** `web e2e` had never passed inside `verify.sh`. Two compounding
causes, neither an assertion: Playwright sizes workers at cores/2, so a 16-core box ran 8 Chromium
instances ("Page crashed" is browser OOM), and the lane ran beside four others on one machine (the
60s timeouts and "Loading..." states that followed were starvation). Workers are memory-bound, not
CPU-bound, so the count now derives from `MemAvailable` at ~2.5 GB each - measured: 4 crashed, 2
passed 39/39 at 5.4 GB. The browser phases moved to a second wave that starts after the parallel
lanes drain; coverage is identical, only local wall time changes.

An earlier version of the cap exempted `process.env.CI`, reasoning that 2-core hosted agents were
already safe. That was wrong and self-defeating: **CI=1 is also set by local agent harnesses**, which
silently restored the 8-worker default and is precisely why this failure looked machine-specific for
so long. Bounding unconditionally cannot regress real CI, because the cores/2 term is retained: a
2-core agent still resolves to 1 worker.

**Consequences:** poller fallbacks went 2-of-3 to 0-of-6 across melbourne, sydney, goldcoast,
mildura, perth and demo-coast - all six aired a real 30.0s bulletin. `verify.sh` passes every phase
including `web e2e` (181s) and `web perf budget` (90s) for the first time, at 429s wall.

**Not fixed here:** the grounding reviewer is an LLM, so a genuinely novel abbreviation can still
cost one bulletin before someone maps it; the fail-open helper does not cover a detector's `Detect`
call, only `Repair`.

## 2026-08-04 - The director's expertise belongs in the user template, not the agent shim

**Status:** committed and gate-verified; NOT deployed (PIM elevation lapsed mid-session)

**Decision:** add worked before/after examples to `prompts/director.md`. Leave the `arn-director`
Foundry agent instruction as the neutral shim, and leave its `reasoning_effort` at `none`.

**Rationale:** asked whether the director's *system prompt* should be reconfigured to make it better
at tone, the answer is no - and an earlier claim of mine that "part of the director's behaviour is
not in version control" was WRONG. `deployment/scripts/provision-foundry-agents.sh` provisions
`arn-director` with a deliberate three-sentence neutral shim ("Follow the instructions in the user
message exactly..."), drift-checked by `check-foundry-agent-drift.sh`. The documented convention is
that JSON-returning roles (refine/attribute/safety/director) keep a neutral shim because a
writer-style agent instruction breaks a JSON role, and that git is the source of truth while Foundry
is a deployment target. So `prompts/director.md` already IS the director's whole instruction - it is
the system prompt in all but delivery mechanism, and improving it is the correct lever.

**Context:** the real deficiency was that `director.md` stated rules but carried ZERO worked
examples, on what is fundamentally a formatting/judgement task. Measured by calling
`gpt-5.6-luna` directly with the shim as instructions and the rendered template as input - 4
configs x 3 cases x 3 repeats, 36 calls:

| config | palette used | run-to-run consistency |
|---|---|---|
| control (as deployed), effort none | **no tags at all, 9/9** | consistent but empty |
| control, effort medium | tags appear | INCONSISTENT (2 variants on one case) |
| few-shot, effort none | `[firmly]` / `[firmly]+[urgently]` correctly | **consistent 3/3 on every case** |
| few-shot, effort medium | identical to effort none | consistent |

So the deployed director's modal behaviour is to emit NO tag and fall back to capitals plus an
exclamation - which is exactly the reported symptom ("I only ever get `[firmly]`", and often not
even that). Few-shot examples fixed both the palette use and the run-to-run variance. Raising
reasoning effort bought nothing over few-shot, so it stays `none`: no added latency or cost.

**Safety held.** Word immutability 36/36 across every config, and the gravity rule (energy asked for
on a bulletin containing a death) produced 0 violations in all four configs - adding examples did not
weaken the guard it must respect. Blocking eval `arn-director-contract-v1` PASS 3/3.
`./scripts/eval.sh --script-only` held the 71% (n=3) baseline with the same pre-existing
fabrication/underfill failures, run in an isolated git worktree because the main tree carried
unrelated concurrent work that does not compile.

**Consequences:** a station's palette is still the ceiling on expressiveness - ARN Drive Authority
offers only `[firmly]`/`[urgently]`, so "make it excited" cannot become bright there by design. What
changes is that the director now reliably uses the palette it HAS instead of silently declining.

**Not done:** deploying it. `Microsoft.Web/sites/config/list/action` is denied on the expired PIM
window, so both the SCM and ARM zip paths return 403/AuthorizationFailed. The change is committed and
every runnable gate passes; it needs `az` PIM re-activation and one publish.

## 2026-08-04 — 2026-08-04 — Per-voice filler cart, cached per voice version

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The dead-air filler cart was ONE evergreen WAV per environment (Broadcast__FillerCartAudioUrl), read by the same voice for every station. The ask: each voice gets its own cart clip speaking the SAME script, cached per (voice x settings x model) so a voice-profile version change naturally produces a new cached clip. The filler-statement audio cache (FillerAudioCacheService, key FillerAudioCacheKey.Build + _t2 self-invalidation suffix) is the exact precedent to reuse.

**Decision:** Treat the cart script as a pseudo filler statement (id __cart__) and reuse the ENTIRE existing filler audio cache machinery unchanged: new FillerCartAudioKey.Build appends a stable SHA256-8 script hash to the filler statement key; IFillerAudioCacheService gains ResolveCartUrlAsync (shared ResolveClipAsync pipeline, cache hit returns the blob's bare URL); a new PerVoiceFillerCartResolver resolves the clip for a job's OWN voice config; BulletinFallbackService.TryFillerCartAsync and JobService.RejectToFallbackAsync apply per-voice-first, evergreen WAV second. The cart script rides the existing Broadcast__FillerCartScript app setting (IaC, QT-001) and is the transcribed wording of the approved evergreen WAV (never invented).

**Rationale:** Reuses the proven cache machinery unchanged (key bump self-invalidation, trim/normalize pipeline, blob + table metadata) instead of a second cache implementation; lazy caching matches filler statements exactly (first fallback for a voice pays one ~5s synthesis); per-voice clips land in the same broadcasts container with the same URL shape so delivery (ZettaFileDeliveryService/BlobAudioUrlProvider) needs zero changes; jobs whose voice config has no concrete settings (broadcast default voice) deliberately keep the evergreen cart since the cache key requires settings.

**Consequences:** Voice-profile version edits now change the cache key and produce a new cart clip per voice on first use; old clips orphan harmlessly. Feature is inert until Broadcast__FillerCartScript is set (empty disables it); bicepparams ship the transcribed wording in all three environments. First fallback for a new voice pays one ~5s synthesis at deadline (acceptable; generation runs ahead of airtime) — a warm-up timer is a deliberate non-goal. Inherits the pre-existing filler-cart console-playback quirk (QT-003: Audio.Data.Url empty for cart references). New tests: FillerCartAudioKeyTests (7), ResolveCartUrlAsync hit/miss/synth-failure, PerVoiceFillerCartResolverTests (5), per-voice-first fallback + reject-to-fallback tests.


## 2026-08-04 — Pace boost owns BOTH ends of the acceptance band; boosted word targets aim just inside the ceiling

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Dev job `b6e03354088c4ce1bd8205d02011a406` (melbourne, 30s, Dolly Male Young v4, `PaceBoostWpm=40`, `eleven_v3`) took 104.6s where comparable melbourne jobs take 21-51s. 70.0s of that was FOUR ElevenLabs renders across two generation passes. Measured on the live API (same voice, same 635-char script): `eleven_v3` renders in 12.0-19.9s vs 4.3-5.0s for `eleven_multilingual_v2` and 1.8-3.2s for `eleven_turbo_v2_5`; TTFB ≈ wall (transfer is only 0.35-0.93s), and normalization on/auto/off, `pcm_24000`, `mp3_44100_128`, `/stream/with-timestamps` and `seed` all move it by less than the run-to-run noise. v3 latency is `1.76s + 17.9ms/char` (R²=0.976). ARN is keeping v3 for voice quality, so the only lever is RENDER COUNT — and four renders was guaranteed, not unlucky:
- `WordTargetOvershoot` (1.15) was applied ON TOP of `PaceBoostWpm`. Algebraically `W = slot × (wpm+boost)/60 × overshoot` gives a natural read `D = slot × factor × overshoot`, while acceptance requires `D ≤ slot × factor` — so acceptance requires `overshoot ≤ 1.0`. Every pace-boosted render overran by exactly 15% and paid a measure-then-trim re-synthesis (109-word target = 48.5s natural against a 38.0s ceiling).
- Even unstacked, the boosted target aims at `slot × factor` EXACTLY — the ceiling itself — where integer rounding alone can put it out of reach (94.8 → 95 words = 38.10s vs a 38.02s ceiling), and the measured ±2.3s render-to-render variance of `eleven_v3` on identical input makes it a coin flip.
- `MaxSlowDownFactor` is 1.0 in `appsettings.json` (overriding the 1.10 code default), pinning the floor at the slot. The band `[30.0 .. 38.0]s` is 8.0s wide while sentences are 4-9s each, so exactly ONE integer sentence count fits and the trimmer's only escape from an overrun is to step one sentence too far and undershoot the floor. Verified: pass 1 trimmed 102 → 63 words → 29.3s → content-limited → an entire second pass.

**Decision:** The pace boost now owns both ends of the band, and boosted targets aim at its middle.
- `WordTargetCalculator.ComputeWordTargetFromWordsPerMinute` drops `overshoot` whenever `paceBoostWpm > 0`. Unboosted callers are untouched.
- New `WordTargetCalculator.ComputeEffectiveMaxSlowDownFactor(wpm, paceBoostWpm, configured, absoluteCeiling)` grants the extra slow-down EARNED by the boost at half its rate — a boost needing 1.20x speed-up permits 1.10x slow-down — capped at `1 + (AbsolutePaceBoostSpeedUpCeiling-1)/2 = 1.175`, never below the configured value, and an exact passthrough at zero boost. Half, not full, because slowing a read drags audibly sooner than compressing one tightens.
- New `WordTargetCalculator.ComputeBoostedWordTarget` aims a boosted script at `ceiling × (1 - 0.08)` natural seconds — just inside `slot × speedUp`, floored at the slow-fill floor — instead of at the ceiling itself. The 8% margin is sized from two dev measurements: eleven_v3 render-to-render duration variance on IDENTICAL input is ±2.3s (~±5% of a 45s read), and the draft undershoots its word target by up to 7%. On the motivating voice/slot that is 82 words with ~3.0s of ceiling clearance.
- `maxSlowDownFactorOverride` is threaded alongside the existing `maxSpeedUpFactorOverride` through `IAudioPipelineService.SynthesizeWithDurationTargetAsync` / `FineTuneToTargetDuration`, `AudioDurationFineTuner.FineTuneToTargetDurationCore` / `SlowFillToTarget`, `ScriptGenerationEngine` (including the `DurationController.Plan` predictive-fit gate, which was passing the CONFIGURED factors and so ignored the boost on both sides) and `AudioFinalizer`'s re-voice path.
- `BulletinEditingBand.Compute` derives its floor/ceiling from the SLOT rather than from the already-rounded target. This fixed a real operator-facing bug: the ceiling was `round(target × factor)` with the boost already inside `target`, applying it TWICE — a 30s slot at 150 wpm + 60 boost was advertised as 142 words, a 56.8s read that is still 42s after maximum compression.
- `AiSettings:ElevenLabs:Seed` set to `20260804` (was null). Measured effect: duration spread on identical input 4.64s → 0.48s. No latency change; it makes the aim point deterministic instead of a lottery.

**Rationale:** Staying on `eleven_v3` fixes the render cost at ~13-16s each, so the only available win is landing the FIRST render inside the band. Aiming just inside the ceiling keeps the boost the operator actually asked for while clearing the render variance that made the old ceiling-exact aim a coin flip. Measured on the live API with the job's real script: 63 words = 27.8-28.8s, which the old 30.0s floor rejected and the new 26.5s floor accepts; 81 words = 36.2-38.1s. Half-rate slow-down keeps the extra allowance tied to what an operator actually asked for via `PaceBoostWpm` rather than loosening the global config for unboosted voices, and it stays a safety net for draft undershoot rather than something the aim leans on.

**Consequences:** Boosted word targets drop (109 → 82 for the motivating voice/slot; at that voice's current 137.8 wpm calibration the old formula still yields 102 words = 45.8s natural against a 38.7s ceiling, i.e. a guaranteed trim). Unboosted voices keep today's word targets exactly; only their operator-facing band ceiling moves by ±1 word (no more compounded rounding). Two `BroadcastOrchestratorTests` NSubstitute stubs needed the new 12th optional arg — a stub pinned to the old arity silently stops matching a BOOSTED call only, which is why 619 of 621 tests passed while the two `PaceBoostWpm_Positive` tests failed on a null Result.

**Rejected first attempt — aiming at the band MIDPOINT (kept because the failure mode is not obvious):** the midpoint of `[slot / slowDown, slot × speedUp]` is by construction about half the boost, and draft undershoot pushes it lower still. Deployed to dev and trialled on three real bulletins (`bfcc2f61`, `992209ef`, `f08e3fb4`; melbourne 30s, Dolly Male Young v4, `PaceBoostWpm=40`, `eleven_v3`). It fixed the render count exactly as designed — target 109 → 73-75 words, **1 render each, 0 trims, 0 content-limited, audio phase 70.1s → 10.3-12.2s** — and it silently stopped delivering the boost: compression 1.107x / 0.990x / 1.017x, i.e. **+14.3 / -1.4 / +2.4 wpm of the 40 requested (36% / -3% / 6%)** against 84% under the old code. `992209ef` aired SLOWER than the voice's natural pace because the newly earned slow-down headroom was spent stretching a read that was meant to be compressed. Lesson: a duration-fit change must be judged on DELIVERED PACE, not just render count; `WordTargetCalculatorTests.PaceBoostedTarget_ActuallyDeliversMostOfTheRequestedBoost` now pins ≥60% delivery and forbids sub-1.0x compression on a boosted voice.

**Dev trial of the shipped rule (ceiling − 8%), same voice/slot/config, 3 bulletins:** `63afe348` target 82 → 84 words → 36.2s natural → 1 render, 1.207x, **72% of the boost**; `8d76f0d7` target 82 → 76 words → 31.0s → 1 render, 1.033x, 12% (draft 7% under target AND read 147 wpm against a 138 wpm calibration — both variance sources compounding on the low side); `c48410b6` target **104** → 4 renders, 3 trims, 115.4s — the ORIGINAL failure in full. Boost delivery across the three: 72% / 12% / 70% (mean 52%) against mid-band's 13% and the old code's 84%. The aim rule is right; `c48410b6` failed on its INPUT, not the rule — see the residual below.

**Residual, and after the dev trial the DOMINANT remaining risk:** the boosted aim is computed from `calibratedWpm`, and that input is unstable by ±35% run to run. `c48410b6` (02:28:56Z) implied a `calibratedWpm` of **186.1**; `8d76f0d7` three minutes earlier implied **138.3**. All six attempt-level calibration writes in that window measured 136-147 wpm, and moving the row from 138 to 186 at α=0.3 needs a single measurement of ~298 wpm — which `RecordActualDurationAsync`'s 90-240 wpm sanity gate makes impossible. `CalibrateVoiceAsync` (the 37-word/60-syllable synthetic `ReferencePhrase`) has NO sanity gate, and `RunCount` advanced 212 → 220 across the three runs while only 6 attempt writes occurred — 2 unexplained. [INFERENCE] a reference-phrase recalibration wrote an out-of-family rate mid-sequence. Underlying causes, all still open: (1) `VoiceCalibrationService` EMAs two populations into one row — the reference phrase reads 158.6 wpm and is ALWAYS rendered on the configured default model regardless of the profile's own model (`CalibrateVoiceAsync` passes no `modelOverride`), while real bulletin reads are 128-147 wpm; (2) the calibration key (`{voiceId}_{speed}_{stability}_{similarity}_{style}_{boost}`) omits the MODEL, and the same voice reads 135.6 wpm on `eleven_v3` vs 159.4 on `eleven_multilingual_v2` vs 170.0 on `eleven_turbo_v2_5`; (3) at α=0.3 the effective memory is ~3 measurements, so `RunCount: 220` implies far more confidence than the value carries; (4) `WordsPerMinute` is derived as `EMA(syllablesPerMinute) / EMA(syllablesPerWord)`, which is not `EMA(wpm)` when the populations differ in syllables-per-word (1.622 reference vs ~1.53 real). Next slice: sanity-gate every calibration writer, rate-limit the per-write EMA delta, restrict the reference phrase to bootstrapping a COLD row, and put the model in the key.

**NOT attributable to this change (earlier claim retracted):** the mid-band critique blamed a dropped fuel close on the tighter word budget. The trial does not support that. Fuel-close presence: pre-change base rate **15/20 = 75%** across melbourne jobs with fuel enabled and fuel data present; mid-band 2/3; ceiling − 8% 1/3 — on a LARGER budget than mid-band. With n=3 per arm this is writer variance, not budget pressure (at p=0.75, P(≤1 of 3) ≈ 0.16). `BulletinDurationFitter.LockedTailStart` protecting the close from the TRIMMER but nothing protecting it at DRAFT time remains a real structural gap, but it is pre-existing and unmeasured here.

## 2026-08-04 - The director, measured against real pipeline inputs: 64% -> 98%

**Status:** committed and gate-verified; NOT deployed (PIM elevation still lapsed)

**Decision:** rewrite `prompts/director.md` lean with explicit emphasis budgets and NO worked
examples; render an empty tag palette as a sentinel rather than a blank; retry in code when a
required tag is missing; and move grave-bulletin tag selection into the delivery style's tone.

**Rationale:** iterated against 18 REAL captured pipeline director inputs (from
`llm-call-captures`, 16 jobs) plus 9 gravity cases augmented onto real scripts, scored by a
deterministic 12-check rubric encoding the calls I would make, 3 repeats per case (n=81). Guidance
came from OpenAI's own GPT-5.6 prompting guide, which prescribes exactly this method: "Remove one
group of instructions, examples, or tools at a time, then rerun the same evals."

**Context:** iteration was driven entirely by captured production inputs rather than invented
ones, which is what surfaced every finding below.

**Context - what real inputs exposed that synthetic ones hid:**
- The previous few-shot version CAPS-flooded real bulletins: up to **9 capitalised words** in one
  read. The examples were 2-sentence toys, so their per-sentence density exploded on a real 60-100
  word script. A bulletin with every road status capitalised is shouted flat.
- **Removing the worked examples IMPROVED the result** (85% vs 80% with them, and 41% shorter). The
  examples leaked their specifics: they taught `[firmly]` onto an EMPTY palette, then taught capitals
  to calm reads. Explicit numeric budgets did the work the examples were supposed to do. Directly
  contradicts the previous day's decision to add them - measured, not argued.
- Adding gravity prose degraded it every single time (three attempts: 74%, 81%, 73% vs 85% lean).
- Empty-palette tag invention traces to the TONE, not the examples: shown a blank list, the model
  turns "Firm, clear and direct" into `[firmly]` on 3 of 3 runs. Naming the absence removes the cause.
- A tone amendment reading "place it on the sentence carrying the travel advice" made the model
  INVENT advice ("take", "instead") on real bulletins that have none - a word mutation on 6 of 81
  runs. Synthetic cases all had an advice sentence, so this was invisible until real inputs.

**Measured, and where I was wrong:** temperature is NOT the lever - 0.3 scored identically to 1.0
(69/81 both), which kills the hypothesis recorded the previous turn. `reasoning: low` was slightly
WORSE than `none` (22 vs 23 of 27) and costs latency, so `none` stays.

**The floor was structural, not textual.** Prompt wording alone gets a tag onto the read ~85% of the
time and no rewording moved it - the reported "I only ever get `[firmly]`, and often nothing" symptom.
Emitting at least one tag from a non-empty palette is a CHECKABLE postcondition, so it is now enforced
