the way word-immutability already was: nudge and retry, keeping the best take. A take that only lacked
a tag still ships (its capitalisation and pacing beat an undirected read) rather than being discarded.

**Consequences:** 64% -> 89% on the prompt alone -> **98% (53/54)** with the sentinel, the retry and
the amended Drive Authority tone. Blocking eval `arn-director-contract-v1` PASS 3/3;
`eval.sh --script-only` held its baseline band; 3336 backend tests green.

**Not done:** deployment, still blocked on PIM. The ARN Drive Authority tone update IS live on dev
(styles are data, not code) - so until the backend ships, dev runs the new tone against the old prompt.

## 2026-08-04 - The operator rewrite is one agent-routed role, not a raw-model call

**Status:** deployed to dev and verified live

**Decision:** route the operator-facing delivery rewrite (`POST /jobs/{id}/retone`) through its own
Foundry prompt agent `arn-delivery-writer`, give it a delivery-specific system prompt for the
raw-model fallback, and teach it what "energy" means when the news is bad.

**Rationale:** asked to "dramatically energise the tone of the script", the rewrite returned
`[firmly] Important road update...` - authority, not energy. Two causes, both structural.

**Context:** two structural causes, both found by measuring against the CAPTURED deployed
request rather than the prompt files on disk.

**Context - the system prompt was fighting the request.** `DispatchLlmAsync("DeliveryWriter", ...)`
passed no `systemInstructionsOverride`, so the raw-model path fell back to
`PromptLibrary.SystemInstructions`. Captured live, that is **18,607 characters** of composed
bulletin-writer editorial prompt whose third line reads "plain, direct, conversational, and
grounded. You are not a presenter persona." An 18.6 KB system prompt built to keep copy plain,
wrapped around a 2 KB request for presentation, wins. Reproduced 4/4 with the real instructions; a
4 KB approximation using `prompts/system.md` alone did NOT reproduce it, which is why measuring
against the captured request rather than the file mattered.

Measuring it also caught a worse defect: on the old path the rewrite trimmed **-3% to -37%** of the
words and dropped up to 2 road facts. On a fixed 30s slot a third of the bulletin missing is dead
air the fitter has to cover.

**Why an agent rather than only an override.** `ResponsesTransport.SendToAgentAsync` does not accept
`systemInstructionsOverride` at all - an agent call carries the agent's own neutral shim and can
never inherit the writer's editorial prompt. That is exactly why the Director, which was already
agent-routed, never had this bug. Agent routing makes the class of failure impossible rather than
fixed, so `arn-delivery-writer` is provisioned alongside the other role agents (neutral shim,
`json_object`, effort `none`) and `DeliveryWriterAgentName` selects it.
`PromptLibrary.DeliveryWriterSystem` remains as the raw-model fallback for any environment without
the agent configured.

**Context - `[firmly]` is not energy.** `prompts/delivery-writer.md` listed `[firmly]` and
`[urgently]` together as one "firm" family and carried energy examples only on all-clear bulletins.
Given three closures the model picked the sober half - the same failure mode the Director had. The
prompt now separates the registers explicitly: brightness for good news, URGENCY AND PACE for bad
news that is not grave, nothing lifted for grave news, and `[firmly]` named as authority rather than
energy.

**Consequences:** the rewrite now does what the operator asks, measured live (12 runs on the
deployed dev endpoint, one real Mildura bulletin, 4 registers):
"dramatically energise" -> `[urgently]` (+`[brightly]` on the good news), "sound much more excited"
-> `[urgently]`+`[brightly]` 3/3, "read this calmly and with respect" -> `[quietly]` 3/3, "just read
it straight" -> no tags and 0% growth 3/3. Word growth -1% to +9% against the +/-10% slot rule, and
**zero facts lost in all 12**. Captures confirm `Model: agent:arn-delivery-writer` with system
instructions down from 18,607 to 78 characters.

**Still open:** `/jobs/{id}/direct` (the word-immutable director exposed as an operator tool) is not
wired to any UI control - only `/retone` and `/audition` are. It duplicates a concept the pipeline
already applies automatically per station and is a candidate for removal.

**Not re-run for this change:** backend E2E. It hangs under Azurite port contention in a detached
worktree; the change is two prompt files plus three one-line wirings and touches no queue or HTTP
lifecycle. 3890 other backend tests pass.

## 2026-08-04 — Station bookends: per-station intro/outro wrapped around every bulletin

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Filler statements were the only station-flavoured text, and they fire only when real content leaves a gap in the slot (ScriptGenerationEngine's fillerGapSeconds). ARN asked for a guaranteed, controlled opening and closing phrase per station — 'Looking over Melbourne today' / 'That's it for Melbourne traffic' — with brands (KIIS, GOLD, regionals) sharing wording while each station names its own city.

**Decision:** Two independent shared libraries (Intros, Outros), versioned, mirroring the DeliveryStyle library pattern: Bookend aggregate + BookendKind + kind-partitioned TableStorageBookendRepository (radioBookends) + BookendService + BookendsHttpTrigger at bookends/{kind}. Stations assign one of each via MarketSchedule.IntroBookendId/OutroBookendId, each with an optional BookendRotationPolicy (Single/RoundRobin/TimeOfDay) mirroring VoiceRotationPolicy and sharing one BookendRotationCursor. Templates carry {token} placeholders resolved by BookendTokenResolver: built-ins city/market/station derived from the schedule, overridden per station by MarketSchedule.BookendTokens. Bookends are synthesised IN THE SAME TTS TAKE (BulletinBookendComposer wraps the finished read after every LLM stage); their spoken cost is subtracted from the writer's word target BEFORE drafting; the writer is shown both texts as fixed context in prompts/draft.md so it writes only the middle. When a station has an outro AND filler is selected, the filler text goes INLINE before the outro instead of being stitched after it.

**Rationale:** A shared library with placeholders answers the 'copy to' request by making it an assignment rather than a copy, and prevents a station inheriting another's wording — the risky part (the city name) is per-station data. Same-take synthesis avoids an audible seam exactly where it would be most noticeable, between the body and a fixed closer. Subtracting the bookend budget up front is mandatory: unlike filler (topped up afterwards) a bookend is unconditional, so drafting to the full slot would overshoot and burn duration-fit retries on every bookended bulletin. Inline filler is the price of correct ordering — a stitched clip plays AFTER the closer, so the bulletin would announce it was over and keep talking. No cap on bookend length: the operator sees the squeeze in the studio's resolved preview, which is a better guard than a number.

**Consequences:** Inline filler forfeits the exact-duration guarantee and the post-synthesis filler rescue (FillerRescueOvershootToleranceSeconds), which measures the true residual gap after synthesis and cannot stitch behind a closer; outro stations fall through to the existing content-limited retry instead. Measured on the stratified 10-fixture fallback replay panel: filled 2/10 (76% mean best fill) vs 1/10 (71%) pre-change — improved, no regression. {city} derives best-effort from the market id, so 'goldcoast' yields 'Goldcoast': the schedule studio's live resolved preview plus an OVERRIDDEN marker on the derived row is the only guard, and the schedule API rejects an assignment whose tokens cannot all be filled. Job gains IntroBookendId/Version + OutroBookendId/Version provenance; regeneration replays the pinned version via JobService.ResolveBookendsAsync. Poller resolution is fail-soft: a missing, archived, or unfillable bookend drops that end rather than failing the slot.


## 2026-08-04 — Act on predicted OVERRUNS, and stop the calibration row from being poisoned

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Follow-up to "Pace boost owns BOTH ends of the acceptance band" (same day). That change got 2 of 3 dev bulletins to a single render, but the third (`c48410b6`) reproduced the original failure in full — 4 eleven_v3 renders, 3 trims, 115.4s — because its word target came out **104** instead of 82. Inverting the aim formula showed why: `calibratedWpm` read **186.1** at 02:28:56Z where the run three minutes earlier read **138.3**. Every one of the six attempt-level calibration writes in that window measured 136-147 wpm, and moving the row from 138 to 186 at α=0.3 requires a single measurement of ~298 wpm — which `RecordActualDurationAsync`'s 90-240 wpm gate makes impossible. `RunCount` advanced 212 → 220 while only 6 attempt writes occurred. Measuring the remaining error budget: draft-vs-target mean **−3.3%** sd 4.2% (biased short, and the `SlotFitPlanner`/`DraftWordBudget` dead zone is −16%/+15% with no correction inside it); content read-rate CV **3.3%** (133.5-147.1 wpm across 9 takes); same-text render variance ±5% → ~1% once seeded. Sum of the controllable terms is ~5.4% sd against an 8% aim margin, so ~7% of runs overrun on merit — but a 35% calibration error swamps all of it.

**Decision:** Two changes, cause first then safety net.
- **Calibration writers hardened.** `CalibrateVoiceAsync` (the synthetic 37-word/60-syllable `ReferencePhrase`) had NO plausibility gate while real-bulletin writes did, making it the only path able to store an impossible rate; both writers now share the same bounds (2-12 syll/s, 0.8-3.0 syll/word, 90-240 wpm) and a rejected reference render is never saved. `VoiceCalibration.RecordMeasurement` rate-limits every rate to `MaxPerMeasurementDrift` (10%) per measurement, so one bad write costs one step instead of a third of the row. The reference phrase now bootstraps a COLD row only — it reads 158.6 wpm against 128-147 for real bulletin copy, so blending produced a number describing neither; on a warm row it only refreshes the staleness clock. It also honours the caller's model (`modelOverride` threaded through `IVoiceCalibrationService.GetCalibrationMetricsAsync`/`CalibrateVoiceAsync`), because the same voice reads 135.6 wpm on `eleven_v3` vs 159.4 on `eleven_multilingual_v2` vs 170.0 on `eleven_turbo_v2_5` and the reference render previously used the configured default regardless of the profile's model.
- **`FitPlan.TrimBeforeSynthesis`.** `DurationController.CorrectableWindow` returned `(Lower, Upper)` and `Plan` destructured `var (lower, _)` — the upper bound was computed and thrown away, so `FitPlan` had no overrun outcome and every overrun cost a full render to discover. `Plan` now takes `canTrim` and returns `TrimBeforeSynthesis` when the ENTIRE predicted interval is past the compression budget (mirror-image conservatism to the underrun gate). `ScriptGenerationEngine` responds by trimming the script text before synthesis, using `BulletinDurationFitter.EstimateSentenceSpans` + a new spans-based `FitByTrimming` overload so the pre-synthesis trim shares the post-synthesis trim's arithmetic AND its weather/fuel close protection.

**Rationale:** Fixing the aim without fixing its input just moves the failure. The calibration work removes the condition that produced the bad target; the overrun branch means that if any future input error does push the aim past the ceiling, the correction is free string work rather than a 13-16s eleven_v3 render. Sharing `FitByTrimming` between the two call sites is what guarantees a pre-synthesis trim and a post-synthesis trim cannot disagree about what is droppable.

**Consequences:** Dev trial, 3 bulletins, melbourne 30s / Dolly Male Young v4 / `PaceBoostWpm=40` / `eleven_v3`: targets **83 / 83 / 82** — stable, with the calibration row holding 138.1 wpm across all three (223 runs) and no spike. **1 render each, 0 trims, 0 content-limited.** Boost delivered **46% / 59% / 68%** (mean 58%) against mid-band's 13% and ceiling-aim-without-hardening's 51%; never below 1.12x compression. Weather/fuel close present **3/3**. Totals 31.4-35.2s (higher than the previous arm's 23-30s only because HEAD no longer skips review/refine — that is unrelated concurrent work, and the render count is what this change owns). **The overrun branch did not fire in the trial** — correctly, since the aim now sits inside the band and nothing confidently overran; it is covered by unit tests, not by this trial, and exists for the `c48410b6` shape. Cross-arm ledger for the same voice/slot: old code 4 renders / 84% boost; mid-band 1 render / 13%; ceiling−8% 1-4 renders / 51%; this change 1 render / 58%.

**Still open:** the calibration ROW KEY (`{voiceId}_{speed}_{stability}_{similarity}_{style}_{boost}`) still omits the model, so a voice used on two models shares one row. The bootstrap-only rule plus the drift limiter bound the harm, and profiles pin a model, so this is latent rather than active — but it is a data migration (row keys change, rows re-bootstrap) and was deliberately not bundled here. Also unaddressed: the draft's −16%/+15% uncorrected dead zone and its negative bias, which is now the largest remaining controllable error term.

## 2026-08-04 — Bookends are one paired library, not separate intro and outro libraries

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Bookends shipped on 2026-08-04 as TWO independent versioned libraries (Intros, Outros) with two per-station assignments, two rotation policies and two nav sections — the option chosen when the design was first put to ARN. On review the operator surface was the problem: two galleries to keep in step, two selectors per station, and a wrong-kind failure mode (an outro id in the intro slot) that the API had to defend against.

**Decision:** Collapsed to ONE library of intro+outro PAIRS. BookendKind is deleted. BookendTemplate carries IntroText + OutroText together (either may be blank, not both); the aggregate id prefix is 'bk-'; the repository uses a single 'Bookend' partition; routes are plain /api/bookends with no {kind} segment; preview resolves both lines in one call. A station assigns one MarketSchedule.BookendId with one BookendRotation policy and one BookendTokens override map. The context, both queue messages and the job record each carry a single ResolvedBookends (IntroText, OutroText, Id, Version) — Job drops from four provenance columns to BookendId + BookendVersion. The web app has one 'Bookends' nav section, one gallery whose cards show both lines, one studio editing both lines in one form, and one per-station selector whose options are labelled 'intro + outro' / 'intro only' / 'outro only'.

**Rationale:** An opener and its matching sign-off are one editorial decision, so making them one record matches how they are actually written and removes the risk of a station carrying a mismatched half. It deletes an entire failure class — a wrong-kind assignment is now impossible by construction, so the API check and its error message are gone rather than merely unreachable. It halves the operator surface (one gallery, one selector, one rotation policy) and the persisted surface (two job columns instead of four, four schedule columns instead of six). One-sided pairs preserve everything the two-library shape could express.

**Consequences:** Clean cutover, no compatibility shims: the old IntroBookendId/OutroBookendId/IntroRotation/OutroRotation schedule columns and the four job columns are abandoned in place. TableStorageScheduleRepository degrades a row carrying only the old column names to an unassigned schedule rather than throwing, so pre-existing dev rows load cleanly but lose their assignment and must be re-assigned — verified on dev. Bookends created under the two-library shape are not migrated. Rotation now cycles whole pairs, so an intro set and an outro set can no longer rotate at different rates; nobody had asked for that. Everything else — same-take synthesis, the word-target subtraction, filler inline before the outro, fail-soft poller resolution, the studio's resolved preview as the guard against a derived {city} — is unchanged from the 2026-08-04 bookends decision, which this supersedes only on library shape.

## 2026-08-04 — The slot-fit trim must protect the station's closer

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** A dev quality pass across all bookend paths (2026-08-04) found three defects that unit tests could not have caught, all in the seams between bookends and pre-existing machinery. The worst: an overrunning read is fitted by BulletinDurationFitter dropping trailing sentences, and the outro is the last thing in the take — so the closer was silently deleted. Observed on adelaide job 7a33aa7160cd: a 93-word read trimmed to 82 words dropped 'Closer only for Adelaide.', and the timeline said only that the weather/fuel close was kept.

**Decision:** BulletinDurationFitter.FitByTrimming takes an optional lockedSuffix; LockedTailStart locks that suffix FIRST and unconditionally, then continues over the contiguous weather/fuel close as before, so the overrun comes out of the traffic items. The suffix is threaded from the resolved pair through IAudioPipelineService.SynthesizeWithDurationTargetAsync and is also passed at the pre-synthesis predictive trim. Matching is on letters and digits only (delivery tags stripped, punctuation and casing ignored) and the suffix must be accounted for IN FULL — a partial match locks nothing, because half a sign-off is worse than none. Two further fixes: JobService.RegenerateJobAsync now resolves the pair BEFORE RequestRegeneration (which clears BookendId/Version), and ConfigExportBuilder now emits the Bookends section.

**Rationale:** The closer existing at all is the feature's entire premise — 'the closer always has the last word'. A trim that deletes it is worse than a trim that shortens the traffic, because the station loses its branding rather than one road mention, and it fails silently. The locked-tail mechanism already existed for exactly this reason (the weather/fuel close was being trimmed away, published job 19be05d7), so extending it is the smallest change consistent with the design rather than a new special case. The regeneration bug repeated a trap the code already warns about for delivery style, and export-without-bookends made config transfer one-directional, quietly losing a library when moving between environments.

**Consequences:** A bookended read now sacrifices traffic content instead of the closer when it overruns; on a tight slot that means fewer roads mentioned. When the close plus closer alone cannot fit the budget the fitter still degrades to the plain prefix trim, which can drop the closer — unavoidable and extreme. Adding lockedSuffix changed the SynthesizeWithDurationTargetAsync arity, so every NSubstitute stub of it needed a matcher (44 call sites across 5 test files). Separately measured and NOT fixed: on a 15-second slot a 6-word pair costs ~13% of the word budget and pushed thin-market portlincoln from success into the filler-cart fallback, where the same station succeeded without a bookend — the length cap declined on 2026-08-04 remains declined, and BookendTemplate.MaxTextLength is where a slot-relative cap would go if the fallback rate on short slots becomes a problem.

## 2026-08-04 — The pace floor must weigh the script the extend would grow, not the post-trim survivor

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** A 5-bulletin dev trial on eleven_v3 at PaceBoostWpm=40 (jobs 92b70b85 / 18e28387 / 45b1cacd / 175950d0 / ca77fee5, 2026-08-04) measured every duration error term per run. Calibration bias is now -0.3% (claims 141.0 wpm, measured 140.6) so the calibration hardening worked, and all 5 files shipped at exactly 30.0000s. But 175950d0 burned a second 38s eleven_v3 render that could not change anything: the drafter produced 90 words against an 83 target, the read overran, the trim cut it to 72, and the pace floor then compared 72 against the 75-word floor and fired an extend whose baseline was the untrimmed 90-word script.

**Decision:** The pace-floor condition in ScriptGenerationEngine now measures attemptResult.ValidatedScript - the script ExtendScriptAsync would actually grow - instead of attemptResult.WordCount, the post-trim survivor. Filler still qualifies: trading a stopgap bed for grounded content is what the branch exists for. Two tests in BroadcastOrchestratorDecoupledFitTests pin both directions, and they share an explicit 13-arg AnySynthCall matcher because a boosted run passes a non-null maxSlowDownFactorOverride that a defaulted stub silently misses.

**Rationale:** The floor asks 'did the drafter under-produce?', which is a question about the drafted script, not about what survived the fitter. A trim is positive proof the slot could not hold those words, so extending from the untrimmed script can only re-overrun and re-trim to a byte-identical read - provably futile, not merely unlikely to help: ExtendScriptAsync saw 90 words vs MinAcceptableWords(83)=70, expanded nothing, and returned its input unchanged. This is the same untrimmed-baseline mixing already fixed in the content-limited extend path, surviving in its sibling.

**Consequences:** Removes a guaranteed-wasted render (38s of 95s on the measured job) with no behavioural change to the genuine-undershoot case, which is why the new undershoot test passes on both the old and new condition. Deliberately NOT addressed: the draft's word-count error is now the dominant remaining term at 8.4% sd against an 8% aim margin, which predicts a 22% ceiling-breach rate and matched the observed 1-in-5. Shrinking it means touching script generation, and raising the margin trades boost delivery away (measured curve: 12% margin gives 12% breach at 46% boost, 16% gives 6% at 28%) - so the margin stays at 8% and breaches stay absorbed by the trim.

## 2026-08-05 — Developer documentation is published as a seventh group, not withheld or relabelled

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN receives the repository and a DevOps project administrator role, but the published site had no page describing the code or the pipeline. Code architecture was absent by design and CI/CD was one diagram plus one paragraph; the command reference told the reader to 'select the platform deployment pipeline' without naming it. 2,261 lines of accurate material existed internally in CONTRIBUTING.md and docs/CODEMAPS/, unpublished. Three reasons kept it out: audience (correct), the 2026-07-28 client-readiness decision (correct in intent), and the leak guard mechanically blocking repository paths, .cs filenames and PascalCase code spans (a guard that had quietly become the decision rather than enforcing one).

**Decision:** A third audience, AUD_DEV, is published alongside AUD_ARN, rendered as a seventh site group 'For developers' in develop/. Six pages: two new (solution-structure, delivery-pipeline) and four promoted (local-development plus the three test-harness documents withdrawn in July). Pages in develop/ are exempt from five leak classes (repository path, repository file, code identifier, project jargon, internal tooling) via DEV_EXEMPT. The other six classes stay enforced: naming an individual, our organisation, an internal defect or risk id, a commercial term, or a TBD still fails the build there. A new sidebar-coverage check fails the sync when a placed group is missing from astro.config.mjs.

**Rationale:** The three harness documents were withdrawn for audience reasons, not classification reasons, which is a placement question with a placement answer. Keeping developer material in a separate group preserves the property that makes the site work, one reader per group, while closing a real hole: whoever ARN puts on this codebase in six months had nothing to read. Scoping the guard exemption to one directory gives implementation vocabulary a principled boundary instead of the ad-hoc per-page exemptions it would otherwise need, and keeps the engagement, people and commercial classes enforced everywhere. The sidebar check exists because the first attempt built six unreachable pages: Starlight's sidebar is declared in config, so a group can render nothing while the build stays green.

**Consequences:** 37 published pages in seven groups, up from 31 in six. Promoting the harness pages needed one round of removing engagement identifiers (SG3, SC-01, SoW) from load-testing.md prose; the guard caught all five. The signed cover's documentation-set table, the handover pack artefact index, and docs-site/README.md now name seven groups and must be updated together. docs-site/astro.config.mjs duplicates the group list by necessity and is now guarded rather than trusted.

## 2026-08-05 — Azure Portal screenshots are tracked files captured through a signed-in browser, not build output

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The monitoring page told an operator to open Resource groups, choose a resource group and select Workbooks, with no picture, and the published corpus held 416 console screenshots and zero Azure images. Portal captures cannot be produced the way the other two image classes are: the Portal needs an interactive Entra sign-in against real deployed resources, so no CI agent can regenerate them. Puppeteer could not capture them either, because its fixed protocolTimeout is exceeded by Page.captureScreenshot on the Portal and is not configurable from this harness.

**Decision:** A third image scheme, portal:, sourced from docs/assets/azure-portal/ and listed in TRACKED_SCHEMES so the gitignored-build-output cache does not apply. scripts/capture-portal-screenshots.mjs drives the operator's already-signed-in Chromium over its DevTools endpoint using raw CDP, one dedicated tab per target with focus emulation enabled, and redacts the signed-in account and avatar from the Portal header before every capture. Five captures: the workbook gallery, Operations Overview, Pipeline Latency, the Logs blade showing one traced bulletin, and the alert rules.

**Rationale:** Tracked rather than generated because there is nothing for a cache to stand in for and no pipeline that could rebuild them. Raw CDP because Puppeteer cannot complete the call. Focus emulation because Chromium throttles timers and stops compositing in background tabs, so the first parallel attempt had four of five targets time out at 120s while only the focused tab rendered; with it, five captures complete in 84s. Redaction because the Portal header renders the signed-in account on every blade, and publishing a consultant's email address on five client-facing images is exactly what the named-individual leak class exists to prevent. The Logs capture carries its query in Azure's own gzip-and-base64 share-link format rather than typing into Monaco, because the editor sits in a cross-origin iframe behind a first-run overlay that swallowed the click.

**Consequences:** Five tracked PNGs, roughly 900 KB, refreshed by one command. The captures show the development environment, so resource names read DEV and the reader substitutes their own; production is normally parked and its workbooks would render empty. The rig also revealed that the Logs blade opens a Queries hub overlay over its results by default, which is dismissed per-run by attaching to the blade's own iframe target.

## 2026-08-05 — Delivery devices are chosen by measurement, not by name

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** An operator asking to energise a bulletin got a single [urgently] tag. Measuring 50 text-level devices (364 generations, Welch t-test vs an 8-run unchanged control) showed why: NONE of the 9 deployed delivery-style palettes contained a single audible tag, and three of their tags ([cheerful], [emphatic], [upbeat]) are not in ElevenLabs' documented vocabulary at all. The writer prompt separately listed [urgently] as its firm-register tag and BANNED the breath family that actually works.

**Decision:** A device may only enter a palette or a prompt if it passes the measured audibility rule: it inserts non-speech (voiced fraction <=-6%), shifts pitch (>=10%), or changes duration (>=7%). Pitch-span and velocity changes are inaudible and must not be optimised. Tags are never placed on the opening line. Tag strings are treated as an exact lookup, never inflected. Energy comes from sentence structure, not from tags.

**Rationale:** Ear-confirmation validated the rule 18/19 with zero false positives, and span was inversely correlated with audibility, which is exactly why the old palettes measured as having effects while sounding identical. Placement outweighs tag choice: [whispering] is inert at the script start and drops pitch 22.7% one sentence in.

**Consequences:** prompts/delivery-writer.md rewritten (verified against the real model: OLD 4/4 runs produced [urgently], NEW 0/4); web/src/features/delivery/cues.ts regrouped by measured effect with an explicit Unverified group so existing styles keep readable labels; the six ARN delivery styles repaletted on dev; docs/reference/delivery-device-map.md records the dataset. Numbers are voice-specific and must be re-measured per voice and per ElevenLabs model release.

## 2026-08-05 — An overrunning toned read is reduced in measured cost order, never stripped wholesale

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Operators reported tags disappearing after a re-voice. Job de45b38b logged 'Operator delivery tones applied: 3 tag(s)' then 'Delivery tones dropped: the tagged read could not fit the slot without cutting content'. The guard was right that a tone may cost time but never content; its premise that 'tags slow the read' was wrong. Measurement (2026-08-05, 4.9% duration noise floor) shows the cost is dominated by pause punctuation and sentence structure - extra sentence breaks +12.3%, em dash +8.1%, ellipsis +5.3% - while among tags only the sound-inserting ones cost anything, and the manner tags are FREE OR FASTER than plain: [brightly] -6.2%, [firmly] -5.5%, [excitedly] -3.2%. Two of the three tags on that job were time-negative, so dropping them recovered almost nothing and destroyed the operator's register for it.

**Decision:** When a toned re-voice overruns and the duration fitter would trim content, reduce the read in measured cost order instead of discarding the tone: first flatten pause punctuation keeping every tag, then additionally remove only the time-costing (sound-inserting) tags, and only then fall back to the plain approved read. Each rung preserves the spoken words, and the rung that aired is logged with the tag count kept.

**Rationale:** The expensive devices are the ones removed first, so the operator keeps as much of the register as the slot allows. Classification is by measured duration cost (DeliveryTimeCost.TimeCostingTags), not by tag family, so a free manner tag is never spent to buy time it cannot buy.

**Consequences:** New DeliveryTimeCost helper in Domain/Services with 31 tests; AudioFinalizer.RevoiceExistingScriptAsync walks the ladder. Verified live on the reported job: 3 tags in, 2 kept on air ([excitedly], [brightly]) where the old path kept none. Costs up to two extra syntheses on an overrunning toned read, only in the case that previously discarded the tone outright.

## 2026-08-05 — Audio tags are gated at the synthesis boundary, not per caller

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Only eleven_v3 interprets inline audio tags; every other ElevenLabs model SPEAKS them. Measured on 2026-08-05 against the live dev app: the same tagged text sent to eleven_multilingual_v2 airs as "Excitedly, the Monash Freeway is closed city bound. Exhales sharply. Burke Road is clear?" A survey of the codebase found SEVEN ways a tag could reach synthesis and exactly ONE was gated (the director, via DeliveryTags.SupportsTags at LlmScriptGenerator.cs:700). The ungated paths were the operator's TonedScript on regenerate, the delivery writer behind POST /jobs/{id}/retone (whose prompt mandates at least two tags and which took a ttsModel parameter it never read), the neutral-delivery-policy pass-through in DeliveryDirector, the audition preview, and POST /synthesize. This was live, not theoretical: the dev voice profile 'Jeffrey (original)' is eleven_multilingual_v2 and is the voice on station KIIS 101.1, so operator tone requests on that station were producing tags for a voice that would read them out.

**Decision:** Gate tags at the ElevenLabs synthesis boundary as the load-bearing guarantee: ElevenLabsAudioSynthesizer strips every tag when the EFFECTIVE model (modelOverride ?? configured ModelId) does not support them. That is the single point all paths converge on and the only place the model actually sent is known. Keep per-source gates as courtesies so operators are not offered levers that cannot land: the delivery writer is told not to use tags (prompts/delivery-writer.md {{#if noTags}}) and its output is stripped; an operator TonedScript on a non-v3 job is refused with an explicit job-log line naming the model; the neutral-policy exit strips on the way past; the audition reports the tag count that was actually heard; and the web review UI withholds the palette and the rewrite control entirely, showing why. The web mirror of the rule is tone-marks.modelSupportsTags, a substring test on "v3" matching the backend rather than an equality check on eleven_v3.

**Rationale:** Gating N callers means the N+1th forgets. A choke point at the wire cannot be bypassed by a future caller, and it is the only layer that sees the true effective model, which can differ from what the pipeline believed when context.Model is absent. The per-source gates exist for honesty rather than safety: a v2 voice still gets the writer's strongest measured levers (sentence splitting, clause endings, ellipses, CAPS), so tone degrades gracefully instead of disappearing.

**Consequences:** DeliveryTags.ForModel is the shared helper, allocation-free when the text has no tag so it is free to sit on the synthesis path. Verified live end to end: raw v2 speaks the tag words, the deployed app on the same voice/model/text does not; on the deployed dev app /retone yields 3 tags on a v3 job and 0 on a v2 job across 4 runs each while both still get the structural rewrite; a toned re-voice on a v2 job logs 'Delivery tones not applied: this voice (eleven_multilingual_v2) cannot use audio tags'. Any station on a non-v3 profile silently loses tag-based delivery styles, which is correct but means voice-profile model choice now decides whether the tone feature exists for that station.


## 2026-08-05 — On a slot too short for both, the traffic wins and the bookend is dropped

**Status:** accepted (supersedes the "No cap on bookend length" position in "Station bookends: per-station intro/outro wrapped around every bulletin", 2026-08-04, and the "declined length cap is still declined" note in CONTEXT.md)

**Context:** The 2026-08-05 bug bash measured what the declined length cap actually costs. Dev job `f9907416a33342adbc5df52017780691`: a 15-second slot (portlincoln is the platform's only one) with the shared 17-word pair — intro "Looking over Adelaide today, your traffic update." (7 words) plus outro "That is it for Adelaide traffic on ZZ Test FM." (10 words) — spiralled through 4 generation attempts and 4+ ElevenLabs renders (14.0s → 17.4s → 13.0s → 11.0s), never converged, and landed on the generic filler cart with `ScriptText=null`. The aired audio contained NEITHER the traffic read NOR the station's top-and-tail. Subtracting the bookend budget up front is correct and unchanged; the defect was that an arithmetically impossible configuration was only discovered by burning four LLM calls and four synthesis renders, and the failure mode was the worst available one.

**Decision:** Prefer the traffic content. `BookendSlotFitPlanner` (Application/Broadcasting, pure and deterministic) evaluates `bookendSeconds + MinimumViableTrafficSeconds <= slotSeconds` BEFORE any drafting, and `ScriptGenerationEngine` drops the pair when it cannot fit, restoring the full word budget and recording an operator-legible reason in the job log. `MinimumViableTrafficWords = 21` is a word count, not a seconds constant, converted at the voice's calibrated pace so the threshold moves with the voice and the schedule gate and the engine can never disagree. The schedule PUT surfaces the same calculation as an advisory (`ScheduleSummaryDto.BookendFitWarning`) so an admin learns at assignment time; the assignment is NOT rejected, because generation now degrades gracefully and one short station must not veto a fleet-wide pair.

**Rationale:** Airing traffic without a station top-and-tail is a mild degradation; airing a canned filler cart with no traffic at all is a product failure. The constant is calibrated against the measured envelope rather than guessed: 8.2s of remaining room demonstrably did not converge on a 15s slot, so the floor must exceed it, and 21 words (8.4s at 150 wpm) is the smallest whole-word increment that does while still retaining the pair on a 16s slot (7.2s + 8.4s = 15.6s). 22 words was rejected because it lands the 16s case exactly on the boundary. A hard length cap was declined and remains declined — this is a fit check at generation time, not a limit on what ARN may author.

**Consequences:** The primary regression test encodes the REAL 17-word pair on a 15s slot, not a synthetic one — an earlier draft of this work passed only because its fixture mis-counted its own outro as 11 words, which made the case genuinely fit and left the observed failure unguarded. The 30s and 16s cases assert the pair is RETAINED, so the ordinary path is provably unchanged. Lowering `MinimumViableTrafficWords` back to 20 reopens the exact job above; the constant's doc comment says so. Reject-to-fallback now measures the cart's duration and warns when it under-fills ("covers 16.0s of the 30s slot — 14.0s of dead air if approved as-is"); the automatic path additionally pads toward the slot with distinct filler, while the operator path is visibility-only because padding there would run TTS-on-cache-miss inside a synchronous HTTP call.


## 2026-08-05 — Market place names come from one shared table, not from slug munging or the schedule name

**Status:** accepted (supersedes the "{city} derives best-effort from the market id" / "the preview is the guard" position in "Station bookends", 2026-08-04)

**Context:** `BookendTokenResolver` derived `{city}` by splitting the market id on `-` and title-casing it, and emitted `{market}` as the raw slug. Measured across all 13 live dev markets on 2026-08-05: `{market}` aired `cairns-4ca` including the call-sign suffix, and `{city}` produced `Portaugusta`, `Portlincoln` and `Demo`. Because those values are non-empty they passed the unfillable-token gate, so the console never blocked them and the mangled word aired. The 2026-08-04 position was that the live resolved preview is the guard; the bug bash showed a guard an operator must notice is not a guard.

**Decision:** One shared `MarketNames` table in Domain/Services, promoted from the private `CityMappings` that `LlmScriptGenerator` already used for prompt-side city derivation, holding the 13 live market ids plus the short codes and aliases the LLM path depends on. `{city}` and `{market}` resolve from it; `DeriveCity`'s slug munging is deleted with no forwarder. An unknown market id yields an EMPTY value, so the existing unfillable-token 400 fires at assignment time instead of a wrong word airing. Per-station `BookendTokens` overrides still win.

**Rationale:** The schedule's `Name` is a program name ("Adelaide Drive Traffic", "Cairns Star 102.7 Traffic"), so threading it through would air "for Adelaide Drive Traffic traffic on…" — worse than the slug. The place name is domain knowledge, not an LLM concern, and two tables holding the same city names would drift; the same wave fixed a defect (an inline `Contains("v3")` duplicating `PronunciationRule.PhonemeRulesSafeFor`) whose entire cause was a duplicated predicate. Failing the assignment gate is preferable to airing a mangled word, and it fails loudly at the moment the admin can fix it.

**Consequences:** `LlmScriptGenerator.DeriveCity` now reads the shared table and is behaviour-identical (exact lookup, then substring scan, then capitalise fallback), guarded by its existing `LlmCityDerivationTests`. A new market must be added to `MarketNames` before `{city}`/`{market}` will resolve for it — deliberate, since the alternative is a silent wrong read. A 13-market theory test asserts every configured market id yields its human-readable place name.


## 2026-08-06 — A station's own schedule is operator-editable within their assigned markets

**Status:** accepted (narrows the "everything else mutating → Admin" default in "Two AAD app roles, Operator and Admin", 2026-05, for this one route)

**Context:** An ARN operator (TEST) opened `/stations` and got the full-page "Admin access required" placeholder. The backend was never that strict: `GET /schedules` and `GET /schedules/{marketId}` are Operator, so the wall was purely a frontend route gate (`App.tsx` `requiredRole="admin"`, `routes.ts` nav metadata) sitting in front of an API that would have answered. The station's configuration is exactly what an operator needs to read and adjust for the market they are on call for — slot times, voice, delivery style, pronunciation dictionary, coverage, content toggles — and every other per-market operational surface (priority roads, filler statements, market guidance, verified pronunciations) is already Operator.

**Decision:** `PUT /api/schedules/{marketId}` resolves to Operator in `RouteRoleMatrix`; `DELETE` stays Admin. The route is unchanged otherwise: `ScheduleHttpTrigger.CreateOrUpdateSchedule` already runs `EnsureMarketAccessAsync`, so a scoped operator can only write a station they are assigned to, and "create a new station" — which is the same PUT with an unassigned market id — 403s for them without a second rule. Frontend: `/stations` is an operator route in both `App.tsx` and the nav metadata, and the three Admin-only actions are withheld from the row/card menus rather than left to fail — New station, Duplicate, Delete (`DELETE /schedules/{m}`) and Trigger now (`POST /broadcast`, Admin and market-unguarded). View details, Edit and the enable switch are shown, because all three are the operator-permitted PUT or a GET.

**Rationale:** The trust boundary that makes this safe is the market guard, not the role — the same reasoning that put publish and retone/audition with the operator on 2026-08-05. Withholding a control whose backend route is Admin is the other half: the bug bash's finding 9 was Rewrite/Audition rendered for operators against Admin routes, and shipping an Edit button that 403s would recreate it inverted. Delete is excluded deliberately: removing a station stops its automatic bulletins and the operator has no way to undo it, so it is not an operational act. Trigger is excluded because `POST /broadcast` carries no market guard at all, so relaxing it would be unscoped by construction.

**Consequences:** The reflection guard in `AuthorizationMiddlewareTests` — every Operator non-GET route must be market- or job-scoped — now recognises a third scoping shape, `/api/schedules/{marketId}`, alongside `/markets/…` and `/jobs/…`; without that it fails, which is the intended tripwire for any future unscoped Operator write. An unscoped operator (no market assignment) can edit every station, exactly as they can already act on every job. Opening the page also made three Admin-only calls newly reachable, each now withheld rather than left to 403: the station History step in both schedule studios (`GET /api/activity*` is blanket-Admin, and its feed renders a 403 as "No activity recorded" — a 403 disguised as absence), the resolved-bookend preview in the Speech step (`POST /bookends/preview`, Admin because it carries no market guard), and the reverse case in the command palette, whose Stations jump group was gated `isAdmin` although `GET /schedules` is Operator. Create and Duplicate stay Admin by choice, not by the matrix. Published docs updated: `operator-guide.md`, `first-time-sign-in.md`, `per-station-configuration.md`.


## 2026-08-06 — A studio save shows the server's reason, and the rule set is validated before the request

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Reported as "can't save a new alias once more than 10 have been added… it's like I'm locked at 15 alias for Cairns". There is no cap. Dev's `Cairns Roads` (`pd-ecc2853e59734b5bb56651dc0e9dabe1`, 15 rules, v8) rejected 51 saves with HTTP 400 in ~5ms each — before storage and before ElevenLabs — because the editor held a second `Manunda` rule ("Man-under" beside the stored "Mahnoonduh") and `PronunciationRuleMapping.ParseRules` refuses two rules for one word and type (one would be applied, the other silently dead). Reproduced against the live dev API: the response body says exactly that, naming the word and both respellings. The operator never saw it: `PronunciationDictionaryStudio.doSave` caught the error bare and toasted "Your changes were not saved. Try again." — advice that can never work — and `DeliveryStyleStudio` and `BookendStudio` carried the same swallow, which also hid the version-size wall and revision conflicts.

**Decision:** Two layers. (1) The three studios surface `ApiError.message` as the toast description; the axios interceptor already lifts the backend's `{ Error }` body into it, so nothing else was needed to make the real reason legible. (2) `ruleSetProblem` (pure, in `pronunciation-form.ts`) resolves the two rejections the backend makes on a rule set — a duplicate word for a type, and a word with no respelling — and the studio blocks Save with that message as the `disabledReason` while flagging the Rules step. Word-less rows are ignored: that is the empty row `+ Alias rule` adds and the studio drops it on save.

**Rationale:** A generic "try again" in front of a deterministic rejection is worse than no message, because it sends the operator round the same loop and invites a wrong theory about the cause — here, a rule cap that does not exist. Mirroring the two rule-set invariants client-side is duplication of a validation, not of the invariant: the domain remains the authority (the same rules also arrive by CSV import and config transfer), and the copy names the offending word so the fix is mechanical. The server message stays wired for everything the client cannot know — the 32,768-char version-history wall, ETag conflicts, upstream ElevenLabs text.

**Consequences:** Any save rejection now reads as an instruction. `ruleSetProblem` is unit-tested against the reported case, including case- and whitespace-insensitive duplicate matching (as the backend's `OrdinalIgnoreCase` key does) and the alias+phoneme pair for one word, which is legitimate and must stay saveable. A follow-up audit found two more rejections of the same shape in the same dialog, both now mirrored: `CreateAlias` refuses a word respelled as itself (case-insensitively; phoneme rules are exempt), and the rules header counted rows the save silently drops, so it disagreed with the saved version's count. The remaining unmirrored rejections across the other editors are registered, not fixed — see the 2026-08-06 audit summary in CONTEXT.md.

## 2026-08-06 — Style Rules Merge Into the Writer Prompt Tab

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The standalone Style Rules feature — a single global, versioned house-style library behind the "Style rules" tab in Bulletin rules, the /api/style-rules API, and a style-rule preview — duplicated what the Writer prompt tab already did per section. Prompt sections already carry per-section version history and ARN-editable content, so a second global voicing library meant a parallel editing surface with its own storage row, its own API and its own preview, and config-bundle exports carried a StyleRules section alongside the editorial sections.

**Decision:** The standalone Style Rules library was retired. Its "Style rules" tab, the global versioned library and the /api/style-rules API were removed together with the StyleRules types: `StyleRule`, `StyleRuleSet`, `StyleRuleDefaults`, `IStyleRulesRepository`, `TableStorageStyleRulesRepository`, `StyleRulesService`, `StyleRulesHttpTrigger`, their DI registration and the config-transfer StyleRules section. The content folded into the 14 writer-prompt sections on the Writer prompt tab (`EditorialLibraryManager`, the editorial library): the road-feel language, closures, numbers, anchors and length/complete-sentence sections absorbed the rule set, with the two code-embedded defaults and the one custom rule ("Never say motorists — say drivers", folded into the road-feel-language section) mapped onto existing section seeds so the dev-published v5 rule set lost no content. The script-level preview (`StyleRulesService.PreviewAsync`) was ported as `EditorialScriptPreviewService` behind `POST /api/editorial/blocks/preview-script` on the Writer prompt tab: editing any of the 14 sections now offers a **Preview read** that runs the draft generator twice — current blocks versus the edit — over a canned busy or quiet scenario, side by side. Admin-only, as before.

**Rationale:** One editorial surface with per-section version history and a single script-level preview is simpler for operators than a separate global library duplicating the same machinery, and it removes a second storage row and API surface to maintain. Writer-prompt sections already resolve at generation time, so folding the style content into them preserves the "a saved change applies to the next bulletin" contract with no behavioural gap.

**Consequences:** Config-bundle exports no longer carry a StyleRules section; the 14 writer-prompt sections are the sole ARN-editable voicing surface, each versioned per section, with the script-level preview available while editing any section. This entry supersedes the 2026-07-02 "Style Rules Become an ARN-Editable Versioned Library" decision. Docs updated in the same wave: the operator guide's Bulletin-rules table and escalation tiers, FAQ, first-day and first-time-sign-in checklists, glossary, handover pack and UAT materials now describe writer-prompt sections with **Preview read**.

## 2026-08-06 — The Cockpit Counts Down The Deadline That Binds, Not Operator Dwell Time

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Every urgency signal in the operator console was driven by getSecondsRemaining = lastUpdatedAt + APPROVAL_WINDOW_MINUTES (8): the red DecisionDock counter, the audible chime (use-alarm), the browser-tab alarm, the nav badge, the queue-rail ordering (QueueBeam), the board's lane ranking (lane-condition), the "Review most urgent" CTA and the hotter-job banner. WS2-001 sets the ~8-minute window correctly, but it is DERIVED from the slot (generation ~15 min before airtime, >=5 min reserved for the Zetta push, 30s listen), so the anchor should be the air slot, not the last write. Three consequences, all verified: slotStateForJob took no "now", so 'missed' was reachable only when no bulletin existed at all and a passed slot was indistinguishable from one ten minutes out; Approve stayed enabled past the slot and confirmed with the same "Approving cannot be undone" either way; and because JobStatusUpdater stamps LastUpdatedAt on every write, revising a bulletin RESET its urgency to +8:00 while its airtime did not move, so the most at-risk bulletin looked calmest precisely because the operator touched it. findAirSlot was used in exactly one place and rendered as a static grey chip. The path was also unreachable locally: all 13 seeded schedules were disabled and the job fixtures' station names shared no values with the schedule fixtures', so findAirSlot returned null in every mock session.

**Decision:** resolveBindingDeadline(job, airSlotAt, now) in job-meta/urgency.ts returns the EARLIER of the air slot and the approval window, which of the two it is, and whether the slot is missed beyond SLOT_MISS_THRESHOLD_MS. DecisionDock counts that deadline and names the clock ("on air 9:05 am" vs "approve by 9:06 am", and "Slot missed" with how long ago). slotStateForJob(job, slotTime, now) now takes the slot and the clock, so a live WAITING_APPROVAL or in-pipeline bulletin whose slot has passed reads 'missed' on the board; ad-hoc riders pass slotTime null and are unchanged. The air-slot vital turns destructive once the slot passes. The approve confirmation escalates independently for a missed slot and for contradicted claims. ReviseDialog receives the remaining seconds and warns when its own regenerate estimate cannot make the deadline. A shared useAirSlot hook replaces the cockpit's local resolution so the vitals and the dock cannot disagree. Two enabled demo schedules were added to dev-data.json so the path is exercised in mock mode. Deliberately NOT changed: the queue rail, the nav badge and both alarms still order and fire on the 8-minute dwell SLA; Approve is re-confirmed past the slot, never blocked.

**Rationale:** The product exists to put a bulletin to air before its slot, so the loudest signal in the console must measure that and not operator dwell time. A signed counter next to a static clock time was compatible with two opposite readings ("approve now, it airs in ten minutes" and "the slot passed ten minutes ago and the station aired nothing"), and the reset-on-write behaviour actively inverted the ordering it was supposed to drive. min(approvalDeadline, airSlot) is a strict improvement without inventing configuration; the fully correct anchor is airSlot minus the Zetta push buffer, which is a config value not yet expressed in code and is registered as a follow-up rather than guessed. Approve stays permitted past the slot because airing late is sometimes the right call and the UI should not make that decision; it only has to stop describing a missed slot as ordinary lateness.

**Consequences:** A latent bug had to be fixed for any of this to be reachable: enumerateSlots requested only pastCount * 3 + futureCount occurrences across the 6h lookback, which truncated any dense schedule. A station firing every 15 minutes has ~24 occurrences in that window, so the 10-occurrence request stopped roughly two hours short and NO past slot existed, making 'missed' unreachable for the busiest stations including the real Cairns "0,15,30,45 6-9,15-18" schedule; it now enumerates the window and takes the tail. One slots.test.ts case was passing for the wrong reason (an every-minute cron whose "most recent past slot" was actually ~6h old) and was rewritten against a sparse cron. Covered by new ReviewPane tests for the missed-slot confirmation. Follow-ups registered, not done: anchor the approval deadline to the air slot minus the Zetta push buffer; move the queue rail, nav badge and alarms onto the binding deadline so the rail stops reading "+2:00" beside a dock that reads "Slot missed"; and decide whether "Use fallback audio" should be promoted to the primary action when a regenerate cannot make the slot. Reviewed as before/after screenshots in web/audit/proposals/index.html.

## 2026-08-06 — Pronunciation studio drops the whole-dictionary preview step

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The pronunciation dictionary studio had three steps (Rules / Preview / History). The Preview step synthesised a canned sample sentence through the SAVED dictionary via POST /pronunciation-dictionaries/{id}/preview, with a model picker and a platform-wide-layer toggle. Since the per-rule audition landed in PronunciationRuleTable (POST /pronunciation-dictionaries/preview-rule, which validates an UNSAVED candidate rule through the same domain construction a save uses), the step could only ever audition rules already persisted, in a sample sentence most rules do not appear in.

**Decision:** Remove the Preview step from PronunciationDictionaryStudio and delete PronunciationPreviewPanel.tsx, the usePreviewPronunciationDictionary hook, DictionaryPreviewResponseSchema, PreviewDictionaryRequest, the pronunciationDictionaryPreview path helper and the mock adapter/store branch. The studio is now Rules + History. The backend endpoint POST /pronunciation-dictionaries/{id}/preview is left in place and is no longer called by the console.

**Rationale:** The per-row play button auditions the rule the operator is actually editing, in the voice the station airs with, on unsaved text — strictly more useful than a fixed sample through the saved version, and it does not need a save first. Keeping both meant two audition paths with different capabilities and two synth costs per press.

**Consequences:** Operators lose the aggregate applied/skipped rule counts and the stacked platform-wide-layer audition; the per-row disabled-reason tooltip already names the model-specific reason a phoneme rule will not apply. The backend Preview trigger is now dead from the console's point of view — remove it in a backend cleanup wave if it stays unused.

## 2026-08-06 — One "Ask for a change" control, and the station's own copy is never rewritten

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The script editor carried two LLM passes side by side: an unlabelled box + "Rewrite" (delivery register, `POST /jobs/{id}/retone`) and a `Rewrite the content` box + "Rewrite script" (content, `POST /jobs/{id}/rewrite`). Two text fields with identical affordances, two buttons both reading "Rewrite…", both showing "Rewriting…" in flight, distinguishable only by a tooltip an operator had to open and read; all their instruction lived in placeholder text that vanished on focus. They sat ABOVE the script, pushing the editable text ~500px down the panel. The delivery pass overwrote the draft in place with no undo and no diff, while its content sibling returned a reviewable preview — the same category of action with two different safety models. Separately, a rewrite of an already-composed bulletin handed the station's bookend lines and filler statements to the grounding reviewer, which correctly reported "Download the iHeartRadio app…" and "Roadworks … are updated weekly on the Cairns Regional Council website." as unsourced and refused the WHOLE rewrite — a refusal no instruction could fix, on every bookended or filler-topped bulletin.

**Decision:** Two changes, one to each half.

_UI_ — `ScriptAssist.tsx` is the single "Ask for a change" section: one input, one Rewrite button, and a Delivery|Content segmented control (withheld on a non-v3 voice, which cannot act on tags, exactly as the tone palette already is). Each mode keeps its own instruction so switching lever does not bin what was typed; the mode's explanation is permanent helper text under the field, not a placeholder. BOTH modes now return a preview with a diff and Apply/Discard — the delivery pass no longer overwrites the draft. Refusals render through `parseRewriteRefusal` as a named gate, one row per rejected claim (quote + scope chip + reason) and a next step, instead of one unbroken red string. The script and its word counter move to the TOP of the editor with the tone palette as their toolbar; the action row gains a rule, Cancel is pushed right away from the two buttons that keep the draft, and a disabled Re-voice now says why.

_Backend_ — `StationLineSplitter` (Domain/Services) peels the station-authored head and tail off a script before any LLM pass sees it and puts them back verbatim afterwards, using the pipeline's own statement identity (`FillerStatementSelector.Normalize`) plus literal-fragment matching for a bookend template whose `{city}`-style tokens the job does not record. `JobStationLineResolver` (Functions/Triggers/Http) gathers those lines from the market's filler statements and the job's bookend id/version, fail-soft. Both `ScriptRewriteHttpTrigger` and `ScriptRetoneHttpTrigger` use it, and both responses gained `PreservedLines` so the console can say why a line came back unchanged.

**Rationale:** Two controls that differ only in a tooltip are one control with a missing mode switch. Making the delivery pass a preview costs one click and buys the diff, which is the actual product — nobody spots what moved in an 80-word read by re-reading it. On the backend, the reviewer was right and the input was wrong: filler and bookends are ARN's own editorial content, appended after every LLM stage during generation and never checked against traffic evidence, so the fix is to stop showing them to the rewriter rather than to weaken the grounding gate. Peeling head and tail is exact because those are the only positions `BulletinBookendComposer.Compose` ever places them.

**Consequences:** `BulletinBookendComposer.Join` is now public and shared, so a script taken apart and put back together rejoins exactly as the pipeline composed it. `RetoneScriptResponseDto`/`RewriteScriptResponseDto` and their Zod schemas gained `PreservedLines` (defaulted, so a pre-deploy backend still parses). Word counts in both responses cover the WHOLE read, preserved lines included, so the operator's slot maths still adds up. The mock adapter reproduces both new states offline — it peels the market's filler statements and refuses an instruction that asks to ADD content — because a state the mock cannot reach is a state the UX harness never audits. Not covered: a body whose last sentence is unpunctuated defeats the peel; the pipeline's own `Join` punctuates every part before the filler, so that shape does not occur in a generated script.

## 2026-08-06 — Voice change during review is a server-resolved profile override on the existing regenerate flow

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Operators needed to regenerate a bulletin with a different voice (e.g. the read is wrong for the daypart, or a station wants to hear an alternative before approving). The words in a bulletin do not depend on the voice except through slot fit: each voice has its own calibrated WPM, model (v3 tags vs multilingual phoneme rules), settings, pace boost, and filler cart. Separately, RegenerationQueueMessage never carried PaceBoostWpm, so every regeneration silently ran with pace boost 0 and the re-voice headroom math in AudioFinalizer was dead code.

**Decision:** POST /api/jobs/{id}/regenerate and /audition gain an optional voiceProfileId. The backend resolves the profile's CURRENT version server-side (hard-fail naming the profile when unresolvable, the CreateJobAsync trust rule; a client-supplied voice snapshot is never accepted). The resolved JobVoiceConfig plus new Job VoiceProfileId/Version provenance pins are persisted BEFORE enqueue (the RISK-31 ScriptText pattern) so a FAILED retry replays the chosen voice. A model-cross override drops the operator's TonedScript so the delivery director re-derives tags for the new model; a same-model override keeps it. In the console, a voice change is a Revise-tray chip: voice-only (or voice+pronunciation) batches apply as a re-voice, never paying the LLM; any content change escalates to regenerate as before. The audition endpoint doubles as the fit probe: it reads the actual script with the candidate voice and its DurationSec is compared to the slot band client-side. RegenerationQueueMessage now carries paceBoostWpm, populated from job.VoiceConfig.

**Rationale:** Re-voice is the cheapest correct loop for a voice swap (~5s audition, ~15s re-voice, one synthesis, zero editorial risk since the approved words are unchanged and evidence is preserved), and the audition-first UX lets the operator HEAR the candidate before spending anything - which also covers the fact that v3 audio-tag behaviour is voice-dependent and undocumented. Server-side resolution keeps the established snapshot trust boundary. Persist-before-enqueue keeps retries faithful to the operator's choice.

**Consequences:** Regenerations of pace-boosted jobs now honour the boost (behaviour change: previously dropped to 0). The job table gains two provenance pin columns (VoiceProfileId/VoiceProfileVersion), also set at both creation sites for parity; schedule-default fallbacks pin nothing. A voice override applies to that bulletin only - the station schedule and rotation cursor are untouched. A new voice's first bulletin may use the evergreen filler fallback until its per-voice cart warms, and an uncalibrated profile's fit verdict starts from the 150 WPM default.

## 2026-08-06 — The writer-prompt editor's verdict belongs to the text, not to a fourth button

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The writer-prompt section editor's footer carried four same-weight controls — `Revert to default`, `Preview read`, `Check`, `Publish` — three of them `variant="outline"`, so the commit action had no more visual authority than the escape hatch and the two identical outlines beside it read as one control split in half. Nothing else in the app does this: `FillerStatementsManager` (the canonical dialog footer) is a ghost escape hatch on the left plus exactly one outline and one primary on the right. `Check` was the odd one out in a second way: it ran `POST /editorial/blocks/check`, a DETERMINISTIC server-side lint (`EditorialRiskLinter.Inspect` — no model call, no cost), behind a button an editor had to know to press. Because it was manual the component had to carry a `verdictIsStale` flag and a "text changed since the last check" warning, i.e. a verdict for wording that no longer existed could sit on screen while a blocking phrase was typed underneath it. The nested "Preview with your edit" dialog had two separate action zones (a primary `Run preview` inline beside the scenario select, a lone `Close` in the footer), a three-line jargon description, and a `w-[min(960px,94vw)]` that never took effect because `DialogContent`'s own `max-w-lg` capped it at 512px — so the side-by-side comparison the dialog exists for had been rendering in ~230px columns since it shipped.

**Decision:** The check runs itself, debounced 400ms on the text, and its verdict renders beside the character counter (`checking…` / `no issues found` / `N to look at` / `cannot be published`) with the findings under the textarea. A report is only trusted when `check.variables.text` equals the text on screen, and `Publish` is held while a verdict is outstanding — so `verdictIsStale` and its warning are deleted rather than reworded. The footer becomes the app's standard shape: `Revert to default` as a ghost on the left, then `Preview read` (outline) and `Publish` (primary). In the preview dialog, `Run preview` moves into the footer beside `Close` as the primary, the scenario select gets a real `FieldLabel`, the description says what it does in one sentence, an empty state names what will appear, and `max-w-lg` is replaced with `max-w-4xl`.

**Rationale:** A verdict that costs nothing to compute should never be something to remember to ask for; making it live deletes the whole stale-verdict class of bug instead of guarding against it, and turns the footer's four buttons into two. The button weights are not cosmetic — an operator scanning a dialog reads weight as "this is the action", and four outlines say nothing is.

**Consequences:** `POST /editorial/blocks/check` now fires roughly once per typing pause instead of once per explicit press; it is a pure in-process lint over ≤4000 characters with no storage or model dependency, so the extra calls are cheap, but any future work that makes it expensive must re-introduce an explicit trigger. The "No issues found — safe to publish" toast is gone (a toast per keystroke pause is noise) and the same fact is stated inline. `EditorialBlockEditor.test.tsx` is new and is the only test coverage the editorial components have ever had; it pins the live check, the outstanding-verdict hold, and the two-button footer.

## 2026-08-07 — One-shot dev deploys via arn deploy all; ARM caches permissions per token

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Deploying to dev required an LLM operator to hand-chain PIM activation, RBAC-propagation polling, two builds and two deploy CLIs. On 2026-08-07 a deploy stalled 25 minutes on AuthorizationFailed even though PIM Owner was Provisioned: ARM caches a permission snapshot per TOKEN, so an az access token minted before the activation keeps 403ing for up to ~30 min, and az account list --refresh does not remint it. The effective-permissions API showed * while resource-provider actions still 403d.

**Decision:** arn deploy all --env <env> is the single deploy command: cmd_deploy's preflight now self-heals auth (activates Owner when inactive, treats RoleAssignmentExists as already-active, waits for the assignment, and remints the ARM token by evicting AccessToken entries from ~/.azure/msal_token_cache.json when the token iat predates the Owner assignment createdOn), then deploys api (Functions zip-deploy + restart + Running poll) before web (SWA build + deploy) so a fresh UI never outruns its API. deploy web retries the SWA token fetch 5x15s with one remint. A ~/.local/bin/arn launcher makes the documented arn spelling real.

**Rationale:** The failure mode is deterministic and detectable (token iat vs assignment createdOn), so the CLI should fix it instead of documenting a polling ritual. Evicting only AccessToken entries keeps the refresh token, so the fix needs no interactive login. api-before-web ordering removes the window where deployed UI expects fields the deployed API does not serve.

**Consequences:** LLM/operator deploy is one command with no auth choreography. Token iat is backdated ~5 min by Entra for clock skew, so a just-minted token can trigger one redundant remint (harmless silent refresh). pim wait now also remints after the role is active. The msal cache edit assumes the plaintext json cache az uses on Linux; if it is missing or encrypted the CLI warns and falls back to az account clear guidance.

## 2026-08-07 — System alerts route to the environment Teams channels; SMS/email receivers deferred on ARN's direction

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN directed that SMS/email alert receivers not be pursued for now and that system notifications (alerts about the platform being down etc.) go to the environments' Teams channels. Live inventory showed the alert-to-Teams path (routeAlertsToTeams) was enabled and verified on dev only (31 Jul); the TST and PRD action groups carried only the interim Arinco email receiver, and both environments' notification Logic Apps still ran the pre-31-Jul workflow whose Compose_card fails on a common-alert-schema payload (proven: a test notification through the TST action group produced a Failed run in Compose_card, formatDateTime on null).

**Decision:** Enable routeAlertsToTeams=true in main.test.bicepparam and main.prod.bicepparam, apply the equivalent live change (az monitor action-group update adding the TeamsAlerts webhook receiver with useCommonAlertSchema against each environment's own Logic App trigger), and bring the TST/PRD workflow definitions up to dev's alert-branch version by a surgical ARM PUT of the workflow definition only, preserving each environment's authorised Teams connection parameters and swapping the three env-specific values (channel id, Environment card fact, console URL). The interim Arinco email backstop stays on every action group.

**Rationale:** The action group and Logic App run independently of the (parked) prod Function App, so alert delivery works without resuming anything; a full env deploy was rejected because prod is parked (a deploy restores SKUs) and a module redeploy of the Teams API connection risks resetting its authorisation. Keeping the email backstop is deliberate: a Logic App inside the subscription cannot be trusted to report that subscription being down.

**Consequences:** Proven end to end in all three environments: az monitor action-group test-notifications through each env's own action group produced a Succeeded Logic App run and an alert Adaptive Card in that environment's Teams channel (dev 00:49Z/03:20Z, TST 03:23:27Z, PRD 03:24:01Z on 7 Aug). IaC now matches the live state, so the next full deploy converges instead of stripping the receivers. The formal SoW SMS/phone written election and ARN's ops-channel nomination remain open ARN items; the alert cards carry an Environment fact so the interim shared team hosts all three channels unambiguously.


## 2026-08-07 — Wording changes are previewed in the script editor; Revise regenerates only from source changes

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The review cockpit had regained two instruction paths after the script editor grew the grounded **Ask for a change** preview. In **Edit**, an operator could ask for a content or delivery rewrite, inspect the diff, apply it to the editable script and re-voice the exact words. In **Revise**, `ChangeComposer` still offered “Describe a change to regenerate”, category pills and a blind instruction queue that rejected the current bulletin and sent it through the full generation pipeline with no preview. Both surfaces claimed to change wording, but only one showed the result before committing and the second could rewrite an already-reviewed script again.

**Decision:** The script editor is the only wording-change surface: edit directly, or use **Ask for a change**, inspect the preview/diff and apply it, then **Re-voice** the exact text. Remove `ChangeComposer`, instruction/comment review-change kinds and the console's regenerate-feedback/delivery-intent payload. **Revise** remains the decision surface for changes that exist outside the script: pronunciation and voice changes re-voice; incident inclusion, corridor order and flowing-road selection regenerate from the selected source data; a failed candidate-voice fit may be explicitly escalated with **Regenerate instead**. With nothing queued the footer says **No changes to apply**, rather than presenting Regenerate as the default.

**Rationale:** An operator should never describe a wording change to one control and discover the rewritten words only after rejecting the current bulletin. The editor already provides the safer and cheaper contract: the final script is visible, grounded AI changes are previewed, manual edits remain possible and TTS reads the accepted text verbatim. Regeneration still has one precise meaning: rebuild the bulletin because its source selection changed, or because the chosen voice cannot fit the approved words and the operator explicitly permits a rewrite.

**Consequences:** `useBulletinReview` no longer owns free-form feedback state; source curation now supplies a scope-honest rejection-history note and the existing structured regeneration fields. The backend's optional feedback fields remain accepted for API compatibility, but the console no longer emits them. The local mock adapter matches that console contract. `ReviseDialog` explains whether the queued batch keeps the script or rewrites it, while fallback and outright rejection remain in their separate destructive section. Verified locally on mock job `arn-job-00008`: Revise showed no instruction composer and a disabled **No changes to apply** state; Edit showed **Ask for a change** plus **Re-voice**. Four targeted files passed 43 tests; `tsc --noEmit` and scoped ESLint passed.

## 2026-08-07 — Rejection audit, correction routing and future writer lessons are separate contracts

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** A reject click used one free-text `notes` value for two incompatible purposes. It correctly entered the job's rejection history, but it also entered a market-wide `marketfeedback` table automatically and was replayed into every later bulletin as `<operator-notes>`. Consequently workflow notes such as “Script edited and re-voiced” and one-off pronunciation or data defects could become durable AI instructions. The July dedupe policy reduced repetition but did not fix the trust-boundary error: a failed bulletin is evidence that something was wrong, not evidence of a safe reusable instruction. The old corpus was market-scoped, had no expiry, and exposed only an admin promotion queue while continuing to teach the writer before promotion.

**Decision:** Rejection now has three explicit, independent outcomes. (1) A required closed `RejectionReasonCode` plus required notes enter only the job audit history. (2) Fixable reasons route to the existing correction tools: pronunciation, source selection or the script editor; they can never enter writer memory. (3) For the four teachable reason families only, the operator may separately enable **Teach this station for future bulletins**, select a typed category and write an imperative lesson. The backend re-validates reason eligibility, category, length and enum validity; clients cannot bypass it. An accepted lesson is station-scoped, deduplicated by SHA-256 identity, expires after 90 days, merges repeated teaching by refreshing expiry, and is replayed only for that station. Admins can inspect provenance, promote a lesson to standing guidance, or dismiss it under **Bulletin rules → Future lessons**. The old automatically accrued market corpus, formatter, policy and prompt variable are removed with no compatibility shim or data migration; historical rows remain inert in the existing table.

**Rationale:** Audit facts, operational corrections and reusable editorial instructions have different trust and lifecycle requirements. Making the reusable instruction a separate opt-in field forces the operator to state what the writer should do rather than asking a model to infer policy from a failure report. Existing deterministic correction tools are more reliable than prompt memory for pronunciation and evidence defects. Station scope prevents one brand's lesson changing another station in the same market, while expiry and dismissal stop memory from becoming permanent sediment.

**Consequences:** `RejectJobRequest` now carries `ReasonCode`, `Notes` and optional `FutureLesson`; integer or unknown enum values fail at the HTTP boundary. Both reject and reject-to-fallback validate the same contract. `FutureLessonEntry`, `IFutureLessonRepository` and `TableStorageFutureLessonRepository` replace the old feedback names in code while retaining the deployed `marketfeedback` table name. Draft generation receives `<future-lessons>` only when the broadcast carries a station id. Promotion and dismissal operate on the station-keyed candidate rows. The console presents a plain-language reason picker, separate audit notes, conditional teaching controls and direct correction actions; it never silently teaches from rejection notes.

## 2026-08-09 — Release 9d5217e promoted dev-test-prod through pipeline 108 and proven live in production

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The 4-8 Aug wave (voice swap on regenerate, future lessons, filler availability windows, bookends, delivery styles, alerts-to-Teams, adjacent-audit remediation) sat uncommitted while dev/test/prod ran older commits. Acquiring production confidence required the release to ride the real pipeline and be proven on production itself. Encountered and fixed on the way: three fresh npm audit advisories (undici/brace-expansion/postcss); a Lighthouse TBT budget breach on /jobs whose root cause was the cron occurrence enumerator constructing an Intl.DateTimeFormat per candidate minute and walking its full 5000-step cap for sparse crons (fixed: per-timezone formatter cache + an until bound; TBT 1474ms->~0 on the agent path); the dev SWA enterprise edge re-triggering its stuck Enabling transition on every full deploy (param now false, retry out of band); and a real product bug where manual bulletins carried the raw location as Station so future lessons taught on them were invisible to station-keyed lookups.
