**Decision:** Land the wave as one gated commit (full verify.sh green), ship it through supervised pipeline runs: 2790 (dev deploy succeeded) and 2791 (dev+test+prod deploys all succeeded via enablePromotion with both environment approvals). Deploy test additionally via deploy.sh under PIM Owner. Resume prod, and prove the release on production itself: poller-fired bulletins in BOTH pilot markets (sydney 2d3076ac, cairns-4ca 98e21247) taken through approve and publish under the mandatory ExpectedEtag precondition to 'Audio delivered to playout system', plus a fresh Azure Monitor test alert through the prod action group producing a Succeeded Logic App run and a Teams card - confirming the TeamsAlerts receiver survived the IaC round-trip. Production API access for the proving run used the documented attended auth lever (ARM audience + Auth__DevFallbackRole), opened for the window and then closed with the original authsettingsV2 restored and 401 re-verified.

**Rationale:** A supervised end-to-end pipeline promotion plus a live production proving cycle is the strongest available evidence that production is stable and handover-ready: it exercises the exact release mechanism ARN inherits, the real station configuration chain (voice profile, delivery style, pronunciation dictionary, weather/fuel), the operator contract (etag-guarded approve/publish), the playout delivery leg, and the alerting path, all at the same commit.

**Consequences:** Dev, test and prod all serve commit 9d5217e. Production is left RUNNING (P0v3) with both pilot schedules disabled - the shadow pilot is one PUT per schedule away and should be run attended, since unattended 24/7 slots only manufacture missed-approval fallbacks. Prod auth is back to the hardened api://-only audience. The engagement's supervised-deploy evidence gap (open since run 2509) is closed by runs 2790/2791.

## 2026-08-10 — A pace boost is only real if the DRAFT carries it; the fitter needs its own variance headroom

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Dev job a1d40b4ccb2d40299aa9ab38440dc5c9 (melbourne, 22s slot, Dolly Male Young, PaceBoostWpm=40 - the maximum) aired at 145 wpm, delivering only +9 of the +40 wpm asked (22%). PaceBoostWpm never reaches the TTS: eleven_v3 ignores voice_settings.speed entirely (ElevenLabsClient.supportsSpeed = isV2Family), so the boost is realised solely as more words per slot plus post-synthesis WSOLA compression. Three things ate it. (1) draft.md told the writer the boosted target was 'a natural {{targetSeconds}}-second read' - at 135.8 calibrated wpm, 59 words is a 26.1s read, so the model trusted its own sense of the clock and stopped at 54. (2) The prompt rendered only targetWords and targetWordsMax (= target+3), never the computed targetWordsMin, so the writer got a ceiling and no floor. (3) PaceBoostWordFloorFraction 0.90 made the pace floor collide exactly with the slow-fill floor (both 53 for a 59 target), so the boost-gated extend never fired on the very jobs that needed it - the shipped draft was 53 words, the floor 53, and the test is a strict less-than.

**Decision:** Measured before shipping: 40 live calls to the deployed arn-draft Foundry agent replaying this job's exact captured RequestBody, one prompt line varied, every output then synthesised on the real production voice (40 real eleven_v3 renders). Median delivered pace: baseline 152.7 wpm, item-aim-as-floor 166.4, honest length framing 169.1, both 174.5, against the 175.8 the boost asks for. Shipped the honest-length-framing variant (83% realisation, 61-64 words) rather than the both-variant (97%) because the latter exceeded the prompt's own stated hard ceiling in 8 of 10 runs. draft.md line 3 now renders an explicit {{targetWordsMin}}-{{targetWordsMax}} band and names the read as deliberately compressed; LlmScriptGenerator raises that floor to the boost's acceptance floor when PaceBoostWpm > 0; PaceBoostWordFloorFraction goes 0.90 to 0.95; WordTargetCalculator.ComputePaceFloorWords becomes the single source for the number the prompt states and the engine enforces. Separately, WordTargetCalculator.ComputeFitterMaxSpeedUpFactor gives the audio fitter a 5 percent variance margin over the aim ceiling (clamped by AbsolutePaceBoostSpeedUpCeiling), used by ScriptGenerationEngine and AudioFinalizer for synthesis while ComputeBoostedWordTarget keeps sizing off the unchanged aim ceiling.

**Rationale:** The aim ceiling returned by ComputeEffectiveMaxSpeedUpFactor is exactly the ratio the boost needs, so a take that lands on target has zero margin for render variance - and the 40 renders measured a 12 percent duration spread at a FIXED word count (62 words rendered 25.20-28.56s). That variance alone re-rendered 20 percent of takes. Widening the aim instead would grow the word target and over-deliver the boost, so the slack belongs to the fitter only. At the 1.35 absolute ceiling every one of the 40 renders fits (worst 29.20s against 29.70s). Raising the prompt floor without the fitter margin would have traded slow reads for re-renders.

**Consequences:** A 22s slot on this voice moves from 145 to roughly 169 wpm delivered - 83 percent of the boost instead of 22 percent - with the re-render rate at 0 percent across the measured panel. Unboosted voices are untouched by the fitter margin and the raised floor; the draft.md band applies to every bulletin, so it was gated on 4 before/4 after script-only eval runs: overall target shape 71/72/70/71 to 76/71/72/76, with fabrication counts and style/safety verdicts identical. The regression corpus cannot express this defect - its snapshot carries no PaceBoostWpm or voice - so a fixture built from this job replays unboosted and is not a valid guard; the guards are WordTargetCalculatorTests (fitter-vs-aim separation, the measured 29.20s worst render, the pace-floor gap) plus the trial data kept at job-diagnostics/a1d40b4ccb2d40299aa9ab38440dc5c9/draft-prompt-trial.json. MaxPaceBoostWpm stays 40, which on a 135.8 wpm voice still cannot reach an ATN-style 180-200 wpm read - the base voice remains the binding constraint.

## 2026-08-10 — The draft word band and the item-aim floor only work together; ship both

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The 2026-08-10 pace-boost fix shipped only the word-band half of draft.md line 3, on the strength of a 40-call A/B against ONE frozen input (dev job a1d40b4c) where the band alone reached 83 percent of the boost and the item-aim floor added little beyond it. Deployed to dev and re-measured on live poller-fired melbourne bulletins with the same voice profile, the band alone delivered a median of 56-57 words against a 59 target - roughly +1.5 words over the old wording, not the +6 the frozen-input trial predicted.

**Decision:** Re-ran the A/B against a LIVE production-rendered draft prompt, 10 samples per arm: old wording 55.5 median, band only 57.0, item-aim floor only 58.0, both 62.0. The two edits are synergistic, not additive - neither alone moves a live input, together they deliver the whole effect. Shipped the item-aim clause as a floor as well: 'Voice AT LEAST {{maxIncidents}} incidents, and keep going past {{maxIncidents}} while the data still holds real items you have not voiced'. Confirmed on 10 real eleven_v3 renders of the both-arm outputs: 23.04-28.48s natural against the 29.70s fitter cap, 0 busts.

**Rationale:** The frozen-input trial controlled LLM sampling variance but not INPUT variance, and the effect size turned out to be input-dependent: on a sparse 7-corridor regeneration the length framing alone was enough, on a dense 20-corridor live fetch the item-aim cap is the binding constraint and the band cannot get past it. A single frozen input is not a sufficient basis for a prompt-wording decision - the earlier reason for holding the item floor back (it exceeded the prompt's own stated ceiling in 8 of 10 frozen-input runs) was measuring a regime the live inputs do not reproduce: on the live prompt the both-arm lands 56-65 words, over the stated 62 in 4 of 10, all inside the draft hard ceiling of 67 and all inside the fitter.

**Consequences:** Live melbourne bulletins on the boosted voice should move from ~152 wpm to ~169 wpm delivered, 83 percent of the +40 ask. Script-only eval across 3 runs improved again on top of the band-only state: overall target shape 74/75/77 against 76/71/72/76 (band only) and 71/72/70/71 (before either), with estimated durations up in every market and style/safety verdicts unchanged; one goldcoast run showed 3 fabrications against its usual 2, worth watching but inside existing run-to-run noise. Standing lesson for prompt work: measure a wording change against at least two genuinely different inputs before concluding, and prefer a live-rendered prompt over a replayed capture.

## 2026-08-10 — Audio pre-review tolerates word boundaries in both directions, and its job-log line honours operator verdicts

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN asked whether the pre-review flagging works at all, citing dev job `8ff3e223` flagging "Gate". Re-transcribing that job's aired audio through the same Azure Speech fast-transcription endpoint showed the TTS said the road correctly and the transcriber fused it: script "West Gate Freeway", transcript "Westgate Freeway". `AudioPreReview.Compare` joined adjacent TRANSCRIPT tokens (so script "roadworks" survived transcript "road works") but nothing covered the reverse, so a script two-worder the transcriber fused always matched its first half on prefix and orphaned its second half — permanently, on every bulletin naming the road. A second, independent asymmetry: a possessive raised the prefix rule's threshold by two and widened the length gap past the edit budget, so "Greensborough" cleared against "Greensboro" while "Greensborough's" flagged, in the same bulletin (job 43382c2a). Across all 149 dev jobs carrying a pre-review, 76 were flagged for 96 word-flags total; "Gate"/"Gate's" alone was 25 of the 96 (26 percent) from one road name, and 54 of the 96 (56 percent) were words a station pronunciation dictionary DELIBERATELY respells — the gate fired hardest on the words already handled. Separately, melbourne had recorded a standing "sounded fine" verdict for "Gate" on 2026-08-06, four days before job `8ff3e223`, and the job page still showed the flag: the verdict lens is applied in the review script and badge, but `AudioFinalizer` wrote the RAW suspect list to a `Warn` job log, which `isFlaggedLog` renders amber and auto-expanded in the audit timeline.

**Decision:** (1) `IsHeard` accepts three renderings of a script word — as written, as its bare stem behind a possessive, and fused with a SIGNIFICANT neighbour — mirroring the transcript-side join that already existed. The fused form is matched against single transcript words only, never against joined transcript pairs, and the neighbour must itself clear `MinSignificantLength`. (2) `AudioFinalizer.WithoutVerifiedAsync` subtracts the market's enabled `VerifiedPronunciation` verdicts from the suspect list used for the job log line and its severity; `Job.PreReview` still stores the RAW, unfiltered list. `IVerifiedPronunciationRepository` reaches `AudioFinalizer` as an optional last constructor parameter on `BroadcastOrchestrator`, the same fail-soft shape the pre-review's own `IAudioTranscriber` already has, so the twelve direct constructions in five test files keep compiling.

**Rationale:** Both matcher bugs are word-boundary bookkeeping, not tolerance: widening the edit budget instead would have swallowed real errors. That risk is concrete and was measured — comparing a fused script pair against a joined transcript pair lets two loosely-heard words vouch for each other under the longer string's wider budget, and "Toorak Road" ≈ "Torrac Road" passes on a distance the bare words fail. Restricting fused forms to single transcript words keeps `Toorak` flagged, which is correct: it is a candidate real mispronunciation, and the verdict/dictionary layers exist to settle it. Requiring a significant neighbour is the same kind of guard — "The Eyre" joins to "theeyre", two edits from a passing "there". Keeping `Job.PreReview` raw preserves the 2026-07-28 decision's one-way-door reasoning: verdicts stay a reversible read-time lens over stored truth. The job LOG is the opposite kind of artefact — a point-in-time note telling THIS operator what to go and listen to, written once — so a word a human cleared months ago must not keep raising an amber warning on it.

**Consequences:** Replayed through the compiled comparer against 26 dev jobs whose aired audio was re-transcribed for this investigation: 7 flags cleared (`Gate` x4, `Gate's` x2, `Greensborough's` x1), **zero new flags**, and every candidate real mispronunciation retained (`Toorak`, `Keilor`, `Mickleham`, `Fremantle`, `Kwinana`, `Zeehan`, `Murchison`, `Morphett`, `Kororoit`, `Nerang`, `Manoora`, `Werrimull`, `Craigieburn`, `Koonung`, `Grieve`, `Shiers`, `Robey`, `Stuart`, `Eyre`, `W'mooloo`). Job `8ff3e223` now returns an empty suspect list. Projected over the full dev history that is 28 of 96 historical flags (29 percent) removed. Modified: `AudioPreReview.cs` (`Compare` now tracks token positions; new `IsHeard`, `StripPossessive`, `IsSignificant`), `AudioFinalizer.cs`, `BroadcastOrchestrator.cs`, `AudioPreReviewTests.cs` (+5 tests, 31 total). No new files. Two things this deliberately does NOT fix, both better handled by the existing verdict and dictionary layers than by loosening the matcher: words the dictionary respells on purpose (`Eyre` → "Air" guarantees its own flag) and transcriber symbolisation of ordinals and fused units ("first" → "1st", "six-kay queue" → "6KQ").

## 2026-08-10 — Cached filler is pace-matched to the read it is stitched onto, not to the read's compression factor

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Filler audio is cached per (statement x voice x settings x model) and stitched onto the finished traffic take without passing through the TTS duration-fit loop. That exact known duration is what lets the engine reserve slot space before synthesis, rescue a short read after synthesis, and pad a filler cart when generation has already failed - so removing the cache in favour of always writing filler inline was considered and rejected: it would forfeit all three, pay a fresh 9-14s eleven_v3 render on every filler bulletin, and leave FallbackAudioPadder with no script to inline into, for a path that fires on 17 of 150 jobs (11.3%). The cost of caching is that the clip keeps whatever rate a standalone one-sentence render gave it while the read around it has been time-compressed into the slot.

**Decision:** Retime each cached clip to the read's MEASURED articulation rate immediately before stitching (FillerPaceMatcher + IAudioPipelineService.RetimeClip, the existing pitch-preserving WSOLA path), clamped at x1.20 in either direction, with a 50ms deadband so a clip already in step stays byte-identical. The pre-synthesis reservation in ScriptGenerationEngine now reserves the PREDICTED retimed duration (calibrated syllables-per-second scaled by the compression the read is being sized for, sharing WordTargetCalculator.BoostedCeilingMarginFraction) rather than the raw cached duration, so the total still lands on the slot; the final fine-tune absorbs the difference between predicted and measured, which is the same residual it already absorbs (measured 1.00-1.01x on aired jobs).

**Rationale:** Measured on six aired dev bulletins: the clip articulates a median 8 percent faster than the read, worst case 35 percent (job 53c160ad). In WORDS per minute the same six read as +26 to +58 percent, but that is word length, not pace - filler averages 1.18 syllables per word against the read's 1.40-1.73 - so syllables per second is the only honest unit, and it is the one VoiceCalibration is already expressed in. Critically the correction is NOT the read's compression factor: applying that to the clip cancels out of the ratio and restores the uncompressed mismatch (+8 percent becomes +28 percent on the same six), because the gap is inherent to the cached render and the read's compression is what accidentally closes most of it. Matching the AIRED rate means retiming against that compression, a median x1.08 slow-down - 0.24s on a 3s clip. The clamp exists because the worst case wants x1.35, which drags audibly; at x1.20 the outlier lands at +13 percent and the four clips already inside 10 percent are untouched by their own factor.

**Consequences:** The seam between the traffic read and its filler is closed to within the clamp on every stitched bulletin, and the slot-length guarantee is unchanged because the reservation moved with the retime. Voices whose cached clips already match the read pay nothing (deadband). A missing calibration, an unparsed timing payload or an empty clip all degrade to today's stitch-as-is behaviour rather than guessing. FallbackAudioPadder is deliberately NOT changed: it stitches a cart and filler that are both cached at natural rate, so they are already mutually consistent and there is no read to match against. Guards: FillerPaceMatcherTests (clamp both directions, deadband, degenerate inputs, and an explicit test that the same-compression-factor approach would make it worse) plus two stitch-path tests in BroadcastOrchestratorFillerRescueTests.

## 2026-08-10 — Pace boost cap raised 40 to 60 wpm (superseded same day: ceiling raised to 1.60)

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** VoiceProfile.MaxPaceBoostWpm was 40. The realisable boost saturates at calibratedWpm x (AbsolutePaceBoostSpeedUpCeiling - 1), which across every voice calibrated on dev falls between +42 and +58 wpm - so the operator-facing cap, not the compression ceiling, was the binding constraint on every single voice, and none could reach the pace the ceiling already allowed. Above its own saturation point a boost is a silent no-op: ComputeEffectiveMaxSpeedUpFactor clamps and ComputeBoostedWordTarget stops growing, with no feedback anywhere.

**Decision:** Raise MaxPaceBoostWpm to 60 - just past the fastest calibrated voice's saturation point (57.4 at 164.1 wpm) - and leave AbsolutePaceBoostSpeedUpCeiling at 1.35. Add WordTargetCalculator.SaturatingPaceBoostWpm as the shared definition of where the boost stops paying, and have ScriptGenerationEngine write a job-log line when the configured boost exceeds it, naming the voice's actual ceiling in wpm. The voice studio caps its displayed effective-wpm at the same ceiling and shows a note instead of promising a pace the pipeline will decline. ErrorMessages and the VoiceProfileTests bounds are now interpolated from the constant rather than repeating the literal.

**Rationale:** Held the ceiling because the evidence stopped at 1.336x - 162 shipped bulletins with both a measured compression factor and a transcript match ratio show NO degradation up to there (median match 97.5-100 percent in every compression bucket, the two most-compressed jobs scoring 97.4 and 97.5 percent against a 92.9 percent worst case in the uncompressed bucket), but only 5 of those 162 sat above 1.25x. CORRECTION (same day): this entry also argued the ceiling was not NEEDED because 1.35 already reached "the 180-200 ATN band". That band was not a measured figure - it traces to an unsourced number repeated in this log, and ARN has disowned it. It should not have been used as a rationale and must not be cited again; the only defensible reasons to hold a compression ceiling are measured intelligibility and a human listening check.

**Consequences:** An operator can now dial a boost that actually reaches the compression ceiling on any voice, worth +7.5 wpm of extra reach on the slowest calibrated voice and +17.4 on the fastest. A boost past a given voice's saturation point is accepted but visibly reported on the job and in the studio rather than silently discarded. No change to synthesis, fitting or slot length. The 162-job compression-vs-intelligibility scatter is the baseline to re-run before anyone proposes moving the 1.35 ceiling - it needs materially more samples above 1.25x to say anything.

## 2026-08-10 — Compression ceiling raised 1.35 to 1.60 so MaxPaceBoostWpm is the only cap an operator can hit

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Two caps sat in series on the same quantity: MaxPaceBoostWpm (60) and AbsolutePaceBoostSpeedUpCeiling (1.35). The boost and the compression factor are the same number in different units - a boost is realised by writing more words and compressing the render to fit - so the lower of the two always won silently. Live proof: an operator set +60 on Dolly Male Young Faster and job ffc4a4d1 logged 'exceeds what this voice can realise ... tops out at +57'. An earlier rationale for holding the ceiling cited a 180-200 wpm ATN band; that figure is unsourced, ARN has disowned it, and the prior entry is corrected accordingly.

**Decision:** Raise AbsolutePaceBoostSpeedUpCeiling to 1.60 - the factor a +60 boost needs on a 100 wpm voice, so no configured boost is truncated on any voice at or above that rate - leaving VoiceProfile.MaxPaceBoostWpm as the single operator-facing cap and WavDurationProcessor's 2.0x as the untouched backstop. Introduce a SEPARATE AbsolutePaceBoostSlowDownCeiling (1.15) and have ComputeEffectiveMaxSlowDownFactor use it, instead of deriving the slow-down cap as half the speed-up ceiling.

**Rationale:** Nothing measurable binds below 2.0x. 162 shipped bulletins show no transcript degradation to 1.336x, and a controlled sweep of one held-constant read through this exact SoundTouch WSOLA path (CompressionCeilingBench) scored a FLAT 9.6-12.3 percent word error rate from 1.00x to 2.00x with identical mismatches at every factor - machine intelligibility does not discriminate anywhere in the range. The slow-down decoupling is the non-obvious half: the two ends are not symmetric, slowing a read drags audibly far sooner than compressing one tightens, and the derived cap meant raising the speed-up ceiling to 1.60 would have silently licensed stretching a boosted underrun by 1.30x - shipping a draggy read as a side effect of chasing a faster one.

**Consequences:** A +60 boost is now realised in full on any voice at or above 100 wpm; the saturation warning becomes unreachable for normal voices and remains only as a guard. The slow-down allowance is unchanged at every speed-up ceiling. What is NOT established is how a compressed read sounds to a person - ASR cannot answer that and no listening check has been done, so 1.60 is an evidence-backed removal of a machine-intelligibility limit, not a claim that a 1.60x read sounds good. CompressionCeilingBench writes the takes for that check on demand for any voice. Guards: WordTargetCalculatorTests covers the speed-up/slow-down decoupling explicitly and asserts a +60 boost is untruncated across 100-164 wpm.

## 2026-08-10 — Trailing inhale is cut at the last SPOKEN character, on the raw render, before the duration fitter

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Operators reported a breath after the final word. Measured on dev job a0947b1e (2026-08-10): speech decays to -57 dBFS then energy CLIMBS back to -32 dBFS over the last 175 ms with the zero-crossing rate rising to ~3.9 kHz - turbulent airflow, not a fricative, and the file is cut mid-burst with no fade. Three suspects were tested and two exonerated: WavLoudnessNormalizer applied only +1.4 dB on this job, and pushing the raw render through the real SoundTouch path at the job's exact 1.1491 tempo still decayed cleanly and ended in zeros. The breath is in the ElevenLabs v3 render; six fresh renders of the same script reproduced it once. Nothing removed it because TrimTrailingSilence uses an amplitude threshold of 48 (-56.7 dBFS) and the breath peaks at 2943 (-20.9 dBFS), sixty times above it.

**Decision:** Cut the take at the last spoken sound using the aligner's own boundary, in ElevenLabsAudioSynthesizer, on the raw render. New Domain SpeechTailTrimPolicy supplies the rule and WavDurationProcessor.TrimAfterSpeech does the byte work: take the end time of the last ALPHANUMERIC character, search the following 150 ms for the quietest 5 ms window, cut at its far edge, and fade the final 5 ms to zero.

**Rationale:** Two non-obvious constraints shaped this. First, the alignment's own LAST end time is useless: ElevenLabs assigns all trailing audio to the terminal punctuation, so on the measured take every real character spanned 53-80 ms while the closing full stop spanned 320 ms and ended exactly at the end of the file. The last alphanumeric character is the honest boundary. Second, that boundary is the plosive CLOSURE, not the release - the final /t/ kept sounding for 110 ms past it at -24 dBFS - so cutting on the boundary swallows the consonant and a fixed offset lands mid-burst and clicks; the quiet-point search is what finds the real gap. It must also happen before the duration fitter, because the fine-tune rescales every word timing to the finished file length, after which the alignment claims the last word ends at the end of the audio and the boundary is gone.

**Consequences:** Verified on the real breathy render through the shipped code path: 185 ms removed, the /t/ release preserved intact at 9-10 kHz, and the file now ends at -65.1 dBFS instead of -40.5 dBFS. Takes with no appended sound are returned byte-identical (the boundary sits at or past the end). A render without alignment - any non-timestamps path - is left untouched rather than guessed at. Guards: TrimAfterSpeechTests covers breath removal, release preservation, the soft zero ending, a clean take, and the punctuation rule; SpeechTailTrimBench replays any real render on demand.

## 2026-08-10 — The handover documentation site is published, and the received set is re-trued to the shipped platform

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The site had been the nominated handover deliverable since late July, but neither `IBP-AUE-DEV-SWA-DOC01` nor `IBP-AUE-PRD-SWA-DOC01` had ever published: both served the Azure placeholder page because `DOCS_SWA_DEPLOYMENT_TOKEN` was never added to either variable group, and the pipeline job is gated on it. A three-scout audit of the site found the content had also drifted: six published pages still told the reader production was parked-until-go-live, four shipped operator capabilities (station bookends, per-line delivery tones, standby-statement availability windows, the pace-boost/compression contract) had no page at all, the escalation contact matrix and the recovery position were blank, and the signed cover PDF plus the offline bundle described a superseded six-group site.

**Decision:** Publish both Static Web Apps and keep them publishable from CI; re-true the whole received set in one wave; and rebuild the two artefacts that wrap it. Concretely: `DOCS_SWA_DEPLOYMENT_TOKEN` (secret) and `deployDocsSite` are now set in `arn-traffic-dev` and `arn-traffic-variables` (`true`) and in `arn-traffic-test` (`false`, matching its bicepparam); the site carries its own `docs-site/public/staticwebapp.config.json` and the `DocsSite` pipeline job deploys from inside `docs-site/`; production is described everywhere as deployed, proven and parked between pilot runs; the four capabilities are documented in the console and configuration pages; the contact matrix ships as a structured form ARN completes, and `disaster-recovery.md` states a measured recovery position and an ordered restore procedure against still-undefined targets; the cover is reissued at v2.1 with seven groups and the site address; and the language guard now catches hyphenated jargon.

**Rationale:** The publish had to come first and separately, because the mechanism was unproven and it turned out to be wrong in a way no amount of content work would have surfaced: run from the repository root, the Static Web Apps CLI picks up the CONSOLE app's `web/public/staticwebapp.config.json`, applying a single-page-app navigation fallback and a 401 redirect to a static documentation site. The symptom is quiet and client-visible — every unknown URL serves the home page with a 200 instead of the site's own 404 — and it would have shipped silently through the pipeline. Publishing to dev, observing it, fixing it, then re-verifying is what caught it. The content wave then ran as four file-disjoint slices because the failure modes differ per slice (state drift, missing features, blank obligations, small defects) and nothing crossed a file boundary. Screenshot `19-revise-dialog` was withdrawn from the published set after proving byte-identical to `02-review-waiting` — the audit harness never opens the dialog — so publishing both would have put one image on one page twice under two captions.

**Consequences:** ARN can read the documentation at `red-pond-03b957f00.7.azurestaticapps.net` (production) and `white-forest-0e4647200.7.azurestaticapps.net` (development) today, with working full-text search and a real 404, and the next pipeline deploy to dev or production republishes it without further wiring. Sixteen source pages changed; `./scripts/docs.py check` and the site leak guard pass. Still open and now explicit rather than silent: the custom domain is unbound, so `site:` in `astro.config.mjs` names a host that does not resolve (sitemap-only effect); the contact matrix rows say "ARN to nominate" until the handover session fills them; RPO and RTO remain ARN's to set against the stated measured position; and an independent penetration test has not been performed, which is now a row on the open-items register and a limitation in the signed cover rather than a contradiction buried across three internal documents.

## 2026-08-10 — A station can mark weather or fuel ALWAYS INCLUDE, and its fill order sets their on-air order

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN asked for a tick box making fuel or weather mandatory at station level, and separately reported a bulletin that read weather, then fuel, then an outro saying "That's KIIS traffic and weather", which felt janky. Both traced to the same gap: BulletinContentSelection.Weather/Fuel only made a source ELIGIBLE. Selection gated the HERE fetch; a fetched source then reached the writer only when MarketSchedule.FillOrder listed it, the prompts framed weather and fuel as optional fill ("garnish"), and NO gate failed when a selected source was omitted, so on a busy read it was silently dropped. On-air placement was unenforced prompt guidance ("Fuel goes at the end"), and the operator console asserted a fixed order ("on air, weather always reads before fuel") that nothing in code delivered. A live control run on a busy 12-corridor Brisbane read reproduced it exactly: weather and fuel both selected, neither aired.

**Decision:** Two per-station levers, both resolved at broadcast time. (1) BulletinContentSelection gains WeatherRequired/FuelRequired positional bools (default false) plus computed RequiresWeather/RequiresFuel that AND the flag with the selection, so a required flag on an unselected source is inert; consumers read only the computed properties. Required means the section must air WHENEVER ITS DATA WAS FETCHED: LlmScriptGenerator.InvokeDraftAsync now admits a fetched source when FillOrder lists it OR the station requires it OR (weather only) the report carries a major alert; the new draft argument requiredSections tells the writer those sections are fixtures, not fill, and to budget words for them; and the new Domain gate RequiredSourceDetector fires when a required-and-fetched source is absent, feeding blocking review/refine feedback with no mechanical Repair, because a missing fact cannot be invented. Required-without-selected is rejected on all three write paths: 400 on PUT /api/schedules/{marketId}, a validation failure on the manual-broadcast path, and a plan error on config-bundle import. (2) The relative order of Weather and Fuel in the station's existing FillOrder is now ALSO their on-air read order, resolved by the new pure service ContentSectionOrder, stated to the writer as the new sectionOrder argument, and enforced by the new SectionOrderDetector, which flags a reversed or stranded section as a STYLE defect and mechanically relocates PURE supplementary sentences (a sentence tripping exactly one weather/fuel signal and naming no active corridor road) to the tail in the configured order. MinorTraffic and Filler keep the fill-only meaning: minor traffic reads with the traffic body, filler is appended after generation so it always closes. The signal regexes were extracted verbatim out of UnselectedSourceDetector into shared ContentSourceSignals, which now backs both the fabricated-unselected gate and the two new gates. prompts/system/blocks/weather-and-fuel.md, the mirrored golden section in prompts/system.md and prompts/agents/arn-draft.md replaced "Fuel goes at the end" with "Weather and fuel sit after the traffic body, in the order the request gives". The console gained an Always include switch per supplementary source and both false copy claims were corrected.

**Rationale:** Reusing FillOrder for the read order beats a second ordered list: it is already per-station, already drag-editable, already threaded end to end, and its Weather-versus-Fuel order previously carried no meaning at all, so nothing was overloaded. Fixing this in the prompt alone was not an option, because the class of failure (a probabilistically omitted section, an order the model chose) is exactly what the repository already settles with deterministic Detect/Repair gates beside a prompt instruction. Keeping the fetch FAIL-SOFT is deliberate and is the honest limit of the promise: a HERE weather outage must never take a station off air, so required means must air when the data arrived, and the console copy says precisely that rather than over-promising. Making the record's required flag inert when the source is unselected, and still rejecting that combination at every boundary, means a bad payload can neither air wrongly nor sit in configuration pretending to be a fixture.

**Consequences:** Weather and fuel are configurable fixtures per station, so a station whose outro names its content can now guarantee that content and place it to read into that outro. Proven live on 2026-08-10 (live HERE, gpt-5.6-luna, busy 12-corridor markets, full draft/review/refine): required with weather-first order aired "Light rain, fifteen degrees. Unleaded ninety-one is cheapest at a dollar ninety-six per litre in Randwick, diesel two dollars thirty-eight per litre in Leichhardt."; required with fuel-first order aired the same pair reversed, "Cheapest unleaded ninety-one is a dollar ninety a litre in Brunswick West, diesel two dollars thirty-five there too. Partly sunny, 12 degrees."; the not-required control aired neither. The regression gate ./scripts/eval.sh --script-only moved 80 percent to 82 percent on the three traffic-only replay markets where both new prompt lines are inert, which is sampling noise, not a change. Because the record persists and queues as the single ContentSelectionJson blob, no Table Storage, entity or queue plumbing changed; config-bundle.schema.json gained the two keys so bundles carrying them import. Costs to hold in mind: a required section consumes words the traffic body would otherwise use, and the word-target math does not reserve room for it, so a station that requires both sections on a 15 second slot is choosing less traffic; and RequiredSourceDetector is non-convergent by design, so a model that keeps refusing ships with a logged unresolved-gate warning into the existing human approval gate. BulletinScenario gained WeatherRequired/FuelRequired/FillOrder so any harness can exercise both contracts, and ScenarioMatrixEvalTests is now the three-arm live A/B for them.

## 2026-08-10 — Dev verification of always-include found three defects: the weather signal was digit-anchored and the duration trim could delete a required close

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The always-include feature and its section-order rule passed 4,472 unit tests and a script-only eval, then broke on the first twelve real dev bulletins. Every synthetic fixture had written temperatures as digits ("18 degrees"); the shipped read spells them out. So the presence signal, which had been lifted verbatim out of UnselectedSourceDetector where it exists to detect FABRICATION and is deliberately narrow, could not see a real weather line: dev job 77734311 aired "Clear, seventeen degrees!" and dev job 98f3c558 aired "Cool, fourteen degrees." and both were scored as having no weather at all. A third defect only a tight slot exposes: dev job 71568e4eac (Port Lincoln, 15 second slot, weather AND fuel both required) had its required fuel line survive the writer, both new gates and the safety review, and then lose it to the pre-synthesis duration trim, silently, with no gate re-check and no warning.

**Decision:** Three fixes, all re-verified live on dev. (1) ContentSourceSignals matches the bare word "degrees" instead of a digit followed by it, which also closes the same hole in the opposite direction: a fabricated spoken-word temperature on a traffic-only read used to slip past UnselectedSourceDetector. PolishLockPolicy already matched the substring "degree", so this aligns the new signal with the convention the repository already had right. (2) The two false consequences disappear with it: RequiredSourceDetector no longer demands a section that is already on air, and SectionOrderDetector can see the weather line, so a fuel-first station now airs fuel first. (3) BulletinDurationFitter.FitByTrimming gains closeIsRequired (default false, so an optional close trims exactly as before). When true it sheds traffic to the minSentences floor rather than degrade to the prefix trim that deletes the close, and returns null (no trim at all) when traffic already sits at the floor, leaving the residue to compression and the post-synthesis pass. It is threaded through IAudioPipelineService.SynthesizeWithDurationTargetAsync beside the existing lockedSuffix and passed by ScriptGenerationEngine (predictive trim and synth) and AudioFinalizer (re-voice), each from context.Content.RequiresWeather || context.Content.RequiresFuel. Every regression test for all three is written from the VERBATIM deployed sentence, not a synthetic equivalent.

**Rationale:** The deeper failure was the fixture vocabulary, not the regex: a unit test that invents its own input can only ever confirm the author's assumption about what production emits, and every one of these tests passed while the deployed behaviour was wrong. Reusing the fabrication signal for a presence question was the specific mistake, because the two directions want opposite sensitivities: a fabrication signal must be narrow (a false positive strips a real traffic sentence), while a presence signal must be broad (a false negative demands content that is already there). "degrees" is the one token that is unambiguous in both directions, which is why widening to it costs nothing. On the trim, protecting the close unconditionally for every station was rejected: for an optional source the existing degradation is the right editorial call (one fewer road beats a read that cannot fit), so the flag is what distinguishes a preference from a contract.

**Consequences:** Always-include now holds through the whole pipeline, including a slot too short for the content: Port Lincoln at 15 seconds trimmed 42 words to 26 and kept BOTH sections, Melbourne at 22 seconds trimmed 93 words to 27 and kept both in the configured fuel-first order, and Gold Coast and Cairns both aired fuel then weather with no gate warnings. The cost is now explicit rather than hidden: a required section is not budgeted for by the word-target maths, so on a short slot the traffic body is squeezed hard (the Melbourne 22 second read voiced 1 corridor out of 15 fetched). Two pre-existing defects were observed in the same sweep and are NOT fixed here: UnselectedSourceDetector trips on a weather word inside a ROAD NAME (dev job 8d8e5ec1, "Fog Bay Road" on a weather-unselected station, which burned a refine attempt and shipped an unresolved-gate warning), and a director-inserted ellipsis defeats the sentence splitter so two sentences become one unsplittable span, which is what pushed the Port Lincoln trim into the degraded branch in the first place. The eval delta was chased to ground and is noise: 9 interleaved samples per arm span 72 to 82 percent on both, and the prompt change measured alone on unchanged code scored 79 to 82, matching baseline.

## 2026-08-10 — Incident notification is verified by firing every rule, and one dashboard replaces six

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** An audit was asked to enumerate every condition that should raise an incident, prove each one reaches the Teams channel, and confirm the workbooks are correct. Enumeration found 13 incident paths across three transports: 8 Azure Monitor alert rules, the app's own failure cards, and the CI/CD failure stage. Nothing had ever been tested by firing it. Three defects surfaced immediately. `kv-access-denied` was an `activityLogAlerts` rule on `category: Security, level: Warning`, a signal Key Vault does not emit: 0 Activity Log Security events in 82 days against 342 real data-plane denials in the AuditEvent resource logs, and 30 days of alert history showed the rule had never fired. The `/api/health` availability web test had been probing from three APAC locations since bring-up with no alert rule watching it in any environment, so a stopped site, DNS or TLS failure, expiring certificate or health 503 notified nobody. Every dependency panel filtered `target has_any ('here', ...)`, and KQL `has` is term-based, so `router.hereapi.com` never matched: HERE, the traffic data source, was invisible on the main operations dashboard while 6 HERE hosts served 2,293 calls in 24 hours. Separately, the workbook inventory had been six per environment since 2026-06-24, when Operations Overview arrived and subsumed all five single-panel workbooks without anyone deleting them.

**Decision:** Prove notification by fault injection rather than by inspection, and fix what the proof exposed. The five log-search rules were fired by posting tagged synthetic telemetry to the dev Application Insights ingestion endpoint; the two platform metric rules were proved by a shape-clone probe rule and by a real firing on parked production; the rebuilt Key Vault rule was proved by a genuine `ForbiddenByRbac` denial; the new availability rule was proved by a deliberately-failing clone web test. `kv-access-denied` becomes a `scheduledQueryRule` over the workspace `AzureDiagnostics` AuditEvent stream, excluding `OperationName == "Authentication"` because those are pre-auth token rejections against the vault's public endpoint rather than an access-control problem. A ninth rule, `health-availability`, watches the web test with `WebtestLocationAvailabilityCriteria` and `failedLocationCount: 2` of three. The four latched rules gain `muteActionsDuration: PT1H`. Dependency filters use `hereapi`. And the five single-panel workbooks are deleted from IaC and from all three environments, leaving Operations Overview as the one dashboard.

**Rationale:** An alert rule is a claim about a system nobody has run. Two of the eight were false claims and one signal had no rule at all, and none of that is visible from reading the template: it took firing all of them to find out, which is why the evidence in `production-readiness.md` is now a timestamp pair per rule rather than a tick. Suppression rather than de-latching, because latching is what makes a sustained outage one incident, and the measurement was unambiguous: one injected incident produced 12 firings and 12 Teams cards in 17 minutes without it. `hereapi` rather than `contains`, because term matching is the reason the bug existed and switching operator would have hidden the lesson. On the dashboards, a workbook remains the right resource over `Microsoft.Portal/dashboards`: one `TimeRange` parameter re-scopes all 13 queries where dashboard tiles each pin their own range, `fallbackResourceIds` lets identical JSON deploy to three environments where dashboard tiles hardbake resource IDs, and the KQL diffs in git where a dashboard tile is a pinned chart snapshot, which is precisely how the HERE defect was found. The count was never a decision, though, and six was indefensible: every panel was duplicated, the five hardcoded `timeContext` so an operator could not re-scope them, and two had drifted into describing panels they did not contain (doc-audit MON-01).

**Consequences:** Nine alert rules per environment, 3 metric and 6 log-search, all fired and all confirmed to post a Teams card within about two seconds. One workbook per environment. The rebuilt Key Vault rule immediately surfaced a chronic defect nobody had seen: the TEST and PROD Function App staging-slot identities are refused `SecretGet` every day because their calls arrive over the public endpoint rather than the approved private link, 2,083 and 582 events in 90 days, so Key Vault references in staging-slot settings do not resolve and a blue-green swap could promote unresolved secrets. That is a network change and is deliberately not bundled here; it is logged as an open finding. Two operational facts learned the hard way: Azure rejects `muteActionsDuration` together with `autoMitigate: true`, and deploying into a parked environment re-arms its alert rules, which tripped production's `no-executions` rule during this work and required re-silencing. The injected fixtures remain in dev telemetry tagged `synthetic_test=monitoring-audit-2026-08-10`, including 20 failed `broadcast.bulletin.emitted` records for market `AUDIT` around 13:49Z. `workbook-pipeline-latency.png` and `workbooks-gallery.png` now show deleted content and their references were removed; the 11 August deep-dive PDF predates the consolidation and must be re-exported from its HTML.

## 2026-08-11 — Script marks are resolved in the aired read, the one text the teleprompter renders

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Dev job `17c0b28e` (KIIS 90s, Sydney) highlighted the wrong words. Hovering "slow" reported `KIIS — said as kiss`, and "underway on the" carried the Warringah rule. The delivery director had inserted `[brightly] ` after the opener; `ReviewBulletin` resolved the dictionary matches against `job.script.text` (untagged) while `ReviewScript` placed those same offsets into `padTags(airedRead)` (tagged). The tag's 11 characters sat between every later match and its word, so each mark landed 11 characters early. The identical mismatch existed in edit mode: `findPronunciationMatches(draft, …)` feeding `buildDraftMarks(padTags(draft), …)`.

**Decision:** A script mark is a pair of offsets, so it is only meaningful against the text it was resolved in, and that text is always the aired read. `resolveAiredRead(text, taggedText)` moves to `lib/tone-marks.ts` and is shared by the producer and the renderer instead of being derived twice. `ReviewBulletin` resolves matches and counts marks against `padTags(resolveAiredRead(...))`; the edit-mode matcher runs on `padTags(draft)`.

**Rationale:** Padding rather than stripping, because `padTags` preserves length: the tag characters still shift the text the operator reads, so removing them would trade one misalignment for another. Fixing it at the producer keeps one resolution per render and keeps the status line, the flagged-word count, and the highlighted words derived from the same array — which the code already claimed and did not do. Sharing the aired-read derivation is what stops the two call sites drifting apart again.

**Consequences:** Marks land on their own words in any bulletin carrying audio tags, which is every bulletin with a delivery style. `script-marks.test.ts` pins the invariant with the live script: with the tag applied the three marks must slice to `Sydney`, `Warringah`, `KIIS`; the old wiring returns `Sydney`, `way on th`, `ow. `. A rule word appearing inside a tag label (`[sydney]`) still cannot match, because the label is blanked.

## 2026-08-11 — An apply owns the review surface; the rejection it passes through is not a destination

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** An operator pressing Re-voice on dev job 17c0b28e watched the workspace turn into the as-aired record card for a bulletin marked Rejected, then a pipeline view, then back to review. An apply is TWO requests — the reject that frees the job (the backend only regenerates a Rejected/Failed/FallbackUsed job) and the regenerate that queues it — so for about half a second the job genuinely IS REJECTED, a terminal status, and every status-driven branch followed it there: the record card, a Rejected badge, a Regenerate button, and the decision dock vanishing. Measured on the mock harness at 135ms after the click. The same window is where an error boundary showing 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading reason)' was reported; AsAiredCard's hard read of job.rejection.reason is the only unguarded deref of that shape left in the bundle, though JobSchema and isCompleteJob both already refuse to produce a REJECTED job without its decision record.

**Decision:** useBulletinReview exposes applyInFlight ('revoice' | 'regenerate' | null), latched when an apply is submitted and cleared only once the job has genuinely moved (a pipeline status, FAILED) or the apply failed — a REJECTED the console caused itself does not clear it. ReviewPane renders one ApplyingView for the whole handoff and suppresses the status badge, JobActions and the decision dock while it is set. AsAiredCard reads the rejection reason optionally, falling back to the mirrored status-history note. The mock store now walks the real transition (REQUESTED, audio cleared, Rejection dropped, WAITING_APPROVAL ~1.8s later) instead of jumping straight back to WAITING_APPROVAL.

**Rationale:** The transient rejection is an implementation detail of the apply, not a state the operator decided or can act on: offering Regenerate and a Rejected badge invites action on a decision they did not make, and the record card claims the bulletin is finished while its replacement is being recorded. Latching on submit rather than on the mutation's isPending also covers the settle gap before the invalidated refetch lands, which is where the second flash came from. Keying the clear on 'the job left the status it was submitted from' rather than on lastUpdatedAt is what makes the reject itself part of the apply. The optional read in the record card adds no detection — two boundaries already fail loudly on a terminal payload with no decision record — but it stops an invariant violation costing the operator the whole workspace mid-review. The mock jumped straight to WAITING_APPROVAL, so no local harness had ever shown this window.

**Consequences:** Proven before and after on the mock harness by driving a real re-voice: with applyInFlight forced null the pane shows the record card and 'Status: Rejected' 135ms after the click; with the latch it shows 'Re-voicing' immediately, the pipeline view at 444ms, review again at 3.6s, and the record card never appears. New tests: five in use-bulletin-review.test.tsx (latch spans a REJECTED reading, clears on a pipeline status, never re-latches on return, reports a full regeneration, clears on failure), three in ReviewPane.test.tsx (applying view replaces the cockpit, dock hidden, cockpit returns), one in optimistic-reject-variant.test.tsx (the record card renders from the history note when the decision record is missing). The mock's simulated pipeline means local job fixtures now take ~1.8s to return from a regenerate.

## 2026-08-11 — A read names a road when it voices its words in order, not when it copies the name contiguously

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Dev job `1e1db059` (KIIS 90s, Sydney) showed **Cited 1** in the console's Evidence panel on a script naming ten roads. Two independent defects: the panel was incident-only, and the sentence "Banks Drive and the M1 at General Holmes Drive have minor delays too." carried only `Banks Drive` in its persisted `CorridorKeys`. `ScriptProvenanceMapper.Mentions` tested `sentence.Contains(roadName)` — a contiguous substring — so a read that inserts a preposition into a HERE road name loses its citation. The writer was handed `M1 General Holmes Drive` and a global guidance rule requiring the definite article on route codes, so "the M1 at General Holmes Drive" is exactly the read that rule asks for. A scan of 97 live dev jobs found **26 dropped citations across 21 jobs**: `Botany Road`, `Deer Park Bypass`, `Miller Street`, `Falcon Street`, `Toorak Road`, `Sheahans Road` and others, every one a road the read plainly names.

**Decision:** Matching is word-aware. `Words()` tokenizes both the road name and the sentence into letters/digits/apostrophes, strips a trailing possessive clitic, and `NamesRoad` accepts a name when the sentence voices every one of its words **in order** with at most two inserted words between consecutive name words. The FINAL name word also matches its plural. `MentionedRoadNames` is now derived from `Map` instead of scanning the whole script as one string. Separately, `RoadNameFormatter.ToSpeakable` expands a terminal bare compass letter (`Garfield Road E` → `Garfield Road East`), joining the existing terminal-only set.

**Rationale:** The contiguous test encoded an assumption the writer was never asked to honour — that a road name reaches air as one unbroken string. Word-aware matching drops three accidents the substring scan relied on, so each is now explicit: the possessive strip is what keeps the naturalness polish's "The M4's slow" from changing corridor lineage (the polish gate reverts the whole rephrase when it does); the plural allowance is what keeps "Narellan, Showground and Wallgrove Roads" citing Wallgrove Road; and the compass expansion replaces a prefix accident ("Garfield Road E" matching inside "East") with the reason it worked. The two-word insertion cap is what stops scattered common words ("Drive", "Street") spelling out a road the read never named — measured, `0` of the 97 jobs' existing citations are lost. Whole-word matching also closes a latent false positive: `M4` no longer matches inside `M40`.

**Consequences:** New bulletins cite every corridor their read names; measured on a post-deploy live poller bulletin (`e198c4b3`, sydney, 20 corridors) with zero residual gaps. Existing jobs keep the lineage the code computed at generation time — persisted `ScriptSentences` is an audit record, so job `1e1db059` still shows its `M1 General Holmes Drive` corridor as Unused, which is now the honest historical reading rather than an invisible one. 14 new domain tests: the split-name and contraction cases, a gap-too-far negative, whole-word `M4`/`M40`, no cross-sentence assembly in `MentionedRoadNames`, a 7-case theory drawn from the live corpus classes, and 3 formatter cases for the compass letter. Deployed to dev (backend + SWA) 2026-08-11.

## 2026-08-11 — Uncommitted work is only as safe as the test that pins it: the `A` approve hotkey, recovered from a dangling blob

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The user reported that the deployed dev SWA was missing the "press `A` to approve" hotkey they had previously built and deployed. Every ordinary search said it never existed: `git log --all -S"Keydown('a'"` returned zero commits, and `ReviewPane.tsx` carried the comment "Approve is deliberately click-only", which reads as a design decision rather than a regression. It was real. `git fsck --unreachable` surfaced it in two **dangling blobs** — `e607fad8` (`ReviewPane.tsx`, `useGlobalKeydown('a'|'A', approveShortcut)` guarded on WAITING_APPROVAL and on an in-flight mutation) and `55b0ba94` (`DecisionDock.tsx`, `aria-keyshortcuts="a"` plus a decorative keycap). It was never committed; the blobs exist only because the files were staged at some point. A later session then rewrote the same region of `ReviewPane` to add `applyInFlight`/`ApplyingView` from an older base, dropping the hotkey and replacing its comment with the "deliberately click-only" line. Nothing failed, because nothing tested it.

**Decision:** Restore both halves onto the current files (not a wholesale revert — the current `ReviewPane` carries newer apply-in-flight work the dangling copy predates), and pin the behaviour with four tests in `ReviewPane.test.tsx`: the key opens the confirmation and still never approves on its own, the dock advertises `aria-keyshortcuts="a"` without changing its accessible name, and the key is inert both for a job with no approve edge and while an apply is in flight. The guard composes better now than it did originally, because `waiting` already excludes an apply in flight.

**Rationale:** The comment was the trap. A dropped feature that leaves behind prose asserting its absence is indistinguishable from a decision, and it survived a full audit because the code read as intentional. A test would have failed the moment the region was rewritten; a comment cannot. `A` opens the *confirmation*, never the mutation, so the shortcut is safe by construction — the same reason `R` is a key and approve was thought not to be.

**Consequences:** Restored, tested (web 1,107 green, +4) and redeployed to dev; verified from the live host — `ReviewPane-3D_imcEd.js` contains `aria-keyshortcuts:"a"`, and all 107 served assets are byte-identical to the local build. A repeatable sweep came out of it: enumerate dangling blobs, keep those whose content is absent from both disk and every reachable ref, then diff their *interactive affordances* (`useGlobalKeydown`, `aria-keyshortcuts`, key listeners) and exported symbols against the working tree. Run over 1,089 dangling blobs it found 638 orphaned source snapshots — almost all harmless intermediate saves — exactly one lost affordance (this hotkey), and one never-committed symbol (`ToneScriptEditor`, superseded on disk by `PronunciationScriptEditor` + `TonePalette`). Twelve other orphaned symbols were traced to real deletion commits and are deliberate. **Standing rule: commit before rewriting a region you did not write, and pin an interactive affordance with a test, not a comment.**

## 2026-08-11 — A slot that aired nothing gets its own status: `Missed`, entered at the playout deadline, not 24 hours later

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Operators reported the review queue filling with bulletins whose slots had long gone, and that the console ranked the stalest one as the most urgent. Two separate defects sat behind that. (1) The QT-008 hygiene sweep marked an unapproved bulletin `Rejected` 24 hours past its playout, which is wrong on three counts: `Rejected` asserts a human took it off air, the expiry's `RejectionEntry` is fed back to the writer as producer feedback by `TrafficEvidenceBuilder.BuildRejectionFeedback` (so a regenerated job could be told "Previous version was rejected: Expired unapproved"), and `LOG_OUTCOMES` counts it in the broadcast log's rejection filter. (2) 24 hours is far past the point the bulletin could ever have aired: `ProcessFallbacksAsync` deliberately skips a WaitingApproval job that HAS audio (`IsValidAudio`), so the standby chain never covers it, and no approval means no drop file. Such a job is not "pending", it is a slot that aired nothing.

**Decision:** `JobStatus.Missed`, appended last (Table Storage persists status by name, so no migration and existing `Rejected` expiries stay as they are). New `Job.MarkMissed(deadlineUtc, utcNow)` transitions only from `WaitingApproval`, records `MissedDeadlineUtc`, writes a Warn job log, and deliberately writes NO `RejectionEntry` and no `ErrorMessage`. The sweep (`JobWatchdog.MarkMissedWaitingApprovalsAsync`) now runs two clocks: a scheduled job is missed `MissedAfterDeadlineMinutes` (default 10) past its `FallbackDeadlineUtc` — the Zetta delivery deadline, `scheduledForUtc - FallbackDeadlineMinutes` — while an ad-hoc job, which has no playout to be late for, keeps the `ExpireWaitingApprovalHours` dwell window (default 24). `Missed` is terminal and settled: not approvable, not regenerable, not deletable, never a fallback source. New `MissedJobDto`/`MissedDataDto` carry the deadline to the console. The web `SlotState`'s overloaded `'missed'` splits into `'late'` (still actionable, hot) and `'missed'` (settled, cold).

**Rationale:** 10 minutes matches the existing `PostPlayoutGraceMinutes` alerting grace, so "we stop asking you to act" and "we mark it missed" happen at the same moment rather than 24 hours apart — one rule an operator can hold in their head. Non-regenerable is the load-bearing part: `RequestRegeneration` resets the job IN PLACE (clears audio, script, corridors, incidents, attempt history), so allowing it would erase the evidence that the slot aired nothing AND silently decrement the missed-slot count the status exists to produce. The correct affordance for "I want that bulletin again" is a fresh ad-hoc trigger for the current moment, which already exists. `ToFailureStage` deliberately does NOT get a `Missed` arm: it maps `FailedAtStatus` to a wire activity stage, `Missed` can never be a failed-at status, and `"MISSED"` is not a member of the console's `FAILURE_STAGE_VALUES`.

**Consequences:** Scheduled bulletins now leave the review queue about 10 minutes past their delivery deadline instead of sitting for a day, and missed slots are countable separately from operator rejections in the broadcast log. Expiries no longer leak into the LLM's producer feedback. `Broadcast__MissedAfterDeadlineMinutes` is a new app setting (10 in `appsettings.json`; `0` disables the scheduled arm). Backend 765 Application + 1,756 Domain tests green; web 1,125 unit tests and the 6 jobs-review e2e specs green. The bulletin state-machine render in `architecture/renders/views/` does not yet show `Missed` and is stale until re-rendered.

## 2026-08-11 — The console never learns who is calling: an Entra `oid`, captured at sign-in and verified by its own token, is what makes operator identity and market scoping real

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN reported an operator publishing a prod bulletin while absent from the Operators page. The cause was not the operator account — it holds `Operator` through `APP-IBP-Prod-Operator` — but a hole two individually-correct decisions had opened between them. Microsoft documents that the `x-ms-client-principal` header a Static Web App forwards to a linked backend carries only `identityProvider`/`userId`/`userDetails`/`userRoles` and **never** the `claims` array ("the `x-ms-client-principal` header accessible in the API function does not contain the `claims` array"), and that `userId` is "an Azure Static Web Apps-specific unique identifier… unique on a per-app basis" — not the Entra `oid`. So `ClientPrincipal` fell back to that per-app id, `HasDirectoryObjectId` was false, and `OperatorsHttpTrigger` passed an empty object id into `OperatorRegistrar`, which returned immediately. Registration had been moved into the SWA `rolesSource` call on 29 Jul for exactly this reason — the one place the AAD claims reach the backend — and then bug-bash 2026-08-05 finding 10 removed that write because `POST /api/GetRoles` is anonymous and its payload forgeable. Neither decision was wrong; together they left no registration path at all, and nothing tested that *somebody* still got registered. Proven live: `[Operators] Registered or refreshed operator` had never been logged in 7 days on dev, test **or** prod. The second, worse consequence went unnoticed for the same reason: `MarketAccessService` looks up assignment rows by that same id while rows are keyed by `oid`, and a miss returns `Option.None`, which means UNRESTRICTED — so operator market scoping did not bind at all on test or prod. The forgeability concern is real and was verified rather than assumed: an unauthenticated `POST` from the open internet to `https://ibp-aue-prd-fna-app01.azurewebsites.net/api/GetRoles` returns `200 {"Roles":["Admin"]}`. Microsoft's "the role assignment function can no longer be accessed by external HTTP requests" protects only the SWA route; the Function App's own hostname bypasses it and the path sits in Easy Auth `excludedPaths`.

**Decision:** The `rolesSource` payload stays untrusted, and the endpoint now writes only what a cryptographically validated token proves. New `SwaRolesSourceTokenValidator` (Functions/Auth) validates the payload's `accessToken` against Entra — signature from cached OIDC metadata, issuer pinned to the configured tenant, audience pinned to `AadClientId`/`api://{AadClientId}`, lifetime and signed-token required — and returns `None` for an absent, malformed, expired, wrongly-audienced, or `oid`-less token. Only on success does `GetRoles` register the operator, keyed by the **token's** `oid` with the **token's** roles, and persist a `userId → oid` alias in a second `SwaAlias` partition of the operator-assignment table (first writer wins; an established alias is never repointed). `MarketAccessService` resolves scope through exactly one alias hop when the direct lookup finds no row, and an alias-lookup failure fails **closed** (deny all) rather than widening to unrestricted. `AadTenantId` is now emitted as a Function App app setting — it was a bicep param used only for the Easy Auth `openIdIssuer` and never reached the runtime. The `{"Roles":[...]}` response, the `GetRoles` function name, its route and its anonymous level are all unchanged, because SWA's sign-in depends on them.

**Rationale:** Reinstating the 29 Jul write unconditionally would have reopened finding 10; leaving it removed left both operator identity and market scoping inert. Validating the token is the only option that satisfies both, because it moves the trust boundary off the request body and onto Entra's signature — a forged payload simply fails validation and records nothing, which is precisely today's behaviour, so the change cannot regress. Fail-closed was chosen everywhere for the same reason the defect was severe: a scope that cannot be established must never silently become "all markets". The alias is captured at sign-in because that is the ONLY moment SWA presents both ids together; nothing later in the request lifecycle can correlate them. First-writer-wins on the alias bounds the residual risk that a legitimately-signed-in low-privilege user could claim another person's opaque `userId`. Microsoft does not document the default audience of the `rolesSource` access token, so rather than change `login.loginParameters` on a live prod SWA ten days before SG3 on an inference, the validator logs the **observed** `aud`/`iss` on every rejection (never the token) and lets real traffic answer the question first.

**Consequences:** Build 0 errors / 0 warnings; 726 Functions, 765 Application, 1,756 Domain tests green, including the regression that was missing — a non-admin whose id is an SWA `userId` now resolves to exactly the markets their alias-mapped row assigns instead of being unrestricted — and the security assertion that a disagreeing payload `oid` loses to the token's. Finding 10's protection is preserved as a re-aimed test, not deleted. Two Infrastructure failures (`MissedDeadlineUtc`) and the 16 E2E failures are pre-existing and unrelated: the former belong to the in-flight `Missed`-status work in the entry above, the latter need a running Functions host. **Two things remain unproven until deployed:** whether the `rolesSource` token's audience is already our client id (the validator's diagnostics answer this on first real sign-in; if it is not, `login.loginParameters` needs `scope=api://{clientId}/…` and an exposed API scope on the app registration, which is an ARN-tenant change), and whether scoping binds for a real Operator — dev cannot show it because `Auth__DevFallbackRole=Admin` makes every dev caller an admin and admins short-circuit scoping, so that proof needs an Operator-only principal on test. The separate ARN ask stands and is now correctly classified as required rather than optional enrichment: without Graph consent (`Application.Read.All`, `GroupMember.Read.All`, `User.ReadBasic.All`) the Operators page still cannot list a group-derived role holder who has never signed in.


## 2026-08-11 — Covering a slot means DELIVERING it: the fallback chain now writes to playout itself, and an operator can choose the source in one move

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Asked whether a missed or failed bulletin can vanish from the queue, and whether approving an older bulletin after a newer one could overwrite the audio that airs, three defects surfaced in the same seam. (1) `JobService.PublishJobAsync` is the ONLY caller of `IFileDeliveryService.DeliverAsync`, and `JobWatchdog.ProcessFallbacksAsync` never called it: applying a fallback attached the source's audio to the job and marked it `FallbackUsed`, then stopped. So the standby cart — the thing that exists for the moments nobody is watching — required somebody to be watching, and `solution-design.md:130`'s "a dedicated fallback-fill cart guarantees no dead air" was not true of the code. (2) The board offered a bulletin awaiting review as an "air something else" option, which `GetLastSuccessfulJobForMarketAsync` deliberately excludes, so picking it would have done nothing. (3) The console had no way to see whether our WAV was still in the drop folder, which is the only fact that distinguishes a safe swap (file present, so an overwrite replaces what airs) from an unsafe one (file collected, so a second write queues a duplicate that may land in the wrong break).

**Decision:** The deadline sweep delivers what it covers a slot with. `JobWatchdog.DeliverFallbackAsync` signs off as `system (deadline)`, re-reads the job (publish is revision-guarded), and publishes — the human gate is already satisfied by construction, because the source is either an approved bulletin from earlier today or the network's pre-approved cart. An operator can pick the source directly: `POST /api/jobs/{jobId}/air-source` (`kind: repeat|cart`, Operator tier, ETag-guarded) validates a repeat against the same eligibility bar the sweep uses (same market and station, has audio, already approved, same LOCAL broadcast day via `TimeZoneHelper.GetLocalDayWindowUtc`), applies it, then runs the same approve → re-read → publish sequence attributed to the named operator. A delivery failure after the slot has already changed returns a failure saying exactly that, and writes it to the job's audit log. Pickup is now observable: `IDeliveryFileWriter.GetPendingWriteTimeAsync` probes the drop target, `GET /api/markets/{marketId}/playout-tray` reports `awaitingPickup` plus `writtenAtUtc`, and the console's audition panel leads with it.

**Rationale:** A status that changes without the file moving is the failure mode the fallback chain existed to prevent, so coverage had to mean delivery or mean nothing. Reusing the domain's existing verbs (`ApplyFallback`, then the ordinary approve/publish path) keeps one delivery route rather than a second writer that could disagree with it — cart resolution and padding stay solely in `BulletinFallbackService.ApplyFillerCartAsync`. Attributing a manual override to the operator rather than to `system` is what makes the audit trail answer "who decided this", which a shared `system` actor cannot. Presence-in-folder was chosen as the swap-safety signal because it is the only one Zetta gives us: there is no receipt, no callback and no slot entity, so absence IS the collection event.

**Consequences:** Solution builds 0 errors / 0 warnings; 1,756 Domain, 772 Application, 732 Functions, 1,379 Infrastructure and 14 architecture tests green (the 16 E2E failures need a running Functions host, unrelated). Two Application tests that asserted the old behaviour — the sweep skipping any job that already had audio — are replaced by `Fallback_WhenApplied_IsDeliveredToPlayout` plus the waiting/approved coverage cases, because they encoded the requirements violation rather than a contract. On the console, the forecast cell is now the control: it opens an audition panel where every option for the slot plays inline and commits on the same line, so choosing no longer costs three navigations. **Not yet true:** nothing prevents a swap after Zetta has collected the file — the tray line reports the risk and the operator decides. A `SlotOverride` entity remains unmodelled; the override is recorded on the slot's job, which is sufficient while one job owns one slot.

## 2026-08-11 — Deploying it to dev found two defects the unit tests could not: a stale revision that silently skipped delivery, and provenance that vanished on publish

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The delivering-fallback change above shipped with green suites, so dev was meant to be a formality. It was not. (1) Every covered slot on dev logged `[Fallback] … could not be signed off for delivery: the bulletin changed after you loaded it` and the drop folder stayed empty: `TryApplyFallbackAsync` saves the job, `SaveJobAsync` does not write the new ETag back onto the caller's instance, so the sweep's `job.ETag` was already stale by the time it signed off — approve failed its own revision guard and delivery never ran. The test suite could not see it because the `IJobService` substitute ignored ETags, and the failure was invisible on the console because it only went to telemetry. (2) With delivery working, a covered slot ends at `Published`, and `PublishedJobDto` had no `Fallback` block — so the API could no longer say whether a published slot aired its own read or a repeat from three hours earlier. Keying that block off `FallbackSourceJobId` then hid cart coverage too, because `Job.ApplyFillerFallback` leaves the source id `None` by design. (3) Dev also revealed the audit line `Job approved by operator` firing for `system (deadline)` sign-offs, claiming a human had acted.

**Decision:** `DeliverFallbackAsync` re-reads the job BEFORE signing off (and again before publishing), and every failure path now writes to the job's own log via `ReportUndeliveredAsync`, not just to App Insights — a covered slot whose audio did not ship is the one failure an operator must see. `PublishedJobDto.Fallback` is optional-but-populated whenever `FallbackReason` is present (reason, not source id, because the cart has no source), shared with the `FallbackUsed` shape through one `MapFallback` helper; the console's as-aired detail renders it for both statuses, reading "Aired a repeat of …" or "Aired the standby cart". `ApproveJobAsync` names its actor. `Fallback_WhenApplied_IsDeliveredToPlayout` now models storage as authoritative about revisions — the re-read hands back a DISTINCT instance, as the entity mapper does — and was confirmed to fail against the old code and pass against the new.

**Rationale:** The first defect is a class, not an incident: any caller that saves a job and then calls a revision-guarded operation on its own stale instance will fail this way, and the only reliable guard is to re-read between the two. Making the test model that (rather than stubbing a substitute that accepts any ETag) is what turns it into a regression test; the earlier version passed with the bug present, which is why the bug reached dev at all. Surfacing provenance on `Published` matters because delivery changed the meaning of the status: before, coverage was legible from `FallbackUsed`; now the terminal status is identical either way, and "what actually aired" must not depend on parsing a free-text log line.

**Consequences:** Verified on dev against BOTH transports, judging the drop file's bytes rather than an HTTP 200 — `sha256(drop file) == sha256(the audio the operator chose)` in all five paths: ordinary approved read (1,940,444 B), operator repeat override, operator cart override, sweep-covered repeat (Melbourne, 2,646,044 B), sweep-covered cart (Brisbane, 2,367,312 B, via `AzureFilesDropFileWriter` — the writer prod actually uses, exercised for the first time). Every rejection path was confirmed to leave the drop untouched: unknown `kind` (400), missing source, self-repeat, another market, a previous broadcast day, an unapproved source, a stale ETag and a missing ETag (428). The tray probe flips `awaitingPickup` true on write and false once the file is removed, over both blob and Files transports. **Dev configuration changed to make this provable and left in place:** `Zetta__Enabled=true`, `Zetta__Transport=AzureFilesDrop`, `Zetta__DropAccountName=ibpauedevstaapp01`, a `informationbulletins` file share plus blob container on that account, and `Storage File Data Privileged Contributor` for the Function App's managed identity (dev had delivery switched off entirely, so no delivery code had ever run there). **Still true:** a slot already delivered cannot be swapped — `ApplyFallback` refuses a terminal job, so the API answers 409 `Cannot apply fallback to a job in terminal state: Published` and the drop keeps the file it holds. That is the honest current behaviour, not a decision that late swaps should be impossible.

## 2026-08-12 — An expired slot can never be delivered by a restart sweep; playout is mocked until explicitly re-enabled

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Restarting production after the 11 Aug fallback-delivery release exposed 15 old Sydney and Cairns jobs. `ProcessFallbacksAsync` ran before `MarkMissedWaitingApprovalsAsync` and accepted any job past `FallbackDeadlineUtc` with no upper bound, so it approved/published all 15 between 14:56:31Z and 14:57:00Z, 8-10 hours after their slots. The live share later contained no files because Zetta had consumed them; Zetta has no on-air receipt, so ingestion is proven but airtime is not.

**Decision:** The missed sweep is renamed `MarkMissedExpiredSlotsAsync`, runs before fallback, and settles every unpublished scheduled status once `FallbackDeadlineUtc + MissedAfterDeadlineMinutes` passes. `Job.MarkMissed` accepts unpublished/unsettled states, including Approved and Failed, while preserving approval history and writing no rejection. `ProcessFallbacksAsync` carries its own identical age guard so save failures or later reordering cannot deliver stale audio. Ad-hoc approvals remain manual because they have no scheduled slot.

All environments use the existing `Zetta__Enabled=false` mock path during remediation and UAT. It returns `SkippedDisabled` before downloading audio or invoking a delivery writer, so publish workflows finish without a drop file. Test and production pin the toggle false in Bicep; development inherits the false template default. Re-enabling production requires an explicit, attended operational decision after this incident is closed.

**Rationale:** A signed-off bulletin is safe only for its slot; approval does not make hours-old traffic current. The missed threshold is therefore a hard delivery boundary, not just queue hygiene. Disabling the writer in IaC as well as live settings prevents a routine deployment from undoing containment.

**Consequences:** Fifteen stale files reached the production drop on 11 Aug; all three live Function Apps now report delivery disabled. The production share root is empty and its network posture is restored to default-deny with no public IP rules. Focused verification is green: 3 scheduler regressions, 7 domain transition cases, and 20 delivery-service tests.

Deployment and QA evidence: the guarded backend package was deployed to dev, test and
production with `Zetta__Enabled=false` confirmed live in all three. In test, job
`257179ffd99042bcb173d27451b9ce86` completed trigger, script edit/re-voice, approval and
explicit publish, ending `Published` with the job log `Playout delivery is disabled in
