this environment — audio retained in storage, not sent to playout.` The full Application
(779) and Domain (1,763) suites passed, the focused delivery-service suite passed all 20
cases, and the Bicep template built successfully. A read-only browser walk covered every
production console surface while both pilot schedules remained paused.

## 2026-08-12 — A gate that only passes on the author's machine is not a gate: verify in a detached worktree

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Syncing the tree to ADO and dev exposed three failures that had nothing to do with the code being pushed, and one that did. `verify.sh` verifies the WORKING TREE, so with another writer editing concurrently the gate judged their half-finished work and failed on it. Running the gate against a detached worktree at the exact commit found the real defect: two documents pointed `see_also` at `docs/elevenlabs/python-sdk/AGENTS.md`, which is gitignored vendored SDK content, so the docs harness resolved it here and would fail in any clean clone. Separately the machine's toolchain had drifted out from under the repo: `global.json` pins .NET SDK 10.0.301 and only 10.0.109 remained installed (rollForward latestFeature cannot go down a feature band), `func` was absent so backend E2E could not start, and Node had reached 26.4.0 against CI's pinned 22.x. Node 25+ ships an experimental built-in `localStorage` global that is undefined without `--localstorage-file`; Vitest copies Node's globals onto the jsdom window, so that undefined value shadowed jsdom's Storage and killed every test touching storage - 16 across OperatorsPage and OperatorAssignmentTable.

**Decision:** Verification of a push is done against the commits, not the tree: `git worktree add --detach /tmp/arn-verify HEAD` with node_modules symlinked, then `verify.sh --full` there. The unresolvable `see_also` lines are removed rather than the vendored docs un-ignored. `web/src/test/storage-shim.ts` is registered as a vitest `setupFiles` entry and installs a Storage ONLY when the host has shadowed it, so a real jsdom Storage still wins and a genuine jsdom breakage stays visible. The pinned .NET SDK is installed to `~/.dotnet` and `func` to `~/.local`, rather than weakening `global.json` to match a downgraded machine.

**Rationale:** Both classes of failure are invisible where the work happens and certain where it lands. A `see_also` resolved against the filesystem passes for whoever generated the ignored file and fails for everyone else, which is the same shape as the leak guard depending on `web/audit/` screenshots that `.gitignore` excludes - that gate cannot pass from a fresh clone at all. A test suite that depends on which Node happens to be installed reads as a code regression when it is a host artifact, and the wrong fix is to edit the tests. Weakening the SDK pin would have made the local build stop matching CI, trading a visible failure for an invisible one.

**Consequences:** Every gate is green at the pushed commit in a clean checkout except `docs leak guard`, which needs gitignored generated screenshots and so is unrunnable from a fresh clone - pre-existing, now written down rather than rediscovered. The pre-push gate then passed all gates on the real tree and `d5acbcab..aeae7cee` reached ado/master. Dev was deployed FROM the clean worktree, not the dirty tree, so it carries the commits and not another writer's in-flight managers: 113 of 113 assets byte-identical to the build, index.html identical, and a live poller bulletin (`a7b94ce7`, sydney, 22s) ran clean with zero residual lineage gaps and a 100% pre-review transcript match. GitHub `origin` remains unpushable: its URL names a personal Arinco guest account that 404s for the signed-in personal credential, so ADO is the only synced remote.

## 2026-08-12 — Voiceover renders on a library voice, and the Voices page opens to operators

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN asked for a way to use a configured voice with any script to produce a downloadable audio file for advertisements and similar production work, reachable by operators as well as admins. No endpoint did this: /voices/profiles/preview synthesises a FIXED sample script, /jobs/{id}/audition takes arbitrary text but is job-addressed and market-guarded, /synthesize takes raw voice fields with no profile resolution and returns only a bare blob filename. The frontend /voices page was admin-only, like every other library page.

**Decision:** New VoiceoverHttpTrigger with two routes. POST voices/profiles/{id}/voiceover resolves the profile server-side to its CURRENT version (BaseVoiceId + Version.Model + Version.Settings, the audition trust rule), synthesises the caller's script verbatim, saves voiceover_{profileId}_{ts}.wav and returns a RELATIVE url plus the file name. GET voices/voiceovers/{fileName} streams those bytes back through our own origin, Range-aware, with Content-Disposition attachment, and refuses any name that does not match the voiceover pattern. The POST is Operator in RouteRoleMatrix and is the one deliberate exemption to the market/job-scoping assertion in AuthorizationMiddlewareTests. ROUTE_VOICES is now requiredRole operator; VoicesPage gates create/duplicate on useIsAdmin (cards and rows get a focusable Record button instead of the actions kebab) and VoiceStudio shows a non-admin only the Voiceover step with no submit. Pace boost and station pronunciation dictionaries are NOT applied.

**Rationale:** A cross-origin SAS url cannot deliver the feature: browsers ignore an anchor download attribute on another origin, so the operator would land in a media viewer instead of a saved file - hence the same-origin streaming GET, whose name pattern stops it becoming an unguarded reader for bulletin audio in the same container. Operator on the POST is justified because it mutates nothing (no job, no schedule, no shared config) and a voice belongs to the library, not to a market, so there is no market to scope it to; the cost is bounded by the existing 5,000-character synthesis ceiling. Pace boost is slot-fitting compression for bulletins and an advertisement has no slot; a pronunciation dictionary is per-station and a voiceover has no station.

**Consequences:** New files: src/ArnBulletinGenerator.Functions/Triggers/Http/VoiceoverHttpTrigger.cs, test/ArnBulletinGenerator.Functions.Tests/VoiceoverHttpTriggerTests.cs, web/src/features/voices/components/VoiceoverSection.tsx. The scoping assertion in AuthorizationMiddlewareTests now carries a named /voiceover clause - any OTHER unscoped Operator write must still fail it. VoiceProfileTable and VoiceVariantCard take canManage (default true). Operators can now see the whole voice library read-only, which is a widened read surface accepted with the change. Voiceover WAVs land in the broadcasts container with the standard published=false tag and are covered by its retention rules.

## 2026-08-12 — Priority-road names are typed, not validated: a road-name autofill was built, reviewed and reverted the same day

**Status:** superseded by "A good run airs only a name the flow feed returned" (same day) — the autofill is REVERTED and must not be rebuilt without answering the objection below

**Context:** The priority-roads composer is a free-text Input with only a maxLength. A priority road takes effect by NAME (`PriorityRoads.IsMatch` against corridor road names), so a misspelling boosts nothing, silently. Built a typeahead to close it: `ITrafficProvider.GetRoadNamesAsync` + `CorridorAggregator.DistinctRoadNames` over HERE flow (`functionalClasses=1,2,3`, `minJamFactor=0`) behind `GET markets/{market}/road-names`, keyed on the market's own `MarketSchedule.Coverage`, successes cached 12h. Went through two rounds of correction — the first cut dumped the top 8 names as a browse list, which is an arbitrary sample of hundreds presented as a menu; the second gated on a 2-character query, added "+N more", and stopped warning while loading or when the vocabulary was empty.

**Decision:** REVERTED in full. Operators type the name. No endpoint, no third-party call on a config screen, no cache, no suggestion list, no spelling warning.

**Rationale:** The vocabulary can never be authoritative, so nothing built on it can be either. It is one point-in-time flow snapshot cached 12h — HERE returns only the segments it had data for in those tiles at that moment — gated by the coverage shape and limited to FC 1-3. "Not in the list" therefore does not mean "wrong", so the warning is unreliable, and an unreliable warning on a config screen is worse than none: once it is wrong a few times it is noise on every row. Measurement killed it: of 389 distinct real HERE-derived road names in `test/corpus/regressions/`, 11 are ALL CAPS and 3 embed a direction (`WEST GATE FREEWAY (EASTBOUND)`). Clicking that suggestion configures a name whose token run `IsMatch` requires — it matches a direction-named corridor but NOT a plain `West Gate Freeway` one, while typing "West Gate Freeway" matches both. **The feature could hand an operator a strictly worse answer than their own typing.** It was also solving the wrong problem: the harm was never the silent no-op, it was the pipeline airing the typo, which is a backend defect and needs no UI.

**Consequences:** Deleted: `RoadNamesHttpTrigger` + its tests, `ITrafficProvider.GetRoadNamesAsync` and both implementations, `CorridorAggregator.DistinctRoadNames` + its tests, `MarketRoadNamesDto`, `web/src/features/schedules/api/road-names-hooks.ts`, the `marketRoadNames` path, the mock store method/type/route and its tests, `RoadNameSuggestions`, and the `RuleComposer.footer` prop added for it. The row redesign from the same session (`Incidents` / `Good runs` toggle group) is UNAFFECTED and stays. If this is ever revisited, the honest shape is to report match evidence AFTER the fact from job history ("this road has matched 0 corridors in 30 days") — observed, not predicted.

## 2026-08-12 — A priority road's two jobs are one multi-choice control, not a pill beside a select

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** A priority road does two independent things in the pipeline — `BoostIncidents` (an impact multiplier on its incident corridors) and `FlowTier != None` (it competes for a slot while flowing) — and the row expressed them with two different idioms. `BoostPill` rendered the bare word "Incidents" as a `role="switch"` whose off state was only a missing tint, so it read as a label rather than a choice. Beside it, `FlowTierSelect` offered "Don't mention / Normal / High / Critical": bare adjectives that never said which dimension they graded, plus a THIRD off switch duplicating what a toggle should own. Nothing on the row said the two settings were independent, or that a road could be listed and do nothing at all.

**Decision:** One `ToggleGroup type="multiple"` per row — `Incidents` and `Good runs` — replaces both the pill and the select's off value. The strength select renders ONLY while Good runs is on, keeps just the three real strengths, and each option carries a one-line description of what that strength does. Turning Good runs off writes `flowTier: 'none'`; turning it back on restores `DEFAULT_FLOW_TIER` ('high'), the same default a newly added road gets, rather than reviving a level the operator can no longer see. Each item carries a Check (on) or Plus (off) glyph, matching `AssignOperatorDialog`'s selected-chip pair, and hover moves only the text colour. The group is labelled per road (`What {road} is used for`). "Good runs" is the term `RundownTable` and `AdjustMapExplorer` already show operators, so config and review now name the same thing the same way.

**Rationale:** The two axes are genuinely independent, so the honest control is a multi-select, not two controls of different weight; and "which jobs does this road do" is the question an operator actually has. The glyph is not decoration: measured live, the shared outline toggle's `hover:bg-accent` is close enough to `data-[state=on]:bg-primary/10` that an OFF chip on the hovered row read as ON — colour alone could not carry the state, and could not carry it at all without colour. The strength stays a Select rather than a third segmented control because it grades one job rather than choosing one, and a second segmented control in a 28px row would compete with the group for the same reading.

**Consequences:** `BoostPill` is deleted; `RoadUseToggle` and `handleSetUses` replace it and `handleToggleIncidents`. `FLOW_TIERS` no longer contains `none`, so the tier select cannot be the place a road stops being a good-run candidate. `rowInert` now reads "enabled with no job selected" from one derived list instead of two fields. Toolbar hint, empty state and `docs/reference/per-station-configuration.md` all describe the two jobs. Controls measure 28px, matching the row's existing density. The wire contract, the domain model and the pipeline are UNCHANGED — this is a presentation change over the same `BoostIncidents` + `FlowTier` pair.

## 2026-08-12 — One row-pill scale across the Bulletin-rules hub, and a category pill always lives in RuleRow's `badge` slot

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Audit of every `RuleRow` caller in the hub after the priority-roads row was rebuilt. Two real divergences, and one thing that only looked like one. (1) A CATEGORY pill sat in a different slot on two tabs: Editorial guidance put its type pill in `badge` (the fixed `sm:w-28` column `RuleRow` documents for exactly this), while Banned words put its kind pill in `actions` on the right — hand-widened to `w-24 justify-center` to fake the alignment the slot already provides, and occupying the position other tabs use for per-row controls and state. (2) The `actions` slot carried two type scales: filler statements at `text-xs` with a `size-3.5` icon (agreeing with the `Badge` primitive's `px-2.5 py-0.5 text-xs`), and the new priority-road controls at `text-[11px]` with `size-3`.

**Decision:** A category pill goes in `badge`, styled exactly as Editorial guidance styles it (`variant="outline"` plus the tint map, no width or alignment classes — the slot owns the column). Banned words moved, and `w-24 justify-center` and its now-unused `cn` import went with it. The one row-pill scale for the hub is the `Badge` primitive's: `text-xs`, `px-2.5`, `size-3.5` icons, interactive controls at `h-7`. Priority roads moved onto it. Filler statements was already there and was NOT changed.

**Rationale:** Filler statements' ghost Button was the initially suspected outlier and is not one: it opens a dialog, so it is an ACTION, and the shared-row conventions explicitly keep a control that carries its own UI out of a menu and in the row as a button. Aligning it to the pills would have made an action look like a state — the exact confusion this pass removed from the priority-road row. Anchoring the scale to `Badge` rather than to the smaller custom size means a pill and a badge sitting side by side in one row cannot disagree, which is what `text-[11px]` next to the `text-xs` "Not in use" badge did.

**Consequences:** Verified live in mock mode by measurement, not inspection: all 14 Banned-words badges render at one x (435px) and one width (112px = `sm:w-28`), in switch → badge → label order; the priority-road chip and strength select both measure 12px type, 28px tall, 14px glyph. `RuleRow` itself is unchanged — both divergences were caller-side. Remaining differences across the family are deliberate: `Badge` pills are text-height (21px) while interactive controls are `h-7` touch targets, and filler's borderless ghost button keeps `px-2` rather than a bordered pill's `px-2.5`.


## 2026-08-12 — A good run airs only a name the flow feed returned; a watched road is never synthesised from config

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** `FlowPoolBuilder.MarkWeightedFlowRoads` ended with a recovery loop: for every watched priority road (`Enabled` + `FlowTier != None`) with no matching incident corridor, it added a synthetic `FlowRoad` to the pool, named from `PriorityRoads.FindGoodRuns` — i.e. from the OPERATOR'S configured string, scored from an assumed arterial class. Two defects in one. (1) **It aired the typo.** A misspelling can never match a corridor, so it always satisfied the "no corridor" condition, was always injected, and `FindGoodRuns` returns the configured string verbatim — so the misspelling could be read on air as a flowing road, indefinitely. (2) **"No incident" is not evidence of flowing.** A watched road standing still at jamFactor 8 with no reported incident was aired as a good run, which is simply false.

**Decision:** Delete the recovery loop. A watched road reaches the flow pool ONLY from the provider's own flow data, so both the name and the claim come from measurement. `MarkWeightedFlowRoads` loses its now-unused `allCorridors` parameter (corridor exclusion was already handled downstream by `GoodRunPolicy.ExcludeCorridorRoads`), and `PriorityRoads.FindGoodRuns` loses its last production caller and is deleted with its tests. To preserve the legitimate capability the loop was covering — a watched arterial that IS flowing but ranks below the fetch cap — `FetchFreeFlowingRoadsSafeAsync` now requests `FlowMatchPoolSize` (200) instead of 18. Weighted roads sort first and `FlowPoolCap` (20) still bounds what is persisted, so widening the fetch changes which watched roads are FOUND without changing what is stored.

**Rationale:** This is the fix the road-name autofill was decoration over, and it holds whatever the operator types — which is why typing needs no validation. The fetch widening is free: same HTTP response, less truncation, no extra provider call. Deleting the loop rather than gating it keeps one rule that is easy to state and impossible to regress: nothing enters the flow pool that the feed did not name.

**Consequences:** A watched road that the feed does not report as flowing (jamFactor ≥ 4, or absent from the response) is no longer reported as a good run — correct, and a behaviour change worth knowing when a market's good-run count drops. `BroadcastOrchestratorTests.PriorityRoads_BoostIncidents_AndFlowTier_ReportGoodRuns` encoded the old contract and now stubs `GetFreeFlowingRoadsAsync`; new `WatchedRoadAbsentFromFlowFeed_IsNeverReportedAsAGoodRun` proves a misspelling reaches neither `GoodRunRoads` nor the persisted `FlowPool`. Suites: Domain 1,759, Application 780, Infrastructure 1,386, Functions 748.

## 2026-08-12 — Secrets reach the app by reading the vault, not by App Service Key Vault references

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** `IBP-AUE-PRD-FNA-APP01-kv-access-denied` (Sev2) had been firing repeatedly and was assumed to be fallout from the same-day playout emergency-off. It was not. Key Vault audit logs show `Forbidden` on `SecretGet` every day back to at least 13 July — the limit of the workspace's 30-day retention — in a textbook once-per-day burst of 7 that drifts about an hour earlier each day and re-phases on restart. That is App Service's ~24h Key Vault **reference** refresh. The correlation over three days is absolute: 44 `Forbidden`, every one from the site's public outbound IP `52.237.246.162`; 100 `OK`, every one from a private endpoint (`10.61.0.61`/`10.61.0.62`). App Service resolves `@Microsoft.KeyVault(...)` app settings in its platform configuration layer, which does not honour VNet integration, and test/prod vaults set `publicNetworkAccess='Disabled'` — under which `bypass: 'AzureServices'` is inert. So the four references (`Here__ApiKey`, `AiSettings__ElevenLabs__ApiKey`, `Webhook__EndpointUrl`, `AadClientId`) could never resolve on the first attempt. Nothing broke only because `Program.cs` already registers `AddAzureKeyVault` over the private endpoint *after* `AddEnvironmentVariables`, so vault values take precedence anyway. The alert rule was authored in IaC on 1 June but only reached the subscription on 10 August, which is why a months-old condition looked like a new incident.

**Decision:** Delete all four `@Microsoft.KeyVault(...)` app settings from `modules/function-app.bicep`; the runtime vault load is the single secret path. `AadClientId` becomes a plain app setting fed from the existing `aadClientId` param — a client ID is public, is already inline in the Easy Auth registration and in every bicepparam, and needed no vault round trip. The webhook secret is renamed `webhookEndpointUrl` → `Webhook--EndpointUrl` in `key-vault.bicep` so the runtime provider's `--`→`:` mapping binds `WebhookOptions.EndpointUrl`; the old flat name only ever worked through an explicit `SecretUri` reference. `kvRef`/`kvDns` and the now-unused `keyVaultName` param are removed with their `main.bicep` argument.

**Rationale:** The two options were to stop using platform references or to weaken the vault (public access plus an IP allowlist). The second trades a documented production network posture for a convenience the app does not use. The first deletes a redundant, permanently-failing code path and makes failure honest: `HereOptions.ApiKey` is `[Required]`, so a vault that genuinely cannot be read now fails startup validation instead of silently handing HERE an unresolved `@Microsoft.KeyVault(...)` literal.

**Consequences:** Rotation procedures change — a new secret version needs a Function App restart, not an app-settings re-save; `runbook.md`, `notifications.md`, `as-built.md`, `dependencies.md`, `manual-steps.md` and `deployment/README.md` are updated accordingly. Adding a secret now requires naming it to match its options section (`Here--ApiKey` → `Here:ApiKey`), documented in `deployment/README.md#why-there-are-no-key-vault-references`. Two secrets are orphaned in each existing vault (`webhookEndpointUrl`, `AadClientId`); they are harmless — the provider bulk-loads them to config keys nothing binds — but should be deleted as vault hygiene, and until then the stale `AadClientId` secret still wins over the new plain app setting, so the two must not be allowed to drift. **Verified on TEST 2026-08-12** (deployed with `deployment/scripts/deploy.sh`, the environment that actually reproduces the fault — `publicNetworkAccess='Disabled'` and private endpoints, same as prod). Before: 4 references and 12–92 `Forbidden` a day, 100% of them from a public caller on exactly those 4 secrets, plus a burst on every restart. After: references 0, and the alert rule's own KQL returns `AggregatedValue = 0` against a threshold of 1. Every secret now resolves `OK` over the private endpoint, including the renamed `Webhook--EndpointUrl`, and `/api/health` reports `elevenLabs: HTTP 200` — that probe sends the real credential, so a 200 proves the runtime vault load supplies it with no app-setting reference. Dev was deployed first via pipeline 108 (build 2836) but cannot prove the fix: its vault allows public access, so it never had the denial.

One residual, unrelated to this change: running `deploy.sh` from outside the VNet still logs `Forbidden` against the locked vault (the operator's own IP, seeding secrets it cannot reach) and will itself trip the alert. That is the documented public-access round-trip, not an application fault.

## 2026-08-12 — Container and queue existence is ensured once per process, not once per bulletin

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Measured over 7 days in prod (2026-08-12): 5,682 Warning-or-worse trace rows, of which 3,537 are a single Azure SDK line, `409 The specified container already exists` — 62% of the warning channel over the week, ranging 37% on a quiet day to 88% on a busy one. (An earlier figure of "4,475 of ~4,700 daily warnings, 95%" was wrong on both the count and the share; the largest single day is 1,640 warnings.) **That noise is NOT ours and this change does not remove it.** Correcting an earlier misdiagnosis: matching the SDK response to its request line by client-request-id shows the container is `azure-webjobs-hosts` — the Azure Functions runtime's own singleton/host-id container, recreated by the host on its own timer. Over three days every one of 3,331 container-create calls in prod was a runtime container (`azure-webjobs-hosts` 3,325, `azure-webjobs-secrets` 6) and **zero** were application containers. Verified after deploying this change to test and prod: the rate is unchanged at ~1.2/min in both. Suppressing it would mean filtering the `Azure.Core` log category in `host.json`, which also hides genuine SDK retry/throttle warnings — deliberately not done here.

What IS ours, and what this change fixes: `AzureBlobBroadcastOutput.SaveAsync` issued `CreateIfNotExistsAsync` on every audio save and `QueuePublisher` on every dispatch. Those are real redundant round trips on the generation path. They were invisible in the prod sample only because prod was not generating bulletins during the measurement window.

**Decision:** Ensure existence once per process, using the flag-plus-lock shape `TableRepositoryBase` already established. `AzureBlobBroadcastOutput` gets a `volatile bool` + `SemaphoreSlim`; `QueuePublisher` gets a `ConcurrentDictionary` keyed by queue name because it serves both Broadcast and Regeneration. For those flags to mean anything the instances must outlive a request, so `BlobServiceClient`, `QueueServiceClient`, `IQueuePublisher` and `IBroadcastOutput` move scoped → singleton — the same lifetime the table repositories already use. `FillerAudioCacheService` stays scoped deliberately (it has captive scoped audio providers); its guard only dedupes the within-invocation burst.

**Rationale:** Azure SDK clients are thread-safe and built for reuse, so singleton is their intended lifetime; scoped → singleton is the legal consumption direction, and every dependency involved (`TokenCredential`, `IOptions<StorageOptions>`, `ILogger<T>`) is already a singleton, so no captive dependency is created. Suppressing the SDK log category instead would have hidden genuine 409s and kept the wasted call.

**Consequences:** Cold start still creates the container or queue when genuinely absent, and a failed create leaves the flag unset so the next attempt retries; real errors propagate exactly as before. The emulator public-access semantics are preserved — `CreateIfNotExistsAsync(PublicAccessType.Blob)` once, `SetAccessPolicyAsync` still re-asserted per save so an Azurite restart recovers the ACL. Prod's warning volume does NOT drop — see the correction above; the once-a-minute line belongs to the Functions host. The gain here is one fewer storage round trip per bulletin saved and per message dispatched, which only shows up under generation load.

## 2026-08-12 — A playout SMB sharing violation is retried, because it means the file is being collected

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The only exception prod raised in seven days was `Azure.RequestFailedException` / `409 SharingViolation` writing `[SYD]KIIS90s_TRAFF.wav` to the Azure Files drop, during the 11 Aug restart sweep. `AzureFilesDropFileWriter` caught it, logged Error and returned `Result.Failure` — treating "playout currently has this file open over SMB" as a permanent failure. It is the opposite: a held handle is positive evidence the playout side is mounted and collecting, and it clears in seconds.

**Decision:** Retry only `RequestFailedException` with `ErrorCode == "SharingViolation"`, three attempts total with 300ms then 900ms backoff, cancellation-aware against both the caller token and the write timeout. Everything else still fails on the first attempt. Each retry logs Warning; exhaustion keeps the existing Error log and the existing `Result.Failure` message text verbatim so the runbook and any log-based alerting still match. Matched on the string error code rather than the SDK enum to stay version-tolerant, following the `WebhookRetryHandler`/`RateLimitRetryHandler` test-seam precedent since Infrastructure has no shared retry helper.

**Rationale:** Distinguishing transient contention from a real fault is the difference between a bulletin reaching air and a false delivery failure. A permission or path error must still fail fast — retrying those would only delay the truth.

**Consequences:** Three new tests cover clears-on-attempt-2, never-clears, and not-retried-when-non-transient (8/8 in the class). `GetPendingWriteTimeAsync` is untouched: it is a read-only probe and sharing violations apply to the write path. This does not change the emergency-off posture — `zettaEnabled` stays `false` until the delivery incident is closed by an attended decision.

## 2026-08-12 — Detour avoidance sends Routing v8 segment IDs, not Traffic v7 segment refs

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Prod logged `HERE Routing detour failed. Status: BadRequest` on repeated polls for one Cairns origin/destination pair. Reproducing the exact prod request shape live against HERE with the dev key returned two distinct, real defects rather than a flaky vendor. First, `avoid[segments]` was being fed Traffic API **v7** `segmentRef` identifiers — compact `$0:<tile>:$1:<seg>#<dir><off>..<off>` or full `hrn:here:data::olp-here:...` forms — while Routing **v8** accepts only `here:cm:segment:<id>[#direction]`, with no catalog prefix and no offset range: `400 E605001 Invalid topology segment`. HERE validates `avoid` before the rest of the request, so this masked the second defect: `spans=names` was sent with `return=summary`, which is `400 E605013 Spans requested but no polyline requested`.

**Decision:** Convert segment refs at the boundary — a new `ToRoutingAvoidSegmentId()` in `HereTrafficProvider` normalises both compact and full forms to `here:cm:segment:<id>#<dir>`, strips offsets, and passes already-correct refs through idempotently. `GetSafeDetourAsync` requests `return=summary,polyline`. Verified live: the fixed request returns HTTP 200 for the exact Cairns pair (1 route, 679s, 12,577m).

**Rationale:** This was never a logging problem. Detour avoidance has been failing wherever incidents contributed avoid segments, so every affected bulletin silently degraded to `Detour=None` — the log line was the only symptom of a real capability being off. Severity stays Error precisely because the pair is demonstrably routable now, so any future 400 is a genuine defect and no longer expected noise.

**Consequences:** Detours work where avoid segments are present. The error path already read and logged HERE's response body and already redacted `apiKey=***` from the URL; the body is now redacted too, as defence in depth. Every logging statement in Infrastructure was audited for key leakage — none outside `HereApiHelper` log URLs or keys. Three new tests cover the segment-ref conversion shapes, the polyline requirement, and that a 400 log carries HERE's cause with the key redacted.

## 2026-08-12 — The Azure SDK's own chatter is filtered at Error; the health signal that shares the channel is not

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The dominant line in prod's warning channel is `409 The specified container already exists`, and it is not ours: matching each SDK response to its request by client-request-id shows the container is `azure-webjobs-hosts`, the Functions runtime's own singleton/host-id container. Over three days every one of 3,331 container creates in prod was a runtime container and zero were application containers. Measured over 7 days: 3,537 of 5,682 warning rows are that one line — 62% of the channel over the week, 37% on a quiet day and 88% on a busy one. (An earlier figure of "4,475 of ~4,700 daily, 95%" was wrong on both count and share and has been corrected wherever it appeared; the largest single day is 1,640 warnings.)

An earlier attempt to categorise these rows concluded they had no log category, which would have made a `host.json` filter impossible. That was a wrong field, not a missing value: host-emitted rows carry `Properties.Category`, while `Properties.CategoryName` is the worker-side key and is blank on them. The category is `Azure.Core`.

**Decision:** Add `"Azure.Core": "Error"` to `logging.logLevel` in `host.json`. Measured collateral, prod, 7 days: `Azure.Core` carries 3,537 Warning rows and **zero** at Error, so nothing actionable is lost at the level being suppressed. Prefix matching also covers the sibling `Azure.Core.1` — a further 24 warnings of the same class (404 queue-existence probes, occasional 503 ServerBusy, slow-response notices) — and roughly 795,000 Information-level SDK request/response header dumps across the two categories, about 114k a day of pure ingestion.

**Rationale:** Storage and dependency health survive in better channels than a text log: `AppDependencies` records every call with its result code independently (104,029 rows in prod, and every one of these 409s appears there as a dependency result), and `AppExceptions` is untouched. The genuinely actionable storage-health warning — an `AuthorizationFailure` signal, 1,981 rows in 30 days — sits in a different category entirely and is unaffected. The alternative was to leave 62% of the warning channel as noise and rely on operators to mentally filter it, which is how a real signal gets missed.

**Consequences:** `host.json` is strict JSON and cannot carry the reasoning, which is why it is here. The proof after deploying is two queries: `AppTraces | where Properties.Category startswith "Azure.Core" | summarize count() by SeverityLevel` should show no Warning rows arriving after the deploy, and `AppDependencies | summarize countif(Success == false)` should be unchanged in rate — dependency failures must still be visible. If a future storage problem needs SDK warning text to diagnose, raise the level temporarily rather than permanently.

## 2026-08-12 — kv-access-denied counts application identities, and the availability detector was fired for real

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Two separate problems with the same rule family, both found by measuring rather than reading.

First, `kv-access-denied` counted raw `Forbidden` rows, so it could not tell *the application cannot read its own secrets* from *a human at a laptop was refused by the vault firewall*. The second is the firewall working. Measured 2026-08-12: the rule fired on TEST and PROD purely because an operator ran read-only `az keyvault secret list`/`list-versions` against the locked vaults while investigating, and it fires on every deploy because `deploy.sh` seeds secrets from outside the VNet — during the prod deploy, 4 denials at 13:21:29 from the App Service outbound IP (the platform's last resolution of the old references mid-write) and 3 at 13:23:24 from the operator's own workstation. Denials split cleanly by `identity_claim_appid_g`: application identities on one side, the Azure CLI app ID on the other.

Second, `health-availability` (Sev1) had **never fired in any environment**. Its only prior verification used a deliberately-failing *clone* webtest and *clone* rule — the real detector was untested, which the docs stated honestly.

**Decision:** Exclude the interactive client app IDs (Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, Azure Portal) from the rule. Rows with no appid claim are deliberately NOT excluded, so an unrecognised caller still fails loud. Then prove the availability detector on a real failure instead of a clone: stop the dev Function App, wait, restart.

**Rationale:** An alert an operator is trained to ignore is worse than no alert. Scoping to the identity whose failure actually matters keeps the signal and removes the noise. And a detector that has never fired is a hypothesis, however carefully it was written — the only way to know the rule, the action group, the Logic App branch and the Teams connection all still line up is to make it fire.

**Consequences:** Both measured. Two-sided validation of the query — the operator-noise window returns **0**, the pre-fix window returns **52**, so nothing real was traded away. Proven on the next real deploy: the test deploy produced 3 Key Vault denials and the alert stayed silent, because all 3 were the CLI identity; application-identity denials were 0 on both test and prod. The drill fired `IBP-AUE-DEV-FNA-APP01-health-availability` at 16:53:53Z on a genuine outage, and the notification Logic App run started 16:53:55Z and **Succeeded** — 1.6 seconds, first end-to-end proof of that detector anywhere. `no-executions` also fired, at 17:04:31Z — 17 minutes after the stop, consistent with its 15-minute window plus evaluation lag. An earlier check at 17:03:18Z concluded it had not fired; that check was 73 seconds too early, and the conclusion was wrong. Both detectors returned to Resolved after the restart, so the resolve path is proven too. Net result of the drill: the two availability detectors that had never fired in any environment both fired on a real outage and both cleared.

## 2026-08-13 — Operators can read the bookend library in every environment; authoring stays Admin

**Status:** superseded by "Operators author bookends too; only deleting a pair stays Admin" (2026-08-13, below) — ARN's follow-up was that operators should be able to EDIT, not only read. The read-side reasoning and the frontend-only diagnosis in this entry still hold and are why the page was already operator-reachable.

**Context:** ARN asked whether operators can be given access to bookends in all environments. Today they cannot, and the reason is frontend-only: GET /api/bookends and /bookends/{id} already resolve to Operator through the GET default in RouteRoleMatrix (operators consume the library inside the station studio's BookendSelector, rotation editor and token gate), but App.tsx and the nav metadata gated /bookends at requiredRole 'admin'. The asymmetry was invisible on dev, where Auth__DevFallbackRole=Admin plus the SWA built-in provider make useIsAdmin() true for every authenticated caller, so the page appeared open; on test and prod, which forward real Entra app roles through the custom provider + rolesSource bridge, an Operator-only caller got 'Admin access required' in front of an API that would have answered. Operators own the station assignment (PUT /api/schedules/{marketId} became Operator on 2026-08-06) yet could not read the pair they were assigning.

**Decision:** Open /bookends to Operator in App.tsx and APP_ROUTES and gate authoring inside the page, mirroring the VoicesPage canManage pattern: BookendGalleryPage passes canManage=useIsAdmin() to BookendCard and BookendTable (a 'Read pair' button replaces the EntityActionsMenu so the keyboard path in survives), the New affordance and the empty-state CTA are admin-only, BookendStudio takes canEdit=useIsAdmin() so an operator sees read-only inputs, no change note, no save (Cancel becomes Close) and no LiveAssignmentNotice, BookendVersionHistory hides Restore, and BookendTokenInsight only fires POST /bookends/preview when canEdit. No backend change: every bookend write and the preview route stay Admin by the RouteRoleMatrix default. There is nothing per-environment to configure - the same code answers dev, test and prod.

**Rationale:** The library is ONE shared set of pairs with no market to scope a write against, so an operator edit would change the wording other markets' stations air; the market guard that justified the Operator grants on publish, retone and the schedule PUT does not exist here, and the AuthorizationMiddlewareTests tripwire (every Operator non-GET route must be market- or job-scoped) would correctly fail if a write were granted. Reading is the actual ask: the operator owns the read that airs and is assigning the pair, so being unable to see its exact sentences is the defect. Withholding the resolved preview rather than granting the Admin route repeats the RGP-3 remedy from the 2026-08-06 adjacent-bug audit (the same panel once rendered 'Preview failed: Forbidden' under every pair) and keeps the frontend gate in agreement with the backend matrix, which is the failure mode that produced both ARN-reported defects of 2026-08-06.

**Consequences:** The operator nav gains a Bookends tab, so routes.test.ts's operator-visible label list now includes it. Dev cannot verify the change - the dev bypass makes every caller Admin, and StartupSafety refuses to boot with Auth__DevFallbackRole set on a TST/PRD site - so it was proven against the mock build with VITE_DEV_USER_ROLES=operator (page reachable, 4 pairs readable, no New button, no actions menu, read-only studio with only Close, version history without Restore, no preview call) and re-checked with VITE_DEV_USER_ROLES=admin (New, full actions menu, editable studio, Save, sample resolution resolving 'Looking over Adelaide today.'). Test/prod behaviour follows from the same code once deployed; confirm on test with a real Operator-only app-role assignment. New web test BookendCard.test.tsx covers the canManage split in both card and table view plus the route-role entry.

## 2026-08-13 — Operators author bookends too; only deleting a pair stays Admin

**Status:** accepted (supersedes "Operators can read the bookend library in every environment; authoring stays Admin", same day)

**Context:** The read-only grant landed earlier the same day and ARN came straight back: operators should be able to SEE AND EDIT bookends, in every environment. The read-only design was internally coherent — the library is one shared set of pairs with no market to scope a write against, so it failed the `AuthorizationMiddlewareTests` tripwire that every Operator non-GET route be market- or job-scoped — but it left the people who actually hear the top and tail of every read unable to fix a word in it without an admin. Nothing about this was environment-specific: the role matrix is the same code in dev, test and prod, and dev's `Auth__DevFallbackRole=Admin` was the only reason it ever looked open.

**Decision:** Grant Operator every bookend route except DELETE. `RouteRoleMatrix` gains one clause — `m != "DELETE" && path.StartsWith("/api/bookends")` → Operator — covering POST /bookends, PUT /bookends/{id}, POST /bookends/preview, archive, unarchive and versions/{n}/restore; DELETE falls through to the Admin default. The tripwire is not weakened, it is extended with a SECOND named exemption beside `/voiceover`, spelling out that this one really does mutate shared config and why that is accepted, so a third unscoped Operator write still fails loudly. Frontend: the read-only variants added hours earlier are deleted rather than re-gated — `canManage`/`canEdit`/`canRestore`/`canResolve` were all unreachable-false once writes are Operator — and a single `canDelete = useIsAdmin()` replaces them, so the gallery offers the full actions menu and the editable studio to an operator and withholds the Delete item alone. `EntityActionsMenu.onDelete` becomes optional, matching the existing optional `onArchive`/`onUnarchive`.

**Rationale:** The market guard that justifies the other Operator writes genuinely does not exist here, so this grant is defended by different controls rather than a pretended scope: every write mints an immutable version carrying its author and change note, `ActivityLoggingMiddleware` records the mutation, any version is restorable in one click, and a pair in use cannot be deleted (409 `library.in_use`). Scoping the write instead — "only pairs assigned solely to your markets" — was rejected because it leaves an unassigned or brand-shared pair editable by nobody but an admin, which is the defect restated with more machinery. Delete is the one thing held back for the same reason `DELETE /schedules/{marketId}` is: archive is reversible retire-in-place and gives the operator the outcome they need, where a delete is unrecoverable and strands every station pointing at the pair. Deleting the read-only UI rather than inverting its flags matters because those branches were already telling the reader, in comments and copy, that writes are Admin — leaving them would have left the code arguing with itself.

**Consequences:** An operator can now change wording that other markets' stations air, and the audit trail is what makes that recoverable rather than a guard preventing it — worth knowing before assigning the Operator role broadly. `EntityActionsMenu` no longer requires `onDelete`, so any future caller can offer a menu without a destructive item. Proven on the mock build, which is the only way to exercise an Operator-only principal (the dev fallback makes every caller Admin, and StartupSafety refuses to boot with `Auth__DevFallbackRole` on a TST/PRD site): with `VITE_DEV_USER_ROLES=operator` the page shows New bookend, four actions menus, a menu reading View/Edit/Duplicate/Archive with **no Delete**, a fully editable studio (5 inputs, 0 read-only) with the live-assignment notice, change note and "Save new version", and "Restore as new version" in the history trail; re-run with `admin` the same menu gains Delete. Backend: 763 Functions tests green including the reflection tripwire and 9 new explicit matrix rows, an Operator-only principal reaching POST/PUT/preview and 403ing on DELETE. Web: 1,143 tests green, `tsc -b` clean, eslint + oxlint clean. **Deployed to test and prod the same day** — see "The operator RBAC wave is live on test and prod" below for the promotion evidence and the mid-promotion divergence it exposed.

## 2026-08-13 — The operator RBAC wave is live on test and prod; the working tree moved mid-promotion

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The bookend-authoring grant (`f28ba062`) was promoted straight to test then prod on ARN's instruction. Prod's Cairns station is enabled and the poller fires every 15 minutes 06:00–18:00 Brisbane, so the Function App restart had to miss a live slot. Separately, and not noticed until after prod was published, ANOTHER writer edited `AuthorizationMiddleware.cs` in the shared working tree at 06:10:55Z — the `/rewrite` operator grant — which is between the test publish (06:06:53Z) and the prod publish (06:23:55Z). Test therefore ran the bookend change alone while prod ran the bookend change PLUS an uncommitted clause, and prod was executing code that existed in no commit.

**Decision:** (1) Sequence a live-station promotion around the poller instead of around convenience: deploy the SWA first (atomic, no backend impact), then wait for the in-flight slot to leave generation and land the Function App restart in the gap. The 06:15 bulletin was left at `WAITING_APPROVAL` — generation complete, awaiting a human — and the restart went out at 06:24, clear of both 06:15 and 06:30. (2) Resolve the divergence forward, not backward: commit the other writer's `/rewrite` clause (`6521fbff`) rather than reverting prod, because it was already executing in production and a second prod restart against a live station costs more than it buys, then deploy that commit to test so both environments run identical code again. Attribution is in the commit message.

**Rationale:** Rolling prod back to `f28ba062` would have removed a tested, additive fix for a 403 operators were actually hitting, and spent a second restart window on a live station to do it — while leaving the same reproducibility problem for however long the clause stayed uncommitted. Committing what is already deployed makes production describable, which is the property that matters at 3am. The deeper lesson is that "build from a clean tree" is not a one-time check: the tree was verifiably clean of dirty artifact paths when the promotion started, and it was the PROMOTION WINDOW ITSELF — two publishes seventeen minutes apart — that let a third party's edit into one artifact and not the other. A detached worktree at the commit, used for BOTH publishes, is the only version of this discipline that holds when other people are typing.

**Consequences:** Test and prod both run `6521fbff`. Verified rather than asserted: identical SWA bundle by content hash on both (`index-c_wCOFGg.js`, `index-D8Z9BlRy.css`, matching the local `web/dist` byte-for-byte), 120 functions and `Running` on both Function Apps, `smoke-test.sh` OK on both, and a three-route parity probe returning identical status AND body across environments (`POST /jobs/{id}/rewrite` → 404 "Job not found", so past the role gate and into the handler; `POST /bookends/preview` → 200 with the same token resolution; `/health` → 200). Full bookend write path round-tripped on test against the deployed code: create v1 → edit v2 → archive → restore v3 → delete 204, library back to its 5 pairs. Prod's first post-deploy poller slot (`2ab97bd1`, 06:30:01Z) PUBLISHED at exactly 22s, opening on "Checking out the roads......" and closing on "Johnny and Inkie back for breakfast tomorrow…" — so the bookends, the 22-second slot, the delivery style and the re-tuned voice promoted earlier the same day are all airing on the new build. Still outstanding and unchanged by deployment: the Operator-only boundary has never been exercised against a real Entra Operator app-role assignment, because neither dev nor the mock build can produce one; that confirmation needs an ARN operator account on test.

## 2026-08-13 — Test is re-trued to production's pilot configuration, not to dev's sandbox

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** After promoting the filler-statement edit, a full three-way audit (code, infra, settings, config data) asked whether test and prod carry everything dev has. Code and infra were already identical: all three Function Apps expose the same 120 functions, all three SWAs serve the same content-hashed bundle (17 assets from the same HEAD build), the 69 app-setting keys match with 10 deliberately env-specific values, and az deployment sub what-if against main.{test,prod}.bicepparam returned zero resource Creates or Deletes (only RP-defaulted/read-only property noise). The gaps were entirely in the ARN-editable config plane, and all of them were on TEST: both pilot schedules had DeliveryStyleId null, the Bookends library was empty (prod: 5 sets, one assigned per pilot schedule), the sydney market Lexicon guidance was absent, two junk Global guidance rows ('no breaths in voice') were present that prod never had, cairns Weather/FuelRequired were false against prod's true, cairns FillOrder was weather-first against prod's fuel-first, sydney was assigned Dolly Traffic instead of prod's Male Sarah - AM - KIIS/Regional HOT AC, and the shared cairns profile ARN Sarah - Younger Female carried different synthesis settings (Speed 1 / Stability 0.45 / Similarity 0.9 / Style 0.15 / boost on) from prod's tuned values.

**Decision:** Sync test to PROD, not to dev: dev is the 14-market sandbox whose extra markets, styles, dictionaries and calibrations are experiments, while test exists to rehearse production. Applied through the audited config-transfer endpoint (dry-run then ?dryRun=false, upsert-only) in four bundles: delivery style + 5 bookends + per-market bookend assignment; the sydney market Lexicon; content-required flags and cairns fill order; and the two voice profiles with prod's exact settings. The two junk Global guidance rows were removed with DELETE /api/guidance/{id}?scope=Global (import is upsert-only and cannot delete). Nothing was written to prod. Test's own 3 unused delivery styles, its 15-minute UAT cron grid against prod's 60-slot ATN clock, and cairns Enabled=true in prod only were left alone as deliberate.

**Rationale:** A test environment that reads in a different voice, with different synthesis settings, no bookends and no delivery direction is not a rehearsal of production, and every one of those differences changes the audio a UAT reviewer hears. Promoting from prod rather than dev also avoids importing sandbox experiments (12 extra markets, 11 extra dictionaries, 36 calibrations) that would make test noisier than the system it is meant to mirror. Config transfer already carries the dry-run/apply parity and the audit trail, so no hand-editing of table rows was needed.

**Consequences:** Test's two pilot schedules now match prod field-for-field except sydney's cron and cairns' Enabled flag; guidance is byte-identical (6 entries); bookend names, intro/outro text, safety terms, filler statements and priority roads all match; both assigned voice profiles match prod by name AND by settings. One prod content question is OPEN and deliberately not actioned: the cairns filler statement airs 'Download the iHeartRadio app to take us anywhere - search KIIS or 4CA Cairns' in prod and test, while dev carries what looks like the corrected line for a Star 102.7 station, 'Download the free iHeart app to take us anywhere - search Star one oh two point seven' (phoneticised for TTS). Cairns is enabled in prod and airing, so the copy is ARN's call; a ready bundle applies it and prod's second-approver gate will park it for a different admin. Prod also holds zero VerifiedPronunciations against dev's three markets, which is review evidence rather than config and was left unchanged.

## 2026-08-13 — The operator's own "Ask for a change" content rewrite is an Operator route

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN asked whether operators can rewrite a bulletin's script and tone from the prompt box in the script editor. Half of it already worked and half was dead: `ScriptAssist`'s **Delivery** lever calls `POST /jobs/{id}/retone`, granted to Operator on 2026-08-05 with `/audition` and `/direct`; its **Content** lever calls `POST /jobs/{id}/rewrite`, which shipped a day later (2026-08-06, "One Ask for a change control") and was never added to the operator POST allowlist in `RouteRoleMatrix`, so it fell through to the Admin default. This is finding 9 of the 2026-08-05 bug bash recurring one endpoint later: the console renders the control on job status alone (`EDITABLE_STATES`, no role check), dev's `Auth__DevFallbackRole=Admin` hides it, and in test/prod an operator-only user typed an instruction, pressed Rewrite and got 403.

**Decision:** `RouteRoleMatrix` grants Operator `POST /jobs/{id}/rewrite`, in the same clause as approve/reject/publish/regenerate/air-source/pronunciation-rules/retone/audition/direct. No frontend change: the control was already ungated, and the gate that was wrong was the backend's.

**Rationale:** The trust boundary is the market guard, not the role, and `ScriptRewriteHttpTrigger` already runs `EnsureJobAccessAsync` — the same guard as approve/reject/retone — so a scoped operator can only rewrite a job in a market they are assigned to. It is also the least dangerous LLM route in the cockpit: it mutates nothing, returns a preview the operator reads as a diff, refuses anything ungrounded against the job's persisted evidence (hard block) or caught by content safety, and the words can only reach air through the existing verbatim re-voice path, where the safety reviewer sees them again. Holding it at Admin while `/retone` is Operator gives the operator the lever that reshapes only the read and withholds the one that fixes what the bulletin says — the wording change they are most likely to need.

**Consequences:** The `AuthorizationMiddlewareTests` route table and the Operator-only `Invoke` theory both gained `/rewrite`; the reflection tripwire (every Operator non-GET route must be market- or job-scoped) passes unchanged because the route is job-addressed, so no new exemption was needed. Reproduced before fixing: both new cases fail without the clause (the middleware short-circuits the Operator-only principal with 403) and pass with it; 765 Functions tests green. Dev cannot demonstrate either state — the dev fallback makes every caller Admin — so the middleware theory is the proof, and the live confirmation belongs on test with a real Operator-only assignment. **Deployed.** It reached prod ahead of its own commit — it was still uncommitted in the shared working tree when the prod artifact was published at 06:23:55Z — and was committed as `6521fbff` and pushed to test immediately afterwards to restore parity; see "The operator RBAC wave is live on test and prod; the working tree moved mid-promotion" for the sequence and the lesson.

## 2026-08-13 — Ask Entra for the console's OWN audience so rolesSource sign-ins can be validated

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** SwaRolesSourceTokenValidator (06cf9f8a, 11 Aug) made operator self-registration require a cryptographically valid ACCESS token, because /api/GetRoles is externally reachable and an attacker could invent a payload. But SWA had only ever been told to request 'openid profile email', and with no resource scope Entra defaults the access token's resource to Microsoft Graph. Every sign-in on test and prod therefore arrived with aud=00000003-0000-0000-c000-000000000000, which this app can never validate (IDX10511, 'Number of keys in Configuration: 0'), and was discarded. The hardening silently disabled the only mechanism that writes an operator row: test kept the rows real sign-ins wrote on 5-7 Aug (operator sign-ins 06 Aug 01:07:15 and 06+07 Aug), prod had only the Arinco deploy operator's 30 Jul row, and ARN read the empty Operators page as 'nobody is defined' while operators were signing in and working normally.

**Decision:** Request the app's own audience alongside the OIDC scopes: auth.identityProviders.azureActiveDirectory.login.loginParameters = ['scope=openid profile email <clientId>/.default']. Because loginParameters entries are literals (SWA expands clientIdSettingName, but not the contents of loginParameters) and the client id is per environment, the config is RENDERED, never copied: deployment/static-web-app/render-rbac-config.py injects the scope, reading aadClientId from the same main.<env>.bicepparam that provisions the Function App. All three deploy paths (arn deploy web, deploy-stage.yml, deploy.sh) call it; a direct cp no longer exists anywhere.

**Rationale:** Measured against Entra before changing anything, via an authorize probe with prompt=none: the bare '<clientId>/.default' is accepted and issues a code, while 'api://<clientId>/.default' fails AADSTS500011 invalid_resource because these registrations expose no identifierUris and no oauth2PermissionScopes. Guessing the api:// form would have broken sign-in for every user. The validator already accepts aud in [<clientId>, api://<clientId>] and both Entra issuers, so only the audience needed to move - no code change, and the 11 Aug hardening is preserved rather than relaxed. Rendering from the bicepparam keeps ONE canonical config (no test/prod drift, the exact fault class fixed earlier the same day) and binds the console's audience to the same declaration that sets the backend's AadClientId, so the two cannot disagree. The canonical JSON deliberately ships the OIDC scopes only, so any future path that copies instead of rendering degrades to 'no self-registration' rather than to a locked-out sign-in.

**Consequences:** Proven live end to end, test first then prod: the live authorize request now carries '<clientId>/.default' (captured by intercepting the redirect), and '[Operators] Registered or refreshed operator ... the Arinco deploy operator with role(s) [Admin]' logged on test at 11:57:44 and prod at 12:05:03, each matching that row's UpdatedAtUtc moving (07 Aug -> today on test, 30 Jul -> today on prod). Zero SwaRoles validation failures after propagation; the failures logged 12:00-12:04 on prod were the propagation poll itself, using the pre-propagation config. Sign-in and role mapping unaffected (userRoles still [anonymous, authenticated, Admin]) and all three SWAs still serve index-c_wCOFGg.js, so only auth config changed. Everyone who signs in from now on appears in the Operators tab, so market scoping becomes usable without waiting on ARN. SWA config propagation lags a deploy by ~1-2 min: verify by capturing the authorize scope, not by signing in immediately. Dev is untouched by design - it has no auth block and no rolesSource, and uses the built-in provider. The ungranted Graph consent (Cause A) is unchanged and now buys only pre-population of people who have never signed in, plus group provenance.

## 2026-08-14 — Curating the shared libraries is operator work; only deleting stays Admin

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The owner asked why operators are prevented from doing things at all, given they run the network day to day. The honest answer was that the boundary encoded SCOPABILITY, not consequence: MarketAccessGuard can only run when a market or job appears in the route, so anything addressed by library id fell to the Admin default. That produced a boundary nobody chose. POST /jobs/{id}/pronunciation-rules already let an operator mint a new pronunciation-dictionary version, so the IDENTICAL mutation was Operator through a job and Admin through the library — a difference of URL shape. Seven endpoints that mutate nothing at all (voice/style/dictionary previews, remix, editorial check and preview-script) were Admin purely by falling through. And POST /broadcast was Admin while /publish was Operator, so an operator could put a bulletin to air but never make one.

**Decision:** RouteRoleMatrix grants Operator every non-DELETE route on /api/voices, /api/pronunciation-dictionaries and /api/delivery-styles — create, edit, archive, unarchive, restore-a-version, calibrate, remix and every preview. GET /api/activity becomes Operator. POST /api/broadcast becomes Operator and BroadcastHttpTrigger now runs EnsureMarketAccessAsync on the RESOLVED market before CreateJobAsync, so an operator can only generate for a station they are assigned to. DELETE stays Admin on every library, station and job. Admin keeps exactly five areas: /editorial/* (system prompt and house style), /safety/terms (banned words), global guidance + promote, the /operators assignment register, and /config/* bulk transfer. Frontend follows: the Pronunciation, Delivery and Activity pages open to operators, and each library page carries one canDelete = useIsAdmin() so only Delete is withheld — the BookendGalleryPage pattern.

**Rationale:** The bookend grant (2026-08-13, earlier the same day) already accepted an unscoped Operator write over shared config, justified not by a market guard but by the control set around it. That control set is generic, not bookend-specific: LibraryReferenceGuard refuses to delete anything a station still points at (409 library.in_use) for every library, VoiceProfile.Archive and DeliveryStyle.Archive are the reversible retire-in-place paths, every write mints an immutable version with author and change note, and ActivityLoggingMiddleware records the mutation. Voices, dictionaries and delivery styles therefore satisfy the same test, and consistency demanded extending the grant rather than defending an accident. DELETE is the one action that breaks the argument, because there is no undo and Archive already gives the operator the outcome; keeping it Admin costs them nothing. Content safety stays Admin for a different reason entirely: banned words are the guardrail applied to the operator's own output, so an operator who could delete one could lower the floor that reviews them.

**Consequences:** The scoping tripwire was RE-STATED rather than relaxed. It now requires an Operator non-GET route to be market/job-scoped OR an audited library write OR free of side effects, and it still walks the real deployed surface from functions.metadata — so a future route with none of those three properties fails the build. Replacing a proxy rule with the property actually being protected is the point. Backend 4,747 tests green including two new BroadcastHttpTrigger tests that prove an operator assigned to sydney gets 403 on a melbourne trigger and that the refusal creates no job and publishes no queue message; web 1,153 green (+10). Proven on the mock build, the only way to exercise an Operator-only principal: as operator the nav carries On air/History/Stations/Voices/Delivery/Bookends/Pronunciation/Activity/Bulletin rules with Operators and Data transfer ABSENT, /operators renders 'Admin access required', and the Pronunciation page offers New dictionary; as admin both pages return and Delete comes back. Still Admin and unchanged: POST /synthesize (raw TTS, left alone as out of the agreed scope, and now the last remaining accident of the default). Deployed from a detached worktree because another writer's HERE data-fidelity work was in flight in the same tree.

## 2026-08-17 — HERE data validity enforced at the data boundary, not in the prompt assembler

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Pilot day-1 operators rejected phantom closures (Warringah Fwy scheduled sub-closure aired as live news), invented directions, and stale same-day replays (53/54 measured replays contradicted their own fetch). The parked data-fidelity branch fixed these inside TrafficNarrativeSummarizer, welding validity policy to the prompt assembler and forcing the script-generation rewrite to ship with it.

**Decision:** Claims a record cannot support are demoted or withheld by IncidentEligibility (Domain) immediately after IncidentFactBuilder reduces each HERE record to an IncidentFact, BEFORE corridor aggregation. Scheduled project sub-closures demote to roadworks; closed ramps demote to hazards naming the ramp; unplaceable closures demote to their cause; unresolved-identity or unknown-condition records are withheld from corridors but persisted with WithheldReason. BulletinFallbackService refuses a same-day replay whose closure claims the current job's own fetch contradicts (ReplayContradictionPolicy), covering with the filler cart instead. The summarizer and prompts are untouched; the parked script-generation work ships separately on its own merits.

**Rationale:** The boundary makes bad claims unrepresentable to every consumer at once (writer context, stored job, operator console) instead of guarding one renderer; it keeps validity decisions pure, unit-testable, and pinned by a golden corpus of live-captured HERE payloads; and it leaves a single seam where future official-source adapters (Live Traffic NSW, QLDTraffic) plug in with per-source parsers producing the same IncidentFact shape.

**Consequences:** Scheduled worksite closures now air as roadworks, never closure news, until a corroborating source confirms a live closure; every reduction is ledgered on the job (withheld:*/demoted:* in JobIncident.WithheldReason) so caps and gates are auditable; ITrafficEventSource is deliberately deferred to the first second-source slice so the interface lands with two implementations and a real merge caller.

## 2026-08-18 — The Event Ledger's trust ladder is deleted, and omission is the only verdict

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The Event Ledger shipped a trust ladder: `EventLedgerFold.ComputeTrust` combined corroboration (two independent feeds) with an operator verdict into a Low/Medium/High tier, carried on `LedgerEventDto.TrustTier` and parsed by the web zod schema. An end-to-end audit of what the backend ships against what the frontend consumes found `trustTier` had ZERO usages in `web/src` — the trust chips were deleted during the Desk UX pass and the backend half was never retired with them. Worse, `High` was unreachable through the product at all: it required `vetted`, `vetted` required a `Confirmed` verdict, and after the omit-only Desk cutover no UI control could write one. The only way to produce a `High` was a direct API call. The same audit found `corroborated`, `jobsFolded` and `generatedAtUtc` unread, and `EventDelta.Vetted` always-false.

**Decision:** Delete the ladder rather than give it a UI. `TrustTier`, `LedgerTrust` and `ComputeTrust` are gone, with the `TrustTier`/`Corroborated` DTO fields, `TRUST_TIERS` and the zod entries. `VerdictKind` collapses to a single member, `Omitted`, which is what the omit-only Desk already meant. That made `EventDelta.Vetted` dead (removed), which left `ComputeDelta`'s `verdicts` parameter unused (removed), so per-job deltas no longer load verdicts at all. `LedgerDto.GeneratedAtUtc` and `JobsFolded` are removed. `TableStorageEventVerdictRepository.ParseKind` now returns null for anything it cannot positively recognise as an omission, and `GetVerdictsAsync` drops those rows.

**Rationale:** A computed-but-invisible tier whose top value is unreachable is worse than either alternative: it implies a capability the product does not have, and it costs a field in every ledger payload. Wiring it instead would have added an operator obligation the omit-only model deliberately removed (the Desk's premise is that everything airs unless omitted, so "confirming" is homework nobody owes). The `ParseKind` change is the one behavioural difference and it is deliberately safer: the previous fallback promoted any unrecognised string — including legacy `Confirmed` rows, which VOUCHED for an event — into something that reads as a verdict, and the only thing a verdict does is keep a road off air.

**Consequences:** Behaviour is preserved because only `Omitted` ever suppressed an event. `POST /ledger/{market}/events/{key}/verdict` now rejects `Confirmed`/`Flagged` with 400 ("Expected Omitted, or null to clear"), verified live on dev along with the fields' absence from the ledger response. The auto-publish groundwork the ladder was intended to feed is discarded with it; if that ships, its bar should be "nothing omitted" rather than "everything confirmed", which needs no per-event tier. Separately, the omission WIRING gained its first tests (`BroadcastOrchestratorDeskOmissionTests`) — `DeskOmissions.Apply` was unit-tested but no test had ever constructed `TrafficEvidenceBuilder`, so the verdict lookup, the market it uses, and the incident key it matches on were uncovered — and `ApplyDeskOmissionsAsync`'s previously silent skips now log, which is what distinguishes a real enforcement failure from omitted keys that simply left the HERE feed.

## 2026-08-19 — The writer's word target must carry the model id, and the history loader must read PascalCase

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** `DurationPrediction__Mode` is set to `HistoryBased` in `deployment/modules/function-app.bicep` for every environment, so `HistoryBasedDurationPredictor` — weighted-distance interpolation over past `(voice, model, speed, syllableCount) → achievedDuration` — is what produces the word target in every prompt (`LlmScriptGenerator.GetTargetSyllables`, interval midpoint / 1.5). Two defects meant it was often not running on the data it was built from. First, the pre-generation call built its `PredictionContext` with only `VoiceId` and `Speed`; `ModelId` defaulted to `""`. Both history lookups filter on an exact `ModelId` match, and `AudioPipelineService` records the model that actually voiced each read, so the query could only ever match rows written before a model override existed — 307 of the 850 committed records, blind to all 129 `eleven_v3` rows, which is what the pilot voices render on. `ScriptGenerationEngine`'s post-generation `PredictDuration` call had always passed `ModelId`; only this one had not. Second, `InMemorySynthesisHistoryRepository.JsonOptions` serialises camelCase with no case-insensitive read, so loading any PascalCase history file — including the committed replay corpus — deserialised nothing and the failure was swallowed.

**Decision:** Pass `ModelId = context.Model.GetValueOr(string.Empty)` in the word-target `PredictionContext`, matching the pattern `ScriptGenerationEngine` already used. Add `PropertyNameCaseInsensitive = true` to the repository's serializer options, keeping camelCase on write.

**Rationale:** Measured, not inferred. For a voice whose history carries a real model id (`9KesAUJoZzq3yyT2bJ3G`, `eleven_multilingual_v2`, 217 records — the voice two replay fixtures use), a 22-second slot resolved to **46 syllables / 31 words** as production called it versus **79 syllables / 53 words** with the model id: a 71% under-target, using 2 reference records instead of 5. Below `MinDataPointsForPrediction` the call silently returns `StaticRateDurationPredictor`'s constants while the deployed setting still reads `HistoryBased`, so the degradation had no signal. Voices whose history happens to carry an empty model id were unaffected, which is why chronic under-fill looked like a prompt problem rather than a lookup problem. Both fixes are one field each and both are pinned by tests that fail on the previous behaviour.

**Consequences:** Word targets rise for every voice whose history carries a real model id, which is the direction that reduces under-fill and filler-cart coverage — but the magnitude is per-voice and unverified on air, so this needs watching on dev before the pilot leans on it. Every length figure measured before this fix was taken against a target from the defective path: the fallback-replay panel has no `DurationPrediction` configuration at all and therefore ran `StaticRate` throughout, so prior prompt-versus-prompt length verdicts compared arms fairly but never exercised the history model. The replay harness cannot validate the fix either — `SimulatedElevenLabsSynthesizer` is fitted from the same 850-record corpus the predictor interpolates, so prediction and simulation would share their training data and the loop would look artificially accurate. Validation belongs on dev against real ElevenLabs, comparing predicted against achieved duration per voice and model.

## 2026-08-19 — The slot fit must compress an overrun, never guillotine the last word

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Prod job 8d37ced0782b43c3bd28261a564afaf2 (cairns-4ca, Star 102.7, 22s slot, 2026-08-18) aired a bulletin that stops mid-word: the script ends "...Unleaded's a dollar ninety-eight in Manoora," and the final word never airs. The delivered WAV is 970,200 samples = exactly 22.000000s, ends on sample -2390 with magnitude RISING into the file end and NO fade, and re-transcribes (whisper small.en) as "...Unlettered's $1.98 in...". ApplyFadeOut ramps a faded tail to exactly 0, so the last stage to touch those bytes was ResizeDataBytes. Cause: AudioPipelineService.LogWaterfallAndSucceed calls EnsureExactDurationIfPossible as a final sample-level guarantee that EVERY success path funnels through, and WavDurationProcessor.EnsureExactDuration would discard whatever sat in the last <=0.5s to hit the slot -- voiced speech included -- via bytesToCopy = Math.Min(targetDataBytes, DataSize). EffectiveToleranceSeconds (0.15) admits audio that far over target into that call, and 0.15s is a whole syllable at broadcast read rate. Two routes reach it holding an overrun: a fine-tuner that leaves the read alone, and (live on DEFAULT options) a post-synthesis strategy proposal adopted without a re-run of the fine-tuner. Nothing downstream could see the damage: IsSlotFilled only checks |final-target| and trailing silence, so an exactly-22.000s file with zero trailing silence scores perfectly, and WordTimingBuilder clamps the last word's end to the file duration, hiding it in the karaoke data too. The one gate that DID detect it was muted: the pre-review found MatchRatio 0.9394 with SuspectWords [hole, Manoora], but AudioFinalizer subtracted the market's operator-cleared verified pronunciations, and Manoora had been cleared as a transcription respelling, so the operator was told only "1 suspect pronunciation(s) - hole". The job itself then reached air by missed-window fallback: it generated a clean take at 23:41, nobody approved it, and JobWatchdog copied this 22:46 take onto it (script, audio, timings and PreReview) at 23:52.

**Decision:** Two changes, both narrow. (1) EnsureExactDuration keeps its early-outs and its 0.5s refusal guard, but before delegating to ResizeDataBytes it now scans the block-aligned byte range it is about to discard (existing IsSilentBlock, the same amplitude threshold 48 TrimTrailingSilence uses) and, when that range carries voiced speech, fits by pitch-preserving WSOLA retime (TimeStretchToTarget) instead of truncating. Padding, already-exact, silence trims, >0.5s deltas, non-16-bit audio and TrimToDuration are all untouched. (2) AudioPreReview.Result gains UnheardTailWords -- the trailing run of significant script words with no transcript counterpart -- and a new pure Domain type AudioPreReviewReport owns the whole operator-facing reporting rule: a verified-pronunciation clearance may mute suspect PRONUNCIATIONS and the non-final members of the tail, but never the tail's final word, which is the anchor evidence that the read stopped before the script did. AudioFinalizer's WithoutVerifiedAsync becomes ClearedPronunciationsAsync and simply supplies that list. The persisted AudioPreReviewOutcome, its DTO and the web schema are deliberately unchanged -- the new signal drives the job log, which is the point-in-time "go and listen to this" artefact.

**Rationale:** The exact-duration contract is a hard playout requirement, so refusing to fit was not an option; compressing the whole read honours the slot AND keeps every word, and the machinery already existed one method away. The blunt trim was never intended to eat speech: TrimToDuration is the deliberate "I already measured what to discard" variant, and EnsureExactDuration's own guard comment says large deltas should be surfaced to the orchestrator, not masked -- cutting a word masks exactly that. Splitting the pre-review signal was forced by real data, not theory: the synthetic test passed with UnheardTailWords == [Manoora], but replaying the ACTUAL aired transcript returned [Unleaded's, Manoora], because Unleaded's did air (mispronounced as "unlettered's") and so has no counterpart either. Naming it as cut off would resurrect a flag cairns-4ca had deliberately silenced, which is what the anchor rule prevents. A blocking gate on the pre-review was considered and REJECTED: the comparer's false-positive rate is precisely why the clearance list exists, so auto-failing a take on it would trade a rare truncation for frequent needless fallbacks.

**Consequences:** A read that overruns its slot by up to 0.5s is now compressed rather than decapitated, so the last word always airs; reads beyond that still surface to the orchestrator unchanged. Regression cover: EnsureExactDuration_ExcessIsVoicedSpeech_CompressesInsteadOfDiscardingTheTail plus both pipeline routes into the final guarantee (threshold and post-synthesis-strategy), all three verified RED against the unfixed processor with peak tail amplitude 0 (expected >48), and AudioPreReviewCutOffReadTests, which replays the real aired script against the real re-transcribed WAV. Verified in an isolated worktree at HEAD carrying only this change: 0 warnings / 0 errors, 4989 unit tests pass. NOT fixed here, and separate calls: the operator-supplied script itself ended mid-clause on a dangling comma (nothing validates terminal punctuation, in the cockpit or at POST /jobs/{jobId}/regenerate, and an unterminated final clause is also the worst possible input to eleven_v3 -- blocking a re-voice on it is a product decision); and a 22s slot aired a 66-minute-old take because approval lapsed, which is the fallback working as designed but is why a 22:46 defect surfaced on a 23:52 job page.

## 2026-08-20 — UI job feeds use a rolling 24-hour bounded window

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The operator console's ordinary jobs consumers called GET /api/jobs without limit, which selected the backend's unbounded list path and made every refresh scan all historical jobs as radioJobs grows. The History page already has its own cursor-based loader for older settled jobs.

**Decision:** Make useJobs add an exact rolling 24-hour from timestamp and limit=500 to every ordinary UI jobs request. Keep the query cache key minute-bucketed, while the request timestamp follows the shared wall clock. Leave useJobsHistory as the explicit on-demand path for older history.

**Rationale:** The backend only applies from when limit selects its bounded newest-first path.
