## 2026-08-21 — Slot-fit by variant selection, reviewer-safe repair ladder, and the Foundry prompt states returned to git

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** On 2026-08-20 the test environment's bulletin quality collapsed mid-afternoon after a strong morning. The Foundry versions API showed the full cause chain: `arn-draft` sat at v1 (11.6 KB full writer prompt) from 16 Jul until 14:52 UTC, when a compacted 3.2 KB prompt was provisioned three times in 26 minutes (v2-v4) — the compaction dropped the road-feel label rule (so "has minor impact" aired verbatim), the no-driving-advice rule (so "Slow down." aired), the weather/fuel framing guidance, and continuity. At 15:55 UTC `arn-refine` was re-provisioned with `arn-refine-sentence`'s single-sentence contract on BOTH envs, so every whole-script refine answered with an envelope the app cannot parse and silently kept the defective script. The good prompt states existed only in Foundry version history — none of it was in git. Separately, the deployed loop redesign had three load-bearing defects: un-ordered reviewer issues were keyword-mapped to a sentence with a default-to-lead fallback; a failed or ratchet-rejected sentence patch KEPT the flagged sentence verbatim, so the next review found the same defect and the job burned its budget (the 02:03 test job failed at the final grounding gate on one weather sentence); and the retry loop relaxed the word target UP toward an over-long failed draft (94 words against a 45-word target bought the next attempt a 59-word budget). Underneath all of it, draft assembly took the first-listed (concise) variant per item and dropped whole sentences when that overshot — the duration predictor set the word target and then went home, so thin drafts shipped listy and dense drafts got compressed.

**Decision:** Four coupled fixes. (1) Prompts: `prompts/agents/arn-draft.md` keeps the compact prompt but restores the dropped craft rules (road-feel not labels, no driving advice, one beat per fact, frame weather as weather, vary the palette); `prompts/review-system.md` extends the weather-vs-traffic rule to market-first phrasing ("Cairns is clear overnight, with temperatures at 18 degrees" is weather, never a roads claim); `provision-foundry-agents.sh` now bakes `json_object` for arn-draft, matching the drift contract; both envs re-provisioned from git and drift-check clean on all 9 agents, including arn-refine back on its whole-script contract. (2) New `VariantSlotFitter` replaces first-variant assembly: exact enumeration of per-sentence phrasing combinations (plus drop for unpinned sentences) under the fit target — feasibility beats fill, fewest drops, closest fill, fuller phrasing on the lead — with same-evidence-set dedup and a greedy fallback past a product-size guard; `DraftWordBudget.TrimToCeiling` stays as the absolute guard. (3) `ScriptReviewLoop` repair ladder: reviewer orders are re-resolved from the reviewer's own quoted span whenever a mechanical repair moved text (stale orders patched the wrong sentence — observed in tests and in the 02:03 job), unresolved issues widen to the whole-script refine per the ReviewIssue contract, a reviewer-flagged sentence whose patch fails or is ratchet-rejected is DROPPED (with `RequiredSourceDetector` guarding a required-fixture carrier into the whole-script path instead), and both ratchets give the deficit axis a small tolerance so a defect-clearing rewrite a couple of words shorter is no longer rejected as "no net improvement". (4) `TryParseRefineSentence` accepts the draft-shaped `{"items":[…]}` envelope the live sentence agent intermittently answers with, and the pre-synthesis retry target may move down but never up after a quality failure.

**Rationale:** Each fix is at the layer that owns the failure: prompts for phrasing (model-facing rules), deterministic code for fit and repair order (never prompt obedience), and provisioning from git so the drift check makes "the good prompt existed only in Azure" unrepeatable. The fitter is selection, not generation: every phrasing it chooses was written by the model against already-committed evidence ids, so a swap can never change what the bulletin claims. The deficit tolerance and the drop-ladder both encode the same principle the incidents taught: a proven defect must be removed, and "shorter" is not "worse".

**Consequences:** Verified on the local repro harness first (`tools/repro_pipeline.py`, which replays captured Foundry draft payloads through the live agents with swappable assembly/refine arms): across 14 runs on three real payloads (thin Cairns, dense Sydney, and the exact payload that failed the 02:03 job), the candidate prompt + knapsack produced no label leaks, no advice lines, no weather misreads, and landed within half a second of the slot allowance where naive assembly under-filled by 2-9s or overshot by 2-4s. Backend: Application 866/866 and the new `VariantSlotFitterTests` (5) + `ScriptReviewLoopPatchFallbackTests` (3) green; the 9 remaining Infrastructure failures are pre-existing in the in-flight prompt-tree/HERE-provider work streams, unchanged by this change. Deployed to dev and verified live on both pilot stations (jobs `b8802fad…` Cairns, `bcf1fdbb…` Sydney): varied calibrated palette, weather framed as weather, no labels or advice, 22.5s/22.9s natural reads gently fitted to 22.0s instead of time-compressed. Test agent provisioning landed the same content (drift-clean). The pre-existing `EditorialPromptSourceTests` parity failure tracks the in-flight prompts/system migration (tree slots vs the system.md golden), owned by that work stream. Open follow-ups: the .NET replay panel as the regression gate for the fitter under the simulated-duration harness, and the item-level cross-contamination seen once locally (a draft item voicing weather/fuel content under traffic evidence ids) needs a citation-completeness guard.

**Verified on TEST the same day** (backend redeploy + agent re-provision, both stations triggered live): Sydney `60774809…` kept its required weather line through the prosody trim ("Partly sunny, 17 degrees.") and led with the measured worst ("Sydney Newcastle Freeway has major delays, traffic crawling") with a varied calibrated palette, 21.0s natural fitted to 22.0s, 100% transcript match; Cairns `39f8b71d…` named roadworks plainly under the condition-honesty rule instead of inventing slowdowns ("Roadworks are also in place on the Bruce Highway through Gordonvale"), both fixtures aired, 21.9s natural, 96% transcript match. The same morning's Cairns job `189542ad…` correctly FAILED at the final grounding gate rather than air a fabricated slowdown — the gate working as designed.
 Also closed the same day: `TriggerStudio` now omits `content` unless the operator changed it in the dialog, so a station's saved Always-include flags are never silently overridden by a mount-time snapshot (the 2026-08-20 trigger that aired without required weather); pinned by `TriggerStudioContent.test.tsx`, dev+test SWAs redeployed.

**Experiment campaign (, captured real payloads × prompt variants × temperatures × knapsack assembly, deterministic defect card + live review gate):** draft temperature is NOT the quality lever — temp 0.5 was WORSE than 1.0 (4/9 runs with defects, label leaks crept back) and 0.8 ≈ 1.0, so agents stay on the service default. The lever that eliminated the defect classes was the prompt: the final `prompts/agents/arn-draft.md` (compact + restored craft rules + condition-honesty + delay-figure-is-not-instruction) produced 0 label/advice/distance/duplicate defects across 16 runs on 4 payloads with zero slot overshoot, and held the advice ban even with advice fields present in the evidence (making an evidence-side advice strip unnecessary). The residual defect source is the REVIEWER's marginal-call variance: it flagged zero-defect Melbourne scripts and then approved the identical script on re-review — mitigation is the shipped repair ladder, not more prompt work.

**Architecture consolidation (same day):** the combinatorial variant-selection algorithm lives in the PRODUCTION generator `StructuredMatrixScriptGenerator.SelectOptimalCombination` (and has since 19 Aug 02:00 UTC — the good-era pipeline). An earlier draft of this change put the fitter in `LlmScriptGenerator.GenerateStructuredDraftAsync`, which has zero callers; that wiring was reverted and the fitter file deleted. The production selector gained: asymmetric slot cost (over-target costs double — compression vs slow-fill), same-evidence-set dedup before permutation, quality penalties for raw data labels/driving advice/voiced distances, an epsilon-corrected tie-break that takes the fuller read at equal fit (float dust had silently defeated it), and an internal-static extraction covered by `StructuredMatrixSelectorTests` (6). The condition matrix (`ScenarioMatrixEvalTests`, 2026-08-21 rewrite) now runs the production generator + live agents per scenario on live HERE data, `Broadcast:UseStructuredMatrix=true` — without that override the matrix measures a pipeline no station runs (the mid-migration on-disk system tree).

## 2026-08-21 — The whole-script LLM refiner is removed; sentence-scoped patching is the only LLM repair

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Later the same day, after the morning's repair-ladder fix was verified live on dev+test, a full read of the refine path against the 77-eval corpus and live job traces showed the whole-script rewrite was a net quality negative: a whole-bulletin rewrite routinely re-wrote most sentences while addressing none of the flagged defects (measured 3 of 7 eval runs), padded with recap filler, and — because the rewrite output was never re-reviewed — shipped unvalidated text (the Baudesert Road place-name swap on job `4417add2` was exactly this). The sentence-scoped patcher (`PatchSentenceAsync`) plus the deterministic ladder (quote-span order resolution, required-fixture splice, drop-the-proven-defect) had already absorbed every job the whole-script pass actually did well.

**Decision:** Remove the whole-script refine path outright rather than leave it as a fallback: `IScriptRefiner.RefineScriptAsync`, its `LlmScriptGenerator` implementation, `TryParseRefine`, the `RefinedScript` contract, the loop's ratchet machinery (`SelectRatchetCandidate`, `AlignRefinedCitations`), the style gate's whole-script fallback, `WordTargetEnforcer`'s whole-script expansion/grounding paths, `prompts/refine.md`, `prompts/agents/arn-refine.md`, and the `refineAgentName` IaC parameter + app setting. The surviving repair surface: reviewer issues with a resolvable sentence order patch sentence-by-sentence; an unresolvable issue defers to the next review attempt; a sentence whose patch fails or is ratchet-rejected is DROPPED, and a required weather/fuel fixture the drop would orphan is deterministically re-spliced from the fetched data (`FixtureLineComposer`); the final grounding gate drops flagged sentences instead of rewriting. Expansion is sentence-scoped growth in `WordTargetEnforcer` (locked weather/fuel lines skipped). `RefineSentenceAgentName` no longer falls back to a refine agent.

**Rationale:** Every mechanism that replaces the rewrite is either evidence-committed (the sentence patcher can only cite supplied evidence and is word-budget-capped) or fully deterministic (splice/drop/relocate). A rewrite the reviewer then cannot re-judge within budget was the one remaining place a bulletin could silently become unvalidated text; deleting the capability is cheaper and safer than bounding it further. The eval harness (`BulletinEval.ReviewRefineAndComplyAsync`) and the skipped live-verification cycle now mirror the sentence-scoped loop so the corpus stays honest.

**Consequences:** Full solution builds 0/0; Application 863/863 (3 tests pinning removed contracts deleted: the whole-script ratchet, LLM-rewrite citation alignment), Infrastructure 1515/1524 with the same 9 pre-existing in-flight failures (HERE-provider, schedule-repo, prompt-tree, audio-trim, WireMock fixture streams) unchanged; Domain/Functions/Architecture/ExternalSmoke all green; E2E red locally as always without a Functions host. Live-side remainder: the deployed `arn-refine` agent still exists in the dev/test Foundry projects but nothing references it — delete it from both projects when convenient (the drift checker no longer tracks it).

## 2026-08-21 — Trim keeps the news: editorial priority in the duration fitter, and drift-proof drop ordering

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The first live exercise of the sentence-only repair architecture (pilot stations on dev) surfaced two real defects plus a crash vector. (1) Port Lincoln job `78fe9db3` (15s slot, sparse): the post-synthesis overrun trim dropped the bulletin's ONLY incident — the Railway Place closure leading the read — and aired a four-road "are clear" sweep, because `BulletinDurationFitter`'s subset objective (fewest dropped, then fewest seconds, then closest fit) had no notion of editorial priority. (2) The final grounding gate's new drop ladder resolved reviewer sentence orders against the pre-drop script while mutating it: dropping order 2 shifted a flagged order 4 onto innocent sentence 5 (the main loop never sees this — it drops one sentence per attempt then re-reviews). (3) `FixtureLineComposer.WeatherLine` indexed `Conditions.Split(...)[0]`, which throws on an empty-string payload from the weather provider, inside the review loop's repair path.

**Decision:** (1) `BulletinDurationFitter` gained an editorial axis: a traffic sentence whose only claim is clear-flow vocabulary (`IsGoodRunSweep`) is shed before any content-bearing sentence at equal dropped count, on both the subset objective and the collapse-floor path. (2) The gate resolves all issues against one pre-drop split, dedupes, and drops highest-order first so removals cannot shift each other; the required-fixture splice runs once after all drops. (3) `WeatherLine` renders a bare "N degrees." on empty conditions instead of throwing. (4) `PatchSentenceAsync` now rejects a multi-sentence return (the splice would grow the script and shift later orders mid-loop). (5) The word-ceiling log line no longer prints "predicted 0.0s against a 0.0s allowance" on the no-calibration fallback paths. Separately, Port Lincoln's three round-robin voices had no calibration rows at all — all three were calibrated live on dev (128–159 wpm measured), so the word-target predictor is now voice-informed there.

**Rationale:** A trim that cannot tell news from filler will eventually cut the only thing worth airing — duration fit is an editorial decision, so the objective encodes it. Drift-proofing the gate mirrors the main loop's proven invariant (one structural mutation per review pass) without paying an extra review round per dropped sentence. The composer and patch guards keep the repair ladder itself un-failable: a repair path that throws or grows the script is worse than the defect it was fixing.

**Consequences:** Regression tests: gate two-sentence drop order, multi-sentence patch rejection, four composer tests (incl. classifier idempotence and the empty-conditions guard), and the fitter's good-run-vs-incident trim. Full suite: build 0/0; Domain 2144, Application 864, Infrastructure 1516 (+ same 9 pre-existing in-flight failures from other streams); Port Lincoln re-run on the fixed build kept the closure at the lead and shed the sweep. Known limitation, not fixed: the embedded prosody model (`spoken-duration-v1.json`) covers only 6 voice rows; Dolly Female Old/Young have empty corpora, so their ceiling gate stays on the word-target fallback until a fitting pipeline runs over real samples.

## 2026-08-21 — The reviewer stops fighting the drop ladder: removed-sentence visibility, bounded continuity, and a novelty screen at the final gate

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Two consecutive live Sydney re-reads on dev failed the final grounding gate (`76f4f8d0`, `b56a431c`) while the sentence ladder itself behaved correctly. The pattern was a whipsaw between the reviewer and the ladder: review flags a sentence -> the patch fails or is ratchet-rejected -> the ladder drops the sentence -> the NEXT review complains the item is missing or demands a cleared-item callback the 22-second slot cannot carry. Both jobs also showed the gate inventing a defect it had never raised in the loop (`76f4f8d0`: a CONTINUITY claim against an untouched lead sentence, with reasoning that conflated a crash with unrelated roadworks), and the reviewer emitting issue rows whose own reason concluded there was no defect. Nothing bad aired — the jobs failed honestly and the fallback covered the slot — but a healthy read was being thrown away on reviewer churn.

**Decision:** Four changes. (1) `IScriptReviewer.ReviewScriptAsync` gained an optional `removedSentences` channel; the loop records every sentence the ladder drops and every later review (loop and gate) receives them, with `review.md` instructing that their absence is deliberate and must never be flagged. (2) `review-system.md` rule 5 (CONTINUITY) is bounded: a callback is only owed for an item the previous bulletin ACTUALLY AIRED, at most one callback in a short re-read, never for a sentence listed under REMOVED THIS RUN, and a missing cleared-item callback is a polish note that can never alone justify NEEDS_REVISION. (3) The output contract now forbids emitting an issue whose reason concludes there is no defect. (4) The final grounding gate screens issues before acting AND before failing: an issue is actionable when it is persistent (same order+defect as the loop's last review) or mutation-adjacent (against a sentence the loop just patched or dropped); a CONTINUITY issue that is neither — first articulated at the gate about untouched content — is logged and ignored, and when nothing actionable or persistent remains the gate ships the loop's script instead of failing the attempt.

**Rationale:** The ladder's whole point is that a proven-defective sentence leaves the read; a reviewer that then demands its return converts a successful repair into a failed job. Continuity is the one defect class the reviewer judges against a read it never heard, and it is the class both failures turned on — so it is the class the novelty screen covers, while factual classes (FABRICATION, WRONG_INCIDENT_TYPE, NOT_FROM_DATA) stay fully actionable at the gate because they are re-verifiable against the supplied evidence. Screening before the failure decision (not just before the drop pass) is what actually saves the bulletin: the second failure died on the gate's LAST attempt, where the old code failed on any rejection regardless of what the rejection was about.

**Consequences:** Application 867/867 with three new gate/ladder tests (removed-sentence visibility, novel-continuity ignored mid-gate, novel-continuity-only rejection on the last gate attempt ships instead of failing); full suite otherwise unchanged (Domain 2144, Functions 827, Architecture 14, Infrastructure 1516 with the same 9 pre-existing in-flight failures). Adding the optional reviewer parameter required updating 42 NSubstitute stub sites — an optional parameter still changes the arity NSubstitute matches on, which is worth remembering before extending a substituted interface. Deployed to dev with `arn-review` re-provisioned from git (drift-clean, all 8 role agents). Both pilot stations then generated clean single-pass bulletins. NOT yet proven live: the continuity fixes need a re-read that actually reaches the reviewer — the verifying Sydney run was clean enough that the conditional audit skipped review entirely.

## 2026-08-22 — A cross-sentence roll-call is a defect: the secondary-item cap becomes deterministic

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Dev job `8b895081` (Sydney, 22s, quiet 02:47 read) aired "Victoria Road is crawling, adding about 10 minutes. Arthur Street is seeing heavy traffic. Park Avenue has a bit of a queue. Rohini Street is taking an extra minute or two. Bay Street has a slight queue. Albert Avenue is a little slower." — six single-road minor items, each with a different idiom. It passed every gate: `RollCallDetector` counts names inside ONE sentence, `SentenceCloneDetector` needs a repeated frame, and the draft prompt's own "Vary the Palette" rule guarantees the frames differ. `prompts/agents/arn-draft.md` already capped secondaries at "1 or 2" — the model simply ignored it, and nothing enforced it. The shape also costs slot: at this voice's fitted coefficients the eight sentence-ends carried 4.0s of modelled pause, so the same facts in four sentences predict 17.2s against the list's 20.5s — the listiness spends roughly eight words' worth of slot on pauses, which then drives the word ceiling to trim real content and leaves the read short enough to need stretching (19.8s natural into a 22.0s slot).

**Decision:** New `SecondaryItemCapDetector` enforces the prompt's own shape: a lead plus at most two named single-road secondaries. Its repair merges the excess into ONE sweep sentence and only ever merges items whose corridors share the same measured `MagnitudeTier`, so the shared state it voices is true of every road it names by construction; items above Moderate are never swept because a Major/Severe corridor is lead material. Wired as a STYLE gate in `ComputeViolationCounts` (so a listy draft also blocks the conditional-audit skip) and as a mechanical repair in the loop's ladder, ahead of any refine decision. `arn-draft.md` was also tightened: "AT MOST TWO" named secondaries, an explicit "Sweep the rest — never list" rule with an example, a note that combining road NAMES under one shared state is encouraged (the Cognitive Load Rule bans stacking cross-streets, not names), and the palette rule no longer reads as licence for a long varied list.

**Rationale:** This suite's standing position is that shape rules the model disobeys become deterministic gates (`RollCallDetector`'s own header says prompt rules for this proved unreliable). Tier-gating the merge is what makes a deterministic sweep safe: the alternative — reusing one item's wording across roads whose data differs — would understate or overclaim.

**Consequences:** Domain 2148 with four new tests, including the exact aired Sydney read collapsing to "Rohini Street, Bay Street and Albert Avenue are all running a little slower." and a Major-tier case that must NOT be swept; full suite otherwise unchanged. Deployed to dev with `arn-draft` re-provisioned (drift-clean). The next live Sydney read (`d41fb7d4`) came back as two closures, one delay item, one three-road sweep and the weather close — 6 sentences for 46 words, the draft producing the sweep itself without the detector having to repair. Residual, tracked separately: the read still landed 20.5s natural in a 22.0s slot (the measured 152 wpm for this voice says the slot holds ~56 words, the ceiling targeted 48), so the ceiling/trim chain leaves ~1.5s to be covered by stretching rather than content.

## 2026-08-22 — The slot-fit selector's search space is bounded; phrasings yield, content never does

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** `StructuredMatrixScriptGenerator.SelectOptimalCombination` walks EVERY combination of the draft's per-item phrasings (plus the empty option for droppable categories) and scores each assembly with a duration prediction and a quality penalty. The combination count is the product of the per-item option counts, and nothing in code bounded it — the only cap on item count is a prompt rule the model demonstrably ignores (dev job `8b895081` shipped six one-road items where the prompt asks for a lead plus at most two). A well-shaped draft is ~100 assemblies; the 9-item draft that same station produced with three phrasings each is ~35,000; 12 items with three phrasings and three droppables is ~1.26 million, each costing a string join, a syllable count, a regex-based penalty pass, and an in-memory kNN history lookup — on the critical path of every bulletin.

**Decision:** Bound the space at 50,000 assemblies. When the product exceeds it, trim PHRASINGS deterministically — take from the widest option list first, never remove an item, never remove a droppable item's empty option, and always leave every item at least one real phrasing — then permute exactly as before. The instance wrapper logs the item count, how many phrasings were trimmed, and the original space size, so a chatty draft is visible as a warning rather than as latency. A memoisation of the duration prediction by syllable count was prototyped and REVERTED: both production predictors derive duration from syllable count alone, but `IDurationPredictor` does not guarantee it (the selector's own test fake is word-based), and the bound already removes the pathological case — a cache that silently assumes an unwritten contract is the worse trade.

**Rationale:** The selector's job is choosing WORDING for content the draft already committed to; the editorial choice space (which items, which drops) must survive intact, so the trim can only ever cost the read some phrasing variety. Bounding beats pruning here because the objective is only computable on a complete assembly (the slot-fit term needs the whole read's duration), so there is no admissible partial bound to prune against.

**Consequences:** Two selector tests added (Infrastructure 1518): a 12-item three-phrasing draft engages the bound, returns within seconds, and still voices all twelve roads; a normal three-item draft is never trimmed. Behaviour is bit-identical to before for every draft under the bound, which is every draft observed in production to date.

## 2026-08-22 — The duration corpus was mislabelled by fallback; refit v2, and a correction to yesterday's diagnosis

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** `harvest-duration-corpus.py` labels each observation by the job's persisted `ScriptText`, but `Job.ApplyFallback` OVERWRITES `ScriptText` with the fallback SOURCE bulletin's text. Every fallback job therefore contributed a pair whose words came from one bulletin and whose measured duration came from another — 151 of dev's jobs. This is exactly the "irreducible noise ... 3.3x the controlled figure ... inputs not actually byte-identical - UNDIAGNOSED" warning the harvester prints, and the v1 calibration was fitted through it. It also produced a false lead of my own: grouping by `ScriptText` showed 27 "identical" jobs spanning 15.9-26.3s, which dissolved once their logs revealed 47/51/54/56/57-word synthesis lines.

**Decision:** New `scripts/build-duration-dataset.py` takes the label from the LOG NARRATIVE, where `Synthesizing audio (N words...)` and `Audio filled to slot: X.Xs natural read` sit adjacent and cannot be crossed, and attaches TEXT only when the persisted script provably is the spoken read (no fallback, no filler stitch, word count matches). Dev yields 732 pace observations, 169 text-labelled. `scripts/fit-duration-models.py` bakes off six candidate forms under leave-one-out per voice; `scripts/emit-duration-calibration.py` emits the winner in the existing schema (`spoken-duration-v2.json`, loader repointed), so this is coefficients-and-coverage, not new model code. The chosen form has ONE free parameter per voice — the syllable rate, fitted through the origin — with word-boundary and pause costs pooled across voices. Leave-one-out ranked the 3-parameter per-voice fit marginally better on MAE (1.04s vs 1.07s) but it is ill-conditioned on this corpus: every observation is a slot-constrained ~45-60 word bulletin, so a free intercept is near-collinear with the rate (the unconstrained fit gave ARN Sarah 0.008 s/syllable with a 10.3s intercept) and the two rate terms are near-collinear with each other (words ~= syllables/1.5, which produced a NEGATIVE syllable cost for one voice). The constrained form has a better p90 (2.07s vs 2.42s) and extrapolates to the longer pre-trim assemblies the word ceiling actually asks about.

**Rationale:** Bias is what matters, not MAE. A symmetric error is corrected downstream by the measured audio fitter; a one-way lean moves the content-versus-length trade on every bulletin. Fitting through the origin is also the physically correct constraint — a zero-word read takes zero seconds — and pause coefficients are clamped non-negative for the same reason (the raw fit put ellipsis at -0.245s, confounded because the station opener carries the only ellipsis in most reads).

**Consequences:** Fleet bias moves from about -1.2s to **-0.09s**, MAE to **1.09s** over 159 measured bulletins; the Sydney voice (Young Female Sarah) goes from MAE 1.71s / bias -1.70s to **MAE 0.68s / bias -0.01s with 80% inside a second**. Coverage rises from 6 rows to 7 including `iKMw2nMnODCnVgY4VQbS` (a Port Lincoln round-robin voice that had no row at all and therefore no calibrated prediction). New `SpokenDurationCalibrationAccuracyTests` scores the shipped calibration per voice against the pinned corpus and gates MAE <= 1.6s and |bias| <= 0.6s for any voice with >= 8 observations, plus a fleet-wide lean check — that suite is what caught two of my own errors during this work (fitting the word term against raw word count when the model charges it on `plainWords`, and the degenerate coefficients above).

**CORRECTION to the 2026-08-22 under-fill analysis:** I previously reported that the predictor ran ~17% slow for ARN Sarah and that this pessimism was shedding content at the word ceiling. That was wrong, and wrong in the same way as the corpus bug: I compared a prediction of the PRE-TRIM script (26.6s for ~53 words) against a measurement of the POST-TRIM read (20.5s for 46 words) — two different texts. On matched text v1 predicts 19.4s against a measured 20.5s, i.e. it runs slightly OPTIMISTIC, and both v1 and v2 agree that roughly 51-52 words fill a 22s slot for that voice. The residual ~1.5s under-fill on job `d41fb7d4` is therefore a TARGETING problem, not a pace problem: the ceiling derived a 48-word target and whole-sentence trimming landed on 46. That belongs to the "four stages each own length" flaw, and is the next thing to fix.

## 2026-08-22 — Duration residuals are word TEXTURE, not punctuation: the prosody apparatus is not earning its keep

**Status:** accepted (findings; model change not yet implemented)

**Context:** With the fallback-free corpus in place (`test/corpus/duration/dataset-v2.json`, 150 usable text-labelled observations over 7 well-sampled voices), `scripts/analyse-duration-residuals.py` mines what the shipped v2 calibration still gets wrong and tests every candidate under leave-one-out.

**Findings.** (1) A per-voice syllable rate ALONE scores MAE 1.155s; the full shipped six-term model scores 1.112s. The word-boundary and pause terms are worth ~0.04s of MAE between them — the prosody apparatus is close to free-riding. Commas add 0.011s, periods nothing until fourth place. (2) The dominant missing signal is WORD TEXTURE. `charsPerWord` alone takes MAE to 1.053s; adding `meanWordSyllables` reaches 0.955s; adding a spoken-form expansion of prices/numbers/initialisms (`spokenSyllableBonus`) reaches **0.888s with p90 1.81s** — a 20% MAE and 17% p90 improvement over the shipped feature set, at zero bias. (3) An earlier hypothesis was REFUTED: the `charsPerWord` correlation is not a syllable-counter defect. A deliberately better counter changed MAE by +0.014s and left the correlation intact, and against a syllable-only model the correlation is only -0.09. The signal appears only when the word-boundary term is present, so `charsPerWord` is largely correcting THAT term's mis-charging. (4) Per voice the deviation patterns differ in KIND and in SIGN: Male Sarah slows on long words (charsPerWord r=-0.45), Young Female Sarah does the opposite (longWords r=+0.49), Dolly (original) rushes monosyllables (r=+0.56), Dolly Male pb40 is dominated by price tokens (r=-0.61), Dolly Male Faster pb60 by longest-sentence length (r=-0.70), Jeffrey by sentence count (r=+0.60).

**Decision:** Record these as the directed next step rather than bolt terms on now. When implemented, the change is: `SpokenDurationFeatures` gains `charsPerWord`/`meanWordSyllables`; the feature extractor applies the pipeline's OWN spoken-form normalisation (`SpokenPriceNormalizer` and number expansion) before counting syllables, rather than carrying a correction term for prices; the calibration schema and `TokenAdditiveDurationModel` carry the two texture coefficients POOLED across voices; and the pause terms stay but are no longer load-bearing. Per-voice texture coefficients are NOT justified at 12-39 samples per voice — the signs differ per voice, so pooling is a compromise that only more data can resolve.

**Rationale:** Expanding prices before counting is principled where a `priceTokens` coefficient is a patch: "$2.18" is one written token and about five spoken syllables, and the pipeline already owns that expansion for the writer. Pooling texture coefficients is the same bias-variance call that picked the one-parameter-per-voice rate: with this much data, constrained beats flexible.

**Consequences:** `SpokenDurationCalibrationAccuracyTests` already gates MAE <= 1.6s and |bias| <= 0.6s per voice, so the improvement is measurable the moment it lands; the budgets should tighten to about 1.1s and 0.3s once the texture terms are in. The residual after that is ~0.9s MAE / 1.8s p90 at 22s slots, which is the honest floor for prediction on mined production data and the reason the measured audio fitter must stay: a controlled battery (designed scripts spanning 20-120 words per voice) is the only way to identify per-voice texture terms and to break the slot-constrained length degeneracy this corpus cannot.

## 2026-08-22 — Duration prediction moves to a pooled token shape with one scale per voice (schema v3)

**Status:** accepted (deployed to the repo; not yet published to dev)

**Context:** The bulletin corpus cannot identify a duration model on its own. All 150 clean observations are slot-constrained 45-60 word reads, so word count and syllable count are collinear (words are about syllables/1.5) and there is almost no length variation to fit a rate against. That degeneracy is what forced the v2 fit through the origin with one free parameter per voice. The job records also carry `WordTimingsJson`, the synthesiser's own per-word alignment. Those spans are SELF-LABELLED, so unlike `ScriptText` they survive `Job.ApplyFallback`: 11,869 tokens spanning 0 to 5+ syllables, which is where a cost function is actually identifiable. Two contamination controls were mandatory. `ApplyFallback` copies `WordTimingsJson` too, so 295 corpus bulletins hold only 185 distinct alignments (one popular source appears five times) and rows are deduplicated by an exact hash. Alignments are also recorded in post-fit time, and converting them to natural time needs `stretch`, which is derived from the same corrupted `naturalSec`, so each alignment is normalised by its own mean token cost and stage A never reads an absolute duration.

**Decision:** Ship a two-stage form (schema v3). Stage A fits 11 SHAPE coefficients from the alignments, pooled across every voice. Stage B fits exactly ONE scalar per voice against clean bulletin durations, through the origin. `scripts/duration-model-bakeoff.py` scored twelve candidates under leave-one-out with the stage-A fit refitted per fold (exact leave-one-job-out by Gram downdate, so no held-out leakage flatters the token models). Winner: MAE 0.857s, p90 1.75s, bias -0.03s, 70% of reads within a second, against 1.094s / 2.15s / -0.06s for the superseded form — a 22% MAE and 19% p90 improvement. Those are speed-normalised seconds; in the actual seconds a slot sees the in-sample figure is 0.830s.

**Rationale:** Three measured patterns drove the form, and each contradicts something v2 assumed. (1) Per-syllable cost is strongly SUB-LINEAR: measured relative cost is 0.72 / 1.25 / 1.57 / 1.71 / 1.89 for one to five syllables, so increments fall (+0.53, +0.32, +0.14, +0.18) and a large fixed per-word onset dominates. A single linear per-syllable rate cannot express that, which is why v2 needed a separate word-boundary term and still mis-priced both ends. (2) Commas do not buy silence: the measured pause after a comma is 0.044s, LESS than the 0.056s after an ordinary word, while only sentence periods carry a real pause (0.143s). What the fitted comma term captures (+0.569 against a period's +0.833) is pre-boundary lengthening of the word itself, so v3 prices a phrase boundary on the WORD, not on the silence. That is why v2's four separate pause coefficients were worth only 0.04s of MAE between them. (3) Numerals are invisible to the shipped counter: `SyllableCounter` strips non-letters, so "12" scores zero syllables while the alignments show it costing a full average token, and "M1" scores one where it speaks "em one". `SpokenSyllableCounter` expands digits and letter-names initialisms, and `alphanumericSec` and `perDigitSec` both fitted clearly positive.

Three alternatives were tested and REJECTED rather than assumed. A per-voice intercept (0.867s) and scaling silence separately from speech (0.892s) were both indistinguishable from the winner under a paired bootstrap on the same folds, so neither earns a second per-voice parameter — notable because the speech/silence split was the standing explanation for the two pace-boosted voices being worst-fit, and it is now refuted. Shrinking thin voices toward the fleet scale was significantly WORSE (0.926s, 95% CI [+0.021, +0.135]). Pooling a voice's pace-boost variants under one scale with a fitted elasticity was also worse (0.932s), so a pace boost is not a simple rate multiplier and each variant still needs its own row.

`longWordCharSec` fits NEGATIVE (-0.033) by design: it corrects `perCharSec` (+0.136), because a twelve-letter word is a single articulation and charging every character at full rate overshoots. The emitter refuses to write a file unless the net rate stays positive, and the embedded contract test asserts the same invariant, because a negative net would let the word ceiling be inverted by padding.

**Consequences:** `SpokenDurationFeatures` gains 11 token-shape fields and a single-pass extractor; new `SpokenSyllableCounter`; `SpokenDurationCalibration` becomes schema v3 (pooled `Shape` plus per-voice `Scale`), deleting the partial-pooling block and the seven superseded per-voice coefficients; `TokenAdditiveDurationModel` keeps its lookup, three-tier degradation and residual inflation and changes only the arithmetic. Only `spoken-duration-v3.json` is embedded and the superseded v1/v2 JSON are deleted from `src/` (provenance stays in `test/corpus/duration/` and git). Accuracy gates tightened from per-voice MAE 1.6s / bias 0.6s to 1.45s / 0.35s, plus a new fleet gate of 1.05s / 0.20s; measured fleet is 0.90s / -0.15s over 159 bulletins. Every gated voice improved: 1.03->0.79, 0.99->0.81, 1.26->1.01, 1.29->1.21, 0.88->0.69, 0.89->0.70, and 0.68 held. Fit/serve equivalence was verified rather than assumed: production passes the TAGGED script to `Predict` while the fit used the tag-free read, and C#-style tag stripping reproduces `plainText` exactly on all 169 labelled rows. Superseded tooling was removed (`fit-duration-models.py`, `analyse-duration-residuals.py`); `scripts/duration-model-search.py` still fits the contaminated pre-v2 corpus and should be retired or repointed.

**Follow-on the same day — the minimum-samples threshold was measured rather than inherited.** The emitter required eight clean bulletins before a voice earned its own scale, a number carried over from the v2 fit and never tested. A learning curve settles it: fit the scale from k random samples of a voice, score a held-out read, 420 folds per k. MAE is 1.207 / 1.057 / 0.991 / 0.903 at k = 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 against an asymptote near 0.87, so the curve is flat by FOUR samples, and TWO samples already beat the superseded form fitted on everything (1.094s). One free scalar simply does not need much data. Holding the threshold at eight therefore bought no accuracy and cost coverage, and the cost was concrete: the pace-boost-20 row has six samples, so it was denied its own scale and inherited a pace-boost-0 row that mispredicted it by -2.06 seconds, the worst row in the fleet. Threshold lowered to four; that row now fits its own scale (0.4376) and its bias collapses from **-2.06s to -0.18s** with MAE 2.06 -> 1.41. Coverage rises to 8 voices over 156 bulletins, and fleet in-sample moves 0.82 -> 0.84s purely because six genuinely harder reads joined the scored set.

**Open:** One thin row is still uncalibrated and visibly wrong (pb55, n=3, bias -1.74s) and four fingerprints have no row at all, so those reads fall back to the word target; pb55 needs one more sample to cross the new threshold. The corpus contains NO repeated (voice, text) pair, so the irreducible noise floor remains unmeasured and we do not know how close 0.86s is to it. The binding constraint is now DATA, not model form: the top five candidate forms were all statistically indistinguishable under a paired bootstrap, so further search on this corpus is not identifiable. Breaking that needs a controlled battery of designed scripts (20-120 words per voice, plus deliberate repeats) synthesised on purpose, which would also supply the length variation this slot-constrained corpus lacks and let per-voice shape deviations be fitted — the per-voice residual drivers differ in SIGN, so today's pooled shape is a deliberate compromise.

## 2026-08-23 — Drafts blew their word budget because the budget was advisory at every writing layer; the guarantee sat after review

**Status:** accepted (deployed to test; dev and prod unchanged)

**Context:** Six poller-fired pilot bulletins on test (sydney KIIS 90s, cairns-4ca Star 102.7, 22s slots) showed drafts arriving far over target — Cairns assembled 91->93 words against a 54-word target, Sydney 58->60 against 45 — and the ceiling then trimming a third of the read away. The first hypothesis, that bookends were not being counted, is WRONG: they are subtracted from the writer's budget up front (2026-08-04), verified live here — Cairns got 54 words for a 22s slot behind a 5-word intro, Sydney 45 behind a 12-word pair. A second claim made mid-investigation, that the shipped reads were blowing the allowance, was also wrong and is corrected: every final read landed 22.3-24.6s against a 24.5s allowance. What blew the allowance was the DRAFT, not the read.

**Root cause:** The word budget was an aim at every layer that writes, and the only hard guarantee ran after the reviewer had already approved the copy. `DraftWordBudget.MaxVoicedIncidents` says so in its own doc comment ("Purely an aim / upper bound — the word-accurate guarantee stays with TrimToCeiling"); the draft JSON schema allowed `maxIncidents + 6` items, described in comment as a "generous" cap; and `WordTargetEnforcer.EnsureWordTargetComplianceAsync` returns early on overshoot by design ("Overshoot is handled downstream by the audio pipeline (measure-then-trim); only a genuine UNDERshoot is expanded here"). The structured-matrix selector cannot rescue this because it may only choose phrasings and drop DISCRETIONARY items — a traffic incident is mandatory, so an over-itemised draft is unfixable downstream. The consequence is not long reads on air; it is that a mechanical trim, whose only editorial input is its drop order, decides what airs out of copy the writer chose and the reviewer passed.

**Decision:** Enforce the budget where the copy is written rather than delegating it to the trim, and treat per-environment agent provisioning as part of a deploy. Two fixes shipped to test: (1) **Agent drift.** test's Foundry `arn-draft` and `arn-review` were stale — test was running NEW code against OLD prompts, so neither the item cap nor the sweep rule nor the review defects-only rule was live. Re-provisioned from git; all 8 role agents now match. Sydney immediately stopped needing the code-side `secondary-item-cap` repair to rescue it. Env-by-env agent provisioning is a standing trap: deploying code does NOT deploy prompts, and `check-foundry-agent-drift.sh` must be run per environment after any prompt change. (2) **Draft schema slack.** `maxIncidents + 6` becomes `maxIncidents + (weather ? 1) + (fuel ? 1) + 1` — slack sized to the non-incident sections the station actually asked for rather than flat headroom for six more incidents. Required fixtures stay protected by the deterministic fixture re-splice, so a tight cap cannot silently lose a weather or fuel line.

**Rationale:** Trimming after review is the wrong place to spend a word budget. The trim has no editorial judgement beyond its drop order, so when it discards a third of the read the effective content selection passes from the writer and the reviewer to a mechanical rule — which is exactly how Port Lincoln came to drop its only closure and air "roads are clear" (2026-08-21). Sizing the schema slack to the sections the station actually asked for keeps the decision upstream, costs nothing when a market is quiet, and leaves the required-fixture re-splice as the safety net. Re-provisioning agents per environment is not optional: prompts live server-side in each Foundry project, so a code deploy alone silently pairs new code with old instructions.

**Consequences:** Cairns' assembled draft fell 93 -> 65 words and its ceiling flipped from `prosody-trim` (predicted 39.6s) to `prosody-fits` (predicted 22.3s) — it no longer writes copy that gets discarded. Its read carried a proper four-road sweep ("work zones on the Bruce, Captain Cook, Mulgrave and Kennedy highways") instead of a road-by-road list. Suite green apart from the 9 pre-existing Infrastructure failures and the environmental E2E set. Zetta delivery stayed contained throughout and was proven positively, not assumed: `Zetta__Enabled=false` verified before, during and after deploy, and both published jobs logged "Send to playout is off for this station — audio retained in storage, not sent to playout."

**Open:** Sydney still drafts about a third over target and still takes a ceiling trim, and reads are still time-warped 6-9% to land on the slot, because the four length authorities (selector, word ceiling, audio fitter, filler) remain independent. Note also that test's `Zetta__DropFileShareName` is the PRODUCTION share name, so the `Enabled=false` flag is the only thing standing between test and the live Zetta share — there is no defence in depth there, and pointing test at a test share would be cheap insurance. Separately, once a bulletin lapses its approval window and publishes the fallback, the job record's ScriptText is EMPTY and `MeasuredDurationSec` reports the fallback's duration (Cairns' 17.020204081632652 recurs byte-identically across jobs), so a reviewer cannot see what was generated from the record alone.

## 2026-08-23 — Every read we reject becomes a permanent test: the subpar-read corpus

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Quality judgements on this project have been verbal, so the same defect has come back more than once after a prompt edit or a model swap. Four shapes aired past every existing gate on 2026-08-23 while being factually correct and fitting their slots exactly, which is precisely why nothing objected: six consecutive one-road sentences (a database read-out); a forty-word compound sentence carrying three roads and joined with a SEMICOLON, which also buried a multi-vehicle accident mid-sentence; and two sentences opening on the identical frame ("A breakdown ... A breakdown ..."). ARN's instruction is unambiguous: these must never air, and every instance we find must become a test case.

**Decision:** `test/corpus/subpar-reads.json` is the standing ratchet. Each entry is a REAL observed read plus the market, source job, the defect in plain words, the prompt rule it breaks, and the deterministic gate that must catch it. `SubparReadCorpusTests` walks the corpus and fails the build if any entry stops being caught. Rules for maintaining it: append the moment a subpar read is identified; never delete an entry; never loosen a gate to make one pass. If an entry cannot be caught deterministically, that is a MISSING GATE and the honest response is to build it.

That rule immediately produced one: `SentenceShapeDetector`, gating four shape defects that no existing detector covered — a sentence past 24 words, a semicolon or colon (no spoken equivalent), a run of four or more short "road is state" sentences, and consecutive sentences sharing their opening two words. It is wired into `ScriptReviewLoop.ComputeViolationCounts` as a style violation, so it drives regeneration in production rather than only failing tests. A companion test asserts a clean, well-shaped read trips NO gate, so the corpus cannot be satisfied by a detector that flags everything.

**Rationale:** This corpus is deliberately separate from `test/corpus/regressions/`. Those are full replay fixtures carrying a traffic snapshot, so exercising one costs live LLM and TTS calls and cannot run on every build. Subpar-read entries are pure text plus an expected verdict, so they run in milliseconds on every build. The two are complementary: replay proves a whole pipeline change improved a specific bulletin, the ratchet proves a shape we already rejected can never quietly return.

One honest limitation is recorded in the corpus itself: `SecondaryItemCapDetector` is the pipeline's repair for the one-road read-out, but it needs `context.Corridors` to identify road names and so cannot run against text alone. The SHAPE is detectable context-free, so that is what a text-only corpus asserts; the repair still belongs to the context-aware detector. Anything that genuinely needs fetched data belongs in the replay corpus instead.

**Consequences:** Three entries seeded, all caught. `SentenceShapeDetector` added and wired. Suite green apart from the 9 pre-existing Infrastructure failures and the environmental E2E set. The bar is now mechanical: "we can't allow these" is enforced by the build rather than by memory.

## 2026-08-23 - Every live-agent harness runs the deployed pipeline, from one definition

**Status:** accepted (in-tree; nothing deployed)

**Context:** The fallback replay corpus is the tool we A/B generation changes with. It set
`Providers:OutputProvider` and nothing else, so it inherited the test config's defaults - the
**legacy raw-model draft path** reading **on-disk `prompts/` markdown**. Dev and test both run
`Broadcast__UseStructuredMatrix=true` with every LLM role bound to a provisioned, drift-checked
Foundry agent whose instructions live server-side. So the harness was measuring two layers that
production does not run, and reporting the result as production's behaviour. `ScenarioMatrixEvalTests`
had the correct wiring hand-rolled in a local dictionary; the replay never got it, and neither did
`FlowPoolCaptureTests`, `BrisbaneRootCauseTests` or `WeatherFuelContinuityLiveTests` - four harnesses
on the wrong path, found only because a guard was written to look.

**Rationale:** A harness on the wrong path does not fail - it passes, writes a report, and prints
percentages, so the error is invisible for exactly as long as nobody checks. Enforcing it structurally
(one definition, plus a test that reads the sources) is the only version that survives the next harness
someone adds.

**Decision:** One definition - `TestConfigurationHelper.DeployedPipeline()` - names the config that
makes a harness exercise what airs, and every harness that stands up real infrastructure builds from
it. `HarnessFidelityTests` enforces both halves: a harness calling `AddInfrastructure` under `Replay/`
or `Eval/` must reference it, and no file may hardcode a pipeline-selecting key (matrix flag, Foundry
endpoint, agent names). Assignment from a variable stays legal, because the `ARN_REPLAY_DRAFT_AGENT`
knobs are how a candidate agent gets A/B'd against the deployed default.

**Consequences:** Measured on the 10-fixture panel, same fixtures, same simulated TTS - the corpus of
dev's own worst jobs, every one of which ended `FallbackUsed` on dev:

| arm | slots filled | mean best fill | attempts |
|---|---|---|---|
| legacy raw model + on-disk prompts (what the harness measured) | 0/10 | 96% | 1.2 |
| matrix + on-disk prompts (half-fixed) | 1/10 | 59% | 2.3 |
| **matrix + live Foundry agents (deployed)** | **4/10** | **83%** | 2.4 |

The legacy arm's 96% "best fill" was prose padded around thin evidence and still filled zero slots;
the deployed pipeline airs four. Routing to the real agents also removed **every** gate rejection:
all six remaining failures are `Content-limited`, five of them honest 22.3-25.5s reads against a 30s
slot. The `RefineSentence returned no text or variants` cascade - which was dropping flagged
sentences, destroying closure leads (Gold Coast: rejected for having no closure lead after the drop
removed it), and silently no-oping `WordTargetEnforcer` expansion - was the raw-model prompt path,
not a defect in the refiner or the selector.

**Follow-on the same day - the config is snapshotted, not hand-listed.** Fixing four harnesses by
hand-listing six settings left the rest of the deployed config still diverging, and would have rotted
at the next app-setting change. `scripts/refresh-deployed-pipeline-snapshot.py` now pulls the deployed
generation config into `test/corpus/deployed-pipeline.json` (30 settings) and `DeployedPipeline()` reads
it; `--check` reports drift. The script excludes secrets, host wiring and **all** `Zetta__*` - a local
harness must never be one config slip from writing to a live station share. `ApplyLocalSettingsCredentials`
now refuses to overwrite any key the snapshot defines, so local settings supply credentials and nothing
behavioural.

That surfaced six more divergences the hand-list missed, two of them behavioural: the harness ran
`MaxReviewRefineRetries=3` against deployed's **2**, and never set `ReasoningEffort=none`, plus four
agent roles (`arn-director`, `arn-polish`, `arn-attribute`, `RefineAgentName`) were unbound and falling
back to on-disk prompts. With all 30 applied, fill DROPPED from 4/10 to 2-3/10 - the 83% was flattering,
bought with an extra refine retry and more reasoning than production gets.

**The headline metric was inverted, and that is what let this hide.** `ARM SUMMARY` led with slots
filled, so a harness accidentally wired to a padding-prone path scored HIGHER - it fabricates, fills
more, and reads as an improvement. The summary now leads with `devAgreement`: how often the replay
reaches dev's own verdict on the same data. On the full deployed config that is 7/10, against 6/10 for
the wrongly-configured arm.

`SpeechDuration:MaxSlowDownFactor` is **1.0** with no `MaxSilencePadSeconds` - deployed cannot slow-fill
at all, so any read that does not NATURALLY reach the slot goes to the filler cart. That, not a
generation defect, is why dev ended `FallbackUsed` on all ten of these and why the honest remaining
failures are all `Content-limited`.

**Open:**
- The corpus is **all negatives** - every fixture is a job dev failed - so `devAgreement` equals
  `10 - filled` by construction here. It can catch a harness that is too generous and can never catch
  one that is too harsh. The corpus needs fixtures dev successfully aired before the metric is load-bearing.
- Fixtures carry no bookends and no filler statements while every production station has both, so a
  content-limited read has nothing to top up with. Same class of gap, in the fixture capture rather than
  the wiring, and it makes `Content-limited` counts an upper bound.
- Fill wobbles +/-1 fixture run-to-run on identical config (agents are nondeterministic), so a single
  run cannot settle a 1-fixture difference.
- Any verdict recorded from this corpus before today is unsafe to trust.

## 2026-08-23 - The replay corpus gets positives, real station config, and a fast loop

**Status:** accepted (in-tree; nothing deployed)

**Rationale:** A harness that takes minutes per run and reports one number is a harness whose verdicts
go unchecked. Every defect below survived because the cost of looking was high and the number on the
front page was the wrong one.

**Context:** After the deployed-config snapshot landed, three gaps remained: the corpus was ALL
negatives (every fixture a job dev failed), station config was opt-in and defaulted off, and outcomes
wobbled +/-1 fixture run to run.

**Decision:** Close all three gaps and make the loop cheap enough that its verdicts get checked.
Fixes, in the order they were found:

1. **`GeneratorInputSnapshot` silently dropped nine generation-relevant fields** - worst `Bookends`,
   which has ~30 references in the generation path and was absent from the snapshot entirely. Added
   all nine (`Bookends`, `FillerStatements`, `SharedRules`, `RoadFeelPalette`, `EditorialSettings`,
   `CuratedCorridorRoads`, `CuratedGoodRunRoads`, `ExcludedIncidentKeys`, `WriterPrompt`), copied in
   `FromContext`, restored in `ToContext`. Additive; all 58 existing fixtures still deserialise.
   Deliberately excluded: `RetryContext`, `RevoiceOnly`, `OperatorAttended`,
   `TargetWordCountOverride` (per-attempt runtime state, not writer input).

2. **Station config was fabricated, not resolved.** Filler came from
   `Substitute.For<IFillerStatementsRepository>()` returning five synthetic statements for
   `Arg.Any<string>()` market - a set built for "what if filler existed" capacity experiments. Turning
   it on by default made all ten fixtures fill (99% mean fill) and would have read as a triumph.
   Dev's markets each carry 4-8 REAL statements (`GET /api/config/export`), so
   `scripts/capture-fallback-fixture.py` now captures per-market filler and schedule-assigned bookends
   into the fixture, and the synthetic set moved behind `ARN_REPLAY_FILLER=graded`. Provenance labels
   (`live-station-config` / `job-snapshot` / `graded-synthetic` / `repository` / `none`) are reported
   per fixture, after a first cut where the console and the written pack disagreed about the same run.

3. **The single `devAgreement` metric was wrong, and it was ours from earlier the same day.** The
   negatives were captured 2-4 Jul and the positives 10-13 Aug - six weeks and most of a pipeline
   rewrite apart. Today's code SHOULD air a July failure; scoring that as disagreement measures
   fixture age, not fidelity. Split into `airedWhenDevAired` (THE gate - dev shipped it, the replay
   must too) and `airedWhenDevFellBack` (improvement candidates, deliberately unscored, resolvable
   only by reading the script).

4. **Eight `Published` fixtures captured and the panel rebalanced 5/5.** Until the corpus had
   positives, the gate that matters - "a job dev aired that the replay will not" - did not exist.

5. **The loop was 5x too slow for the wrong reason.** A blanket 20s sleep between runs serialised
   everything: 200s asleep per panel, TEN MINUTES at `repeats=3`. It was guarding an AOAI rate limit,
   which is a concurrency problem, not a delay problem. Replaced with bounded concurrency
   (`ARN_REPLAY_CONCURRENCY`, default 4) plus launch stagger and per-fixture synthesis-history files
   so concurrent runs cannot cross-contaminate calibration. Panel: **7m30s -> 1m33s**; `repeats=3`:
   **~22min -> 4m25s**. No 429s.

**Consequences:** Fidelity gate `airedWhenDevAired=5/5` on a single run; `4/5 [4-5 over 3 runs]` across
repeats. `filled=8-9/10`, mean fill 100%, mean attempts 1.3.

The band immediately earned its keep: **cairns-4ca flapped 1/3 aired**. A single run had shown it
failing and a later single run had shown it passing - either would have been believed. Its failure mode
is real and reproducible: the draft repeats the fuel prices and the weather across sentences, review
catches it, and refine routing reports "issue(s) not resolvable to one sentence; no whole-script
rewrite", so the read dies at the grounding gate. Cross-sentence repetition has no repair path since
the whole-script refiner was removed (2026-08-21). That is a live pipeline defect on a PILOT station,
not a harness artifact.

**Open:**
- Cross-sentence repetition is unrepairable and therefore fatal - cairns-4ca fails ~2 of 3 attempts on
  it. Needs either a cross-sentence detector feeding regeneration or a bounded multi-sentence repair.
- The eight positives carry `StationConfigSource=live-station-config`: today's station config, not the
  config as it stood when the job ran, because job records did not persist it. Fixture 1 fixes that
  going forward; historical fixtures stay an approximation.
- Improvement candidates (`airedWhenDevFellBack=4/5`) are unjudged. Someone should read those four
  scripts and confirm they are genuinely airable rather than merely long enough.

## 2026-08-23 - Six script defects fixed; the fatal one was a mislabelled failure disposition

**Status:** accepted (in-tree; nothing deployed beyond dev Foundry prompt provisioning)

**Rationale:** Five observed defects were three root causes, and the highest-value fix was one enum
value. Chasing the symptoms individually would have missed all three.

**Context:** Ten replayed bulletins from the deployed pipeline showed cross-sentence repetition, a
cause restated four times, per-market price-format divergence, an inferred spatial relation, and a
malformed road name.

**Decision:**

1. **`Permanent` -> `Retryable` on `broadcast.final_grounding_failed`.** `Permanent` means "retrying
   cannot help"; cairns-4ca aired on 1 of 3 replays of byte-identical evidence and died on attempt 1
   of 4 with three unspent. The retry path ALREADY feeds the failure text forward as draft guidance,
   so the reviewer's own complaint conditions the next attempt for free - nothing needed building.
   Terminal disposition is converted back to `Permanent` at the engine's single exit (`Outcome`),
   because `Retryable` escaping the engine makes QueueFailurePolicy redeliver the whole job and stops
   BroadcastOrchestrator covering the slot - the 2026-07-26 asymmetry. A first cut converted only one
   of the method's TWO attempt loops and was caught by
   `GroundingGateExhausted_NoFallbackAvailable_CarriesPermanentDisposition`, which exists for exactly
   that.
2. **`RepeatedCauseDetector`** wired into `ComputeViolationCounts` as style, so a read restating a
   shared cause can never skip the LLM audit; relational defects route to regeneration, which is the
   only repair mechanism that both exists and is proven (whole-script rewrite removed 2026-08-21).
3. **Draft prompt groups on shared cause/event at any severity**, cause stated once, severity deciding
   lead and order only - the old rule keyed grouping on severity, so four high-severity closures never
   qualified.
4. **Relation-grounding rule**: spans, points, causation, sequence and direction may only be asserted
   when sourced, with neutral phrasings supplied. Two runs on identical evidence had produced
   "closed BETWEEN Petrie Plaza and Northbourne Avenue" and "closures AT Petrie Plaza and
   Northbourne Avenue".
5. **Fuel-scoped price patterns** (`N cents`, bare cents-per-litre, unsigned decimal), scoped to fuel
   context so `16 degrees`, `M7`, `102.7` and years are provably untouched.
6. **`RoadNamePlausibility`**, filtered only on DISCRETIONARY road lists (good-run/flow-pool, where a
   drop is free) and surfaced-never-dropped on incident roads.

**Consequences:** Fidelity gate `airedWhenDevAired=5/5`, stable `[5-5]` across repeats where it was
`4/5 [4-5]`; cairns-4ca stopped flapping entirely. Suite green at the pre-existing 9 with +36 tests.
Verified on live dev agents after provisioning (`check-foundry-agent-drift.sh`: all 8 match git).

Proven fixed in the aired text: cairns fuel `196 cents`/`235` -> "a dollar ninety-six a litre";
brisbane's duplicated Pacific Motorway; sydney's duplicated Western Motorway; adelaide's `$1.93`;
Gold Coast's four-times-restated marathon now grouped into one sentence.

**Open:**
- **Prices are not fully closed.** `SpokenPriceNormalizer` is proven correct on every observed string,
  yet portlincoln and cairns still air "unleaded 91 at $2.23" from the telegraphic
  "<suburb> fuel, unleaded 91 at $X, diesel $Y" shape on the two SHORTEST slots. Normalisation now
  runs at three points (generator, review-loop exit, after word-target expansion) and the residual is
  a mutation after all three. The general lesson holds and is the thing to fix properly: a gate that
  runs before the last mutation does not hold, and this pipeline mutates text in at least six places
  after generation.
- 11eee9bf43 (sydney, 30s) still fails content-limited at 27.6-29.4s of 30s, and flaps.
- `airedWhenDevFellBack` moved 4/5 -> 3/5: the pipeline now REJECTS reads it used to ship (the
  repeated-cause gate doing its job), trading a mediocre aired read for a filler cart. Whether that
  trade is right is a product call for ARN, not a technical one.

## 2026-08-23 - Cleared incidents earn airtime on severity, not on recency

**Status:** accepted (ARN decision; in-tree)

**Rationale:** A listener to a music station hears ONE traffic bulletin, not a sequence, so continuity
between bulletins is a fiction from the audience's side almost all of the time. "The Harbour Tunnel's
reopened" is useful to anyone choosing a route now. "Congestion on the Western Motorway has cleared"
is useful to nobody: not news to someone who heard the earlier bulletin, meaningless to someone who
did not.

**Context:** A live Sydney 22s read spent roughly 40% of the slot on seven cleared roads while the one
live story - a Harbour Tunnel closure - got a single sentence. Three code paths formatted cleared
items and disagreed about how many belong in a bulletin: `IncidentChangeFormatter` capped at 2 with the
documented rationale "the delta is context, not content", while `AppendClearedSection` and
`AppendClearedEvidence` were both unlimited. The second of those is the path production runs, and it
declared `int emitted`, incremented it, and never compared it to anything - the cap was intended and
the comparison was never written.

Separately, `IncidentChanges` is computed by `IncidentStateService` comparing the current HERE fetch
against persisted incident state - by POLLING, not by broadcasting. Nothing checked whether a bulletin
carrying that congestion ever aired, so a first-of-day bulletin, a filler-cart-covered slot or a
schedule gap could each announce that something "has cleared" the audience was never told about.

**Decision:** `IncidentChangeFormatter.IsClearedWorthVoicing` gates cleared items on severity -
high-criticality closures and crashes only, never congestion, never standing footprints - and all
three paths apply it plus the shared `DefaultClearedCap`. `IncidentTypeClassifier` gains `IsCrash`,
which was missing beside `IsClosure`/`IsCongestion` and had been re-derived per caller.

**Explicit continuity is deliberately NOT a feature.** The rejected alternative gated the claim on
broadcast history ("only say it cleared if a bulletin actually aired saying it was there"). That needed
the pipeline to persist what it BROADCAST rather than what it observed - new state, a new way to be out
of sync - to answer a question severity answers better, and it turned first-of-day, filler-covered and
gapped slots into three separate edge cases. Under a severity gate they are one case, because the test
is "is this worth telling a stranger". No "as we mentioned earlier" phrasing.

**Consequences:** Measured on the pilot fixtures. KIIS 90s Sydney before - "The Western, Westlink M7,
Southern Cross and South Western motorways have cleared. The M4 and M5 are also running clear." After -
"The Sydney Harbour Tunnel is closed southbound, with the closure extending through the tunnel. The
road closure on Mitchell Road has now cleared. Traffic is running well on the M4, Western Motorway and
M5." The live closure leads, exactly one cleared item survives and it is a closure, and the freed
airtime went to current conditions. Fidelity gate held at 2/2 across repeats; suite at the pre-existing
9 with +12 tests. `BuildEvidenceUnits_ClearedFactsAreDeduplicatedByRoadAndCondition` was retargeted
onto worthy types - it tests deduplication, and its congestion fixtures would now pass or fail for the
wrong reason.

**Open:** "with temperatures ON 13 degrees" recurs on both pilot stations and is now the most visible
surface defect in the reads.

## 2026-08-23 - One spoken-form sweep, re-runnable after every mutation

**Status:** accepted (in-tree; dev Foundry prompts provisioned)

**Rationale:** A gate that runs before the last mutation does not hold. Four identical copies of a
five-normalizer expression meant that when normalisation had to be re-applied after the review loop,
only one of the five came with it.

**Context:** "with temperatures on 13 degrees" aired on BOTH pilot stations in a single run. No gate
could see it: the read was grounded, fitted its slot and broke no style rule. Fixing it exposed the
real problem. This exact expression existed character-for-character at four call sites (draft, polish
and refine in `LlmScriptGenerator`, plus the structured-matrix generator):

```
SpokenPunctuationNormalizer(TimeOfDayNormalizer(SpokenPriceNormalizer(
    ClearRoadLabelNormalizer(ClosureVerbNormalizer(x))), daypart))
```

When the earlier price work added normalisation back after the review loop and after word-target
expansion, it added `SpokenPriceNormalizer` alone. So a post-generation mutation silently undid ARN's
marked-up "shut" -> "closed" preference (BFN-017), the clear-road labelling ("moving well" ->
"looking good", the flow feed's own wording vs what ATN actually says), the daypart correction and the
punctuation cleanup — while the price fix, being the one that got copied, survived.

**Decision:** `SpokenFormNormalizer.Normalize(script, daypart)` owns the whole sweep, applied at all
four generation sites and both post-mutation points; `ResolveDaypart` moves into the Domain because the
Application layer now needs the same answer. Every rewrite is idempotent, which is what makes
re-running it free. New `WeatherPhrasingNormalizer` fixes the temperature preposition, deliberately
narrow — only "temperature(s) on <number>" — because "on" is a good preposition everywhere else in a
traffic read. The prompt states the preference too, so good phrasing is the default and the normalizer
is the guarantee: the same two-layer split `ClosureVerbNormalizer` already documents after a soft
instruction proved unreliable under sampling variance.

**Consequences:** Across the pilot runs: zero "temperatures on", zero raw `$` prices, zero "moving
well", zero "shut". Fidelity gate 2/2 stable. Suite at the pre-existing 9 with +22 tests.

Three test fixtures were made normalisation-STABLE rather than their assertions relaxed: they pinned
pre-normalisation wording ("this morning", "moving well") incidental to what they test (ceiling
application, the refine ratchet, expansion shipping), so the sweep reaching a second point made them
fail for an unrelated reason. `ScriptReviewLoop` gains `TimeProvider` for daypart resolution.

**Open:** the sydney 30s fixture still fails content-limited at ~27s of 30s with
`MaxSlowDownFactor=1.0` — a complete, airable read dropped to filler over an 11% shortfall. That is a
config question for ARN, not an engineering one.

**Rationale:** Prompts are provisioned server-side PER ENVIRONMENT, so a code deploy alone would have
shipped the code paths without the writer guidance they depend on. Test's `arn-draft` was drifted
before provisioning; dev's was not, because it had been provisioned during local iteration.

**Context:** ARN reviewed the live pilot reads and raised two notes; both are fixed below.

returns "All 8 role agents match git" on each.

`Zetta__Enabled = false` on dev and test, and no delivery-related log entry on any triggered job.
`Zetta__DropFileShareName` remains the PRODUCTION share name on both, so the enabled flag is the only
thing separating test from the live share - unchanged today, still worth pointing a test share at.

**Two notes from ARN's review of the live pilot reads:**

1. **The Light Horse incident was missing from the evidence panel.** Not missing data: HERE returned the
   corridor as `Light Horse Intr`, the writer correctly read "the Light Horse Interchange", and the

2. **Fuel prices always name their location, and the framing now varies.** ARN: "it always says
   'manora fuel, unleaded x and diesel y'". `FormatFuel` keeps each supplied suburb attached to its own
   price line and never infers a missing one; the draft prompt gains four rotatable frames
   (cheapest-first, price-first, compact for short slots, two-sentence for long) with explicit
   never-drop-the-location and don't-reuse-one-frame rules. `FuelLines` stays deterministic - a repair
   path with randomness would break replay fixtures.

**Consequences:** Live pilot bulletins on test, both filling exactly (22s/22s, WAITING_APPROVAL):
Sydney voices the Light Horse queue with evidence attached; Cairns reads "Cheapest unleaded is a dollar
ninety-eight at Manoora, while diesel is two dollars forty in Manoora" - a new frame, both locations
named. Suite at the pre-existing 9 with +30 tests.

**Open:** the new fuel framing REPEATS a shared suburb ("at Manoora, while ... in Manoora"). The old
rigid hint prevented that and was replaced to break the frame monotony; the replacement's softer
same-suburb guidance did not hold under sampling. Per this repo's established pattern that is a
deterministic-gate job, not a prompt job.

## 2026-08-24 - A shared fuel suburb is said once, mechanically; test readied for Zetta

**Status:** accepted (deployed dev + test; Zetta still DISABLED on both)

**Rationale:** The prompt owns variety, a deterministic gate owns the rule. Trying to make one prompt
hint do both produced first a rigid frame, then a repeated suburb.

**Context:** ARN, on a live Star 102.7 read: "Cheapest unleaded is a dollar ninety-eight at Manoora,
while diesel is two dollars forty in Manoora." The original hint ('say "there too", never the suburb
name twice') prevented exactly this but locked the writer into one frame every bulletin - ARN's other
complaint. Replacing it with rotatable frames plus softer guidance fixed the monotony and lost the
no-repeat rule, because soft instructions do not hold under sampling. `ClosureVerbNormalizer` documents
the same lesson.

**Decision:** `RepeatedFuelSuburbDetector` (Detect/Repair, scoped to fuel lines via
`ContentSourceSignals.IsFuelLine`) keeps the FIRST location phrase and drops later repeats, wired into
`ScriptReviewLoop`'s safe-mechanical-repair block beside repeated-preposition. Differing suburbs pass
through byte-identical - the pinned negative case, because "at Kilburn ... in Windsor Gardens" is
correct and must never be collapsed. Corpus entry added so the Manoora read stays rejected.

**Consequences:** Live test read after deploy: "Unleaded is a dollar ninety-eight at Manoora, diesel is
two dollars forty **there**." Suburb once, location never dropped. Suite at the pre-existing 9, +36
tests. Sydney's Light Horse item now voices with its suburb and carries evidence.

## 2026-08-24 - Test armed for Zetta delivery; the station toggle is the operator's control

**Status:** accepted (ARN decision; `Zetta__Enabled = true` LIVE on test, dev remains false)

**Rationale:** Operators need the station toggle in the console to be the real control, not a setting
that silently does nothing because an environment gate is shut behind it.

**Context:** `main.test.bicepparam` already carried `param zettaEnabled = true` and `deployment/README.md`
already documented test as armed - the IaC and docs were AHEAD of the deployed app setting, which was
still `false`. So this change removed a drift rather than creating one.

**Decision:** set `Zetta__Enabled = true` on IBP-AUE-TST-FNA-APP01. Delivery now requires BOTH gates,
exactly as the README describes: the environment flag (now open on test) and the station's own
`MarketSchedule.PlayoutEnabled`. Both pilot stations were verified `PlayoutEnabled = false` at the
moment of arming, so nothing delivers until an operator turns a station on - no unattended overnight
delivery. Verified after arming: `/api/markets/{id}/playout-tray` reports `enabled: true` for both
markets with the correct target filenames, per-station flags still false, drop share still empty.

**A correction to an earlier claim in this session:** test does NOT write to an isolated account.
Production and test BOTH write `informationbulletins` on `ibpauetststaftp01` - same account, same
share, same `{MarketId}_TRAFF` pattern, same market codes. An earlier note in this session said test
was isolated and could not overwrite a production file; that was wrong. Arming the same station in both
environments overwrites one filename from two writers, and per the README it is a race neither side can
audit, because Zetta returns no on-air receipt and the file's disappearance identifies a station's
latest publish rather than a specific job. The one-station-one-environment discipline is therefore a
hard operational requirement, not a preference.

**Consequences:** dev stays `false` and has never delivered. The 2026-08-11 stale-restart class stays
covered - `DeliverAsync` refuses an expired slot before it downloads audio, independently of the
poller/watchdog guards. Any market other than the two pilot stations still has no code in the market
map and fails loudly rather than delivering.

**Open:** test crons remain the UAT grid (Cairns 01:01/02:10, Sydney 01:33/02:10 local), so a station
left armed overnight would deliver at those times rather than at a sensible morning slot.

## 2026-08-24 - Test scheduling made byte-identical to production

**Status:** accepted (test schedules updated; production untouched)

**Rationale:** For operators to switch a station between environments, the two schedules have to be the
same in every respect that affects a bulletin. Otherwise "the same station on test" is a different
product and the trial proves nothing about production.

**Context:** test carried leftover UAT cron grids (Cairns 01:01/02:10, Sydney 01:33/02:10 local) while
production runs a real broadcast clock.

**Reading production took three attempts, and the first two SHOULD have failed:**
- `/api/schedules` on the prod Function App returns 401 to an ARM bearer token - the API wants the
  Entra app-role claim the SWA forwards, which ARM Owner does not confer.
- Prod storage refuses key-based auth outright (`KeyBasedAuthenticationNotPermitted`), and a
  data-plane read is additionally blocked by the account's network rules (private endpoints). Correct
  posture; nothing was changed to work around it. A `Storage Table Data Reader` assignment created
  during that attempt was removed - and was redundant anyway, since three data-plane Contributor roles
  at that scope already existed.
- The route that worked is read-only and uses the operator's own authenticated browser session over the
  local CDP endpoint: open the prod console, same-origin `fetch('/api/schedules')`.

**Decision:** aligned the only two divergent fields. Everything else already matched - timezone, target
duration, voice profile, time-of-day voice rotation, content flags, fill order, bookend, pronunciation
dictionary, coverage polygon, notify/escalation minutes.

| station | field | test was | now (= prod) |
|---|---|---|---|
| cairns-4ca | `CronExpression` | `1 1 * * *` + `10 2 * * *` | `55 5,6,7,8,9,14,15,16,17,18 * * 1,2,3,4,5` |
| sydney | `CronExpression` | `33 1 * * *` + `10 2 * * *` | same as above |
