| sydney | `DeliveryStyleId` | `""` | `ds-f0b248af1ec14f87a26fb7c1eec3c353` |

The delivery style was verified to exist on test under the SAME id before being set - test holds two
styles both named "ARN Bright Contemporary", so matching on name rather than id would have picked the
wrong one.

**Consequences:** a field-by-field re-diff reports **0 differing fields** on both stations. Test now
fires :55 past 5-9am and 2-6pm weekdays in each station's own timezone, exactly as production does, so
an operator turns a station off in prod and the same one on in test and gets the same slots.
`PlayoutEnabled` deliberately remains `false` on both test stations - the environment is armed, the
station toggle is the operator's deliberate act.

**Production was read and never written.** No prod setting, schedule, or role assignment was left
altered.

## 2026-08-24 - KIIS 90s "no traffic this morning": the 5:55 slot fails about half the time

**Status:** accepted (analysis; no prod change made)

**Rationale:** The reported symptom was new to ARN, not new to the system. Answering "why today" mattered
more than answering "what broke", because nothing broke.

**Context:** An operator reported no traffic on KIIS 90s and "the two credits went to air at 6.18am".

**What actually aired (Sydney, Mon 24 Aug AEST):**

| slot | outcome |
|---|---|
| 5:55 | draft 42 words = **18.6s of natural speech for a 22s slot** -> content-limited -> *"Generic filler cart applied (no same-day bulletin available)"* -> standby cart aired. the operator's "two credits". |
| 6:55 | final grounding gate rejected the read twice - *"the Western Motorway congestion is marked new, so 'still' incorrectly re-introduces it as ongoing"* -> repeat of the 6:11 bulletin |
| 6:41, 6:44 | two further attempts, both content-limited -> repeats |
| 6:47, 7:55, 8:55 | approved by an operator - real bulletins aired |

Cairns hit the same pair at 8:40 Brisbane (gate failure -> repeat, then content-limited -> repeat).

**Decision:** record the analysis and hold prod unchanged pending ARN's call. Findings:

1. **`MaxSlowDownFactor` has ALWAYS been 1.0 in production.** It has sat in
   `src/ArnBulletinGenerator.Functions/appsettings.json` since commit `5e67631e` (post-SG2 delta) and
   **no environment overrides it anywhere in the IaC** - not dev, test or prod. Production has never
   been able to slow-fill. This is not a regression and not a recent change.

2. **This morning was not the first time.** The 5am slot across the six weekdays it has run:

   | date | first-slot outcome |
   |---|---|
   | Mon 17 Aug | published, 22s |
   | **Tue 18 Aug** | **fell back - generic filler cart, measured 20.015260770975058s** |
   | Wed 19 Aug | published, 22s |
   | Thu 20 Aug | published, 22s |
   | **Fri 21 Aug** | **MISSED** |
   | **Mon 24 Aug** | **fell back - generic filler cart, measured 20.015260770975058s** |

   The measured duration is byte-identical on both fallback days, which is the padded generic cart's
   fixed length rather than a coincidence - the same cart aired both times. So the first slot has
   failed 2 of 6 mornings and been missed on a third: roughly a 50% success rate, unreported until now.

3. **Why the FIRST slot specifically.** It combines the two worst conditions: 5:55am has the thinnest
   traffic data of the day, so the draft comes up short; and being first, there is no same-day bulletin
   to repeat, so the only remaining cover is the generic cart. Later slots degrade to a repeat, which
   sounds like a stale bulletin rather than no bulletin - far less noticeable. That asymmetry is why
   this surfaced as "no traffic aired" rather than "the traffic was old".

**Consequences:** both failure modes are fixed or improved in the code now on dev and test and NOT on
prod - the continuity/relation grounding rules address the 6:55 rejection class, and the
retry-instead-of-die disposition change gives a short read more attempts. Neither is deployed to
production.

**Open:** `MaxSlowDownFactor = 1.0` is the single highest-value change for the first slot of the day -
a 1.05 pad would have covered 18.6s into the 22s slot outright and is a config change, not code. That
is ARN's call.

## 2026-08-24 - Test outperformed production on the first prod-matching morning

**Status:** accepted (measurement; no change made)

**Rationale:** Test ran its first morning on the prod-matching crons the same morning production
dropped a slot to the standby cart. Comparing the two on the same slots, same markets and the same
HERE data is the cleanest read available on whether the dev/test code is worth deploying.

**Context:** test was made schedule-identical to prod the night before, so both environments ran the
same :55 slots for the first time on the same morning - the one morning production dropped a slot to
the standby cart and ARN noticed.

**Decision:** treat the measured gap below as the evidence for a production deploy, and record that
test's own fallbacks were operator-workflow gaps rather than pipeline defects.

**Measurement** (Mon 24 Aug, all morning jobs, both markets):

| | production | test |
|---|---|---|
| jobs | 16 | 8 |
| reached a full 22.0s read | 11 (69%) | **8 (100%)** |
| content-limited at any point | 11 (69%) | 1 (13%) |
| grounding-gate rejections | 3 | 1 |
| extra operator regeneration jobs | 5 | 0 |

The same-slot contrast is the sharpest form of it:

- **prod** Sydney 5:55 - 42 words -> **18.3s** of natural speech -> could not fill 22s -> generic cart.
- **test** Sydney 8:40 - 56 words -> **23.9s** natural -> trimmed to 22.0s -> filled comfortably.

Same market, same time of day, same provider. Production undershoots and falls back; test overshoots
and trims. That is the word-target/expansion work behaving as designed.

**Test's four Sydney cart fallbacks were NOT pipeline failures.** Every one produced an airable 22.0s
bulletin first. Three read `Job rejected: RevisionRequested. Notes: Source selection changed in review`
- an operator curated the sources (in one case 2 of 25 corridors), the regeneration came back clean at
22.0s, and nobody returned to approve before the deadline. The fourth was simply unapproved. Nobody is
rostered on Sydney in test; An operator worked Cairns in test and took attempt-1 approvals with full
22s reads on every slot.

**Test's one genuine content failure:** Cairns 08:40 - 10.1s of natural speech plus a grounding-gate
rejection on the same "still ongoing" continuity class - degraded to a repeat of an earlier same-day
bulletin, which is the correct behaviour.

**Consequences:** Zetta containment held throughout - every test job logged `Send to playout is off for
this station - audio retained in storage, not sent to playout`, and the drop share is still 0 files.

## 2026-08-24 - Direction and lane impact are parsed from the NSW feed; a bare "blocking" claim is now gated

**Status:** accepted (dev + test; production unchanged)

**Context:** ARN reviewed a live dev bulletin that read **"A crash is blocking the M5 at Mascot."** The
authority's own record (Live Traffic NSW 285537) said **"1 of 2 westbound lanes closed (lane 2)"**. The
road was not blocked and the direction was dropped. ARN's request: add direction impact, and avoid
"blocking" unless the read can say "a lane" or similar.

**Rationale:** the authority already publishes both the direction and the lane split; we simply never
read them, and nothing stopped the writer from asserting a blockage the data did not support. Parsing
what exists is cheaper and safer than teaching the model to hedge.

**Decision:** parse the impact the authority already publishes, and gate the blockage verb the writer
was never stopped from using. Two independent defects, two independent fixes.

**Root causes, both confirmed against the stored job and the live feed:**

1. **The official-feed path never parsed direction or lanes.** `OfficialTrafficEvent` has carried
   `Direction`, `LanesClosed`, `LanesTotal` and `ExtentDescription` all along, and the contract comment
   said they were "optional refinements straight from HERE" - so `ParseNsw` read only
   `roads[0].mainStreet/crossStreet/suburb` and left all four null on every NSW record. The stored M5
   incident proves it: `Direction: null, LaneDetail: null, LanesClosed: null, LanesTotal: null`.
   Direction was already voiced correctly for HERE-sourced items (test Cairns reads say "Westbound
   Mulgrave Road", "Northbound on the Kennedy Highway"); the M5 crash was official-feed-only
   (`Sources: ["livetraffic-nsw"]`), which is exactly why it had none.

2. **`FalseClosureDetector` did not recognise bare "blocking".** Its `ClosureClaimRegex()` was
   `\b(?:closed|shut)\b|\bblocked off\b`, so "blocking" matched nothing and shipped ungated.

**Everything downstream already existed and was NOT rebuilt.** `TrafficNarrativeSummarizer.EvidenceUnits`
already emitted a `direction` unit and already spelled lane counts as "one lane closed" / "two of three
lanes closed"; `TrafficEvidenceBuilder` already tracked coverage of all three fields. The parse was the
only missing link - this change fills it in.

**A near-miss worth recording.** The first implementation keyed the `periods[].direction` fallback off
the PRESENCE of the `impactedLanes` key. Measured live: **310 of 322 records carry that key as an EMPTY
array**, so the fallback would never have run and direction would have landed on ~1% of records instead
of 14%. Nine fixture tests passed while the real feed would have been gutted, because every fixture
omitted the key entirely rather than supplying it empty. Fixed, and pinned by
`NswDirection_FallsBackToPeriod_WhenImpactedLanesIsAnEmptyArray`. The lesson generalises: a fixture that
omits a field does not test a feed that sends it empty.

**Measured on the live feed through the real `LiveTrafficNswFeed` (305 records in a statewide area):**

| field | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| voiceable `Direction` | 0 | **43 (14%)** - Westbound 15, Northbound 12, Eastbound 10, Southbound 6 |
| `LanesClosed` / `LanesTotal` | 0 | 2 |
| `ExtentDescription` | 0 | 12 |
| non-voiceable direction leaked | - | **0** |

Note 93% is the rate at which the field is PRESENT; once `"Both directions"` (587 entries) and
`"All directions"` (140) are filtered - neither is a voiceable direction, and either would air as
"Both directions on the M5..." - the usable rate is 14%. Real example now available to a read:
`Western Distributor [Westbound] 2/4 "Lanes closed"`.

**This change never creates a closure claim.** `RoadClosed` is untouched, and
`periods[].closureType == "ROAD_CLOSURE"` is deliberately ignored because it is a category, not a live
state - one live record carries it alongside `roadextent: "Affected"`. Pinned by a regression test. The
closure side of this work is strictly impact-reducing, which is the only safe direction given the
documented history of false closures reaching air.

**Consequences:** NSW `Capabilities` now classify Direction/LanesClosed/LanesTotal as structured rather
than prose. The draft prompt leads an item with a supplied specific direction and forbids
blocked/blocking/closed/shut without closure evidence, with the corrected read as the worked example
("Westbound on the M5 at Mascot, a crash has one of two lanes closed"). The `arn-polish.md` CRASH
severity palette was briefly stripped during this work and restored: its "with the right lane blocked"
rung is lane-level and exempt by design, "has closed the road" is correct when the data marks a closure,
and "an earlier crash, now cleared" is load-bearing for the 2026-08-23 cleared-severity gate. The
palette is vocabulary; the inviolable rule is the gate; they are two layers on purpose.

**Open - unrelated finding from the same investigation, now CONFIRMED live and escalated to RISK-36
(2026-08-24):** the QLD feed's API key is the hardcoded, published QLDTraffic **public demo key**
(`OfficialFeedsOptions.QldApiKey`), documented by TMR as globally limited to 100 req/min shared with
every other consumer of that key worldwide. Three things were verified after the original note:

1. **Every environment runs it, including prod.** `az functionapp config appsettings list` returns
   **zero `OfficialFeeds__*` settings** on dev, test and prod, and `deployment/` contains **zero**
   `OfficialFeeds` references - so no per-environment override capability exists at all.
2. **It is already degrading air content.** All four test Cairns bulletins on 2026-08-24
   (06:40-09:40 AEST; jobs `5aa54c9d`, `35816e25`, `98855d51`, `1a0bd43a`) aired HERE-only -
   `Sources: ['here']` on 14/14 selected incidents and 15/15 corridors - with
   `[Corroboration] Feed qldtraffic failed: ... 429` in App Insights. A live QLDTraffic pull the same
   morning held **29 events within 60 km of Cairns**, covering **9 of the 10 roads those bulletins
   named** (Bruce Hwy, Mulgrave Rd, Captain Cook Hwy, Kennedy Hwy, Reservoir Rd, Pease St, Anderson
   St, Foster Rd, Riverstone Rd). Controls: test Sydney jobs in the same window corroborated normally
   against the keyless NSW feed (one ran official-only), and dev Cairns corroborated 7/12 - so the
   fusion path is healthy and the fault is isolated to this key. The throttle is nondeterministic
   contention, not exhaustion: 10 sequential direct calls from a workstation returned 200 while test
   was being refused.
3. **It silently re-opens the false-closure class.** `TrafficEvidenceFusion.DemoteIfUncorroboratedStaleClosure`
   gates on `authorityCoversRoad`, which is **always false when the feed returns nothing**, so stale
   HERE closures on Cairns roads air undemoted - the RISK-30/RISK-35 defect class, at the QLD pilot
   station, with no operator-visible signal because the failure never reaches the job record.

Needs dedicated per-environment keys registered with `qldtraffic@tmr.qld.gov.au` (an ARN action -
pilot volume is trivial against a 100 req/min dedicated key, since corridor fetches are 60s-cached),
`OfficialFeeds__QldApiKey` promoted to a bicep param + Key Vault secret, and an operator-visible job
log line on feed degradation. The SA feed separately returns 403 in dev and test.

## 2026-08-24 - A repeated state phrase is now gated at two occurrences, not three words

**Status:** accepted (dev + test; production unchanged)

**Context:** ARN flagged live test job `14dffcb2` for reading the same state phrase twice: *"Victoria
Road is **a slower run**, with delays adding about four minutes. Southern Cross Drive has **a slower
run**, adding about three minutes."* The job's logs show `Script approved by review (attempt 1)` and
`Refine routing: no actionable issues; no refine call` - the LLM reviewer passed it and no deterministic
gate fired. Asked whether this was a faulty path: it was not. Nothing was bypassed and nothing errored.

**Rationale:** the draft prompt's `Vary the Palette` rule already forbids reusing a phrase **twice**,
while the code permitted two. Prompt rules alone are unreliable under sampling - the same market in the
same minute produced a correctly-varied read on dev ("backed up" / "a slower run" / "slight queues") and
the repetitive one on test. That asymmetry is the standing argument for a deterministic floor beneath a
prompt rule, and it is the same lesson the sibling detectors' doc comments already record.

**Decision:** extend `SentenceShapeDetector` rather than add a fifth overlapping gate, and place the
floor at two occurrences of a multi-word phrase.

**Why all three existing gates missed it - each by a documented margin:**

| gate | threshold | why it missed |
|---|---|---|
| `RepeatedStatePhraseDetector` | one word, 3+ times | `"slower"` = 2, `"run"` = 2, `"adding"` = 2; `"delays"`/`"delay"` count as different words |
| `SentenceCloneDetector` | 4+ contiguous shared frame | `"a slower run"` is **3** words - missed by exactly one |
| `SentenceShapeDetector` (opening check) | echo at sentence START | openings differ: `"Victoria Road is"` vs `"Southern Cross Drive has"` |

Lowering either existing threshold was rejected: 4 -> 3 on the clone frame, or 3 -> 2 on the single
word, fires on legitimate reads, and an over-tight gate that drops an airable bulletin to the filler
cart is a worse outcome than a mildly repetitive read. The gate is a style violation driving a
refine, never a hard failure.

**Consequences:** the detector scans 3-5 word contiguous n-grams across sentences, requiring two
distinct sentences, at least one content word, no capitalised token (road and suburb names recur
legitimately), and excluding the standard `adding ... minutes` delay construction. It reuses
`RepeatedStatePhraseDetector`'s curated ignore vocabulary rather than duplicating it - two copies of
that list drifting apart is a failure mode this repo has already paid for. Station-authored bookend and
filler copy is peeled with the existing `StationLineSplitter` via a new `stationLines` argument, not
hardcoded. Wired at all three points its siblings use: `ComputeViolationCounts`, the inline recheck (so
the named phrase reaches the patcher rather than an anonymous +1 to the style count - it was previously
counted but never surfaced, meaning the refiner was repairing blind), and the final deterministic
recheck. The most important test in the set is a NEGATIVE: the correctly-varied dev read from the same
data must not flag, or the gate is too tight to ship.

## 2026-08-24 — Monitored drive-time runs are evidence the operator console can see

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Test job cb5eadd4 (KIIS 90s, Sydney, 2026-08-23) aired "The M4 from Parramatta to the city is a slower run, taking 33 minutes" and the operator console flagged the line "No source found. Verify manually." The claim was correct: "the M4 from Parramatta to the city" is a configured MonitoredRoutes entry and HERE measured it live (independently re-checked: 31 min live / 26 typical / 23 free-flow over 25.4 km eighteen minutes later). Four independent gaps hid it. (1) Job.MonitoredRoutes is persisted but was mapped into NO API DTO, so the Sources rail had no drive-time record to show. (2) ScriptProvenanceMapper.Map only saw corridors, and a monitored route is a ROUTE, never a corridor, so the sentence could not carry lineage. (3) MapRoadPhraseSpans draws only on corridors, flow roads and good runs. (4) Every sentence on that job had empty EvidenceIds: LlmScriptGenerator.GenerateScriptAsync returned `new DraftedScript(normalized, [])` whenever any spoken-form rewrite fired, discarding the citations the structured Draft had just committed, which is why the job logged "0/5 sentence citations (source=none)" while sibling jobs the same hour logged "4/6 (source=loop)".

**Decision:** Monitored drive-time routes are first-class operator-facing evidence. TrafficDataDto carries a new MonitoredRouteDto list (name, live, typical, delay, distance); JobScriptSentence/ScriptSentenceDto carry RouteKeys, populated by ScriptProvenanceMapper.Map from a new monitoredRoutes argument using the same word-aware whole-phrase rule corridors use; the web maps routeKeys to a routeMatched verdict ("Monitored drive-time run - the live and typical figures are in the Sources panel.") and ReviewSources leads with a Drive times card. Separately, GenerateScriptAsync now normalises each drafted sentence alongside the assembled read instead of dropping the sentence list.

**Rationale:** Route lineage is server-owned through RouteKeys rather than a client-side name match, because route names are multi-word phrases and this repo already pays for duplicated matching rules drifting apart; a job with no RouteKeys stays honestly amber. Monitored routes are deliberately NOT added to MapRoadPhraseSpans: that contract is the pronunciation respell target, and "the M4 from Parramatta to the city" is the wrong unit to teach a dictionary. The DTO reports every measured route including ones the writer never saw, because the suppression rules (closure reconciliation, hot-board gate, the 5-minute headline threshold) live in TrafficNarrativeSummarizer and a second copy would drift; the operator's question is what was measured, which is always answerable.

**Consequences:** A grounded drive-time claim now renders sourced with its live/typical figures on screen instead of amber. The citation fix restores EvidenceIds across the whole pipeline, not just route sentences - it was silently emptying them for any draft that needed a spoken-form rewrite. New tests: ScriptProvenanceMapperTests (Map_AttributesSentenceToTheMonitoredRouteItNames and three siblings), JobMappingExtensionsTests (ToDetailDto_MonitoredRoutes_*, ToDetailDto_SentenceRouteLineage_*), LlmScriptGeneratorTests (GenerateScriptAsync_SpokenFormRewriteChangesScript_KeepsDraftedSentenceCitations, verified to fail against the old expression), and web provenance/sentence-status suites. Legacy jobs deserialise with null RouteKeys and map to an empty list.

## 2026-08-24 - Pronunciation rules are pushed longest-match-first; a general rule was eating the specific fix

**Status:** accepted (code fix on dev + test; the live Sydney rule data still needs one operator edit)

**Context:** ARN reported "Warringah" mispronounced on test job `a907ac7b` despite a dictionary entry
for it. The whole chain was verified correct: schedule `sydney` -> `PronunciationDictionaryId
pd-c707ec2c...` -> local "Sydney Roads" v3 -> ElevenLabs `WGzqLVE34C7BWcqpmOG4` version
`QI0wIx7chBhPV5RBiH29`, which is exactly the version stamped on the job. The dictionary was attached and
applied. The app's own pre-review even caught the result (`MatchRatio 0.944`, suspect word "Warringah").

**Rationale:** the dictionary held TWO overlapping rules for the same road, and the operator's later,
more specific fix was inert:

| position | rule | replacement |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | `Warringah` | `Were-rin-gah` |
| **19** | `Warringah Freeway` | `woringguh` |

The version history shows the operator trying twice - v2 *"Added 'Warringah Freeway' from bulletin
review"*, v3 *"Changed 'Warringah Freeway' from bulletin review"* - and getting no feedback either time.

**Decision:** order the wire payload longest `string_to_replace` first in
`ElevenLabsClient.BuildRulePayloads`, so a specific multi-word rule can never be shadowed by a general
one.

**Measured against the live ElevenLabs API before writing any code** (two-rule probe dictionary,
identical text "The Warringah Freeway is busy this morning.", `eleven_v3`):

| rule order sent | heard |
|---|---|
| general first (`Warringah`->banana, then `Warringah Freeway`->kiwi) | "The **Banana** Freeway" |
| specific first (same rules reversed) | "The **kiwi**" |
| re-push of the SAME rules in reversed order via `add-rules` | "The **kiwi**" - the stored lexicon reorders |

So ElevenLabs applies alias rules in the order supplied, first match wins. The third row is what makes
the one-line fix sufficient: every push sends the COMPLETE desired set
(`PronunciationDictionaryService` line ~316), and a re-push in a new order provably reorders the stored
lexicon, so one sort at the wire boundary corrects every dictionary on its next version.

**A hypothesis that was wrong, recorded so it is not re-tried:** `eleven_v3` was suspected of ignoring
pronunciation dictionaries. It does not - a probe alias came through on `eleven_v3`,
`eleven_turbo_v2` and `eleven_multilingual_v2` alike. Model support is not the issue.

**Consequences:** a sequencing trap. The fix is inert on existing dictionaries until something
triggers a version push (`RulesDifferFrom` gates it), so nothing changes on air by deploying alone.
But the next time ANY Sydney rule is edited, the re-push will reorder and the position-19 rule WILL
start firing - and that rule replaces the two-word phrase `"Warringah Freeway"` with the single token
`"woringguh"`, **deleting the word "Freeway"**. Verified: the probe read "The kiwi is busy", not "The
kiwi Freeway is busy". So the rule data must be corrected in the same operator action, either by
deleting the now-redundant specific rule or by making its replacement carry the road type
(`"woringguh Freeway"`). Deploying the code without touching the data is safe; editing the data without
this reasoning in hand is not.

**Open:**
- **No shadow detection exists.** `PronunciationRuleSetEditor.SameWord` compares whole words only, so
  adding `"Warringah Freeway"` beside `"Warringah"` looked like an unrelated new rule. An operator
  should be warned when a rule they add is shadowed by, or shadows, an existing one - that is the
  systemic fix, and its absence is why two edits silently did nothing.
- **Which alias is correct is an ARN decision and cannot be measured.** Six candidates were synthesised
  in the real station voice (`EF2rFRNHqbfaMctIvS2k`); five of six transcribe back as "Warringah" through
  ElevenLabs Scribe, so speech-to-text cannot rank them. Worth noting because the app's own pre-review
  gate relies on that same round-trip signal.
- **Duplicate dictionary names.** Five ElevenLabs dictionaries are named "Sydney Roads" (19/19/7/20/21
  rules) and two local records share the name. Editing the wrong one is silent and would look exactly
  like this bug. Same hygiene class as the two identically-named "ARN Bright Contemporary" delivery
  styles found on 2026-08-24.

## 2026-08-24 - The Warringah defect was test-only: its pronunciation dictionary had drifted from prod

**Status:** accepted (test rule corrected; prod untouched; one alias choice still open with ARN)

**Context:** chasing the mispronunciation on test job `a907ac7b` (see the ordering decision above) led to a
larger finding. Prod's "Sydney Roads" was read read-only through an operator browser session:

| | prod | test (before) |
|---|---|---|
| version | **24**, last edited 2026-08-23T22:45Z (08:45 AEST that morning) | **3**, a 2026-08-20 config import |
| rules | 20 | 19 |
| `Warringah` | `waringa` - ONE rule, no conflict | `Were-rin-gah` **plus** a shadowed `Warringah Freeway` -> `woringguh` |

**Rationale:** prod was never broken. Operators actively curate prod's dictionary from bulletin reviews -
24 versions, one landed the same morning - while test's copy is a frozen import. The reported defect was
an artefact of that drift, compounded by an operator's attempted fix landing in a shadowed position.

**Decision:** correct test's rule now (`Warringah` -> `warringa`, chosen by ARN's ear from six synthesised
candidates; the shadowed word-dropping rule deleted), and treat dictionary drift as the real issue to fix.

**Remaining divergence from prod, all in test's disfavour:**

| rule | prod | test |
|---|---|---|
| `Warringah` | `waringa` | `warringa` (one letter apart) |
| `Pyrmont` | `peermont` | `Pir-mont` |
| `Military` | `mili-tree` | absent |
| `Wah-rin-gah` | `Were-in-gah` | absent - and DEAD in prod too (see below) |

**Consequences:** test is a mirror only for what has been deliberately synced. Schedules were made
byte-identical on 2026-08-24, but pronunciation dictionaries were not, so an operator trialling test will
keep reporting pronunciation faults that production does not have - exactly what happened here. Test also
carries 15 dictionaries against prod's 2, five of them named "Sydney Roads" upstream in ElevenLabs
(19/19/7/20/21 rules); editing the wrong one is silent and looks identical to this bug.

**Two things worth knowing, both measured today:**

1. **`eleven_v3` is non-deterministic.** Two renders of a byte-identical prompt differed in 97.7% of
   bytes at the same duration. So an alias cannot be A/B'd by comparing audio, and a single good-sounding
   sample is a sample, not a guarantee - pronunciation quality carries run-to-run variance. This also
   limits what the pre-review match-ratio gate can promise.
2. **Prod holds a dead chained rule.** `Wah-rin-gah` -> `Were-in-gah` exists to patch the OUTPUT of an
   earlier `Warringah` alias. Now that prod emits `waringa`, the string `Wah-rin-gah` never appears, so
   the rule is unreachable. Harmless, but it is evidence operators resort to chaining aliases when a rule
   appears not to work - which is precisely the symptom the shadowing bug produced.

**Open:** whether test should adopt prod's `waringa` for parity, or prod should adopt the ear-validated
`warringa` - the latter changes production and is ARN's call. Also open: syncing prod's dictionaries into
test the way schedules were synced, and a shadow warning when an operator adds an overlapping rule.

## 2026-08-24 - The road-type expansion map is load-bearing, not polish: measured against the live voice

**Status:** accepted (measurement; no code change)

**Context:** ARN asked whether the Waze Australia abbreviations page (and the TTS thread it links) could
help with pronunciation aliases. Neither helps with aliases, but chasing it produced a measurement worth
keeping.

**Rationale:** `RoadNameFormatter.SpokenExpansions` was built reactively - one token added per observed
bulletin failure, documented as "measured list, surgical by design". Nobody had ever tested which entries
the voice actually needs. Waze's 2012 thread solved that by building a test rig and probing the TTS
systematically instead of waiting for failures; that method transfers even though their results (Nuance
"Samantha", North America, 2012-14) do not.

**Decision:** treat the map as critical infrastructure. Probed all 29 entries through the live station
voice (`EF2rFRNHqbfaMctIvS2k`, `eleven_v3`) in a carrier phrase, transcribed each result.

**Only four of 29 survive unaided** - `Rd`, `Hwy`, `Blvd`, `Pkwy`. Everything else is mangled or spelled
out letter by letter:

| abbreviation | intended | what the voice actually said |
|---|---|---|
| `Fwy` | Freeway | **"Four Way"** |
| `Mwy` | Motorway | **"More Way"** |
| `Mtwy` | Motorway | **"MTW Y"** |
| `Brg` / `Bdge` | Bridge | **"Burg"** / **"Badge"** |
| `Cir` | Circuit | **"Sir"** |
| `Pwy` | Parkway | **"Piwi"** |
| `Byp` | Bypass | **"Bype"** |
| `Ter` | Terrace | **"Tur"** |
| `Intr` | Interchange | **"Intra"** |
| `Cwy` | Causeway | **"CWI"** |
| `Pde`/`Tce`/`Cct`/`Cres`/`Esp`/`Expy`/`Gt`/`Mt`/`HT` | - | letter-spelled or unchanged |

**Consequences:** removing or failing to add an entry is a broadcast defect, not a cosmetic one - "Pacific
More Way" and "Wilson Badge" would air. This is the same failure mode Waze documented in 2012 ("Jr"
without a period reads as "jay are"), so it is a property of TTS engines generally rather than of
ElevenLabs. It also means the map deserves the opposite of the caution it was written with: the risk of a
MISSING entry is far higher than the risk of a speculative one, at least for tokens that genuinely occur.

**Acting on the same method found a live gap.** Scanning every road-name string in `test/corpus`
(51,849 occurrences, 376 distinct terminal tokens) for tokens the voice cannot read as words surfaced
directional suffixes the feeds append to Melbourne freeway names - `Wbnd`, `Ebnd`, `Sbnd`, 26 occurrences
("Westgate Freeway Wbnd", "Mornington Peninsula Freeway Sbnd"). All were UNMAPPED, and the live station
voice reads "Westgate Freeway Wbnd" as **"West Gate Freeway, WBND"** - letter by letter. Now expanded to
`westbound`/`eastbound`/`southbound`/`northbound`, matching the token the rest of the pipeline already
keys on. Not on air today (Melbourne is not a live market) but it would have been the moment it became one.

**Two negative findings from the same scan, both worth NOT acting on.** `Parde` (13x, "Alexandra Parde")
and `Stret` (3x, "Bennett Stret") are misspellings in the source data - but the voice **silently corrects
them**, reading "Parade" and "Street". Adding spelling-repair rules would be wasted work at the TTS layer
(they may still matter to the grounding gate, which compares script text against source text - a different
concern). And `Nsw`/`Qld`/`PTY LTD` appear only in POI and business names, never as a road type.

**Heuristics cannot do this job.** Vowel-density and length filters flag `Way`, `Park` and `North` as
unpronounceable while missing nothing useful; there is no reliable static test for "will the voice mangle
this token". The only dependable oracle is the voice itself, which is why the probe exists rather than a
cleverer regex.

**A second confirmation of v3 non-determinism (see the pronunciation-ordering decision):** `Trl` read as
**"Trail"** in one utterance and **"Trill"** in another minutes later. So a probe must be repeated to be
trusted, and a single good sample never proves an abbreviation is safe.

**Why the Waze lists themselves were not adopted:** the Australia page is the AS/NZS 4819:2011 addressing
table, which governs what Waze EDITORS type. Our strings come from HERE and the state feeds, which use
their own set. Measured: of the 29 AS/NZS abbreviations our spoken path does not handle, **zero appear in
any road name** across 6,480 distinct road-name strings (51,849 occurrences) in `test/corpus`. Several are
also ordinary words or ambiguous (`App`, `Arc`, `Ch`, `Con`, `Gr`, `Exp`), so importing them wholesale
would add false positives with no measured benefit.

**Why their tested results could not simply be reused (asked directly, so measured):** the "Big List"
Google Sheet is still live and was fetched. **24 of our 29 tokens are in it** - so the candidate list does
transfer - but the observed-result columns are almost all empty. Only **93 of 1,117 tokens (8%)** carry any
measured TTS result across both tabs, despite the lead post claiming every entry was tested in 2014. Of our
24 overlapping tokens, exactly three have data: `Rd` -> "Road", `Mt` -> "Mount", and `Pkwy` -> routing
"n/a. Says letters". Everything we actually depend on - `Hwy`, `Fwy`, `Mwy`, `Mtwy`, `Blvd`, `Brg`, `Cir`,
`Cres`, `Expy`, `Trl`, `Ter`, `Byp`, `Av`, `Ave`, `HT` - was never tested. And the one comparable data point
CONTRADICTS our engine: Nuance letter-spelled `Pkwy` on routing, while `eleven_v3` says "Parkway" correctly.
So the probe was not ceremony - it produced 29 results for our own voice in about two minutes, where three
years of volunteer effort produced three usable data points for the same tokens on a different engine.

**What the pages did confirm:** Waze's thread converged on "positional awareness" for the `St`
Street-vs-Saint and `Dr` Drive-vs-Doctor ambiguity - which is exactly what `RoadNameFormatter` already
does (terminal-position switch, plus leading `st` -> "saint" for St Kilda). The alternative the Australia
page recommends - a trailing full stop to mark Saint - is one Waze participants themselves found
confusing in the same thread ("plenty of signs out there that use N. to mean North"). Not adopting it was
the right call.

## 2026-08-24 — Flow-derived corridors get a suburb, from geometry we were already fetching

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN reviewed dev job 872395f7 (KIIS 90s Sydney) on 2026-08-24: "Richmond Road and Marsh road are flagging, but there's no location reference"; "road clumping but no suburb for context, Haig Ave is a good one - I'm not sure which it is"; "not sure on the M1 General Holmes Drive issue, looks all clear". All three are one defect. Every corridor voiced in that read was flow-derived (IncidentCount 0, Suburb null, Latitude null); every corridor that DID carry a suburb was an official-feed incident. HERE /flow is already requested with locationReferencing=shape and the raw HereFlowLocation binds the polyline, but ToCongestionSegmentsAsync projected out the geometry, so CongestionSegment carried no coordinates. A flow corridor therefore had no suburb to inherit and no endpoints, which also made ResolveCorridorEndpoints return null and silently skip EVERY flow corridor in the extent pass. The summarizer has rendered " near {Suburb}" for a long time; it simply never had a value.

**Decision:** Carry the flow row's shape ends through to the corridor and name the place from them. CongestionSegment gains StartPoint/EndPoint (FlowRowEndpoints reads the first and last point of the shape links); CreateCongestionCorridor takes its StartPoint/EndPoint/Latitude/Longitude from the LONGEST segment - the same reading whose length it voices; and a new EnrichCorridorsWithSuburbAsync pass fills Suburb on any ranked corridor that has coordinates but no suburb, immediately before the extent pass so extent (which only fills a None) is unaffected.

**Rationale:** The suburb pass deliberately calls BatchReverseGeocodePlacesAsync, not the BatchReverseGeocodeAsync the extent pass uses: the latter returns PreferNamedStreet(street,label,district) collapsed to its first comma segment, which is a STREET name, and only the Places variant separates the suburb out. Endpoints come from the longest segment because a flow group's segments share only a road NAME with no contiguity, so the ends of any other pairing can sit kilometres apart on unrelated stretches. A suburb that merely restates the road name is dropped (HERE labels 'Wiley Park' as both). No prompt change was needed.

**Consequences:** Verified live on dev job 02ce3c71 immediately after deploy: 15 of 15 flow corridors resolved a suburb, and the read aired "The Hume Highway through Bankstown ... M1 General Holmes Drive at Mascot" - both of ARN's named examples. Cost is bounded by the existing enrichment shape: one batch over the ranked set only (<= maxCorridors), 100 coords per request, sequential fallback capped at MaxParallelReverseGeocode. Any failure degrades to no suburb, never a bulletin error. New tests: CongestionCorridorTests.FlowCorridor_TakesItsLocationFromTheLongestReading and FlowCorridor_WithoutShapeGeometry_StaysUnlocated. Known follow-on: JobCorridor still has no Latitude/Longitude, so the coordinates are not persisted and the console map cannot pin a flow corridor even though TrafficCorridorDto exposes the fields.

## 2026-08-24 - 17 of 19 pronunciation rules were dead weight: ARN ear-reviewed the whole Sydney dictionary

**Status:** accepted (test only, v6; production deliberately untouched)

**Context:** the Warringah investigation established that a bad alias can air for days unnoticed, and that
only one of the 19 rules in test's "Sydney Roads" had ever been checked by ear. All 18 unverified aliases
were synthesised in the live station voice (`EF2rFRNHqbfaMctIvS2k`, `eleven_v3`), each paired with the
plain word, and presented to ARN as an A/B review page.

**Rationale:** every alias is a text substitution the voice cannot be reasoned about statically - speech-
to-text normalises the output back to the intended word, so automation cannot judge an alias (it CAN judge
an abbreviation, where failure shows as letter-spelling). A human ear was the only available oracle, so
the whole set was put in front of one.

**Decision:** ARN's verdict was that the plain word sounded better on **17 of 19**. Those rules are
deleted. Two survive:

| kept | alias | why |
|---|---|---|
| `Warringah` | `warringa` | plain is wrong; chosen by ear from six candidates earlier today |
| `Gymea` | `Guymeah` | the raw spelling gets a soft "j"; the alias forces the hard "g" (`/ˈɡaɪmiː/`) |

Deleted: `Glebe`, `Pyrmont`, `Drummoyne`, `Wahroonga`, `Unleaded`, `Unleaded's`, `Smithfield`, `Sydney`,
`KIIS`, `Turramurra`, `Coogee`, `Bondi`, `san souci`, `lewisham`, `Kirribilli`, `Parramatta`, `Military`.

**Verified after pruning** - a full bulletin line through the v6 dictionary reads correctly:
"Now looking over **Sydney**. Roadworks at **Guy Mia** are adding time, and there's a slight queue
eastbound on the **Warringah** Freeway at Cammeray. That's **Kiss** Traffic and Weather together."
`KIIS` needs no rule at all: the voice already reads it as "kiss". `Sydney` was being fed `Sydne` for no
benefit, on every single bulletin.

**Consequences:** two rules instead of nineteen is not just tidiness. Every redundant rule is a shadowing
hazard - the Warringah defect happened because a general rule sat in front of a specific one, and the
larger the set the likelier that collision. `Military` was added earlier the same day from prod and is
among the deletions, which is the honest outcome of testing an assumption rather than trusting it.

**The systemic lesson:** rules were added on suspicion, at the moment someone thought a read sounded off,
and then never re-checked. 89% of them were unnecessary or harmful. Any alias-style config that cannot be
verified automatically needs a scheduled human re-review, or it silently accumulates.

**Open - production carries the same 18 redundant rules.** Prod's "Sydney Roads" is v24 with 20 rules,
including `Sydney` -> `Sydne`, `Coogee` -> `could-gee`, `lewisham` -> `LOO-ah-shum` and `san souci` ->
`san sooZee`, all of which ARN has now judged worse than the plain word. They are on air today. Prod was
not touched, per standing instruction; whether to prune it the same way is ARN's call, and the same A/B
page can be regenerated against prod's exact rule set on request.

## 2026-08-24 - 22 files had been sitting with unresolved merge-conflict markers, and the tree could not build

**Status:** accepted (resolved; 50 commits pushed to ARN's Azure DevOps master)

**Context:** preparing the engagement handover sync, the repo's own pre-push gate refused the push with
7 failed gates. Investigating those found something worse than a lint problem: **22 files carried
unresolved 3-way merge-conflict markers**, 36 blocks in total, spanning C#, TypeScript, Bicep, shell,
Python and Markdown. `deployment/main.bicep` would not compile (`BCP025`, duplicate
`refineSentenceAgentName`) and the C# Application project had 8 errors. `git` itself reported zero
unmerged paths, so nothing surfaced this in status output.

**Rationale:** the markers pre-dated this session - a recovered stash object from before any of today's
work already contained 20 of them - so they had been in the tree for up to five days, which is the
straightforward explanation for the run of `partiallySucceeded` CI builds. They were surfaced only
because the pre-push gate was exercised for the first time in a while.

**Decision:** resolve all 36 blocks in favour of the "Stashed changes" side after verifying that side on
the merits, block by block. That side was consistently the newer and correct one, established by
evidence rather than assumption:

* `JobMappingExtensions` - `FlowRoadDto` declares `BaseScore`/`BoostAmount` at positions 8-9, so the
  other side was passing `f.FunctionalClass` positionally into `BaseScore`. That was the build error.
  The chosen side uses named arguments. Its companion test file adds the 34-line regression test that
  documents exactly this defect.
* `SourceParseContracts` / `SourceParseCoverageHttpTrigger` - identical code, differing doc comments.
  Confirmed by search that **nothing in `src/` emits `FieldOrigin.Prose`**, so the chosen side's
  "live prose share remains zero" wording is accurate and the other side's was aspirational.
* `deployment/*` and `scripts/foundry-traces.py` - the chosen side removes the whole-script
  `arn-refine` role, which `decisions.md` records as deleted on 2026-08-21. The other side still
  carried it.
* `CorridorSelectionOptions` / `SynthesisHistoryOptions` - both sides delete dead members; confirmed
  unreferenced before accepting.
* `CONTEXT.md` - the chosen side carries the 21-24 Aug entries AND compresses the verbose 13 Aug one,
  which brought the file from 186 lines to exactly its 150-line budget.

**Consequences:** conflict markers are invisible to `git status` once a merge is recorded as complete, so
nothing but a build or an explicit scan will find them. The lesson for this repo is that
`scripts/verify.sh` is the only thing that actually proves the tree is coherent, and it had not been run
against a push for days.

**A second, sharper finding: the `.ngrep` shim silently breaks `verify.sh`.** The repo-local direnv shim
replaces `grep`/`rg` with `ngrep` inside this directory. `verify.sh` uses `grep` internally to detect
errors in each gate's output, so with the shim active EVERY gate lane printed ranked search results and
reported failure - 7 "failures" that were pure artefact. The gate set only becomes meaningful with the
shim stripped from `PATH`. Anyone running the gate locally needs to know this, and it is why `.envrc` is
now gitignored rather than shared.

**Open at push time:** two gates still fail, neither introduced by this work - the 9 pre-existing
Infrastructure test failures already documented in `CONTEXT.md` as in-flight, and web lint errors in
another session's activity/ledger feature work (react-hooks 7 impure-render rule), fixed separately.

## 2026-08-24 — Section order is re-gated after word-target expansion

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN reported an out-of-order read twice on 2026-08-24 (the Gold Coast operator, KIIS 90s): 'did that thing again where it put an incident after the weather'. The aired script closed 'Sunny, sixteen degrees. Pacific Motorway and WestConnex are both MOVING nicely!' — a traffic good run after the weather. The gate was NOT at fault: SectionOrderDetector.Detect flags that exact aired text and Repair fixes it, including with the [brightly] delivery tag present (both pinned in SectionOrderDetectorTests). The hole was WHERE it ran. ScriptReviewLoop gates section order, but WordTargetEnforcer then expands the already-reviewed script ('the expansion refine above grows an already-reviewed script but is never itself reviewed'), and FinalizeExpandedScript re-ran ELEVEN deterministic gates without the section-order one. Nothing downstream re-checks: the naturalness polish is rephrase-only and gated, and the delivery director adds ElevenLabs tags under a word-immutability guard, so neither can reorder. Reproduced in the Application suite: an expansion patch that emits a weather clause ahead of new traffic shipped 'Botany Road... Showers clearing later. The M5 is also slow at Liverpool... Sunny, sixteen degrees.'

**Decision:** SectionOrderDetector.Detect/Repair now runs in FinalizeExpandedScript, LAST, after the other eleven repairs, and joins the unresolved-deterministic-gate warning as 'section-order'. Placed last deliberately: every repair above it reshapes the traffic body and any of them can strand a supplementary line. Repair still relocates only PURE supplementary sentences, so a mixed traffic+weather sentence continues to fall through to the warning by design — unchanged posture, mirroring UnselectedSourceDetector.Repair.

**Rationale:** The gate already existed and was proven correct against the real aired text, so the cheapest correct fix is to close the stage-ordering hole rather than touch detection. FinalizeExpandedScript is the last mechanical net between expansion and synthesis; section order belonged in it from the start.

**Consequences:** An expanded read can no longer ship with a supplementary section stranded mid-bulletin. Section order is one of SIX repairable gates still absent post-expansion — the others are Fragment, RedundantTail, RepeatedFuelSuburb, SecondaryItemCap and EvidenceRestatement; only the reported one was fixed here, and whether the rest belong in that net is an open question. This does NOT reach production: prod runs the 2026-08-17 package and this change is dev/test only.

## 2026-08-24 — Flow rows are named from the map, and clear runs carry a suburb

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN reviewed a dev read on 2026-08-24: "Green looks great, red is still a bit of a curly with Victoria and Elizabeth." Green was "Windsor Road at Baulkham Hills" - a congestion corridor, already covered by the corridor suburb pass. Red was "another clear run on the M4 Western Motorway, its service centre, Victoria Road and Elizabeth Drive", which contained TWO defects. (1) A POI voiced as a road: HERE's flow Location.Description is a label, and ToCongestionSegmentsAsync stamped it in as identity with an Unambiguous verdict - the map lookup was declared for the flow path (the method was async, CongestionSegment carries ResolvedRoadName/Verdict, FlowFunctionalClass takes a RoadIdentity) but never wired; the call passed `default`. Its four guards in HereTrafficProviderTests were among the nine failures the team had been carrying as background noise, asserting exactly this: expected "A3 / Centenary Dr", got "Australian Post Delivery Centre"; expected "Fitzwilliam Rd", got "Wiley Park". (2) No suburb on a clear run: the good-run channel is IReadOnlyList<string> end to end and FlowRoad carried no location, so the corridor suburb work did not reach it.

**Decision:** Flow rows are named from HERE's map, and good runs carry a suburb. ToCongestionSegmentsAsync now batch-resolves every row's own segment refs and calls RoadIdentityResolver.Resolve, using identity.Name, identity.Verdict and identity.FunctionalClass; a row with no single map identity is withheld rather than voiced under its label. FlowRoad gained Point and Suburb, populated from the longest reading's coordinate and a Places reverse-geocode, and BOTH good-run representations now emit it - the prose ContentFormatters.FormatGoodRuns and the structured AppendGoodRunEvidence unit.

**Rationale:** Fixing only the prose formatter would have missed the defect entirely: dev and test run UsePlainTextDraft=false, so the writer receives evidence units, and the prose block never appears in the prompt. That was caught by reading the captured RenderedPrompt rather than trusting the code path, and it is the same never-diverge rule the evidence-unit file opens with. The label fallback is kept for a wholesale map outage only (an unconfigured or failed lookup returns an empty set), because degrading every flow row to silence would empty a congestion-led bulletin.

**Consequences:** Verified live on dev. Job 3dfa6f0a: the good-run pool came back M5, M7, Princes Hwy, Victoria Rd, Pacific Mwy, Hume Mwy, Northconnex - all map identities, no POI. Job d8bd52b5: the writer received [goodrun:M5:suburb] = Moorebank and [goodrun:Eastern Distributor:suburb] = Waterloo, and the read located every item it voiced - "Centenary Drive at Strathfield", "Copeland Street at Liverpool", "Wattle Street in Haberfield", "St Hilliers Road in Auburn". The four flow-identity guards are green; the Infrastructure suite drops from 9 pre-existing failures to 5, none related. Not yet observed: a clear-run SENTENCE voicing a suburb on air, because neither verification read voiced one.

## 2026-08-24 — Test → Zetta re-proven under the per-station arming model, ARN-confirmed

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Test had already delivered to the live share with a witnessed ingest on 2026-07-30 — ARN playout confirmed both pilot stations' reports landed in the live Cairns and Sydney KIIS 90s libraries — so "can test reach Zetta" was not itself the open question. What changed since: 2026-08-20 introduced the per-station `MarketSchedule.PlayoutEnabled` gate and re-pointed test at the live `informationbulletins` share, but that day's proof deliberately ran against the sibling `informationbulletins-test` share that ARN's autoloader ignores, and both pilot stations were left `PlayoutEnabled=false`. So no ARN-confirmed ingest existed for the CURRENT build and arming model, and the residual risk named that day was precisely the `UploadRange` call against `informationbulletins` under the new gate.

**Decision:** Verified live 2026-08-24 and recorded as PROVEN for the current build and arming model: a bulletin published from TEST with the station armed reaches Zetta. Sydney/KIIS 90s job `f7321bd9` was approved 03:26:38 UTC and published 03:26:39 UTC by the Arinco deploy operator with `PlayoutEnabled=true`; the job logged `Audio delivered to playout system` and `[SYD]KIIS90s_TRAFF.wav` (1,940,444 bytes, 22.0s) appeared at the ROOT of `informationbulletins` on `ibpauetststaftp01` — the live production playout folder. The file was gone by 03:27:30 (`ResourceNotFound`) and ARN confirmed Zetta received it. Test is a delivery-capable environment for the pilot, and putting a station on air needs no deploy to prod.

**Rationale:** This closes the residual the 2026-08-20 work explicitly left open — the `UploadRange` against the `informationbulletins` share specifically, a 20-character string difference — and closes it with a real ARN-confirmed ingest rather than by argument, now that the per-station gate sits in front of it. It also settles pilot sequencing: prod stays frozen at the last known-good build as the fallback while test carries new code to air, which is only defensible if test can actually deliver.

**Consequences:** **Test state now:** sydney is `PlayoutEnabled=true` AND its schedule is `Enabled=true` (cron `0,30 6-17 * * 1,2,3,4,5`, Australia/Sydney), so test now airs sydney on its own cron - it is no longer one toggle away, it is live. cairns-4ca remains `PlayoutEnabled=false`. Prod MUST NOT have sydney armed while this holds: same file name, same share, and the race is unauditable.

**NEW FINDING - test can deliver UNATTENDED, and an earlier claim was wrong.** The watchdog's fallback-cover path publishes AND delivers a `WaitingApproval` job with no human involved. Job `00ae9bda` (the poller's own 03:30 slot, never approved by anyone) was covered at 03:27:00 by reusing `f7321bd9`'s audio, logged `Fallback applied from job f7321bd9`, `Job approved by system (deadline)` and `Audio delivered to playout system`, and wrote the SAME file name a second time 21 seconds after the first write. Both writes carried identical bytes (both jobs resolve to blob `broadcast_20260824_032340_f7321bd9....wav`). So the statement that only `Approved` jobs auto-publish is FALSE: `JobWatchdog.DeliverCoveredSlotAsync` -> `JobService.PublishJobAsync` covers a `WaitingApproval` slot, and a covered slot's delivery cutoff is `ScheduledForUtc`, not `FallbackDeadlineUtc`, so it can still deliver after the normal deadline has passed. Approving one bulletin therefore makes it the reuse source for any later unapproved slot the same day.

**Deliberately still unproven:** (1) sha256 byte-identity of the drop file against the approved audio - the verification download raced Zetta's ingest, returning 0 bytes and then `ResourceNotFound`, so unlike 2026-08-20 there is no hash match for this delivery; the 1,940,444-byte size matching the previously verified 22.0s file is the weaker evidence that stands. (2) How many times Zetta ingested - one file, or the same bulletin twice across the two writes. The drop file's disappearance identifies a station's latest publish, never a count.

## 2026-08-24 - The slot-fit envelope is ARN-tunable from the console, not a deploy

**Status:** accepted (in-tree; dev + test deploy pending)

**Context:** `MaxSlowDownFactor` is pinned to `1.0` in `appsettings.json` to honour the 2026-06-25
"never slow the read" decision, while the code default is `1.10`. The measured cost of that policy is
concrete: the 05:55 Sydney slot fell to the standby cart on 2 of 6 mornings and was MISSED on a third,
which is the incident ARN reported this morning. Whether an audible slow-fill beats sponsor credits is
an editorial judgement, and it was locked behind a deploy.

**Rationale:** `EditorialSettings` already exists for exactly this class of value - its own doc comment
says compile-time constants made questions like "should a busy market be allowed more than five
corridors?" *"product decisions blocked on a deploy"*. The slot-fit numbers are the same shape of
question, and they are the most consequential ones ARN could not reach.

**Decision:** four nullable fields on `EditorialSettings`, resolved Station > Market > Global per field
exactly like the existing caps, editable in the console's editorial settings panel:

| field | bounds | what it decides |
|---|---|---|
| `MaxSlowDownFactor` | 1.0 - 1.25 | how far a short read may be stretched to reach the slot; **1.0 = never slow the read** |
| `MaxSpeedUpFactor` | 1.0 - 1.30 | how far a long read may be compressed |
| `MaxSilencePadSeconds` | 0.0 - 2.0 | trailing silence allowed to close a residual gap |
| `MaxSafeOverrunTrimSeconds` | 0.0 - 10.0 | overrun still worth compressing rather than regenerating |

Bounded tighter than the caps because every value is audible; a factor below 1.0 would speed a read
while claiming to slow it, so 1.0 (mechanism off) is the floor rather than zero.

**The effective view reads the DEPLOYED options, not the code defaults.** `EffectiveEditorialSettingsDto.From`
takes the injected `SpeechDurationOptions`, because the two genuinely differ (1.0 deployed vs 1.10 in
code) and "effective" has to mean what a bulletin would really use. Showing ARN a slow-fill allowance the
environment does not have would be worse than showing nothing.

**The bug this work produced, and the rule that prevents it recurring.** The first implementation
collapsed the nullable override into a resolved `double` and passed it at the audio-pipeline boundary.
Same resulting number, but a different contract: the pipeline applies its own configured option when the
argument is null, so a station that had configured nothing no longer made the call it made before the
console existed. **128 Application tests failed.** They were right to. The rule now recorded in code at
three call sites: the non-nullable resolved value is for INTERNAL fit arithmetic, which has no "unset"
case; anything handed to the pipeline stays NULLABLE so an unset console is byte-identical to the
previous behaviour. A filtered `~Broadcasting` run (32 of 874 tests) reported green throughout, which is
the reason the regression reached a full-suite run at all.

**Consequences:** suite green - Domain 2251, Functions 832, Application 874, Architecture 14, and
Infrastructure improved from its 9 pre-existing failures to **5** (the four `HereTrafficProvider` ones
were fixed as a side effect of the conflict resolution). A test-helper matcher that omitted
`maxSlowDownFactorOverride` was implicitly pinning it to null; it now matches explicitly, which is the
kind of accidental over-specification that makes a stub look like a behavioural assertion.

**Open:** ARN still has to choose a value. The panel now states the trade in the UI - at 1.0 a read that
cannot reach its slot goes to the standby cart - but nothing is changed by default. `MaxSlowDownFactor`
stays 1.0 everywhere until ARN sets it, so this decision reopens the 2026-06-25 policy for discussion
rather than reversing it.

## 2026-08-24 — A fallback no longer destroys the bulletin it replaces

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** A fallback overwrote the generated bulletin in place. `Job.ApplyFillerFallback` set
`ScriptText = None` and cleared the sentences; `Job.ApplyFallback` overwrote both with the re-aired
source job's. Measured on the deployed dev + test environments on 2026-08-24: **40 of 49 jobs in a
24-hour window had `Script.Data.Text == ""` and zero sentences.** The operator console therefore
showed no script at all for those jobs, and the writer could not be reviewed after the fact — the
generated words were unrecoverable from the job record, so the single most common outcome in a thin
market produced no evidence of what the pipeline actually wrote.

**Decision:** Retain exactly ONE take — the bulletin that existed immediately before the fallback
fired. New `SupersededTake` domain record (script text, tagged text, its own audio blob reference,
sentences, word timings, pre-review, delivery-style/bookend pins), captured by
`Job.CaptureSupersededTake` from inside BOTH fallback methods, positioned after their guards and
before the first field assignment. Persisted in one size-fitted `SupersededTakeJson` column (it
carries sentences and word timings, so it rides `FitTableProperty`/`ExpandTableProperty`, not a raw
serialize). Exposed on `JobDetailDtoBase.SupersededTake` — the base, not a leaf, because a
`FallbackJob`, the `PublishedJob` that delivered the cover, and a `FailedJob` all need it. The
console renders it as a collapsed-by-default `SupersededTakeCard` in the reading column beneath the
aired script: plain transport, the retained script as paragraph text, and a field-level
`EntityDiffView` against what aired (suppressed when the aired script is blank, which is the common
standby-cart case). A new `AirIntentLine` states what is going to playout and by when.

**Rationale:** Evidence is deliberately NOT copied into the take — corridors, incidents, weather and
fuel stay on the job and describe this same take, so duplicating them would double the row for no
new information. Exactly one take, never a list: a growing list in a table column recreates the size
problem the `OfficialEvidence` four-receipt cap exists to avoid, and a real multi-take archive would
need blob backing. `RequestRegeneration` deliberately does NOT clear the field, for the same reason
it keeps `FallbackDeadlineUtc`: the take is a historical fact about a fallback that did happen.
`AttemptResult` was the rival pattern and was rejected — it carries only timing/success metadata, is
surfaced solely under `FailedJobDto.Failure.AttemptHistory`, and is cleared by regeneration.

**The take's audio does NOT ride the proxy path, on purpose.** `ResolveAudioUrlAsync` returns
`jobs/{jobId}/audio/{render}` under `Broadcast__UseAudioProxy` (true in every environment), and
`GetJobAudio` always streams `job.AudioUrl` — the trailing segment is a cache key, never a selector.
Routing the take through it would have served the CART audio under the take's label, which is worse
than no player. A sibling `ResolveStoredAudioUrlAsync` signs the take's own blob directly and fails
soft to an empty URL; the card then renders the script with no transport. The deployed audio route
is unchanged.

**Consequences:** New: `SupersededTake`, `Job.SupersededTake` + `SetSupersededTake`,
`JobEntity.SupersededTakeJson`, `SupersededTakeDto`, `JobMappingExtensions.MapSupersededTake` (and
`MapPreReview`, extracted so the job's own pre-review and the take's share one mapping),
`JobsHttpTrigger.ResolveStoredAudioUrlAsync`, web `SupersededTake` type + `SupersededTakeSchema` +
`SupersededTakeCard` + `AirIntentLine`. `ToDetailDto` now takes a required second audio URL — every
callsite updated rather than defaulted, so a caller cannot silently pass the wrong blob.
`docs/reference/job-table-schema.md` documents the new column and the seven-column compression set.
Suite green: Domain 2251, Application 874, Functions 832, Architecture 14, Infrastructure unchanged
at its 5 pre-existing failures; web 605 tests across 59 files. Verified visually in mock mode on job
`arn-job-00012` — the card expands to the retained 45s read against the 25s cover, with the diff and
`Use as working script`. Jobs that fell back BEFORE this ships have no take and render nothing:
the field is retroactively empty, not retroactively populated.

## 2026-08-24 — Bookends and mandatory lines are outside the ship-time trim; the underrun check is bounded by the measured read

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Three consecutive reads shipped defective: dev d8bd52b5 (4.1s dead air), test a9109443 (1.2s dead air, outro cut), test 2178f0e2 (outro cut). The operator stated the non-negotiables: the station bookends and any mandatory weather/fuel line must ALWAYS air, and the bulletin must never leave empty space at the end of the audio - it must always fill the slot with spoken audio. All three had one cause: two trim implementations disagree about what is untouchable. BulletinDurationFitter.FitByTrimming (predictive-fit path) protects intro, outro and the required close. ScriptWordCeiling.TrimToCeiling (ship-time ceiling path) has no bookend awareness - it drops TRAILING sentences to hit a word count, and the outro is the last sentence, so it goes first. The ship-time trim fired on all three jobs. It then set preSynthesisCeilingTrimmed=true, which unconditionally suppressed the underrun check, so the resulting hole shipped silently and logged as 'Audio filled to slot'.

**Decision:** The ship-time ceiling trim now passes the station lines and requiredFixtures:true to TrimToCeiling, putting bookends and mandatory weather/fuel outside its budget. The underrun suppression is bounded by the MEASURED read: trimOvershot = underrunSeconds > MaxSilencePadSeconds re-arms the content-limited check on both the primary and the filler branch, so a trim can no longer certify its own hole. BroadcastOrchestratorDecoupledFitTests.CeilingTrimFollowedByUnderrun_IsNotContentLimited asserted the overruled policy and is rewritten to _IsContentLimited.

**Rationale:** Bookend loss, short read and silent failure were one defect, not three. Bounding the trim's excuse by what was actually measured keeps the legitimate half of the original guard (no retry oscillation over a residual the silence pad closes) while removing its ability to launder a real hole into shipped dead air. Collapsing to a single trim implementation is the larger correct change but touches every market's trim behaviour, so bookend protection was patched into the second trim instead.

**Consequences:** Verified live via the scheduled poller on dev (2223b6e6) and test (23b9bb1c): both reads end with the outro, carry weather, and have a 0.0s trailing gap (speech ends 22.0s and 21.995s in a 22.0s file). Both logged a ceiling target BELOW the synthesised word count (47->55, 53->61), proving bookends are excluded from the trim rather than dropped. Backend suites green: Application 874, Domain 2254, Functions 834, Architecture 14. Two trim policies still coexist - collapsing onto FitByTrimming remains open. Separately, the KIIS OutroText is stored truncated ('powered by' with empty Tokens), so the read ends mid-sentence; that is ARN editorial data, not code.

## 2026-08-24 — FALLBACK_USED is a 0.2-second step, not a state, and nothing was watching the ones that stuck

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Challenged on why the console offers "Retry generation", "Approve fallback" and (newly)
"Use as working script" on a status that publishes itself. Measured, rather than argued.

The deadline sweep applies the cover and delivers it in the SAME iteration:
`JobWatchdog.ProcessFallbacksAsync:201` → `DeliverFallbackAsync:285` →
`JobService.DeliverCoveredSlotAsync:735/744` (approve, then publish, actor `system (deadline)`).
Live `StatusHistory` timestamps on dev and test: **FallbackUsed → Published in 0.104s, 0.171s,
0.179s, 0.204s, 0.204s, 0.223s.** Coverage's real representation is `PUBLISHED` + `Fallback`, and
that is what the corpus shows — **dev 504 of 657 published jobs carry a Fallback (77%), test 245 of
323 (76%)**. Three quarters of everything ever published was a cover.

So a job an operator FINDS in `FallbackUsed` is not early — its delivery failed, or the process died
between the two saves. And nothing ever looked at it again:
`TableStorageJobRepository.ListJobsNeedingFallbackAsync:396-409` filters
`Status ne 'FallbackUsed'`, and the sweep's own loop skips the status. **39 such rows across dev and
test, every one 12.7 to 28.7 days old.** The newest is dated 11 Aug — exactly the date inline
delivery landed (`JobService.cs:707`), so these are pre-fix residue rather than an ongoing leak. The
hole in the code is real but narrow: the failure/crash window, which still never retried.

**Decision:** Two changes, deliberately not a state-machine rewrite. `JobStatus` ordinals are
persisted integers under an append-only rule (`Job.cs:9-20`, after the 19 Aug incident where
inserting a member silently rewrote historical rows), so `FallbackUsed` cannot be renamed or removed.

1. **`JobWatchdog.RecoverUndeliveredCoveredSlotsAsync`**, wired into the poller after the fallback
   sweep. Three arms, because a stranded cover is in three genuinely different situations: slot
   still ahead → retry `DeliverCoveredSlotAsync` (as `PublishApprovedBeforeDeadlineAsync` already
   retries an undelivered approved bulletin); slot just passed → alert once, deduped through the
   job's own log via `CoverUndeliveredMarker`, plus `TrackZettaDeliveryFailure(market,
   "covered_slot_undelivered")` and a `FailedNotCovered` card; slot passed beyond
   `MissedAfterDeadlineMinutes` → do nothing at all. That third arm exists so the 39 historical rows
   are left exactly as they are, per an explicit call to leave them: re-alerting on them would page
   someone about weeks-dead air on the first tick after deploy. `ListJobsAsync([FallbackUsed])`
   reuses the existing query `ProceedPastCurationDeadlineAsync` already uses; no new repository
   method.
2. **The console stops offering actions the slot cannot honour.** New `isAirSlotPassed(job)` in
   `job-meta/urgency.ts` keyed on the job's OWN `input.timeWindow.to` (`ScheduledForUtc`) — the same
   value the backend measures a covered slot's delivery cutoff against. `JobActions` renders nothing
   for `FALLBACK_USED` once the slot has gone, and the superseded-take card withholds its
   regeneration seed on the same test. `SlotAudition` replaces "Air this" with "Slot closed" when
   the slot's own job is `PUBLISHED` or `FALLBACK_USED`, which `Job.ApplyFallback` /
   `ApplyFillerFallback` both refuse (`Job.cs:625-627, 674-675`) — it was an action guaranteed to
   fail.

**Rationale:** Retry-then-alert mirrors the shape already proven for an undelivered APPROVED
bulletin (`PublishApprovedBeforeDeadlineAsync`), so the covered case stops being the one path with
no recovery instead of inventing a second convention. The third arm — silence beyond the missed-slot
grace — is what makes the sweep safe to switch on against real history: without it the first tick
would fire 39 cards about slots weeks dead, which is worse than the silence it replaces. Deleting or
splitting `FallbackUsed` would be the cleaner model and is not available: the ordinals are persisted
and append-only, and 39 rows already carry the value. Gating the console on the SLOT rather than the
status is the only test that separates a rescuable cover from a dead one, because the status is
identical in both cases and occupied for two tenths of a second in the healthy one.

**The trap that made the first attempt of (2) a no-op.** `resolveBindingDeadline` returns null for
every status except `WAITING_APPROVAL`, so `resolveBindingDeadline(...)?.slotMissed === true` reads
**false — "slot fine" —** on a covered job whose slot went a fortnight ago. Gating on it changed
nothing, which the live check caught and the unit tests now pin. `useAirSlot` is also the wrong
source here: it derives the slot from the station's cron and returns null for an ad-hoc bulletin or a
station with no enabled schedule. The job's own scheduled time is the only per-job authority.

**What was deliberately NOT changed.** Web `TERMINAL_STATUSES` includes `REJECTED` and the backend's
`Job.IsTerminal` does not. That is not drift: the backend asks "may this still be failed or covered?"
while the web asks "has this stopped changing on its own?" — which drives polling, the as-aired card
and sentence-verification suppression. Aligning the lists would restart a poll with nothing to watch.
The comment on `TERMINAL_STATUSES` now says so, because the audit that found this read it as a bug.
Also left alone: `AUDIO_READY` sits in `EDITABLE_STATES` while `ReviewPane` routes it to
`GeneratingView`, so its editor is unreachable — a real defect, but deciding whether that status
should be editable is a product call, not a truth fix.

**Consequences:** New: `RecoverUndeliveredCoveredSlotsAsync`, `CoverUndeliveredMarker`,
`IsPastCoveredSlotAlertWindow`, `isAirSlotPassed`, `JobActionsProps.slotMissed`,
`AuditionRow.slotClosed`. A stale XML comment on `DeliverFallbackAsync` claiming "nothing delivers
it" — true until 11 Aug, false since, and it misled the audit — now states the history instead of the
behaviour. Tests: 5 sweep cases (retry / alert-once / weeks-old-left-alone / dedupe / no applied-at
stamp), 4 `isAirSlotPassed` cases incl. one pinning the `resolveBindingDeadline` trap, 6
`SlotAudition` cases, 1 `JobActions` case. Suite: Domain 2254, Application 879, Functions 834,
Architecture 14; web 1258 passed across 127 files. Verified live in mock mode on `arn-job-00012`:
with the slot in the past, Retry / Approve fallback / Use as working script are all gone while the
take card and the air-intent line remain. **Not deployed** — the sweep changes what reaches air, so
it wants a what-if and a test-first rollout.

## 2026-08-24 — Reserving the bookends AT THE SELECTOR alone is wrong: the engine already reserves them

**Status:** rejected — tried on dev 2026-08-24 05:19Z, broke generation, rolled back 05:28Z

**Context:** ARN reported the KIIS closer missing from consecutive dev/test reads. The immediate
cause was fixed the same day — `ScriptWordCeiling.TrimToCeiling` drops TRAILING sentences and knew
nothing of a locked prefix/suffix, so the outro was always the first thing cut, and the engine now
peels the station lines before trimming. That closed the symptom and exposed the cause: the trim was
firing on essentially every bookended read. `StructuredMatrixScriptGenerator` scored `slotMiss`
against `context.TargetDurationSeconds` — the WHOLE slot — while `BulletinBookendComposer.Compose`
wraps the pair around the body AFTER the generator returns. The selector is exact: it filled 22.0s
with body, the composer then added 5.2s of top-and-tail, and every bookended station overran by
exactly the pair's length, deterministically. Dev `b8e0a280`: 52-word body ~22.4s, composed 64 words
predicted 27.6s against a 24.6s allowance, `prosody-trim`, closer gone. Replaying that job's own
captured draft menu through the live selector reproduced it — 51 words / 21.99s body, composed
27.17s — and reserving the pair produced 39 words / 16.82s body, composed **21.99s against the
22.0s slot**. The selector hits whatever target it is given to a hundredth of a second; it was being
given the wrong one. This is hard constraint 8 of
("Bookends reserved. The budget is slot minus bookends"), written down and never implemented.

**Decision:** REVERTED. `GenerateScriptAsync` computed `ReservedBookendSeconds` from the resolved
pair and passed `slot − reserved` to `SelectOptimalCombination` as the body's target, priced with
the selector's own `IDurationPredictor`. Deployed to dev at 05:19Z. **It broke generation and was
rolled back at 05:28Z.**

**Why it was wrong: the bookends were then reserved TWICE.** `ScriptGenerationEngine` lines 109-111
already compute `bodyTargetSeconds = TargetDurationSeconds − bookendSeconds` and derive the
attempt's word target from it (`TargetWordCountOverride`, the "target N words" line in the job log).
The selector ignoring that and using the full slot was not an oversight the engine was unaware of —
it was the slack that made the composed read long enough. Subtracting at the selector as well sized
the body for `slot − bookends − bookends`, and nothing downstream could put the content back:
`WordTargetEnforcer` can only expand through the LLM, and expansion is grounded, so on thin evidence
it correctly refuses to invent.

**Measured, dev, same station and slot (22s, KIIS 90s, bookended):**

| | job | outcome | wall | read |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| with the change | `273cddfb` | **Failed** — content-limited | 124s | 16.3s of speech, 4 generation attempts, expansion reverted |
| rolled back | `9d274699` | WaitingApproval | 55s | 22.0s, closer intact |

`273cddfb`'s log is the whole story: `target 40 words` → body trimmed to 27 by the station-line
holdback → `Short bulletin: only 16.3s of natural speech for the 22s slot` → four attempts of
expansion → `Failed: Content-limited: best spoken 19.3s could not fill the 22s slot`.

**Why the tests did not catch it.** The two regression tests drove
`StructuredMatrixScriptGenerator` in isolation with a fixed-rate predictor and asserted the composed
body fits the slot — which it did. They could not see the engine's own reservation, because every
Application-layer test substitutes `IScriptGenerator`. There is no test that runs the selector's
seconds target and the engine's word target against one another, which is exactly the seam that
broke. Any future attempt at this needs one.

**Found while failing, and worth fixing on its own:** the expansion grounding check flags the
station outro as ungrounded — `"That's KIIS traffic and weather together, powered by" is station
branding/sign-off language not supplied by the run context`. `ScriptReviewLoop` strips bookend edges
before the reviewer sees them (`BulletinBookendComposer.StripBookendEdges`) but
`WordTargetEnforcer`'s expansion path does not, so every expansion on a bookended station burns its
grounding retries on config it can never change. Pre-existing; this change only made expansion run
often enough to expose it.

**Rationale:** One layer owns the body budget, not two. The reverted change assumed the selector was
the only place a reservation could live; it is not, and the engine's reservation was load-bearing.
Either the engine stops subtracting and lets the selector be the length authority (the direction
 argues for), or the selector keeps scoring against
the full slot and the engine's word target stays authoritative. The half-measure is what failed.

**Consequences:** The tree is back to the pre-change state and dev is redeployed from it (`9d274699`
verified good). Reconciling the two authorities is the same duration-policy work as the
engine/selector compression disagreement (`ComputeBoostedWordTarget` sizes for a compressed read;
`SlotMissSeconds` charges overshoot 2x/8x) and must not go near a deployed environment without
corpus replay plus a test that exercises the selector's seconds target and the engine's word target
together. Until then the standing behaviour is unchanged: bookended reads overrun and the
station-line holdback protects the closer, which is the shipped 04:32Z state.

## 2026-08-24 — The retime fades the audio's own tail, not the slot's

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN reported test job 23b9bb1c ending mid-word: the read finished '...powered' with no 'by'. The script, the UI and the word timings all carried 'by' correctly, and an earlier render of the same job measured clean, so the defect was in one specific render. The audio served by the page (broadcast_20260824_043528_*) ended on RISING energy at -27.7 dBFS, stepping from sample -283 to digital zero in one sample, with peak 1100 in its final millisecond against a body peak of 27571. Its WavProcessor trace was a single line - AdjustSpeed 24.720s -> 22.000s - with no TrimAfterSpeech and no fade. TrimAfterSpeech is conditional on ElevenLabs returning a usable alignment (ElevenLabsAudioSynthesizer line 94), and it is the only stage that applies a fade-out; when the alignment is absent the retime is the sole tail treatment. TimeStretchToTarget faded only when it TRUNCATED (copy >= targetSamples), on the documented reasoning that a zero-padded short result 'already ends in silence'. This render came up short by 22 samples - 0.5ms - so the fade was skipped and the 0.5ms pad was all that separated live speech from the end of the file.

**Decision:** TimeStretchToTarget now fades the REAL audio's tail - ApplyFadeOut(pcm, 0, copy * 2, info) - unconditionally whenever it produced any samples, instead of fading the slot's tail only when it truncated. The fade therefore lands where the audio actually ends, whether the WSOLA result overran the slot or came up short of it. A new theory in WavDurationProcessorTests drives a full-amplitude tone with no natural decay through both the compressing and stretching paths and asserts the last sample carrying signal is a fade remnant, not a full-level cut.

**Rationale:** A zero pad is only silence when it is long enough to be silence; a sub-millisecond one is a click with extra steps.
