hour window. Foundry's Tracing tab was empty because the raw model endpoint emits
nothing to it. Two `writeFlow` calls returned after 60,002ms and 60,007ms
completely empty, and no operator-visible log line said the flow desk had failed —
that bulletin was built with no flow material.

**Decision:** Manage all six Foundry agents in `provision-foundry-agents.sh` with
a neutral instruction shim and a definition hash. Declare the project's App
Insights connection in IaC. Put agent routing behind a default-OFF
`enableWorkflowAgents` switch. Emit one `DependencyTelemetry` per LLM HTTP
attempt carrying the `gen_ai.*` custom dimensions. Give captures an `Error` field,
real cached/reasoning token counts, and a declared 14-day retention.

**Rationale:** The agent endpoint rejects a request-side `instructions` field
(HTTP 400 `invalid_payload`, "Not allowed when agent is specified.", verified by
direct curl), so the system prompt must travel inside `input` or the per-station
voicing overlay silently stops reaching the model. It also rejects a request-side
`text` field, so the raw route's strict `json_schema` contract downgrades to the
agent's baked `json_object` — a real loss, stated plainly. The app uses the
classic Application Insights SDK 2.x, which is not an OpenTelemetry tracer
provider, so a bare `ActivitySource` span would export nowhere. Migrating the
whole app to the Azure Monitor OTel distro would change how all telemetry is
emitted and risk existing alerts, so `DependencyTelemetry` with `gen_ai.*`
custom dimensions was chosen because Microsoft's own sample queries
`dependencies` on `customDimensions['gen_ai.operation.name']` correlated by
`operation_Id` — the same table and shape.

**Consequences:** This does **not** improve latency. Measured by direct curl,
~19–28% of calls to `gpt-5.6-luna` stall with the server accepting the request,
sending nothing for a precise ~60s, then either answering normally or returning
HTTP 500 `no healthy upstream`; TTFB equals total, TCP+TLS are ~0.1s,
`reasoning_tokens` is 0, and it reproduces on a ~120-token prompt with no app
code involved. The identical probe against `gpt-5.6-terra` and `gpt-5` stalled
0/29 times. The agent route hits the same fault. Client-side telemetry is the
only way these stalls become visible, because Foundry's server-side agent traces
cannot show a client-side wait.

## 2026-08-31 — Fall back to an alternate model deployment when Luna's shared pool rejects

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The `gpt-5.6-luna` shared GlobalStandard pool in `australiaeast` is intermittently oversubscribed. Three symptoms have one cause: HTTP 503 `no healthy upstream`; a precise approximately 60-second stall where curl shows TTFB equal to total while TCP+TLS take approximately 0.1 seconds; and HTTP 429 whose body says "The system is currently experiencing high demand and cannot process your request ... consider switching to Provisioned Throughput", with `rate_limit_source: rapi`. Over seven days, dev (capacity 1,986) recorded 38 x 503 and 32 stalls with zero throttles; test (capacity 150) recorded 26 throttles and 15 x 503. The 429s arrived while our own quota was idle: `x-ratelimit-remaining-requests: 149/150` and `x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens: 149,936/150,000`. Our request rate is not the cause: 6.8 requests/min per bulletin, with a peak of three requests in one second. Retry amplification made the incident user-visible: test's `BroadcastQueueProcessor` p90 reached 578.9s and its maximum 600s on 2026-08-31, against a p50 of approximately 40s all week; `compose2` produced 25 of 41 rejections, and generation can retry up to four times.

**Decision:** On HTTP 429, transient 5xx (500/502/503/504/408), or stall-retry exhaustion, resend the call exactly once immediately, with no backoff, on an alternate deployment before entering the existing throttle ladder. Once switched, the ladder continues on the alternate deployment rather than returning to Luna; fallback is entered at most once, so there is no oscillation. An empty `aiFallbackModelName` leaves the feature off and preserves the previous behaviour, so it is disabled by default. The raw route swaps its `model` field to `gpt-5.6-terra`; the agent route swaps to a `-terra` sibling because the agent request cannot select a model. Ten agents are now provisioned from a per-agent model map: six Luna primaries and four Terra siblings (`arn-wf-write-incidents-terra`, `arn-wf-write-flow-terra`, `arn-wf-compose-terra`, and `arn-wf-edit-terra`).

**Rationale:** Two obvious fixes were ruled out by measurement. Raising `aiModelCapacity` does not address a shared-pool rejection: the 429 arrived with 149/150 requests and 149,936/150,000 tokens remaining, so our own quota was idle. Trimming `max_output_tokens` does not address it either: a controlled test charged exactly 64 tokens at both 200 and 4096, demonstrating that the maximum is not reserved against TPM. The fallback therefore does not pretend that either setting fixes the platform fault. There is no backoff before the fallback because a shared-pool 429 does not clear in two seconds and Terra measured zero throttles; the old 2+4+8+16-second ladder was 30 seconds of pure dead time before trying a deployment that was already rejecting us. The ladder stays on the alternate because Luna is the deployment measured to be saturated; sending those retries back to it would deliberately retry the known-failing endpoint. Terra was healthy throughout the comparison: 5/5 and 12/12 concurrent successes, 0/29 stalls, and zero throttles over seven days, on the same model family and version date 2026-07-09. Two mechanisms are forced by the platform: the agent endpoint rejects a request-side `model` with the exact error "Model must match the agent's model 'gpt-5.6-luna' when agent is specified.", so the raw route can swap a model field but the agent route must select a sibling agent.

**Consequences:** `gpt-5.6-terra` is a different model from `gpt-5.6-luna`, so a bulletin served by the fallback may read differently. That is deliberate: the alternative is a failed bulletin. ARN's standing preference remains Luna; this is an availability measure, not a model change. It is disabled in every environment until `aiFallbackModelName` is set deliberately. `ViaFallback` on the LLM telemetry record identifies after the fact which deployment or agent served each call. This does not fix the underlying shared-pool fault: Provisioned Throughput is the only option measured as removing that fault while keeping Luna.

## 2026-08-31 — Emergency-services data is a separate evidence rail, shown before it is ever aired

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** ARN asked for DataQuoll emergency-services data, with the highest urgency tier always aired and everything else listed in the console. Measuring the live API first changed the design three times over. (1) The API has NO road-impact field anywhere — grepping the whole OpenAPI 1.50.0 spec for `road|closure|lane|detour` returns only incident titles — so a fire whose location reads "BRUXNER HWY" is a fire located on that road, not a closure. (2) The obvious "highest tier" field is disqualified: all 10 `severity: Severe` records nationally in a 500-feature capture were SA Ambulance pager cases ("Stab / Gun - CHELTENHAM", "Cardiac or - YANKALILLA"), because that feed derives CAP severity from case acuity. (3) 279 of those 500 features were `medical`, 106 were duplicate CAP revisions of the same incident, and 100% of NSW RFS records classify as `eventType: other`, so category filters return nothing for the Sydney pilot market. Licences also differ per source: WA DFES is CC BY-ND and SA CFS is CC BY-NC-ND, neither usable by commercial radio.

**Decision:** Ship it in two phases, and phase 1 airs nothing. `IEmergencyIncidentFeed` is a NEW contract, deliberately not an `IOfficialTrafficFeed`: that interface's events flow through `IncidentClassCrosswalk` into corridor fusion, which would attach an emergency incident to the nearest road name. `EmergencyEvent` is carried on `TrafficEvidenceBuilder.MarketContent` so it rides the same parallel fetch window as weather and fuel, but is deliberately NOT applied by `ApplyMarketContent` — `BroadcastWithTraffic` is the writer's context, so the data is structurally unable to reach a script. It travels straight to `StoreIncidentsOnJob` and persists as `Job.EmergencyEvents` / `EmergencyEventsJson`. The airing tier is `EmergencyWarningLevel.EmergencyWarning` (Australian Warning System) and nothing else; CAP severity/urgency/certainty are not even persisted. Air-eligibility is fail-closed: official source AND a licence starting `CC BY` with neither `-NC` nor `-ND`, AND a category in {fire, weather, hazmat, earth, rescue}. Licences are resolved at runtime from the unauthenticated `/attribution` endpoint keyed on `(state, agency)` rather than a hardcoded table. `EmergencyFeeds:Enabled` defaults to FALSE, so the code ships inert.

**Rationale:** Fusing this into corridors would have reproduced the 13 Aug M7 false-closure defect exactly — a geocoded road name near a point becoming a claim about that road. Binding the must-air rule to `severity` would have put a stabbing callout on Adelaide breakfast radio; only `warningLevel` is a public escalation ladder an agency actually issues. Ineligible records are persisted and listed rather than filtered out, with a per-row "not airable" marker and a footer naming the suppressed categories, because RISK-37 taught that silent suppression cannot be distinguished from a broken feed. The licence check reads `/attribution` at runtime because the incident payload carries `source.agency` but no licence, and a hardcoded feed-to-licence map would be a guess that silently rots as DataQuoll resolves its eight "licence under review" sources. Phase 1 stops short of the writer because the two decisions that actually gate airing are ARN's, not ours: a 15-second slot (portlincoln) is about 38 words and an emergency line costs 15-20, and auto-airing a life-safety warning sourced from an aggregator is a news/compliance call that DataQuoll's own terms disclaim.

**Consequences:** Every job now carries a `dataquoll` source diagnostic — `Skipped` when the environment has not opted in, `Failed` on a real outage, so "off" and "broken" stay distinguishable. `SOURCE_IDS` in `web/src/features/jobs/api/schemas.ts` is a closed `z.enum` consumed by the job schema, so the new id had to be added there or every report page would fail to parse. `JobEntityMapper`'s enum-aware JSON options were renamed `NamedEnumJsonOptions` now that two columns share them. The Adjust tab's map drops from filling its column to a fixed 240px with the panel taking the remainder; the same panel appears on `CurationPane`, read-only in both. Deployment plumbing (bicep `EmergencyFeeds__*` app settings, blank `ApiKey`, Key Vault secret `EmergencyFeeds--ApiKey`) is NOT in this change and is required before any environment can turn the feed on. Open with DataQuoll: the NSW RFS `eventType` collapse to `other`, duplicate CAP revisions on `/incidents`, and licence resolution for QLD EMQ, NT PFES and the six SA sources.

## 2026-09-01 — The composer's length loop judges the read against the band it was given, not a second opinion on the voice

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Dev operation `825770ab` made ELEVEN `arn-wf-compose` calls for one bulletin: three parallel candidates plus eight sequential corrections, because the length loop lived inside the compose call and therefore ran on all three candidates, correcting two drafts that selection was about to discard. Moving it onto the chosen candidate cut that to five or six calls. But the deeper fault only surfaced when the corrected reads were inspected. In operation `a73962e5` the prompt asked for 81-89 words, the composer returned 85 — exactly right — and the loop then deleted two stories, and after the editor restored one, deleted two more, ending on a two-sentence 43-word read. The model had obeyed every instruction it was given, including "Remove 2 whole item(s)" and "Remove 1 whole item(s)"; the fault was entirely ours. Two components held incompatible views of one voice. `WordTargetCalculator` sizes the read from `WordsPerMinute` 150 with a 1.15 `WordTargetOvershoot`, an effective ~172 wpm, while `CalibratedDurationOracle` priced the same voice from syllables at about 129 wpm — it reported a 39-word read as 18.1 seconds. Those estimates are 40% apart, so an in-band read measured as eleven seconds over a 28.2-second slot and every correctly sized bulletin was guaranteed to be shredded. Separately, the loop had been silently conditional on a provider detail: a missing `previous_response_id` abandoned the correction outright with no narrative entry, leaving the deterministic trimmer to take the blame for cutting approved copy.

**Decision:** The loop's ceiling is the word band the prompt stated, `aimedWords ± BandTolerance`, with `BandTolerance = 4` as the single constant feeding both the instruction the model receives and the rule it is judged by. A read that obeyed its instruction can no longer be corrected at all. The correction runs once, on the candidate `SelectCandidate` chose, and NOT on the editor's revisions — re-correcting those made the read shrink monotonically and returned 43, 51 and 50 words against 75-word targets. Where no response id exists the same instruction is sent as a standalone turn carrying the read, because continuation is an optimisation and not a requirement. The word count is stated exactly once in the composer prompt, at the tail; the brief header's "Slot: about N spoken words of air." and the mid-prompt "about N words" are gone. `FallbackSyllablesPerSecond` moves 5.8 to 3.82 and `CalibrationDefaults.SyllablesPerWord` 1.45 to 1.58, measured over the 960 usable samples in `test/corpus/fallback-replay/synthesis-history.json`.

**Rationale:** Every number here is measured, and two plausible fixes were rejected by measurement. Consolidating the word count to one statement was expected to fix adherence and did not: the gap stayed at +20 words (+27% to +25%), which is what proved the count was never the operative instruction. Removing `WordTargetOvershoot` was rejected on the committed ten-fixture panel: overshoot 1.0 held the fidelity gate at 5/5 but produced three outright failures, dropped fills from 9 to 7 and raised attempts from 1.4 to 2.0, buying a 2pp mean-best-fill gain that sits inside the measured ±4pp noise band. The overshoot is therefore load-bearing insurance, not waste — the audio path compresses an overrun but can only pad silence under a short read, so aiming long and trimming is the recoverable failure. The syllable constants are a factual correction rather than a tuning choice: 960 real samples give 3.81 syllables per second at speed 0.94-1.00 and 3.84 at 1.00-1.06 (sd 0.24), and 1.57-1.62 syllables per word (sd 0.09), against a measured word rate of 141-147 wpm. The old pair implied roughly 240 wpm for an uncalibrated voice, which is why the loop saw no breach on reads that genuinely overran by ten seconds.

**Consequences:** The replay panel cannot validate the syllable constants: `FallbackReplayTests` seeds a real per-voice `VoiceCalibration` from each fixture's own sample, so neither fallback is ever consulted there. They are justified by direct measurement and will show up on cold-start voices, which is where the dev symptom appeared. `BulletinComposer` no longer takes an `IDurationOracle` — its band is words from the prompt — so the workflow constructs it with options alone. `ComposeAsync` and `RecomposeAsync` return `ComposerReply(Text, ResponseId)` because three candidates are composed in parallel and the id has to travel with each one rather than living on the composer. Three tests pin the contracts that broke: `An_in_band_read_is_never_corrected`, `Word_loop_corrects_the_chosen_read_before_the_editor_sees_it` and `Composer_prompt_states_the_word_count_exactly_once`. Reads still run over target on live dev triggers, and that residue is the deliberate overshoot the trimmer absorbs, not the defect fixed here.

## 2026-09-01 — An editor revision continues the composer's thread instead of re-rendering the prompt

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The length-correction loop already continued the composer's conversation with a ~200-character follow-up, but the editor-revision path did not: `RecomposeAsync` called `CompleteAsync` with a full `RenderPrompt`, measured at 18,560 characters on dev operation `a73962e5`. Everything expensive in that payload — the story briefs, station lessons, voice policy, board state, story budget — is byte-identical to the call that happened seconds earlier. Worse, it quoted the composer's own output back to it under a `PREVIOUS READ:` heading, so the model was re-deriving a bulletin from a transcript of itself rather than editing what it had just written.

**Decision:** Where a thread exists, revise by continuing it: `BulletinComposer.ReviseInThreadAsync` sends the editor's reasons plus the new band, and nothing else. The workflow carries `composerThread` forward from the chosen candidate through the correction and each revision. The full re-render remains as the fallback for the case with no response id to continue, so an agent route that stops returning ids degrades rather than breaks.

**Rationale:** Measured on the committed ten-fixture panel against the same-day control. The fidelity gate held at 5/5 and per-fixture outcomes were unchanged: filled 9/10 in both arms, mean best fill 105% in both, mean attempts 1.4 in both. `llmCallsPerBulletin` fell from 1.0 to 0.9, and fixture `0871f234` needed one attempt where the control needed two. The payload saving is the substance: across 48 dumped compose calls the median full render is 11,462 bytes and the median continuation 805 bytes, 93% smaller per revision. Because the saved bytes are a stable prefix, the fresh path was also defeating prompt caching on every revision.

**Consequences:** `CorrectChosenReadAsync` returns `ComposerReply` rather than a bare string, because the workflow now needs the thread id the correction ended on. Revision quality is no longer measurable by diffing rendered prompts — the instruction is a turn in a conversation, so `ARN_REPLAY_DUMP_CALLS=1` is the way to inspect it. This does not change what the editor asks for, only how it is delivered.

## 2026-09-02 — Carry composed standing guidance into the conversational workflow

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** `TrafficEvidenceBuilder` already resolved and applied the composed, sanitised Station > Market > Global guidance to `BroadcastWithTraffic.Guidance`, but the conversational generator dropped it while constructing `WorkflowRequest`. Consequently neither the writer desks nor the composer model saw operator-authored directives, while the editor should remain independent of them.

**Decision:** Project the composed guidance entries to plain `IReadOnlyList<string>` lines on `WorkflowRequest`. Render a non-empty list as a `STATION GUIDANCE` block in each writer desk prompt and in the composer prompt, immediately after `STATION LESSONS` in the composer. Do not render guidance in the editor prompt.

**Rationale:** Scope precedence, sanitisation and the maximum of eight directives remain owned by `GuidanceComposer` in the application/domain path. A plain-string workflow boundary avoids an Application dependency and makes the prompt contract explicit. Keeping guidance out of the editor prevents operator direction from changing the independent review role.

**Consequences:** Standing guidance now reaches every drafting role that can act on editorial direction and is omitted when empty. Workflow tests pin one occurrence per desk/composer prompt and prove editor isolation.
## 2026-09-02 — Fail closed when the conversational editor is unavailable

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** `BulletinEditor` previously converted malformed, empty, and failed editor replies into `EditorVerdict.Approve`. That silently treated an editor outage as a successful review even though every generated bulletin is already held for operator approval. A rejection on an unavailable editor would spend a revision without actionable feedback.

**Decision:** Require the `edit.json` verdict shape, retry one malformed response with the identical prompt, and return `EditorVerdict.Unreviewed(reason)` after a second malformed response or any transport failure. The workflow records `Editor unavailable - read shipped unreviewed`, performs no revision, preserves the read, and freezes the successful trace with outcome `succeeded-unreviewed`. A generator-level warning mirrors that status for diagnostics.

**Rationale:** Retrying one malformed response recovers transient formatting failures without changing editorial wording. Treating the second failure as unreviewed preserves the operator's existing approval gate and avoids spending revisions on feedback that does not exist. The explicit trace outcome prevents an unavailable review from being confused with approval or rejection.

**Consequences:** Malformed-then-valid replies follow the valid verdict unchanged, while malformed twice ships the intact read with two editor calls and an explicit trace failure. The current generator-level warning is visible to application logging; job `LogsJson` does not yet receive the warning because `WorkflowOutcome` is intentionally not added to the `DraftedScript` contract in this phase.

## 2026-09-02 — Calibrate only natural first renders and partition by TTS model

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** `ScriptGenerationEngine` recorded every outer attempt's duration, including fitted re-syntheses and content-limited candidates. The EMA therefore learned fitter output rather than the voice's natural speaking rate. Separately, `VoiceCalibration` keys contained voice and settings but not the TTS model, despite ElevenLabs v2 and v3 speaking the same voice at materially different rates. There was also no prediction-error signal. The fallback word-rate oracle remained hardcoded to 170 wpm even though the 960-sample corpus measured 147.1 wpm median, 1.57 syllables/word and 3.82 syllables/second.

**Decision:** The audio pipeline marks successful results that came from the first untrimmed synthesis. Calibration updates are accepted only for that natural result and only when the candidate is not content-limited. Calibration keys include the model identifier; existing legacy rows intentionally go cold and use the measured fallback constants until a model-specific sample is captured. Each successful synthesis emits `duration.prediction.error.seconds` with signed error defined as achieved natural seconds minus predicted seconds and dimensions voice, model and speed. The workflow oracle fallback is derived as `DurationPredictionOptions.FallbackSyllablesPerSecond * 60 / CalibrationDefaults.SyllablesPerWord`.

**Rationale:** A trim changes both the text and the population being measured, while a failed candidate must never teach the speaking-rate model. Model partitioning prevents cross-model pacing from being blended. The signed residual makes direction and magnitude queryable in Application Insights. Deriving the oracle from the measured constants removes the stale 170-wpm assumption and yields approximately 145 wpm.

**Consequences:** A natural 25.0-second read against a 27.0-second prediction moves calibration and emits error -2.0; a subsequent fitter re-synthesis does neither. v2 and v3 rows are independent. Legacy calibration rows are not migrated and will cold-start from constants on their next model-specific lookup.

**Implementation correction, 2026-09-02:** the first dev rollout exposed that `RecordActualDurationAsync` still created and invalidated the legacy `unknown`-model row because its call contract did not carry `context.Model`; model-aware reads therefore stayed cold and the same Gold 96FM voice paid a 36.7s first render plus a 32.9s fitted re-render. The recording contract now carries the effective model through `ScriptGenerationEngine` into the calibration key and cache invalidation. This is the missing call-site completion of the accepted decision above, not a new policy.
## 2026-09-02 — Share HERE incident enrichment between corridor and flow paths

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** A cold bulletin started the flow-pool road-name lookup alongside the main corridor lookup. Each path tiled the same HERE incidents area and independently enriched the same incident set, producing two upstream incidents fetches and duplicate enrichment work.

**Decision:** HereTrafficProvider memoises the filtered, enriched incident set in a lazy task keyed by the coverage geometry and the configured three-minute traffic bucket. GetCorridorsAsync and GetIncidentRoadNamesAsync consume that task, preserving each caller's existing filtering, ranking, cap, and road-name projection.

**Rationale:** Sharing at the provider boundary removes the duplicate HTTP and enrichment work without changing ITrafficProvider, application cache keys, or evidence contracts. A lazy task preserves single-flight behaviour for concurrent callers; the bucket key limits reuse to the existing traffic freshness window.

**Consequences:** A cold cycle performs one tiled HERE incidents fetch for the two paths instead of two. Successful forward geocoding is now cached for 24 hours using a normalised query plus radius key, so repeated equivalent coverage lookups issue one request. Failed geocodes remain uncached and retry normally.

## 2026-09-02 — Expose resolved prompts in playbook preview

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** Operators could preview only the compose2 generated read and could not inspect the exact system or rendered user prompt sent to the model. The five supported playbook roles are all valid editing and inspection targets, but only compose2 owns the generated bulletin response.

**Decision:** Extend playbook preview with nullable resolved system and rendered user prompt fields while preserving the existing baseline, generated script, refusal, notes and duration fields. Resolve role-qualified overlays against each role's shipped prompt. Run the existing replay workflow to recover a matching role's rendered user prompt when available; return prompt inspection successfully with null generated text for roles without a generation path. Add a collapsed Rendered prompt disclosure to the Writer prompt studio and expose every supported role in its selector.

**Rationale:** The replay snapshot already contains the evidence required to render the same requests, and the workflow trace records prompts exactly as sent. Reusing those paths keeps preview forensic rather than approximated, while nullable generation makes non-compose roles useful without pretending they produce an aired script.

**Consequences:** Compose2 preview remains backward-compatible and continues to show baseline/generated text. Non-compose previews show the resolved prompt and optional user request without a generated bulletin. Operators can diagnose an overlay before saving it, with the long prompt text hidden until explicitly opened.

## 2026-09-02 — Keep dead continuity caps visible but read-only

**Status:** accepted

**Context:** The conversational pipeline has one live writer path. The Bulletin Rules hub still exposed three continuity-cap fields whose values were persisted and resolved, but never read by that path. The fields were easy to mistake for active controls. The legacy matrix surfaces `SharedRules`, `RoadFeelPalette`, `IncidentVoicing`, `WeatherVoicing`, `FuelVoicing` and the old `WriterPrompt` payload are no longer exposed in the web UI; they were removed rather than replaced with inert controls.

**Decision:** Keep the API and stored values intact. Remove editing controls for `ContinuityNewCap`, `ContinuityOngoingCap` and `ContinuityUpdatedCap`; show their effective values in a collapsed-by-default read-only Continuity caps section with an alert explaining that the live conversational pipeline does not read them and linking to the station Playbook studio. Round-trip stored values on an unrelated Limits save so this UI change does not erase existing data. All other exposed Bulletin Rules surfaces remain editable because they have a live consumer.
